paragraphs: בעקבות המגבלות שהוטלו על שירותי הלוויין של מאסק, צבא אוקראינה נעזר במערכת של חברת HiSKY הישראלית, הפועלת גם בשטח רוסיה. על פי דיווח בארה"ב, המערכת שימשה גם לתקיפות נגד רוסיה

בניגוד לשירותי סטארלינק וסטארשילד של מאסק, שאינם פועלים בשטח רוסיה, המערכת הישראלית פועלת גם בתוך תחומי המדינה. לדברי אחד הגורמים, צוותי כטב"מים אוקראיניים נעזרו בה כדי לאתר משגרי טילים בליסטיים רוסיים. מחברת HiSKY לא נמסרה תגובה לדיווח.

למרות היתרון המבצעי של המערכת הישראלית, היא אינה מספקת פתרון מלא לצרכים היומיומיים של קייב. לדברי אותו גורם, תפעול המערכת דורש מומחיות טכנית גבוהה יותר, כולל נוכחות של מומחים במהלך המשימות, לעומת מסופי סטארלינק הפשוטים להפעלה. בשל כך, סביר להניח כי המערכת הישראלית תשמש בעיקר למשימות בעלות ערך גבוה במיוחד, ולא לגיחות השגרתיות שהכוחות האוקראיניים נדרשים לבצע מדי יום מול הפלישה הרוסית.

articles.title: Israel needs a 'Thin Constitution' to end the battle over judicial reform - opinion
articles.summary: If the change bloc intends to honor the new Knesset speaker’s pledge, it must make clear that rapid repeal is not an end in itself.
paragraphs: In his first address as speaker of the 26th Knesset, Matan Kahana declared: “As long as I am speaker, Israel’s Knesset will comply with court rulings without question.”

He had to state the obvious because others, including the outgoing Knesset speaker and the outgoing chair of the Constitution, Law and Justice Committee, believe that the Knesset, as the representative of the people’s will, need not obey rulings it considers unlawful.

That declaration reveals how low Israel's rule of law has sunk. Yet it was preceded by another statement from Kahana, one far from self-evident: “The incoming government will undertake the necessary reform of the checks and balances among the three branches of government, and will do so by broad consensus.”

Together, these statements point Israel in the right direction. We must uphold the existing rules rather than tear them up – or we will devour one another alive. But the status quo is not sacrosanct: the 26th Knesset must review the rules and amend them where necessary.

Those changes must rest on “broad consensus” rather than be rushed through by a transient majority. Once that consensus is reached, the new arrangements should be enshrined in a constitution focused on the structure of government, a “Thin Constitution” that will stabilize Israeli democracy for generations.

At the same time, the Knesset has begun the legislative process of undoing the judicial reform laws passed by its predecessor. This is an unusual move, to say the least, and its benefits and costs deserve scrutiny. Is it consistent to make the necessary changes “by broad consensus?”

On the one hand, the proposed amendments – due to be debated in special Knesset committees beginning this week – have a conservative aim: restoring the previous arrangements. These arrangements are familiar and well tested, so there is no reason to fear unforeseen problems.
The formal legislative procedures must still be scrupulously observed, but extensive debate over the arrangements themselves is unnecessary. Their meaning and implications are well known.

On the other hand, swiftly repealing a series of laws enacted by the previous Knesset could push Israel further down the path toward democratic instability. We should beware the “righteous zeal” that could drive each incoming Knesset to erase legislation it dislikes. Justifications will always be found.
Adopting a 'Thin Constitution'

Justice Minister Yariv Levin has accused the change bloc of double standards: it demanded thorough debate before these laws were enacted, yet now seeks to fast-track their repeal. The laws he advanced in the previous Knesset, however, introduced new arrangements that required scrutiny, whereas repeal would restore familiar ones.
Still, his warning deserves attention: “Everything you are trying to repeal will return, and with greater force.”

We should distinguish between laws that took effect during the previous Knesset’s term and those whose entry into force was deferred until its successor’s term. As my colleague Prof. Ittai Bar-Siman-Tov has suggested, when a law stipulates that it will take effect only in the next Knesset’s term, this can be read as an invitation from the outgoing legislature to its successor to repeal it in light of the election results.

In such cases, concerns about instability fall away: the previous Knesset’s intent is being fulfilled, not thwarted. This applies, for example, to the law intended to weaken the attorney-general, which was scheduled from the outset to take effect only at the start of 2027.

By contrast, we should think twice before rushing to repeal a law that has already taken effect, such as the law governing the Judicial Selection Committee. Does the immediate gain outweigh the long-term damage to democratic stability? Such action may be justified in extreme cases to prevent irreversible harm, but this is not one of them.

The committee is not due to meet any time soon: no government has yet been formed, so no new justice minister has been appointed to chair it. We should therefore defer this amendment and work toward broad consensus within a reasonable time frame. If no agreement is reached, the previous arrangements can be restored through the normal legislative process.

If the change bloc intends to honor the new Knesset speaker’s pledge, it must make clear that rapid repeal is not an end in itself. It simply returns us to the starting point for reforming the rules governing relations among the branches of government, with all factions of the Knesset working toward a common goal: adopting a “Thin Constitution” by broad consensus.
The writer is president of JPPI – the Jewish People Policy Institute – and professor (emeritus) of law at Bar-Ilan University.

articles.title: Argentina's bid to stop Falklands oil drilling rejected
articles.summary: A joint venture between UK-Israeli companies is set to start exploring for oil and gas, but Argentina sought to block it as part of its claim to sovereignty.
paragraphs: Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.

The Argentinian government had called for the Sea Lion venture to be halted as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected that claim.
Speaking on Saturday, the president of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea said it was the wrong court to rule on questions of sovereignty. The decision was upheld in a vote 18-3.
After the ruling, Argentina's President Javier Milei said "this decision is not the final word" and declared "the Falkland Islands are Argentine".
In a joint statement, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves said that Buenos Aires must "respect the right of the Falkland Islanders to determine their own future".

"Argentina sought to stop the Falkland Islanders making their own sovereign decisions and failed in this attempt," they wrote, urging Argentina to "end its wider economic pressure" against the territory.
The case is the latest diplomatic row between the UK and Argentina, which fought a 74-day war over the islands in 1982.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.

But the Argentinian government claimed the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law, arguing that while it believed there was a territorial dispute over the Falklands, nothing should be done that could change the situation - including the building of oil wells.

The UK responded that the Law of the Sea court had no jurisdiction over the issue, and that pausing the Sea Lion project could have huge economic consequences on the islands' local population and companies connected with the venture.
The tribunal's decision ultimately rested on its own powers - this was a territorial issue, and a maritime court was not the right place to hear the dispute.

Buenos Aires disagreed, writing in a statement after the decision that "Argentina did not ask the court to rule on sovereignty", but to apply the United Nations' sea laws to the UK over its "exploitation of our resources".

It also said that five individuals would face sanctions for their involvement in the oil drilling venture, something Milei had been threatening. The statement did not specify who the sanctions would be against.
"The message is clear: those who participate in the illegal exploitation of our resources will face the consequences," the statement said.

articles.title: Jess Wilson’s rapid rise is hard to believe - but Victorian Labor’s collapse has been years in the making
articles.summary: Labor faces possibility of relegation to crossbench as Coalition claims majority government and Greens celebrate ‘wild’ success Full report: Victorian Coalition wins majority government as Labor suffers historic defeat ‘Worse than anyone feared’: how Victorian Labor unravelled after 12 years in government Victoria election live results: votes tracker, map and seat counts It is difficult to overstate how far the Victorian Coalition has come. In the days after Christmas 2024, Brad Battin toppled John Pesutto as Liberal leader after a court found the Hawthorn MP defamed his colleague. A…
paragraphs: It is difficult to overstate how far the Victorian Coalition has come.

In the days after Christmas 2024, Brad Battin toppled John Pesutto as Liberal leader after a court found the Hawthorn MP defamed his colleague. A million-dollar loan by the party to Pesutto to help cover his legal costs also ended up in court. Battin lasted less than a year before his leadership also came undone and he was replaced by Jess Wilson in November 2025.

A year on, Wilson has become the first woman to be popularly elected as Victoria’s premier and at 36, the state’s youngest leader since federation. As of 10pm, the Coalition had won 53 seats – well above the 45 needed to form a majority government – and her Labor opponents have been wiped out, from 56 seats in 2022 to just six declared seats, according to Guardian Australia’s analysis, with a little more than a quarter of the vote counted.

The Labor leader, Ben Carroll, has secured two unwanted places in Australian political history: becoming the first premier to lose their seat at a Victorian election and the state’s shortest-serving modern premier, in the job for just 123 days.
While the final seat tally won’t be known for a few days, the Coalition has won seats in parts of the state it hasn’t ever held.

The state that had come to regard Labor as its natural party of government has consigned it to the electoral wilderness. At the current count, more people voted for One Nation across the state than Labor, with the party recording a 21% primary vote, though this did not translate into seats.
This was in part due to them overtaking Labor, on 17.6%. The Coalition’s landslide win comes off the back of a 34.78% primary vote, only a small increase from the 29.6% it recorded in its 2022 loss.
There is also a real possibility the Greens, who have won eight seats, will end up being the official opposition, with Labor consigned to the crossbench.
“It is wild, the number of seats we’re in hunt for,” the Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, said on Saturday night.
It’s difficult to see how Labor will be able to rebuild into anything remotely electable in four years.

It’s hard to believe Wilson only entered parliament at the last election after the former member for Kew did not run again after a drink-driving incident in which he crashed his car into a child’s bedroom.
Immediately promoted to shadow cabinet, then to shadow treasurer and now also leader, she’s taken a party that was deeply divided and turned it into an election-winning, unified outfit.

Wilson is relatable, approachable and a small-l Liberal in a state that remains broadly progressive – if you consider the almost 20% of Victorians who voted for either the Greens or the Victorian Socialists. Much of her success can be attributed to her ability to reach beyond the Coalition’s traditional base.

Her rise has also helped attract a new calibre of candidate. She persuaded several female contenders to contest winnable seats, including Samantha Byrne, who has won Niddrie off Carroll. The party has also made a concerted effort to recruit more diverse candidates and build relationships with multicultural communities Labor has taken for granted.
In her victory speech, Wilson acknowledged it was the first time many Victorians had voted Liberals.
“I realise that you have lent us your vote. We don’t own it. And we will work every single day to demonstrate that you were right to place your trust in us,” she said.
Wilson knows winning an election is one thing but governing is another.
Her first challenge will be translating an election victory into a mandate to govern. Many Victorians voted for change but may not know what that involves.

After all, many voters got their first meaningful taste just 48 hours before polling day, when the Coalition’s costings revealed plans to privatise or sell off around $13bn state government assets, including the state’s sewerage infrastructure.

Then, Wilson will have to manage the competing ambitions within her own ranks. She currently holds the shadow treasurer portfolio, a position several colleagues would dearly like to claim in government. She insists she intends to keep it.

The Coalition has a relatively shallow pool of experience on which to draw after 12 years in the wilderness. Bringing someone like Pesutto on to the frontbench would make sense but enrage others in the party room. It’s no wonder Wilson was tight lipped about the prospect when interviewed last month.
She described the election as a referendum on Labor. Now, she has to deliver for all those who gave her a party a chance.

Meanwhile, in Labor, recriminations have already started. In reality, they had weeks ago. Most of the criticism is the same – Carroll’s campaign focused too much on crime and his inability to acknowledge the 12 years of Labor that came before him – epitomised by the moment he avoided uttering Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan’s names in the debate.
But a result like this was years in the making.

After the 2022 election, Andrews vowed to do more for the communities that swung hard against Labor in the wake of the pandemic. Now, it doesn’t have one. Seats such as Kororoit, Kalkallo, Tarneit and Melton in Melbourne’s north and west and Narre Warren North in the city’s southeast, which have never been held by a party other than Labor, have turned blue.
On Saturday night, the deputy leader, Gabrielle Williams, said while the party increased seats four years ago, it ignored the main message voters were sending.
“There were certainly warning signs from the 2022 result that we should have responded to and perhaps didn’t take the opportunity,” she said.
“It should have been an inflection on point that caused us to stop and see what is happening to our base and what they weren’t getting from us.”

Labor missed another opportunity to reset when Allan became premier in 2023. “She just tried to carry on as if she was the new Daniel Andrews, it was continuation of the old government,” a campaign source said.

That government, according to the source, was bogged down by debt, alleged corruption on government construction sites, waste, crime and potholes. The potholes became daily reminders of a government that many Victorians felt was no longer delivering.
“Is there no better symbol that shows we failed to get the basics rights?” they said.
Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

articles.title: Argentina fails to block oil drilling off Falkland Islands
articles.summary: UK government calls on Buenos Aires to end ‘economic pressure’ on islands after international tribunal’s ruling The UK has called on Argentina to stop its economic warfare on the Falkland islands after Buenos Aires failed in a legal attempt to terminate an offshore oil project vital to the future of the British overseas territory. An application by the South American country for suspension of the Sea Lion project was rejected on Saturday by the international tribunal for the law of the seas (Itlos) on the grounds that the issue lay outside its jurisdiction. Continue reading...
paragraphs: The UK has called on Argentina to stop its economic warfare on the Falkland islands after Buenos Aires failed in a legal attempt to terminate an offshore oil project vital to the future of the British overseas territory.

An application by the South American country for suspension of the Sea Lion project was rejected on Saturday by the international tribunal for the law of the seas (Itlos) on the grounds that the issue lay outside its jurisdiction.

In a joint statement, Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary and Ellie Reeves, the attorney general for England and Wales, said: “Argentina sought to stop the Falkland Islanders making their own sovereign decisions and failed in this attempt.

“The UK has no doubt of our sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, our sovereignty and sovereign rights over the surrounding maritime areas, and the right of self-determination of the Falkland Islanders.
“We now call on Argentina to respect the right of the Falkland Islanders to determine their own future and urge Argentina to end its wider economic pressure against the Falkland Islands.”

The ruling from Itlos is a significant blow to Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, who has described reclaiming sovereignty of the Falkland islands, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, as a “national cause”.

The Falklands has a prosperous economy but the Sea Lion oil project is said to offer the potential to double the islands’ GDP. It is seen by the Falkland Islands’ government as a vital way to secure its future as a self-financed British overseas territory.

Milei has previously said that blocking the drilling is part of a wider strategy to force the UK into talks over sovereignty over the archipelago, over which the two countries went to war in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.

In a decision read out on Saturday by the president of Itlos, Maurice Kamga, the tribunal rejected Argentina’s arguments for a suspension of the project, saying there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal was unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.

Kamga said 18 judges had voted to reject Argentina’s claims, while three had voted to uphold them. At a hearing earlier this month, Argentina said drilling should not be allowed until the issue of sovereignty over the islands had been resolved and asked Itlos to issue a temporary injunction until a full arbitration hearing could be held.

Mario Oyarzábal, the chief legal adviser to Argentina’s ministry of foreign affairs, had claimed that the oil money from the drilling would “finance the very military base and presence that sustains the UK’s de facto control of the territory”.

During the two-day hearing, Reeves said that such an order would have “devastating consequences” for the islanders and prevent them from developing their natural resources “as they are entitled to do so, pursuant to their fundamental right to self-determination”.

The Sea Lion project in the North Falkland basin, led by the Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper, will start drilling in March, and oil will be extracted from 2028 and continue for 35 years. It has the potential to double the islands’ GDP, with a cumulative uplift of £8bn over the lifetime of the project.
Milei previously described the companies’ activities as unlawful and launched economic sanctions on people and firms involved in oil exploration around the islands.

An arbitration tribunal will now address the substance of the dispute, but its decision could take years, and by then oil exploitation will have already begun. The Argentinian government is pushing through legislation that would criminalise parties involved in the Falklands economy.
In a statement, a spokesperson for Milei claimed that the tribunal’s ruling was not the “final word” on the dispute, adding: “By history and by right: the Malvinas are Argentine.”

The spokesperson said: “The decision by the international tribunal for the law of the sea in no way legitimises the unilateral exploitation of our natural resources. The national government will continue to take all necessary actions to prevent such exploitation. In this regard, new sanction proceedings were initiated yesterday against five entities for violations of our current legal framework. The message is clear: those who participate in the illegitimate exploitation of our resources must face the consequences.

“The defence of our sovereignty is not the cause of any single government or political party; it is an inalienable constitutional mandate. Argentina will continue to assert its rights through all available diplomatic, legal, and administrative channels, with the firm conviction that no unilateral action by the United Kingdom can extinguish our legitimate sovereign rights.”

A spokesperson for Navitas said: “We welcome the tribunal’s decision to reject all of Argentina’s requests for provisional measures. Navitas remains focused on the continued responsible development of the Sea Lion project, pursuant to licences issued by the Falkland Islands government. We wish to extend our appreciation for the UK government’s continued and unwavering support for the Falkland Islands and the Sea Lion project.”

articles.title: Victorian election 2026: Coalition wins majority government as Labor suffers historic defeat
articles.summary: Jess Wilson to become state’s first popularly elected female premier as Ben Carroll loses seat in 2026 state election, and Greens and One Nation surge Victoria election live results: votes tracker, map and seat counts ‘Worse than anyone feared’: how Victorian Labor unravelled after 12 years in government See all of our Victorian state election coverage Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast Victorian Labor has suffered a historic defeat, ending 12 years of government, with the Coalition winning a majority and the Greens securing a record number of seats. One Nation…
paragraphs: Victorian Labor has suffered a historic defeat, ending 12 years of government, with the Coalition winning a majority and the Greens securing a record number of seats.

One Nation was on course to win more than 20% of the primary vote, but struggled to pick up lower house seats on a night when huge swings and three- or even four-party contests in many electorates made preference flows difficult to calculate.
At 36, Wilson will become Victoria’s youngest leader since federation and the first woman to be popularly elected as the state’s premier – a feat neither Jacinta Allan nor Joan Kirner achieved.
In her victory speech, Wilson spoke directly to Labor voters who had abandoned the party and said her team would “work every single day to demonstrate that you were right to place your trust in us”.
“I know that for many of you this is the first time that you have ever voted Liberal. And for others, it was the first time you have ever given us your preference,” Wilson said.
“I realise that you have lent us your vote. We don’t own it.”

Carroll lost his seat of Niddrie in Melbourne’s north-western suburbs, which Labor had held for its entire 50 year history. It is the first time a Victorian premier has lost their seat at a state election.
In a speech to party faithful shortly after 8.30pm, Carroll took full responsibility for Labor’s crushing defeat.
“This is a significant loss for Labor,” Carroll said. “It’s not the result we wanted, but it is a result we accept.

“As leader of the party, I take full responsibility. Democracy is both beautiful and brutal. Beautiful, because we get to witness the will of the people. And brutal, because it is so difficult and painful to lose.
“But Victorians have spoken. And their message is clear. They want change.”
The Greens were on course to secure eight seats – holding Brunswick, Richmond and Melbourne and winning Pascoe Vale, Preston, Northcote and Footscray from Labor, and Prahran from the Liberals.
If voting trends from Saturday night’s counting continued, it appeared possible the Greens might win more lower house seats than Labor, making it the official opposition.
The party’s state leader, Ellen Sandell, told ecstatic supporters the result was “not an overwhelming endorsement of the Liberals or One Nation”.

“This result is a rejection of the Labor party that has moved so far away from the values they once held, and it is a rejection of the old party politics that just is not working for people,” Sandell said.
“We are sending more Greens to parliament than ever before at a time that could not be more crucial.

“When we say we have to replace the major parties, we are serious. It was always about more than just winning seats in parliament. It was about building a movement and a progressive political force with the courage and the conviction to stand up for what it believes.”

One Nation secured more than 20% of the statewide primary vote – up from 0.22% in 2022 – but seemed likely to gain very few lower house seats. The party is in contention the regional district of Murray Plains, held by the Nationals, and in Sunbury on Melbourne’s north-western fringe, previously held by Labor.

At One Nation Victoria’s campaign event, it was the federal leader Pauline Hanson who addressed the party faithful. The state leader, Warren Pickering, failed to win the seat of Pakenham, which went to the Liberals.
Hanson congratulated Wilson and said she “had a big job ahead of her to clear up Labor’s mess”.
“For Victoria’s sake, I wish her and her team well,” Hanson said.

One Nation’s lower house prospects appear to have been hurt by a complex preference count in Labor-held seats it targeted. As Labor fell to third place in some seats, its preferences flowed to the Liberals.

Early in the night several former Labor seats were called for the Liberals, including Frankston and Mordialloc in the south-east, Hastings on the Mornington Peninsula and Box Hill and Ringwood, in the eastern suburbs. The seat of South Barwon also went to the Liberals, the first time the party has won the seat from Labor since the 1990s.
Kororoit, Tarneit, Point Cook, Sydenham, Werribee and Melton – traditional Labor strongholds in Labor’s west and north – also fell to the Liberals.
Only about a fifth of upper house votes had been counted on Saturday night, but the Coalition looked likely to pick up at least 15 seats, with One Nation on eight and the Greens and Labor on six.
Labor MP Steve Dimopoulous, who is seen by some as a potential leader of the party if he holds on to his seat, offered a sincere apology to Labor faithful.
“This is an absolutely unequivocal report card on the Labor government,” Dimopoulous said.
The deputy Labor leader, Gabrielle Williams, another potential leadership candidate, said she was “deeply saddened” by the result and the party needed to learn from its mistakes.
“Clearly we have to be deeply humbled by the results and take the lessons from them,” Williams said.

Federal Labor sources quickly began to distance themselves from the state election result. One described the result as the “perfect storm-of-shit moment in Victoria” that would not be repeated federally.
“There are upsides federally to the Liberals being in power and cutting and privatising stuff, and One Nation’s bluster and hollowness getting tiring,” they said.

articles.title: Black barrister tells of racist abuse after Rupert Lowe viral tweet
articles.summary: Exclusive: Hard-right MP claimed photo featuring Joseph Ashong was sign of discrimination against white Britons A newly qualified black barrister who took part in a group photo that went viral after Rupert Lowe cited the image as evidence of discrimination against white Britons has said he has never before experienced such racism in the UK. Joseph Ashong, who was in a cohort attending their “call to the bar” ceremony in London, said he was amazed and upset by the reaction to the picture as it was viewed by millions on the afternoon of the ceremony. Continue reading...
paragraphs: A newly qualified black barrister who took part in a group photo that went viral after Rupert Lowe cited the image as evidence of discrimination against white Britons has said he has never before experienced such racism in the UK.

Joseph Ashong, who was in a cohort attending their “call to the bar” ceremony in London, said he was amazed and upset by the reaction to the picture as it was viewed by millions on the afternoon of the ceremony.

Lowe, the leader of Restore Britain, the hard-right rival to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK party, reposted the formal photograph of 80 newly called barristers that was shared by the Middle Temple inn of court on Wednesday.
The Great Yarmouth MP wrote on X: “To those who still say White British men and women face no discrimination in our country, show them this image.”

Lowe’s post has been viewed 2.3m times. It was amplified by the far-right agitator known as Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, and it triggered a wave of racist abuse online. Millions more have since viewed the image and other group photographs shared by Middle Temple this week.

Isabel Oakeshott, the journalist and partner of Richard Tice, the deputy leader of Reform, also posted the photograph. “These are the judges of tomorrow,” she wrote. “One particular demographic appears to be missing. There is something very wrong with our country if we can’t say that there is something not quite right about this.”

According to a survey published in March by the Bar Standards Board, 82.3% of barristers in England and Wales are white. Official government statistics suggest that the proportion of judges from minority ethnic groups is 13% – up from 6% a decade ago. The photograph was just the latest of a series of call to the bar ceremonies held this year at Middle Temple, one of the four institutions entitled to call members to the English Bar as barristers.
Many international students come to the UK because English common law forms the foundation of legal systems in over a third of the world.

Ashong, who is from Ghana but earned a scholarship to pursue a career at the bar in the UK, where he arrived in 2023, was at the front of the image shared by Lowe, which was taken shortly before the ceremony. “If only I had been given a pass for being black,” he said of the tough journey to become a barrister.
Ashong, 36, said it amazed him that an MP had triggered the racism. “There may have been unconscious bias in the past but I have not experienced racism to this extent before,” he said.

Ashong said he had chosen to study at City St George’s, University of London, due to the shared English common law heritage between England and Wales and the Commonwealth countries. The Middle Temple has a strong tradition of taking on members from the Commonwealth.

“A friend reached out to me to say there’s a picture on Twitter which is making the rounds and they’ve seen my face in there,” Ashong said. “So I go to Twitter and I find that the MP is making a statement about discrimination. We know what is being insinuated: people who are supposed to look British, so to speak, now don’t and the bar is a mixed bag of people from all over the place, mostly black and brown people. It is ignorant.”

He added: “In my case, I was awarded the Harmsworth scholarship from Middle Temple. That means going through an intense application, going through interviews before you are finally merited the award.”
The Harmsworth scholarship was established by the great-grandfather of the current proprietor of the Daily Mail.

Ashong said he would apply for a pupillage – the final part of training to become a barrister – in the UK but that he was considering returning to Ghana to build a practice. “It’s a bit sickening because what’s going on out there is pure ignorance,” he said. “An MP of all people should know that there’s no design for immigrants to take over the bar.”
Yi Vonne, 23, who had been studying law at Cardiff University since 2024, was in a later group photograph that was also highlighted on social media as apparently showing bias against white people.

She said she would return to Malaysia in December to start her pupillage but had opted for that day’s call to the bar, which was relatively late in the year, to allow for her mother to organise time off from work and join her on a “special day”. She said: “I’ve never been treated like this before here.”
Vonne said Middle Temple had offered for other groups to opt out of the photograph “because of all this racial abuse that’s going on”. “But of course, who wants to do that?” she said.

On Thursday, the Liberal Democrat MP Al Pinkerton raised the row in the Commons, saying that a “wonderful celebratory photograph of young barristers called to the bar at Middle Temple has become the subject of the most appalling racialised abuse, including, I am very sorry to say, by certain members of this house”.

Alan Campbell, the leader of the House of Commons, responded that it was “beyond inappropriate and entirely unacceptable for anyone to follow up online and make the sorts of comments that he talks about”.

Middle Temple has informed its members that the posts were “considered carefully at the most senior level” but that the “conclusion was that there is nothing to be gained from adding to the comments by Al Pinkerton MP in parliament”.
A Restore Britain spokesperson said: “Rupert’s post speaks for itself on the point he was making.”
Additional reporting by Lyndon Li

articles.title: Channel 4 defends controversial Huw Edwards documentary
articles.summary: Film following disgraced former BBC presenter for almost a year faces fierce backlash ahead of airing on 1 December Channel 4 has defended its controversial Huw Edwards documentary, with the broadcaster saying the film does not diminish the “seriousness” of his actions nor “entitle him to sympathy, redemption or rehabilitation”. The film, Huw Edwards – Guilty, which has followed the disgraced former BBC presenter for almost a year, has faced a fierce backlash before its airing on 1 December. Huw Edwards – Guilty airs on Channel 4 on Tuesday at 9pm. Continue reading...
paragraphs: Channel 4 has defended its controversial Huw Edwards documentary, with the broadcaster saying the film does not diminish the “seriousness” of his actions nor “entitle him to sympathy, redemption or rehabilitation”.
The film, Huw Edwards – Guilty, which has followed the disgraced former BBC presenter for almost a year, has faced a fierce backlash before its airing on 1 December.

Edwards pleaded guilty to three charges of making indecent images of children after he was sent 41 illegal images by a convicted paedophile, Alex Williams. He was sentenced to six months in prison in 2024, suspended for two years.

A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, had “no interest in hearing what” Edwards had to say, adding: “Broadcasters are expected to act responsibly and have appropriate regard to their audiences when making decisions.”

A government minister, Emma Hardy, said the planned documentary made her “feel sick”, telling LBC that Channel 4 was providing a platform to “someone who is on the sex offenders’ register”, while another minister, Anna Turley, told the radio station it made her “deeply uncomfortable”. The shadow culture secretary, Rebecca Paul, said: “This man shouldn’t get a minute of airtime.”

On Saturday, Louisa Compton, Channel 4’s director of news, digital and audience trust, responded to the brewing controversy, saying it was in the broadcaster’s remit to “stimulate debate” and that “interviewing someone is not an endorsement of them”.

She said: “Edwards was one of the most prominent and trusted broadcasters in Britain. He pleaded guilty to serious offences involving indecent images of children and has never publicly faced detailed questioning about his criminal behaviour or the complete collapse of his career and reputation.
“There is a clear public interest in confronting him with those questions rather than allowing them to remain unanswered.
“We are also acutely conscious that behind offences involving indecent images are real children and real victims – including those as young as seven – who have been abused.

“Nothing about making this film diminishes the seriousness of that harm, nor does Edwards’ participation entitle him to sympathy, redemption or rehabilitation. His account is there to be tested, not accepted.”

Compton also said that Edwards had not been paid for participating in the film or had any control over its content. “We should be capable of examining difficult issues rather than looking away because we don’t like what we see. We understand that some people will profoundly disagree with our decision to make this film,” she said.
“But discomfort is not, in itself, a reason for journalism not to ask difficult questions. We believe those questions are in the public interest.”

The film will follow Edwards at home in rural Wales, where he has been since his career ended after his criminal conviction. In a short trailer, the 65-year-old says he had “lost the plot” at the time of his crimes.

The film-makers said that after attempts to “ingratiate himself back into public life”, Edwards was shown being forced to “confront his loss of fame, declining health, fractured relationships and his crimes”.
The fall of Edwards, a veteran newsreader who announced the queen’s death on the BBC in 2022, has already been depicted on television in Channel 5’s drama Power: The Downfall of Huw Edwards.

The former presenter later said the programme was a “one-sided account” and has made a complaint to the media regulator Ofcom. It is investigating the programme under its “fairness and privacy” rules.
The drama became Channel 5’s highest-rated show of the year after its broadcast in March, attracting 3.8 million viewers in four weeks.
The two-part series focused on an earlier allegation against Edwards made by the Sun in July 2023 that claimed a “top BBC star” had paid a teenager more than £35,000 for sexual pictures.
A Channel 5 spokesperson said: “We stand by the programme and will be robustly defending this complaint.”
Huw Edwards – Guilty airs on Channel 4 on Tuesday at 9pm.

articles.title: דורות גדלו על הפלאפל שלהם - עכשיו מישל ואיבט נפרדים
articles.summary: לקוח ותיק בא עם הבן והנכד, ואחר הגיע אחרי שנחת בלילה מהודו. ביום האחרון של "פלאפל מישל" בוואדי ניסנאס, מישל ג'מאל מספר ל"מעריב" על הפלאפל שמכר עוד בבית הספר ועל הבקרים שעוד יעביר עם בנו ויסאם
paragraphs: לקוח ותיק בא עם הבן והנכד, ואחר הגיע אחרי שנחת בלילה מהודו. ביום האחרון של "פלאפל מישל" בוואדי ניסנאס, מישל ג'מאל מספר ל"מעריב" על הפלאפל שמכר עוד בבית הספר ועל הבקרים שעוד יעביר עם בנו ויסאם

אחרי 46 שנה סוגרים בני הזוג את "פלאפל מישל" בוואדי ויוצאים לפנסיה. כשנשאל מה קרה שהחליט לפרוש, מישל השיב בפשטות: "שום דבר", ואחרי רגע הוסיף: "גם לי מגיעה פנסיה, לא?" ואיבט? "האישה לא כל כך מרוצה, אבל אין מה לעשות", סיפר. "אני בן 78 כבר, והיא בת 74".

על הפרידה הודיעו מישל ואיבט אתמול בפוסט בפייסבוק שפתחו במילים "חברים יקרים, אחינו ואחיותינו". בין מי שקראו אותו היו גם לקוחות שלדברי מישל מגיעים לחנות בקביעות כבר 40 שנה. "במשך ארבעה עשורים הייתם בשבילנו הרבה יותר מלקוחות. הייתם משפחה גדולה שגדלנו איתה", כתבו בני הזוג. "בכל בוקר, עם כל ביס, חלקנו איתכם שיחות, חיוכים ורגעים מהחיים".
"הפלאפל שלך טעים, הפלאפל שלך טעים"

מישל מכר את מנת הפלאפל הראשונה שלו שנים לפני שפתח את החנות בוואדי. כילד היה מוכר לחבריו בבית הספר את הפלאפל שהכינו בבית ממתכון שלמד מאימו. "כשבאתי לחיפה, אז התחלתי לעבוד במסעדות, ואחר כך החלטתי לפתוח את הפלאפל שלי", סיפר.
בין הלקוחות, סיפר, היו גם ראשי ערים ושחקנים. וכשביקשנו שיגלה מה הסוד של הפלאפל שלו, ענה: "הסוד זה לילדים שלי". אבל הסוד לכל דבר, לדבריו, הוא לעשות אותו באהבה. "ואני את המקצוע שלי מאוד אהבתי, מאוד".

גם ביום האחרון אמר מישל שיישאר בחנות עד שש בערב. ללקוחות שהפכו לחלק מחייהם כתבו הוא ואיבט: "הייתם הלב הפועם של המקום הזה, והסיבה האמיתית להצלחה ולשמחה שלנו". בסוף ההודעה הוסיפו: "אבל הסיפור שלנו ממשיך!".

articles.title: IDF on high alert for potential Iranian surprise attack, strengthening coordination with US
articles.summary: The IDF is maintaining heightened readiness and close coordination with CENTCOM amid concerns Iran could launch a surprise attack on Israel or US assets.
paragraphs: The IDF is maintaining heightened readiness and close coordination with CENTCOM amid concerns Iran could launch a surprise attack on Israel or US assets.

The IDF is maintaining a high level of operational readiness and close coordination with US Central Command (CENTCOM) amid concerns that Iran could launch a surprise attack against Israel or US interests in the Middle East, Walla reported on Saturday.

In recent months, the head of the IDF Operations Directorate, Maj.-Gen. Itzik Cohen, has held three conference calls a week with CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper and his staff to ensure full coordination regarding developments in the Middle East, military movements, operations, and emerging trends.
The two also met at the Operations Division's command center in the underground bunker known as the "Pit" at the Kirya military headquarters in Tel Aviv during the admiral's visit the previous week.

According to defense officials, the IDF continues to maintain heightened readiness, particularly in the Israel Air Force (IAF), while reinforcing command centers and headquarters around the clock to prepare for any scenario and shorten response times.

The IDF General Staff is aware of the strain placed on IAF ground and aircrews but has clarified that efforts are being made to fine-tune readiness levels and minimize uncertainty as much as possible, particularly given that it was the Americans who prompted the IDF to prepare for the possibility of an attack on Iran several times in recent months.
IDF prepares for potential Iranian surprise attack
A senior defense official told Walla, "The possibility that Iran will try to surprise Israel is a plausible scenario. To that end, the IDF must be prepared both defensively and offensively."
Amid heightened readiness and concerns over a regional escalation, the IDF Military Intelligence Directorate continues to fortify its early-warning model across all fronts.

The aim is to ensure that, if Iran decides to launch a surprise attack against US interests in the Middle East, the IDF will have sufficient time to prepare and, if necessary, launch a preemptive strike.
US assets at risk of being attacked include 50,000 military personnel, bases and infrastructure, advanced weapons systems, naval vessels, aircraft, and air defense systems.

articles.title: Wilson vows to ‘bring back hope’ after historic victory in Vic election – as it happened
articles.summary: This blog is now closed. Full report: Victorian Coalition wins majority government as Labor suffers historic defeat Victoria election live results: votes tracker, map and seat counts ‘Worse than anyone feared’: how Victorian Labor unravelled after 12 years in government Jess Wilson’s rapid rise is hard to believe - but Victorian Labor’s collapse has been years in the making Election winners and losers – in pictures See all of our Victorian state election coverage Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast Federal politicians largely absent from state election Just…
paragraphs: Treaty at stake at this election
What are the parties promising?
Key battlegrounds in the Victoria election – video
Voting in person or by postal ballot: what you need to know
Jess Wilson and Ben Carroll ‘confident’ as they cast votes

Both the Coalition led by Jess Wilson and One Nation have pledged to repeal Victoria’s treaty with First Nations people if they win the election. The treaty established the Gellung Warl, a representative body for Indigenous people which has the power to make rules on a limited number of matters directly affecting First Nations peoples. It does not have the power to veto policy or legislation.
A Parliamentary Budget Office report requested by Wilson earlier this year found that repealing the treaty laws would save taxpayers $948.3m over the next 10 years. Labor disputed the figures.
Just under two hours til polls close

We are less than two hours away from polls closing. The ABC reported there was a late rush at the polling booth at Melbourne town hall, so it seems a few people who were a bit wary of the rain earlier are heading out now.

Our live stream will kick off an hour after polls close at 7pm AEDT, with Barrie Cassidy, Matilda Boseley, and Benita Kolovos bringing you all the news, plus we will have reporters at the Liberal, Labor and Greens election night parties as the results come in.
You can view the live stream on the Guardian website, YouTube or Instagram.
Hanson meets Santa while campaigning
Pauline Hanson has drawn crowds on election day in Victoria, AAP reports.
One Nation’s campaign bus headed to polling booths east of Melbourne on Saturday morning, after touring electorates in the city’s north the previous day.
In Koo Wee Rup, local candidate Nikole Schellekens was happy ceding the floor to Hanson, offering to take photos for supporters keen to get their picture taken with the party leader.
Amid the fanfare, a man dressed as Santa Claus made an appearance, telling onlookers Hanson had “been a very good girl this year” before embracing her.
While Hanson received a mostly warm reception in the electorates of Pakenham, Narracan and Bass, she did meet some opposition at a polling booth in Frankston.
One heckler told her “we do not want racist, Trump-style politics in Victoria” while a group of Labor volunteers shouted “put One Nation last” as she walked by.
One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, told reporters:
double quotation markIf it’s not us that forms government, we will hold whoever does form government’s feet to the fire.
But … we will also work with anyone to achieve better outcomes for Victoria.
Second polling booth closes due to weather
The Victorian Electoral Commission has announced the polling booth at Saints Peter and Paul Serbian Orthodox church hall in Wodonga has shut due to the weather conditions.
This follows Keysborough Gardens primary school shutting earlier due to flooding.
A federal Labor MP appears
Federal Labor MP Josh Burns appears to be on the campaign trail today, posting on Instagram he’s there to support MP Nina Taylor.
Allow Instagram content?
Josh Frydenberg on the campaign trail

The former federal treasurer Josh Frydenberg is out and about campaigning for the Liberals in Victoria, too, posting “Go Jess!” on X, accompanied by a photo of Frydenberg and some volunteers decked out in blue.
This election has primarily been fought over cost of living, infrastructure, health and public safety.
All parties have made promises around these issues and more. You can read about some of them here:
What the heavy rain means for vote-counting
Our political scientist for the election, Luke Mansillo, has sent us this dispatch about what the rain might mean for the election:

double quotation markThe torrential rain in Melbourne has produced a non-insignificant problem for everyone working on the election. Psephologists know that half of the electorate has previously voted ahead of election day and the remaining half of the electorate will vote on election day. These two groups potentially look quite different, so analysts will need to be extra cautious.

However, there are going to be fewer people handing out because they do not want to get drenched in the rain; there will be fewer how-to-vote cards that will survive the rain; and, there will be fewer people willing to accept a how-to-vote card as they run into a polling place trying to stay dry. Political parties’ efforts to direct preferences through deals may be less consequential. For these reasons, there will be a systematic bias in the preference flows by 10 to 15% and, when applied to half the electorate, may change the results by about 1% to 3% and possibly higher rates of informality. Thanks to the weather, we will need to wait for the early votes to be reported for many seats.
Our Victorian state correspondent, Benita Kolovos, opens her book of knowledge to get you up to speed on what to look out for as the election results come in.
Meanwhile, the end of group voting tickets means Victoria’s upper house will be looking very different regardless of who wins government.
More people will be voting in this election than ever before and almost half have already voted. But if you haven’t already voted, here’s what you need to know:
Polling places open from 8am to 6pm on Saturday 28 November. If you’re still in line at 6pm you will still be able to vote.

Legislative council – the upper house – voting has changed. Now voters must number at least five party groups above the line, in order of preference, or at least five individual candidates below the line. Watch our explainer below:
For postal votes, your ballot papers must be sent before 6pm on Saturday 28 November. The Victorian Electoral Commission must receive it by Friday 4 December for it count.
For more information about voting, read this:

Taylor on the moveJust following the last post, it looks like the federal Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, is getting around today for candidates. The Liberal candidate for South Barwon, Libby Pettit, just posted a photo with Taylor, the Victorian Liberal senator Sarah Henderson and state MP Bev McArthur on Instagram.
A few federal Liberals out and about today it seems.

articles.title: Pompeo predicts US blockade will push Iran to escalate, reigniting Israel, US strikes on regime
articles.summary: Pompeo said the US should hit Iran's industrial base, missiles, and drones and "go after the next set of leaders" to end the war.
paragraphs: Pompeo said the US should hit Iran's industrial base, missiles, and drones and "go after the next set of leaders" to end the war.

Former US secretary of state and CIA director Mike Pompeo predicted in an interview released on Friday that the US blockade of Iran will eventually force Tehran to try to break it, setting off an escalation involving Israel and the Gulf states that would lead to a new round of US strikes.

"The blockade is so effective that the regime will have to at some point try to break the blockade," Pompeo said in an interview with Times Radio's "The General and the Journalist" podcast. "And when they do that, I think not only the United States, but Israel and the Gulf states will conclude, we're not going to let the blockade be broken. And this will escalate away."

That, he said, would lead US President Donald Trump to decide "it's time to go again and go at another level of targeting a set of targets that I know very well from my time in service. They are deep. They're exquisite. We know where the assets are."
Pompeo urges strikes on Iran's next set of leaders
Pompeo said ending the war required more than eliminating Iran's uranium enrichment capacity.

"We should let it be unmistakably clear, the regime is intent on building a nuclear weapon if it takes the rest of their lives and that of their children and grandchildren," he said. "You got to take down some piece of their industrial base; you have to take down more of their missile and drone capacity. I would go after the next set of leaders."

The goal, he said, was "an Iran that is sufficiently chastened that they will again drink from the poison chalice." That phrase echoes Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini's description of accepting the 1988 ceasefire that ended the Iran-Iraq War.
Pompeo says Iran regime could fall within months

Asked how long the Islamic Republic could survive, Pompeo said lifting sanctions and letting Iran "collect tolls" in the Strait of Hormuz would keep the regime in power "for another generation." But if the US helps Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar defend themselves and takes down Iran's ability to mine the strait and fire missiles and drones, he said, "we may be talking about years, maybe even months."

He compared it to the fall of the Berlin Wall, which came two weeks after he left his post as a young soldier patrolling the border in Germany in 1989. "No one predicted that," he said. "These things have a way of collapsing. You simply can never predict when."

Pompeo urged Trump to use his final two years in office to support "the good guys," including more weapons for Ukraine, help for Gulf allies, and "continuing our deep, strong relationship with Israel."

articles.title: Trump shares Thanksgiving post claiming GDP figures released before midterm elections were 'fake'
articles.summary: The Commerce Department revised third-quarter GDP growth to 4.3% from 3.4% on Wednesday in what Trump calls a "massive, and purposeful, error."
paragraphs: The Commerce Department revised third-quarter GDP growth to 4.3% from 3.4% on Wednesday in what Trump calls a "massive, and purposeful, error."

US President Donald Trump on Thursday accused the Commerce Department of deliberately issuing incorrect economic growth figures before this month's midterm elections, and called for an investigation. The claim came in a lengthy Thanksgiving post on social media where Trump called the figures a "massive, and purposeful, error" and linked them to Republicans' heavy losses in the November 3 elections, which gave Democrats control of both houses of Congress.

"It was just revealed that the real numbers on the economy, published before the election, were fake, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the government agency that does these numbers," Trump wrote. "Why wasn't the correct number issued before the election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation."

His complaint centers on data the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis released Wednesday. The figures revised third-quarter gross domestic product growth to an annual rate of 4.3%, up from a prior estimate of 3.4%. The bureau routinely revises GDP figures, monthly jobs reports, and other data to improve accuracy on a preset schedule that does not account for the political calendar.

Trump did not provide evidence that the revision was politically motivated. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment, as the government was largely closed for the Thanksgiving holiday.
Trump repeatedly questions unfavorable economic data

The post is the latest instance of Trump casting doubt on economic data that does not match his claims of a historic boom. In August 2025, he fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics after a weak jobs report showed only 73,000 jobs added in July 2025 and downward revisions of 258,000 jobs for May and June. Trump called that report "phony" and "rigged."

Voters have not shared Trump's view that the economy is strong. In the midterms, 76% described economic conditions as "not so good" or "poor," according to the AP Voter Poll, and about two-thirds said Trump's own policies had fueled inflation.

Trump's post also ignored another figure the Commerce Department released Wednesday: The personal consumption expenditures price index, a key measure of inflation, accelerated to an annual pace of 3.8% in October.
Trump's Thanksgiving message targets critics, immigrants

Trump is spending Thanksgiving at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach. His holiday message, according to CBS News, opened by wishing a happy Thanksgiving to the "American patriots who have worked so hard to make our country great!" He then directed holiday wishes at a long list of perceived opponents.

That list included the Commerce Department, immigrants, and "the radical far left," as well as "those that are looking to change our Court System to that of Sharia" and "those who want to redistribute Property." He also took aim at the Somali community, and people who, he says, do not appreciate the White House ballroom he is building.
On Thursday evening, Trump and First Lady Melania Trump called US service members, including members of a unit involved in Operation Epic Fury, and said that Iran "will never have a nuclear weapon."

articles.title: "אתם לא תעבדו פה" - הפרוטקשן הגיע גם לפרויקט הדגל של עיריית חיפה
articles.summary: כרבע מיליון שקלים נגבו מהקבלן המשפץ את פנים השוק בחיפה. כשהגיע קבלן לשיקום החזיתות, נדרש גם הוא לשלם 7,000 שקל בחודש, וסירב. אחד מחמישה כתבי אישום שהוגשו במסגרת מבצע "שומרי הצל" מציג את הפרוטקשן
paragraphs: כרבע מיליון שקלים נגבו מהקבלן המשפץ את פנים השוק בחיפה. כשהגיע קבלן לשיקום החזיתות, נדרש גם הוא לשלם 7,000 שקל בחודש, וסירב. אחד מחמישה כתבי אישום שהוגשו במסגרת מבצע "שומרי הצל" מציג את הפרוטקשן

ביוני 2024 החלה חברה קבלנית בשיפוץ פנים השוק ברחוב סירקין. לפי האישום, אלחאג' פנה למנהל העבודה, הציג עצמו כמי שמתגורר בסמוך וביקש לספק שמירה. מנהל העבודה, שחשש מפגיעה ברכוש ומשיבוש העבודות, העביר את פרטיו להנהלה, וזו קישרה בינו לבין עלי, בעליה ומנהלה הפעיל של חברת השמירה.

מכתב האישום עולה שהשניים סיכמו שהקבלן ישלם לעלי 7,000 שקל בתוספת מע"מ מדי חודש, ומתוכם יועברו לאלחאג' 5,000 שקל במזומן. בגין האתר נגבו כ-231,280 שקל, שמתוכם קיבל אלחאג' כ-140 אלף שקל. לטענת התביעה, השניים לא החזיקו ברישיונות הנדרשים ולא סיפקו את שירותי השמירה שהובטחו בחוזה, אך המשיכו לגבות את הכספים.

לגבייה היה גם תיעוד חשבונאי מסודר: לפי כתב האישום, עלי הנפיק לחברה הקבלנית חשבוניות מס על שם "גלוק ביטחון 2017" בגין התשלומים החודשיים. ממאי 2025 הונפקו החשבוניות על שם חברה אחרת. אלא שלטענת הפרקליטות, מאחורי החשבוניות לא עמדו שירותי השמירה שהובטחו, והכספים נגבו תוך ניצול חששם של מנהלי החברה מפגיעה באתר ובציוד.

החוקרים יצאו לבדוק מה מקבלים הקבלנים תמורת התשלום. בבקשת המעצר מפורטים דוחות פעולה המתעדים בדיקות ליליות באתרי הבנייה בשוק תלפיות ובקריית מוצקין. לפי הבקשה, פעם אחר פעם האתרים נמצאו נעולים וללא פעילות שמירה.
גם בתצפיות באתרי בנייה בשדרות מוריה בחיפה ובדרך עכו בקריות לא נמצאה פעילות שמירה. נתוני התקשורת הצביעו, לפי הפרקליטות, על כך ששניים מהנאשמים אוכנו פעמים בודדות באזור האתר שבו היו אמורים לשמור.

באוגוסט 2025 החל קבלן נוסף להתארגן לשיקום חזיתות השוק. לפי האישום, אלחאג' דרש גם ממנו 7,000 שקל בחודש, תוך שהבהיר כי הקבלן העובד בפנים משלם סכום זהה. מנהלי החברה סירבו. כשאחד מהם הטיח בו כי מדובר בפרוטקשן, השיב, לפי האישום: "למה אתה חושב שאני רוצה פרוטקשן, גם לקבלן למטה עשו נזקים... תישנו על זה בלילה ואנחנו נדבר".

ב-13 באוקטובר בשנה שעברה, בעת שעובדי החברה הקימו קירוי בטיחות וגדרות, הגיע אלחאג' ולפי האישום הפיל גדרות וקרשים, צעק ונצמד לפניו של מנהל החברה. כשהמנהל הזהיר כי יזעיק את המשטרה, צעק לעברו אלחאג', לפי האישום: "המשטרה על הז*ן שלי", והשמיע איומים מיניים בוטים כלפיו וכלפי מנהלת הכספים. "אתם לא תעבדו פה... יש לי שני רוטוויילרים בבית וזה שטח שלי. אני מסתכל על הכול, אתם לא תחנו פה ולא תהיו פה", הוסיף. עוד נטען כי אמר שאינו חושש לשבת בכלא וכי ביכולתו לשלוח את בנו לדקור את המנהל. למרות האיומים, החברה עמדה בסירובה ולא שילמה.

באותו דיון טען עו"ד חליוה כי חלקו של סביחי מצומצם, כי הכספים המתוארים באישום הועברו לחברה ולא לידיו וכי אין הצדקה להמשך מעצרו. הוא ביקש לשחררו לחלופת מעצר גם בשל מצבו הרפואי. הפרקליטות התנגדה וטענה כי האישום המיוחס לו מבסס מסוכנות וחשש להשפעה על עדים.

articles.title: Two Médecins Sans Frontières staff killed by Israeli strike in Gaza, charity says
articles.summary: MSF and head of WHO denounce attack on Gaza City clinic as Israel claims security guards were members of Hamas Israeli forces have bombed a clinic run by Médecins Sans Frontières in Gaza City, killing two of its staff members, the organisation has said. MSF said Israel had directly struck the clinic, despite the fact that its location was known to the Israeli military and that it was well marked with MSF logos. The organisation denounced the attack and said that with the deaths of the two security guards on Saturday, Israel had killed 17 of its staff members during the war in Gaza.…
paragraphs: Israeli forces have bombed a clinic run by Médecins Sans Frontières in Gaza City, killing two of its staff members, the organisation has said.

MSF said Israel had directly struck the clinic, despite the fact that its location was known to the Israeli military and that it was well marked with MSF logos. The organisation denounced the attack and said that with the deaths of the two security guards on Saturday, Israel had killed 17 of its staff members during the war in Gaza.
The head of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, condemned the bombing, saying: “Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked.”
In a post on X, Ghebreyesus also said: “Attacks on health facilities, health workers and humanitarian personnel in Gaza are outrageous and unacceptable … These attacks MUST STOP.”

The Israeli military claimed that the two men whom they killed, Ahmad Abou Hassira and Moaz Alitsbach, were members of Hamas’s military wing. It also added that the strike was “not directed at a hospital” and had caused no damage to the facility.

The Israeli military has often accused Hamas of embedding itself within civilian infrastructure, including hospitals. However, in 2024 the head of the international criminal court’s Palestine investigation said claims about the presence of Hamas fighters in Gaza’s hospitals had been “grossly exaggerated”.

Israel has killed Palestinian medical workers en masse since the start of the war in Gaza. According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, at least 1,700 have been killed by Israeli attacks. Rights groups say the Israeli military has engaged in systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure, including medical infrastructure.
The UN has repeatedly called on Israel to stop its restrictions on the entry of supplies to allow Palestinians to prepare for the winter and begin to rebuild the destroyed strip.
The result is a healthcare system “experiencing systemic collapse, severely undermining its capacity to meet the basic health needs of the civilian population”, according to a UN report in August.
The humanitarian situation is also deteriorating, as heavy rains exacerbate crowded and unsanitary living conditions, leading to the spread of infectious diseases.

Israel has continued to bomb Gaza on a near-daily basis despite a ceasefire signed in October 2025, killing at least 1,705 people since then. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of violating the understandings of the ceasefire.
The war began after a Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 that killed about 1,200 people.

More than 74,000 people have been killed and more than 175,000 injured in Israel’s war in Gaza. A UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court for war crimes. Israel denies these claims.

articles.title: Deal with Epstein lawyer and accountant could block victims’ other claims, experts warn
articles.summary: Concern that settlement to resolve suit against pair may stymie legal claims that involve child sexual abuse material As the clock ticks toward final settlement for a sex-trafficking-related lawsuit against Jeffrey Epstein’s accountant and attorney, some experts are expressing concern that the agreement might stymie survivors’ search for justice in other litigation involving child sexual abuse images. The suit involves Darren Indyke and Richard D Kahn, who for decades worked as Epstein’s personal lawyer and accountant respectively. Both men also serve as executors of Epstein’s estate.…
paragraphs: As the clock ticks toward final settlement for a sex-trafficking-related lawsuit against Jeffrey Epstein’s accountant and attorney, some experts are expressing concern that the agreement might stymie survivors’ search for justice in other litigation involving child sexual abuse images.

The suit involves Darren Indyke and Richard D Kahn, who for decades worked as Epstein’s personal lawyer and accountant respectively. Both men also serve as executors of Epstein’s estate. Indyke and Kahn have insisted they knew nothing about Epstein’s crimes and have rejected allegations of wrongdoing.

In the soon-to-be-settled 2024 Manhattan federal court civil complaint against them, survivors’ attorneys allege that Indyke and Kahn “were personally essential to the Epstein enterprise’s success – among other things, they helped structure Epstein’s bank accounts and cash withdrawals to give Epstein and his associates access to large amounts of cash in furtherance of sex trafficking”.

A final settlement hearing in this trafficking-related case is scheduled for 2 December, during which a judge might sign off on the agreement brokered between survivors’ attorneys at Boies Schiller & Flexner LLP, and Indyke and Kahn. This agreement would establish a $35m settlement pool for survivors who qualify for compensation with these claims, according to court papers.

Epstein, a high-powered financier who counted numerous wealthy and prominent men as his associates, was arrested in July 2019 and charged with sex-trafficking minors following years of allegations against him. The Manhattan US attorney’s office said that his victims were as young as age 14 when he abused them. He killed himself in jail while awaiting trial.

Jennifer Freeman of Marsh Law, who helms other litigation against Epstein, has voiced concerns about the proposed settlement, namely that this deal might set up roadblocks to legal claims against his estate that involve child sex abuse material, or CSAM.

Survivors and law enforcement have said that Epstein possessed, transported, produced and distributed CSAM over decades. Freeman said she fears that Epstein’s estate could try arguing that the proposed Kahn/Indyke settlement protects his estate from any possible litigation brought by CSAM survivors.

“We objected to the settlement on the grounds that CSAM has its own separate claim with its own statutory remedies and this was not, in our view, considered in putting together this settlement,” Freeman told the Guardian.
Freeman represents two women in a 15 September lawsuit involving CSAM claims, as well as several class members of the trafficking-related litigation.

“We fully support the existence of a settlement for survivors, and we want that to go forward, and we very much hope it does,” Freeman said. “However, we believe that the release of [Epstein’s] estate doesn’t make sense here, since the case was not against the estate – it was against two individuals, the lawyer and the accountant.”

Freeman also said she had concerns that survivors might not be aware of the proposed settlement and what she believes might be potential implications on CSAM claims against Epstein’s estate. Freeman wants any Epstein survivor who endured CSAM abuse – including those who participate in the trafficking settlement – to have an opportunity to pursue claims related directly to CSAM.

While the judge on 16 September extended the deadline for survivors to submit or opt out of trafficking-related claims, Freeman said that “we’ve heard from many, particularly those who are outside the United States, [who] had no idea anything was going on”.
“They don’t have class actions typically in their countries, so this would not be a familiar process for them to look out for or understand … that it might apply to them.”

CSAM claims “should not be included in the settlement at all. That should be explicit,” Freeman said of her hopes for the final agreement. “The release of the estate should be at least limited and, in my view, eliminated.”
Asked for comment, attorneys for Indyke and Kahn deferred to prior statements on allegations against them.

In a recent lawsuit against them brought by New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, one of their lawyers said they “emphatically rejected” claims “they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr Epstein’s sexual abuse or trafficking – conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr Indyke nor Mr Kahn was present.

“Not a single woman has ever accused Mr Indyke or Mr Kahn of committing sexual abuse or witnessing sexual abuse, nor claimed at any time that she or anyone else reported to them any allegation of Mr Epstein’s abuse,” the statement also said.

Attorneys for Indyke and Kahn do not agree with concerns that the trafficking-related settlement is over-broad. Daniel Ruzumna, who represents Indyke, said: “As the parties pointed out at the hearing and the court appeared to recognize, the putative class only includes women who were sexually abused and/or trafficked by Epstein.”

“That would include any woman who also may also have a CSAM-related claim, in which case that woman may be entitled to a larger recovery from the settlement fund,” Ruzumna said. “But if a woman only had CSAM-related claims, she would not be part of the class … at the September 16 2026 hearing, the parties made clear that women with CSAM-only claims (ie who were not abused or trafficked themselves) are not part of the class and therefore would not release claims.”

Epstein’s apparent possession of CSAM has been detailed by law enforcement officials, as well as materials released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. An FBI memo, for example, said files included “a large volume of images of Epstein, images and videos of victims who are either minors or appear to be minors, and over ten thousand downloaded videos and images of illegal child sex abuse material and other pornography.”

Maria Farmer, whose sister Annie was abused by Epstein and his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell at age 16, told authorities in 1996 that he possessed nude images of her siblings. “Complainant [Maria Farmer] stated that she is a professional artist and took pictures of her sisters 12 and 16 yrs for her own [personal] Art Work,” the law enforcement report stated.
“Epstein Stole the photos and Negatives and is believed to have sold the pictures to potential buyers,” the authorities’ report on Maria’s allegations also said.
Maria also reported “pictures of young girls at swimming pools” and recounted that Epstein said “if she tells anyone about the photos he will burn her house down”.

articles.title: US oligarchs enriched by ‘transactional’ Trump face fierce scrutiny in new Congress
articles.summary: Democrats pledge aggressive investigations into Trump-allied billionaires and how president’s policies have boosted their bottom lines For an elite circle of Donald Trump billionaire allies who lavished tens of millions of dollars on his campaign, vanity projects and crypto ventures, his second administration has boosted their bottom lines through lax oversight, tax breaks, federal contracts and other perks. But with Democrats winning control of Congress in the midterms, House and Senate investigations are being planned for 2027 into several Maga oligarchs in hi-tech and crypto industries,…
paragraphs: For an elite circle of Donald Trump billionaire allies who lavished tens of millions of dollars on his campaign, vanity projects and crypto ventures, his second administration has boosted their bottom lines through lax oversight, tax breaks, federal contracts and other perks.

But with Democrats winning control of Congress in the midterms, House and Senate investigations are being planned for 2027 into several Maga oligarchs in hi-tech and crypto industries, examining how their firms and the president benefited from his “transactional” governing style, according to Democratic lawmakers and scholars.

Trump allies expected to face scrutiny by congressional panels looking, in part, at how Trump’s pay-to-play modus operandi has financially and politically benefited them include Space X mogul Elon Musk, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, and crypto titans such as Binance founder Changpeng Zhao.
Trump’s own wealth soared by $2.7bn since he won the presidency again in 2024 – due in good measure to “crypto ventures and overseas deals”, according to a Forbes report in September.

Additionally, Trump’s sons, Eric and Donald Jr, have notched sizable financial gains in tech, crypto and other areas since Trump won again, and are expected to face Capitol Hill inquiries into ways their Oval Office ties may have benefited them.

White House and justice department lawyers in November sent threatening letters to key congressional Democrats, warning they could face scrutiny, and perhaps criminal charges, if they investigated some of Trump’s big-money patrons and their federal contracts.

Scholars and legal experts who have tracked some of Trump’s financial moves, boosting his personal fortune and increasing the wealth of his big patrons, see ample evidence that the ties between Trump and some of his leading donors and business allies have hurt American democracy.

“The personal wealth of Trump, his family, and those in his inner circle, as well as Trump’s vanity projects, are being funded by the very tech titans whose own wealth and power has been boosted by this administration’s policies and actions,” Cornell economist Eswar Prasad said in an email.

Prasad earlier this year raised red flags about Trump’s dealings with “crypto tycoons”, telling the Guardian: “Trump and his family have hardly been shy about cozying up to crypto tycoons, and have been quite brazen in their pay-for-play approach to this sector.”
While the Hill investigations are in planning stages, tech leaders led by Elon Musk have clearly been big winners in the second Trump administration.

Trump and Republicans forged especially close ties with Musk, the world’s richest man, who spent almost $300m in 2024 to help Trump win, and then about $450m in the midterms in mostly failed efforts to help GOP candidates.

According to an in-depth report this fall from the nonpartisan Democracy Defenders Fund, Musk firms secured $6bn in government contracts while he was leading Trump’s “Doge” drive to cut federal spending, and another $10bn in contracts since he left his post last year.
Moreover, the study found 25 federal agencies or departments have “taken actions benefiting or potentially benefiting his businesses”.
The DDF report – Trump and Musk, 17 Months Later – also found that Musk’s net worth “more than doubled since he left Doge in May 2025, growing from approximately $419bn to between $900bn and $1tn”.

“The central finding is that the current government ethics framework allows the world’s richest person – a major political donor and former government official – to earn billions from federal contracts while his companies receive favorable treatment across government,” the report concluded.

Before the elections, Musk on X vowed to hit back against those who go after him, writing: “Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them.”

Separately, Huang, who resigned as Nvidia CEO after reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy spurred fears of China gaining significant access to Nvidia’s valuable microchips, looks to have benefited from the president’s pay-to-play governing style.

In a stunning twist, 11 days after Huang quit, and facing clear pressure from Trump and others in his administration, Nvidia announced Huang would return as CEO, a move which fueled bipartisan concerns and calls for hearings next month.
Huang in 2025 was among the biggest known donors to Trump’s prized ballroom, reportedly giving $25m to finance the venture, according to Public Citizen, a liberal watchdog.

Moreover, Trump’s financial disclosures in 2026 revealed Nvidia stock trading over 100 times since he returned to office with a combined transaction value between 27m and 97m, according to Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (Crew).

Trump has said all his stocks are managed solely by independent outside advisers and he has no role in stock trading. Trump has also repeatedly denied any conflicts of interest or quid pro quos as president.

Trump and his billionaire commerce secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly ignored national security intelligence warnings and allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced chips to the Singapore-based datacenter firm Megaspeed, which was until August 2025 run by Alice Huang, the alleged spy who had an affair with Jensen Huang.

According to press reports, Alice Huang was in touch with China’s spy agency for months when her firm sold some of Nvidia’s advanced chips to other datacenters in south-east Asia with China ties, and some of which were suspected of being smuggled to China, fueling bipartisan criticism and some internal administration dissent.

Separately, several major crypto companies have profited from the administration’s lax crypto regulatory oversight, including Binance, the world’s biggest crypto trading platform. Last year, in a complex deal, Binance helped the Trump family’s crypto venture World Liberty Financial, which only launched in the fall of 2024, secure a $2bn infusion from an Abu Dhabi-backed state investment fund.
Trump reported earning over $1.4bn from World Liberty and other crypto ventures in 2025, or about two-thirds of the $2.2bn in earnings his 2025 financial disclosures showed.
Responding to media questions about his stunning earnings last year, Trump told reporters: “You know why I’m profiting? Because the stock market’s going up. Everybody’s profiting.”

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty in 2023 to anti money-laundering and sanctions violations, and Binance agreed to pay $4.3bn in fines and restitution to the government. Zhao, who reportedly owns 90% of Binance stock, served a four-month sentence and was pardoned late last year by Trump in a controversial move.

Since he won a second term, Trump has issued executive orders boosting the crypto industry by easing regulations and oversight by the Securities and Exchange Commission, a huge shift from under Joe Biden, which Trump promised in a talk in mid-2024 at a major bitcoin conference.

Crypto moguls and allied groups poured tens of millions into the midterms, largely trying to defeat Democrats. Legal experts and economists now see ample reason to investigate the close ties between Trump and his crypto and hi-tech oligarch allies.

Former Federal Election Commission general counsel Larry Noble said: “Despite the efforts of Musk and other tech and crypto oligarchs, they are now going to be facing members of Congress questioning their past actions and future plans, and demanding answers about their transactional and mutually beneficial dealings with Trump, not meaningless photo ops and compliments.
“They just learned that democracy is not some computer game or theoretical idea. It’s voters exercising their power in real time, and the voters were not happy.”
Prasad raised similar concerns.

He said: “Trump and his acolytes have openly peddled their influence and twisted the policy apparatus they now control in order to favor tech moguls, who have been equally open about their direct and indirect paybacks to Trump, his family and associates, and his political and other causes.”
A few incoming chairs of House and Senate panels have signaled investigations that in part will look at leading billionaires, including Musk.
