"An entire business community develops around a place like Nvidia. In Tivon, they have nowhere to expand."
According to Levi, the designated land in Kiryat Tivon has already undergone planning procedures, but those plans were not designed specifically for Nvidia's requirements.
He noted that existing plans include facilities for multiple companies, a transportation terminal, and an ecological corridor, some of which he believes would need modification or cancellation.

Levi also raised concerns about the site's proximity to a flood-prone area, existing high-voltage power lines, and the engineering challenges of building a large underground parking facility on clay soil near the Kishon River.
"There is no public transportation there, apart from a bus traveling along the road," he said.

"There are roads with one lane in each direction that cannot be widened because of the surrounding development plans. There are no future residential development plans. Where will 6,000 employees live?"
Nvidia campus may not open until 2034 or 2035, Levi estimates

Asked about Kiryat Tivon Local Council head Ido Greenblum's efforts to establish a railway station near the planned campus, Levi acknowledged his counterpart's efforts but questioned the project's feasibility within the anticipated development timeline.
"Ido is fighting for it, and that is perfectly legitimate. He is doing what he needs to do, but ultimately, there are realities in the planning process," Levi said.

Taking into account the time required to approve development plans, obtain construction permits, and complete construction, Levi estimated that even under favorable circumstances, Nvidia's campus in Kiryat Tivon would not open until 2034 or 2035, approximately eight to nine years from now.
By contrast, Levi argued that the land proposed by the Clal Group in Nesher could accommodate nearby residential neighborhoods, schools, medical clinics, and commercial developments.
"Here, they would live next to their workplace, and a family could give up a car," he said.
However, another major company is already reportedly negotiating over the Nesher site, according to Levi.
Asked whether he remains in contact with Nvidia representatives, Levi confirmed that discussions were ongoing but declined to elaborate on their substance.
"We are speaking with them as well. I know there are conversations. I know there are still conversations," he said.

Nevertheless, Levi acknowledged that establishing Nvidia's campus in Kiryat Tivon would benefit the entire Haifa metropolitan area. He estimated that some of the company's employees could ultimately choose to live in Nesher's Agamei Bereshit neighborhood.
Haifa Bay redevelopment plan raises concerns over employment, economic growth
The question of employment also emerged during the discussion of National Outline Plan 75 (TAMA 75), which concerns the redevelopment of Haifa Bay and the area's transition away from heavy industry.

Levi criticized the manner in which the plan is currently being advanced, arguing that local authorities had been excluded for years from planning developments for which they would ultimately be responsible for providing infrastructure, schools, and municipal services.

Regarding the proposed trade corridor and logistics facilities in Haifa Bay, Levi questioned how many jobs such developments would create and whether they would provide sufficient economic opportunities for future residents.
"Is that what you want? For us to become the storage yard of the State of Israel?" he asked.
Levi expressed concern that land readily available for residential development could be marketed before the government establishes a clear timeline for relocating industrial facilities.
Bazan oil refineries unlikely to close by 2029, Nesher mayor warns
Levi expressed skepticism regarding the possibility of closing the Bazan oil refineries in Haifa Bay by 2029, approximately three years from now.
Asked whether he remained convinced that the industrial complex would not close by the proposed deadline, Levi responded unequivocally.
"Absolutely. There is no doubt whatsoever," he said.
According to Levi, the government must first establish viable alternatives for fuel supplies and storage, as well as for other products the petrochemical complex manufactures.
He declined to provide an alternative closure date, arguing that a realistic timeline could be set only once the necessary replacement infrastructure had been planned.
"When will it happen? When the State of Israel creates an alternative," Levi said.
"When I see plans for an alternative to the Bazan complex, I will be able to tell you that there is a realistic prospect."
Despite Nesher receiving municipal revenue from the Bazan complex, Levi emphasized that he supports its eventual closure.
"Human life comes before everything else," he said.
Until the facilities close, Levi called for stricter enforcement of environmental regulations and substantial financial penalties for violating air pollution standards.
He summarized his message to Bazan representatives during meetings with company officials: "You are not the ones breathing this air. We are the ones breathing it."
Levi calls for universal military service, including Arab, haredi Israelis
While declining to disclose which party he supported in the recent election, Levi outlined his position on military conscription and the rights of Israelis who do not serve.
"I believe military conscription is essential for the State of Israel," he said.

"I am not referring only to the ultra-Orthodox [haredi] sector, as people tend to do. I believe that anyone who does not enlist in the military and has not received an exemption on medical grounds should not enjoy the same rights as everyone else in Israel."
"Everyone needs to contribute, including Arabs. Everyone needs to contribute to the State of Israel," he added.

According to Levi, the government should take the initiative in expanding military recruitment, although he acknowledged that integration into military service among both haredi and Arab communities would likely be gradual.

He pointed to his experience in local government as evidence that cooperation between different sectors of Israeli society is possible, noting that Jews and Arabs, as well as religious and secular Israelis, already work together within municipal frameworks.
Arab political participation could strengthen Israel's next government

Levi also expressed support for Arab political participation in the ongoing coalition negotiations, arguing that greater involvement could help Arab communities address domestic socioeconomic challenges.
"I believe Arabs should also be partners because, ultimately, they need to take responsibility for their own lives," Levi said.

"They need to stop focusing on what is happening in the Palestinian Authority and start discussing how we can live together here and improve infrastructure, education, and social conditions within their communities."
According to Levi, Arab voters participated in the election with the expectation that their elected representatives would improve everyday life in their municipalities.
He argued that the election results gave Israel's political leadership an opportunity to build broader cooperation despite existing divisions.
"There are no winners in this election. Everyone lost," Levi concluded. "And because everyone lost, there is an opportunity to win big."

articles.title: US pushed Venezuela, Iraq to consider leaving OPEC, sources say
articles.summary: The US controls Venezuela's access to state funds following the January ouster of Nicolas Maduro, while Iraq's oil revenues continue to pass through an account at the New York Federal Reserve Bank.
paragraphs: The Trump administration encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving OPEC earlier this year and prevented Venezuela from paying its annual membership dues to the group, according to ten people familiar with the matter.

The previously unreported moves targeted two of OPEC's five founding members, marking an unusually direct challenge to an organization US President Donald Trump has long accused of keeping oil prices artificially high.

US officials were pushing for greater oil production and investment in both countries at the time, and some worried OPEC production limits could eventually constrain those ambitions, according to people familiar with the discussions.

The US pressure on Venezuela went far enough that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened this summer, persuading the Trump administration not to press the issue further, two people familiar with the matter said.

In Iraq, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi raised the possibility of leaving OPEC at a government meeting this summer after discussions with US officials who encouraged the idea, two people familiar with the matter said.
Iraq's oil ministry pushed back, persuading al-Zaidi to keep Iraq in the group and instead seek a higher production quota, the people said.

The United States has powerful leverage over both countries. The US controls Venezuela's access to state funds following the January ouster of Nicolas Maduro, while Iraq's oil revenues continue to pass through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, a relic of the 2003 Iraq War.

The US State Department did not answer questions about whether it had prevented Venezuela from paying its OPEC membership fee. But it confirmed Washington has the power to decide on Venezuela’s use of state funds, now held in a US-controlled account set up after Maduro's removal.

"The Department receives disbursement requests from the interim Venezuelan government and reviews the requests, including against a list of approved and prohibited uses of the foreign Government Deposit Funds," a State Department official told Reuters.

The official said lower-level US officials may have raised the question of leaving OPEC with Venezuela's government earlier this year, but that "it has not been among the issues raised by high-level officials."
The State Department's conversations with Iraq, meanwhile, "have focused on improving energy infrastructure to increase production and transportation of energy, not OPEC," the official said.
Representatives for OPEC and for the governments of Venezuela, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia did not respond to requests for comment.

The US maneuvers add strain to an organization that has already lost four members since 2019, and whose share of the global oil market recently hit a low on the back of disruptions caused by the US and Israeli war on Iran, another OPEC founding member.
"The risk of OPEC fracture is rising," said Dan Alamariu, chief geopolitical strategist at Alpine Macro.

The United Arab Emirates announced its exit from OPEC earlier this year after becoming frustrated with the group’s production caps, while Angola, Ecuador and Qatar quit the group in 2024, 2020 and 2019, respectively. There are no indications the US was involved in those decisions.
From customer to competitor
OPEC was founded in Baghdad in September 1960 by oil-producing countries seeking to assert more control over a global market dominated by a handful of Western oil companies.

Founded by Iraq, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Venezuela, OPEC is now made up of 11 members. It has also formed an alliance with several other producer countries, including Russia, called OPEC+, which regularly meets to set coordinated production levels.

Trump has repeatedly attacked OPEC throughout his decades-long business and political career, calling it a cartel and a monopoly profiting from the rest of the world. Over the past decade, though, the US has become the world's largest oil producer, turning it from an OPEC customer into its main rival for oil market share.

After the US seized Maduro in January, the US State Department opened discussions with Venezuelan officials in Washington on whether the country should leave OPEC, five people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
They did not identify the individuals who took part in those discussions.

Trump wanted US oil majors to revive Venezuela's oil output - something he said would shore up energy security in the Western Hemisphere - and worried that OPEC policy decisions could hinder that plan, the sources said.
Bin Salman intervened, however, persuading the Trump administration not to push further, two of the sources said. Saudi Arabia is OPEC’s top producer and its de facto leader.
In August, Trump said it was up to Venezuela whether to leave OPEC.

US officials also held talks this summer with al-Zaidi, encouraging Iraq to leave OPEC as US oil majors Exxon Mobil and Chevron planned major new investments there, two people familiar with the matter said.
Al-Zaidi later raised the issue at a government meeting. His oil ministry persuaded him to stay and instead potentially seek a higher OPEC quota, they said.
The issue could come up again, as some elements of Iraq’s ruling coalition favor leaving OPEC and OPEC+, which they view as dominated by Saudi Arabia and Russia, the people said.
There is no indication Washington has sought to block Baghdad’s OPEC dues.

After the US invasion of Iraq in 2003, the United States began routing Iraq's oil revenues through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. That structure remains in place more than two decades later.
This year, the US threatened to starve Iraq of its oil money if it didn’t cut Iran’s influence in its government.
OPEC membership fee payments are typically due in the first quarter of each year and fund staff salaries, research, and travel at the OPEC Secretariat in Vienna.
Unlike the United Nations, where dues are scaled to the size of a country's economy, OPEC splits the fees equally among members at around $3.08 million each.
The price tag is tiny compared to OPEC oil revenues, but paying it carries symbolic importance as a marker of continued membership in an organization Caracas helped create.
Washington argued Venezuela could spend the money on more important matters, one person familiar with the country's relationship with OPEC said.
OPEC has the discretion to disregard unpaid membership fees, and is not planning to expel Venezuela over the issue, two OPEC sources told Reuters.
Washington's control of Venezuela's oil revenues and finances has led some in the South American country to refer to their country as a US protectorate, instead of a sovereign nation.

The US Government Accountability Office opened a formal investigation in July into the administration’s management and disbursement of Venezuelan oil revenues, following congressional requests for transparency.
The Trump administration has said Venezuela's oil revenues are being used to meet the needs of the Venezuelan people, including to pay government salaries and fund essential services.
Reuters could not establish when exactly the US rejected the OPEC dues payment request.
Venezuela is currently exempt from OPEC+ oil output quotas as its production has collapsed from historical highs due to years of sanctions and mismanagement.
According to OPEC figures, the country pumped about 1.2 million barrels per day in September. Its state oil company PDVSA has said it plans to reach 1.5 million bpd by the end of next year.

OPEC last regulated Caracas' output with quotas in 2017-2018 when the country’s target was around 2 million bpd. A source familiar with Venezuela's OPEC position said the country's return to the quota system is unlikely until it hits that level again.

articles.title: Tel Aviv man indicted for blackmailing women with AI-generated sexual images
articles.summary: The State Attorney's Office has requested that 44-year-old Liran Tadmor remain in custody until the conclusion of the criminal proceedings against him.
paragraphs: The State Attorney's Office filed an indictment on Thursday against Liran Tadmor, 44, a Tel Aviv resident, at the Tel Aviv Magistrate's Court on multiple charges of extortion by threats and sexual harassment involving AI-generated sexual images and videos.

According to the indictment, filed by attorney Coral Golbary of the Tel Aviv District Attorney's Office, Tadmor allegedly developed a systematic and extensive scheme targeting numerous women, obtaining personal photographs from their Facebook and Instagram accounts without their knowledge or consent.

Using artificial intelligence software, Tadmor allegedly manipulated the photographs to create sexually explicit images and videos falsely depicting the women in various states of nudity or revealing clothing.
Prosecutors allege that Tadmor subsequently harassed the women through phone calls and messages containing abusive language and degrading sexual remarks.
To conceal his identity, he allegedly used dozens of phone numbers and virtual SIM cards.
Defendant allegedly threatened to distribute AI-generated deepfakes on social media

In most cases, according to the indictment, Tadmor threatened to distribute the fabricated sexual content on social media and send it to the women's acquaintances unless they complied with his demands.
In several instances, he allegedly carried out his threats, publishing the manipulated images without the complainants' consent.
Prosecutors further allege that Tadmor used the names and photographs of some of the complainants to create fraudulent WhatsApp profiles, through which he contacted additional women.

The indictment charges Tadmor with multiple offenses, including extortion by threats, making threats, harassment through telecommunications devices, sexual harassment, and impersonation with intent to defraud.
Prosecution seeks continued detention over AI-related sexual harassment offenses
The State Attorney's Office has requested that Tadmor remain in custody until the conclusion of the criminal proceedings against him.
In its detention request, the prosecution described the alleged conduct as a systematic, persistent, and obsessive pattern of harassment targeting numerous women.

Prosecutors emphasized that Tadmor allegedly exploited artificial intelligence technology to produce degrading and abusive sexual content, violating the complainants' privacy and dignity and undermining their personal security.
A publication ban prohibits the disclosure of any information that could lead to the identification of the complainants, including details of their occupations.

articles.title: Netanyahu's coalition trap, Eisenkot's resolve, and the future of Israel’s rule of law - opinion
articles.summary: Developments in Netanyahu's corruption trial could complicate Eisenkot's coalition negotiations, while raising broader questions about the future of Israel's judiciary and the rule of law.
paragraphs: Gadi Eisenkot is a deceptively complex figure. The pro-Netanyahu propaganda apparatus has exploited this extensively, portraying him as politically naive, inarticulate, and manipulated by forces more powerful than himself.
Nothing could be further from reality. Eisenkot has one significant advantage: Attempts to discredit him rarely stick.

In recent days, outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his supporters appear to be discovering that Eisenkot is not the man they portrayed him to be. Netanyahu himself, however, has always known better. Having worked with Eisenkot, he is familiar with his capabilities and is now encountering them under considerably less favorable circumstances.
Eisenkot's military career reveals his political character
I have known Eisenkot reasonably well since 1999, when he served as military secretary to then-prime minister Ehud Barak and subsequently to Ariel Sharon.
He was among the few officers who emerged from the Prime Minister's Office unchanged. He did not develop a taste for expensive cigars, whiskey, or political intrigue.
When he left the office to fight in the Second Intifada, serving in the Judea and Samaria Division, he remained precisely the same officer who had entered it.
My favorite story from Eisenkot's unwritten biography concerns his dismissal from a command position in the Golani Brigade.
As a young commander of Golani's anti-tank reconnaissance company, Eisenkot had granted his soldiers scheduled leave following an extended period of exhausting operational activity.
At a meeting of brigade officers, then-Golani Brigade commander Zvi Poleg, who would later become mayor of Netanya, instructed Eisenkot to recall his soldiers for an upcoming brigade sports day.
Eisenkot refused.
Poleg, who until then had appreciated the young officer from Eilat, insisted. Eisenkot maintained his position, prompting Poleg to dismiss him in front of the brigade's officers.
Years later, Eisenkot acknowledged that, had he been in Poleg's position, he would have dismissed himself as well.
Nevertheless, he had made a conscious decision not to recall his soldiers. He was at the beginning of his military career, understood the potential consequences, and accepted the risk.

After considering leaving the military, Eisenkot decided to pursue academic studies instead. He eventually became commander of the Golani Brigade, commander of the Judea and Samaria Division, head of Northern Command, head of the Operations Directorate, deputy chief of staff, and ultimately IDF chief of staff.
When required to confront authority on behalf of those under his command, Eisenkot demonstrated a willingness to jeopardize his own future.
Eisenkot's composure and political instincts
Another defining characteristic of Eisenkot is his composure under pressure. He witnessed similar qualities in Barak and Sharon, but his own temperament long preceded his service alongside them.
As IDF chief of staff in 2018, he was required to demonstrate that composure during the rescue of an Israeli undercover force following a compromised operation in Khan Yunis.

The same quality was evident during his confrontation with then-defense minister Avigdor Liberman, who advocated military action in Gaza while Eisenkot believed that confronting Hezbollah's cross-border tunnels in northern Israel should take precedence.
Eisenkot succeeded in securing Netanyahu's backing. Liberman found himself politically isolated and subsequently resigned.
That episode reflected both Liberman's willingness to stand by his convictions and Eisenkot's considerable political instincts.
The lesson is relevant today. Eisenkot's soldiers, whose leave he once refused to interrupt, have been replaced by the Israeli public.
My assessment is that he believes he is fighting not for a period of leave, but for the country's future. Personal political considerations are unlikely to dominate his calculations.
Just as he once accepted dismissal from Golani, Eisenkot appears prepared to risk his own political future to replace Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's potential rotation offer could threaten coalition negotiations
What does this mean for the formation of Israel's next government? The outcome remains uncertain.
According to the account presented in this column, Netanyahu told associates earlier this week that preventing Eisenkot from establishing a government would require a "Hanukkah miracle."
An atmosphere of an impending political transition may be developing within Netanyahu's office. Nevertheless, it would be premature to write him off.

The prevailing assessment within Likud, as described in the original reporting, is that Netanyahu could ultimately agree to serve second in a rotation government shortly before Eisenkot succeeds in forming an alternative coalition involving the ultra-Orthodox (haredi) parties, Arab parties, or external Arab parliamentary support.
As Liberman warned on Thursday, such an offer could constitute a political trap.
Netanyahu could use the remaining period of Eisenkot's mandate to prolong negotiations, only to abandon them at the last possible moment and trigger another election.
Developments in Netanyahu's corruption trial on Wednesday, one day before Liberman's warning, appear to have strengthened his political incentive to pursue another election.
Netanyahu may believe that the developments in court can be translated into additional Knesset seats.
Eisenkot understands this. Liberman understands it. One can only hope that Naftali Bennett, who continues to advocate for a unity government with Netanyahu, understands it as well.
Bennett's unity government faces significant political obstacles
I do not question Bennett's motives. His determination to fulfill his electoral commitments deserves recognition.

However, Bennett understands that Netanyahu is unlikely to enter a national unity government without his haredi partners. Their participation would significantly complicate efforts to advance meaningful military conscription reform.
Bennett also understands that Liberman, Yair Lapid, and Yair Golan are unlikely to participate in such a government.

Under the parliamentary configuration described in the source, Netanyahu could enter negotiations with a bloc of more than 40 MKs, while Eisenkot and Bennett would collectively hold approximately 27 to 28 seats.
Such an imbalance would expose both men to considerable political risk. Netanyahu would have substantial leverage over the coalition before its ministers had even settled into office.
Could Eisenkot establish a minority government with Arab support?
What happens if negotiations with the haredi parties collapse and efforts to establish a national unity government fail?
Would Eisenkot have the courage to establish a minority government comprising 48 MKs and relying on external support from Arab parties?
He would have the courage. The more significant question is whether he would have the necessary political partners.

Such a government would not necessarily be established as a temporary arrangement before another election. Eisenkot could seek to expand the coalition from within after securing its initial establishment.
For both Liberman and Bennett, another election could carry substantial electoral risks.
Those predicting the immediate collapse of a minority government should also consider the parliamentary mechanisms that could contribute to its stability.

The emergency regulations governing the application of certain Israeli laws in Judea and Samaria, for example, are scheduled to remain in force until February 2028. Even if an upcoming attempt to renew them fails, their expiration would not be immediate.
Unlike during the previous government of change, Netanyahu could face significant obstacles in attempting to bring down such a coalition.
One of those obstacles is Itamar Ben-Gvir. The prospect of his return to government could provide Arab MKs with a powerful incentive to maintain external support for an Eisenkot-led coalition.
It is a political sword that would hang over them throughout the government's tenure.
Netanyahu's corruption trial and the lessons of Olmert's acquittal
The front-page headline consisted of a single word: "The Acquittal." Alongside it appeared a photograph of the defendant, smiling broadly.

Beneath the headline were several opinion columns by the newspaper's leading commentators. Their titles included "The Attorney-General's Fault," "The Lost Years," "The Failure," "The Victory," and "The Conspiracy."
At the bottom of the page appeared another prominent headline: "A Yom Kippur for the State Attorney's Office."
This was not a newspaper published this week. It was the front page of Yediot Aharonot following former prime minister Ehud Olmert's acquittal on most of the charges against him in 2012.
Israel has been here before.
The difference is that, at the time, everyone waited for the conclusion of the trial. Today, the judges in Netanyahu's criminal proceedings appear interested in shortening the process.
Whether they are reluctant to produce a verdict that would subsequently face Supreme Court scrutiny, frustrated by the proceedings, or concerned about their consequences remains unclear.

There is another fundamental difference. Olmert resigned as prime minister before his trial, following criticism from the then-opposition leader, Netanyahu, who argued that a prime minister under investigation could not make consequential national decisions.
Netanyahu, by contrast, remained in office while standing trial.

In my view, he used his political authority to systematically undermine public confidence in Israel's state institutions, beginning with the police and continuing with the State Attorney's Office, the attorney-general, and the Supreme Court.
Justice Minister Yariv Levin and MK Simcha Rothman's judicial overhaul initiatives subsequently placed the broader legal system under unprecedented pressure.

The legitimacy of state commissions of inquiry and the Central Elections Committee was also challenged. Netanyahu now presents himself as the victim of the very institutions whose credibility he has spent years undermining.
How Israel's judicial system secured Olmert's conviction
What happened following Olmert's initial acquittal?
The prosecution, attorney-general, and police did not abandon their efforts.
Investigators continued applying pressure to Olmert's former bureau chief, Shula Zaken, following an extensive investigation involving his associates and searches of the Prime Minister's Office.
Prosecutors had previously taken the unusual step of securing advance testimony from American businessman Morris Talansky while Olmert was still serving as prime minister.
Despite the closure of several investigations, law enforcement authorities continued pursuing the remaining cases.
When the Holyland proceedings created an opportunity to secure Zaken's cooperation, prosecutors obtained recordings and her agreement to testify against Olmert.
They subsequently sought exceptional permission to introduce new evidence during the appellate proceedings.
The Supreme Court approved the request.
The panel included then-Supreme Court president Asher Grunis, Salim Joubran, Yoram Danziger, Neal Hendel, and Uzi Vogelman.
Several of these justices would subsequently become targets of criticism from Netanyahu's supporters, who frequently portrayed judicial activism as evidence of political bias.

Yet these were the very judges who enabled prosecutors to pursue additional evidence against Olmert, a former prime minister who had moved toward the political Left and offered Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas far-reaching concessions in peace negotiations.

Among the senior legal officials involved in the proceedings against Olmert were former attorneys-general Menachem Mazuz and Avichai Mandelblit, as well as former state attorneys Moshe Lador and Shai Nitzan.
These were some of the same officials whose integrity would later be questioned by Netanyahu's political supporters.
There are judges in Jerusalem. There have always been judges in Jerusalem, even when they make mistakes.

articles.title: International music executives increasingly shun Israel’s talent showcase at Jaffa Port festival
articles.summary: “We’re here to make art, and art has a role that isn’t political,” the festival’s artistic director, Hadas Vanunu, said.
paragraphs: The Israeli music industry had its own take on speed dating this week at a venue built from repurposed shipping containers in the Jaffa Port.
International booking agents and record label executives moved from table to table, slipping on headphones and chatting with Israeli musicians at Beit Hamecholot.

The musicians arrived armed with vinyl records, snacks, bottles of alcohol, and, in some cases, furry costumes - anything that might entice a prospective booker to stop and listen. A few minutes of conversation could determine whether their music would be heard in Berlin, Tokyo or New York.
But getting the people who could make that happen to come from abroad to Israel’s Music Showcase Festival in the first place has become increasingly difficult due to cultural boycotts of Israel.

Of the at least 200 music industry professionals invited this year, 32 attended, down from 55 last year. In previous years, the festival would typically send out between 400 and 500 invitations, but the festival’s artistic director, Hadas Vanunu, said organizers had become more selective about whom they’d approached since the war in Gaza began three years ago.
Vanunu said the way prospective delegates responded was more troubling than the drop in numbers.
From security concerns to political considerations

In 2024, when just 22 international guests came, many cited security concerns and pressure from their families. By 2025, objections were increasingly political, although Vanunu said Israel still elicited a measure of sympathy abroad because of the hostages held in Gaza.
This year, many of those approached simply didn’t respond.

“We were practically begging people to tell us why they wouldn’t come, even if it meant getting angry messages saying, ‘We’re not coming because Israel is doing this or that.’ This year, we didn’t even get that,” Vanunu told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
“What was a trend of hating Israel a year or two ago has now become the norm. Israel is a pariah state. You can really feel it in your blood, just how hated you are,” she said.

Founded in 2009, the festival has helped propel Israeli acts including Noga Erez, Lola Marsh and Garden City Movement onto the international music scene. This year’s six-day event featured some 50 performances across Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, spanning jazz, hip-hop, rock, electronic and Middle Eastern music.

Produced by Jerusalem’s Yellow Submarine music center in partnership with the Foreign Ministry’s cultural diplomacy division, the festival has suffered budget cuts and been targeted by the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement. In 2022, Palestinian boycott campaigners explicitly called on international guests to shun the event, citing its government sponsorship.
Since the outbreak of the Gaza war following the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, even people who attended the festival years earlier have grown wary of being publicly associated with Israel.
“We’ve even had Jews from the diaspora and former Israelis who attended the festival ask us to erase every digital trace of their visits,” Vanunu said.

Where once the festival prominently publicized the identities of its international guests as a measure of its prestige, this year organizers supplied JTA with a list of delegates on the strict condition that neither their names nor their job titles be published.

Among the organizations represented were those affiliated with Warner Records, Germany’s Asphalt Festival, Britain’s National Jazz Archive, South Korea’s Jarasum Jazz Festival and the music publications Rolling Stone and Billboard. Delegates came from countries including the United States, Germany, Britain, Poland, China, Japan, Vietnam, Singapore, Ghana, Zimbabwe and the United Arab Emirates.
No distinction between Israelis and Israel itself, Vanunu says
Some prospective delegates, Vanunu said, wanted the festival’s organizers to clarify their position on the Israeli government’s actions before they would even consider engaging with them.
“There is absolutely no longer any distinction between an Israeli individual and their country,” she said.
The musicians in Jaffa, however, were also grappling with other consequences of the war.

Magi Hikri, who performs as MAGI, was left to fend for herself at the showcase after her manager was called up at the last minute for reserve duty. “What can you do? That’s the reality we live in here,” she said.

With long, tousled blond hair, Middle Eastern roots, and pounding dance beats, Hikri has echoes of the international star Shakira in her persona, including a soccer connection: The singer, of Iraqi and Yemeni Jewish descent, has a track, “Jilala,” on the soundtrack of the wildly popular EA Sports FC 26, the soccer video game from the series formerly known as FIFA.
Despite the setbacks, Hikri saw the foreign delegation as “proof that music prevails and will always have a place.”

Several delegates were willing to speak publicly about their decision to attend. Maciej Nestor, who runs the independent Polish record label V Records, said that having toured western Ukraine during the war, he understood how vital music and culture were to people living through conflict. Yet even some of his Jewish musician friends questioned his decision to come to Israel.
“I don’t justify violence or take political sides,” he said, but added that neither artists nor audiences should be “isolated by political conflicts.”

Nestor pointed to what he had seen both on the streets and onstage: Jews and Arabs “going about their lives” and Israeli and Palestinian musicians performing together at the Jaffa gathering as part of the FeelBeit Ensemble, led by jazz trumpeter Avishai Cohen.
“Culture must remain a space for dialogue and human connection,” he said.

Isaac Green, a New York-based executive at Warner Records, by contrast, said he had encountered no pushback over his decision to attend. Green, who is Jewish, pointed to the considerable Jewish presence in the American music industry.
He was struck by the breadth of musical innovation in Israel, he said, and by the “energy of audiences,” even at jazz concerts.
Green described a set by Ethiopian Israeli rapper Eden Derso, who fuses Hebrew hip-hop with soulful R&B vocals, as “phenomenal.”

Derso said hearing praise from someone who did not understand her lyrics was particularly gratifying. “They don’t understand the words but still love it, that’s crazy to me,” she said. “People are just drawn to it.”
She recalled her first performance in Berlin after the outbreak of the Gaza war, when some audience members visibly recoiled upon hearing she was from Tel Aviv.

Asked if such reactions might make her conceal her nationality abroad, Derso scoffed, invoking her Beta Israel heritage. “My father waited long enough to come to this country,” she said. Hiding her Israeli identity, she said, was “like hiding my Blackness.”

The war has changed the repertoire of Boogie Balagan, a Paris-based Israeli duo whose music draws heavily on Arabic influences. Gabri, one half of the duo, said that since Oct. 7, he now improvises a different lyric instead of singing the word “Palestine” in one of their songs. The word had become difficult to sing, he said, after so many of his friends lost loved ones that day.

In the aftermath of the attack, the duo recorded “Mashiah,” singing entirely in Hebrew for the first time in 20 years together. Muslim audiences had responded positively to the song, Gabri’s musical partner, Azri, said, adding that it was younger people on the French far left who were “particularly obstinate” in their hostility toward the duo as Israelis.

Huy Tuan Bui, a prominent Vietnamese music producer and founder of several major music festivals, acknowledged having “moments of doubt” before coming to the expo in Israel, but he said he was deeply moved by the organizers’ refusal to give up on the festival through years of war.
He described his week in Israel as “unforgettable,” praising the caliber of Israeli musicians and the warmth of the people.
“What I witnessed completely changed my perception of this land,” Bui said, pledging to become a “voluntary ambassador promoting the beauty and kindness of Israel and its people.”
According to Vanunu, the willingness of foreign guests to travel to Israel should not be mistaken for an act of charity toward Israeli musicians.
“They don’t want to help Israeli artists simply out of the goodness of their hearts. They want to help because the artists are insanely talented and the music is incredible,” she said.

Cuts to the Foreign Ministry’s cultural diplomacy budget have also threatened the festival’s future. Last year, the ministry froze an estimated 5 million shekels in funding for international cultural collaborations.
“We’re either fighting what the world thinks of us or fighting over whether our own country even believes in investing in culture at all,” she said.
Vanunu said the music industry needed to collectively resist the pressure to boycott artists.
“We’re here to make art, and art has a role that isn’t political,” she said. “The day will come when everyone understands that, and when everyone does, we’ll still be here, doing what we do.”

articles.title: Australia’s east coast deluged by storms as roads flood and damaging winds forecast for NSW and Victoria
articles.summary: Severe weather and flood watch warnings are in place as a storm band moves from central Queensland through NSW to Victoria and Tasmania Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast The final weekend of Australia’s wettest spring on record for an El Niño year is delivering a deluge of storms and heavy rain. Severe weather and flood watch warnings were in place across the eastern states as a weather band moves from central Queensland through New South Wales to Victoria and Tasmania. Continue reading...
paragraphs: The final weekend of Australia’s wettest spring on record for an El Niño year is delivering a deluge of storms and heavy rain.
Severe weather and flood watch warnings are in place across the eastern states as a weather band moves from central Queensland through New South Wales to Victoria and Tasmania.
The Bureau of Meteorology’s Helen Reid said El Niño attracted great interest but was only one factor to consider when looking at a season and the continent in its entirety.
Allow content provided by a third party?
“El Niño is part of it, and we have had quite a lot of rainfall in the south-east but that’s … also a balance of what we didn’t have earlier in the winter season,” she said.
Tropical humidity has drifted across the continent and is being swept into the eastern states.
“We are looking at a very active system that’s going to be affecting southern Queensland, inland NSW, Victoria and also into Tasmania,” Reid said.
Damaging winds were forecast for the NSW alpine region and Victoria’s central and eastern districts, which were also expecting heavy rainfall.
The heaviest overnight falls in Victoria were 85.4mm at Amphitheatre Reservoir in the northern Pyrenees region and 72.8mm at Bet Bet Creek in the state’s west.
Victorian State Emergency Service volunteers reported a busy 24 hours, with more than 340 calls for help to 6am on Saturday.
Most calls related to fallen trees (105), building damage (96) and flooding impacts (97).
The state’s north-east and eastern ranges can expect six-hourly rainfall totals from 55mm to 70mm on Saturday morning.

A moderate flood warning is in place for Warrill Creek in Queensland, with initial flood warnings in Tasmania for the Meander and Mersey rivers and flood watches for most of the catchments in western, central and north-east Victoria.
Meanwhile, a heatwave in the Northern Territory is easing but intensifying from severe to extreme in Western Australia’s Kimberley and Pilbara regions.
“It’s only going to be a shortlived heatwave but it is going to be a couple of hot days through there,” Reid said.
“Picking out Kununurra as an example, they’re looking at 42 or 43C for the next few days during the daytime but only dropping down to about 27C overnight.”
An offshore trough off WA’s coast would create a low-intensity heatwave stretching to just north of Perth.
Meanwhile, firefighting crews are facing another difficult day as they continue battling raging bushfires on Tasmania’s remote Flinders Island.
As other parts of Tasmania brace for heavy rains and potential flooding, crews on Flinders Island are battling a blaze that had burned 15,000 hectares by Friday - more than 10 per cent of the island.
Forecast heavy rainfall has yet to reach Flinders Island but Tasmania Fire Service incident controller Steven Richardson said it could create further challenges rather than provide relief.

“At this stage, the weather may actually create further challenges for firefighters on the ground, reducing our ability to strengthen containment lines through backburning and creating wet, slippery conditions,” he said.
“While some warnings have been downgraded, our crews are expecting another long day on the ground focusing on containment and asset protection.”

articles.title: From her wedding dress to cancer recovery: The story Kate Middleton tells through fashion
articles.summary: From her royal wedding to her return to public life after cancer treatment, Kate Middleton has spent 15 years using fashion to send messages, blending luxury labels with affordable brands, embracing diplomatic dressing and setting global trends
paragraphs: From her royal wedding to her return to public life after cancer treatment, Kate Middleton has spent 15 years using fashion to send messages, blending luxury labels with affordable brands, embracing diplomatic dressing and setting global trends

“Cancer does change you. It changes your body. It changes you physically. But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you. You know, healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.”

The 30-minute documentary follows Middleton throughout her recovery. Among other things, it shows her taking part in the Three Peaks Challenge, in which she climbed the highest peaks in England, Wales and Scotland within 24 hours last June to raise money for the charity of the Royal Marsden hospital, where she received treatment. Beyond documenting her physical journey, the film seeks to tell a story of recovery, a changing body and life after illness.
Kate Middleton at a cancer fundraiser, 2026
(Photo: Jonathan Brady - Pool/Getty Images)

In January 2024, Middleton underwent abdominal surgery. Kensington Palace subsequently announced that she would not resume public duties until after Easter, without providing further details. After two months of speculation and conspiracy theories on social media, Middleton released a video revealing that post-surgery tests had detected cancer and that she had begun a course of preventive chemotherapy. She did not disclose the type of cancer she had. In January 2025, she announced that her cancer was in remission.
Kate Middleton announces she has completed chemotherapy

The airing of “Heal” comes as Middleton gradually resumes her public duties after an extended absence from royal life. Against this backdrop, her wardrobe, which has long served as a means of public communication, takes on new significance. While her fashion choices once conveyed stability, restraint and her place within the British monarchy, with frequent nods to Princess Diana and Queen Elizabeth II, her public appearances are now inevitably viewed in the context of her recovery from cancer.

This month, Middleton accompanied her husband, Prince William, on an official visit to India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony in Mumbai, one of the leading international awards recognizing efforts to protect the environment and combat the climate crisis. The three-day visit marked the couple’s first joint royal engagement outside Britain since her cancer treatment.
A blue dress designed by Roksanda Ilinčić during a visit to Mumbai, 2026
(Photo: Aaron Chown - Pool/Getty Images)

From a fashion perspective, the visit was also a showcase of what is known as diplomatic dressing – using clothing to pay tribute to the host country’s culture. While her choices have not always been successful, the intended messages were clear. Middleton’s wardrobe ranged from tailored pantsuits and skirt suits to an evening gown made from Indian sari fabric, worn as a gesture of respect for her hosts.

This approach to diplomatic dressing has been a hallmark of Middleton’s style since she joined the royal family in April 2011. On official visits, she typically tailors her wardrobe to the host country, whether by wearing designs by local designers, incorporating cultural motifs or embracing the colors of the national flag.

Throughout the visit, she alternated between a light-colored pantsuit with a mint-green jacket by Veronica Beard, a red skirt suit by Emilia Wickstead and a blue midi dress by Roksanda Ilinčić. She accessorized the latter with earrings from Indian jewelry house Amrapali, which she had worn during the couple’s previous visit to India a decade earlier.
An Emilia Wickstead skirt suit during a visit to Mumbai, 2026

For a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Middleton opted for a plum-colored pantsuit by Indian designer Gaurav Gupta, pairing it with a handbag by British brand DeMellier made from a leather-like material developed by an Indian company using discarded rice husks and straw. It was a carefully considered choice that conveyed an environmental message through clothing.

For the gala, Middleton opted for a red anarkali dress named Neelam by Indian designer Mahima Mahajan. The dress featured a traditional Indian silhouette embellished with gold embroidery and green glass beads. She completed the look with an emerald-and-diamond necklace and matching earrings from Queen Elizabeth II’s collection, originally designed for the monarch, who first wore them in 1989.
A dress by Indian designer Mahima Mahajan. With Prince William at the Earthshot Prize ceremony in Mumbai, 2026
(Photo: Phil Noble - Pool/Getty Images)

This approach to diplomatic dressing has been a hallmark of Middleton’s style since she joined the royal family in April 2011. On official visits, she typically tailors her wardrobe to the host country, whether by wearing designs by local designers, incorporating cultural motifs or embracing the colors of the national flag. During her visit to Pakistan in 2019, for example, she wore several variations of the shalwar kameez, the country’s traditional attire, including a blue kurta.
An Elie Saab gown worn to a dinner with the sultan of Oman at Windsor Castle, 2026
(Photo: Isabel Infantes - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

During a visit to Bhutan three years earlier, Middleton wore a skirt made from traditional fabric specially woven for her by a local artisan. In Canada that same year, she paired a red dress with Queen Elizabeth II’s maple leaf brooch. On a visit to Germany in 2017, she chose a dress by German designer Markus Lupfer featuring a print of eagles, the country’s national bird.

Born in January 1982 in Reading, England, Middleton is the eldest child of Michael and Carole Middleton. Her parents built a successful party supplies business and the family belonged to Britain’s upper middle class. After attending Marlborough College, where her interests included sports and art, she took a gap year during which she studied in Florence and participated in a volunteer program in Chile.
An ensemble by Holland Cooper and a Burberry coat during a visit to Scotland, 2026
(Photo: Martin Grimes/Getty Images)

In 2001, she began studying art history at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, where she met Prince William. The two became a couple a year later. Their relationship attracted intense media coverage, culminating in their 2011 wedding at Westminster Abbey in London, which was broadcast to millions of viewers worldwide. The couple have three children: Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis.

Middleton’s fashion history predates her entry into the royal family. In 2002, she wore a black dress at a charity fashion show. Originally costing around 30 pounds, the dress became a highly coveted item following reports that it had caught Prince William’s attention at the event. In 2011, it fetched 78,000 pounds at auction.

In fact, Middleton’s fashion history predates her entry into the royal family. In 2002, she wore a black dress at a charity fashion show. Originally costing around 30 pounds, the dress became a highly coveted item following reports that it had caught Prince William’s attention at the event. In 2011, it fetched 78,000 pounds at auction.
Kate Middleton and Prince William at their wedding, 2011
(Photo: John Stillwell - WPA/Getty Images, Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images)

Nine years later, her wedding gown, designed by Sarah Burton for Alexander McQueen, made Middleton one of the world’s most closely watched style figures. It also marked the beginning of an enduring relationship with the fashion house, whose designs she has worn on numerous occasions since.

Her choice of McQueen, a British fashion house known for its dramatic and subversive aesthetic, is particularly interesting given Middleton’s understated style. But luxury designers and fashion houses such as McQueen, Jenny Packham, Catherine Walker, Emilia Wickstead and Erdem are not the only mainstays of her wardrobe. Over the years, she has frequently incorporated pieces from more accessible brands such as Reiss, Hobbs, Jigsaw and Zara.
Family style: Kate Middleton, Prince Louis, Princess Charlotte, Prince William and Prince George, 2023
(Photo: Yui Mok - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

One of the defining moments in her fashion history came in 2011, when she wore a 175-pound (770-shekel) dress by Reiss to meet then-U.S. President Barack Obama and first lady Michelle Obama. The dress sold out within hours and caused the brand’s website to crash. The term “Kate effect” has since come to describe the consumer demand generated by each of her appearances.

Another notable feature of Middleton’s style over the past decade has been her willingness to rewear outfits from previous public engagements, presumably to encourage discussion about sustainability and responsible consumption – issues she has not publicly addressed. Yet in an age of instant gratification dominated by fast fashion, repeating an outfit, especially as one of the world’s most photographed princesses, makes a powerful statement without saying a word.
A dress by Self-Portrait at a Buckingham Palace garden party, 2026
(Photo: Aaron Chown - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

One example of how Middleton communicates through fashion came at the 2018 British Academy Film Awards, where stars including Angelina Jolie, Emma Roberts and Lupita Nyong’o wore black gowns in solidarity with the #MeToo movement and the Time’s Up initiative. With members of the British royal family generally refraining from taking public political positions, Middleton opted for a deep green evening gown accented with a black velvet ribbon – a choice that drew criticism.
Her choice of a green dress sparked anger on social media. The British Academy Film Awards, 2018
(Photo: Jeff Spicer/Getty Images)
Social media users took issue with her fashion choice.

“How is Kate not ashamed to sit in the auditorium wearing a green dress when so many women around her are wearing black? Frankly, she should have stayed home if she wasn’t going to support other women,” read a post on the “Meghan and Harry” fan page.
“It’s not a political thing. Its a woman thing!” Nikki Long wrote on Twitter, expressing disappointment over Middleton’s decision not to wear black.
Royal elegance: Kate Middleton and Prince William at Windsor Castle, 2025

Fifteen years after Middleton joined the British royal family, her wardrobe offers a record of her evolution in the public eye. Her fashion choices reflect not only personal taste but also a broader language of symbols, messages and gestures. Now, as she returns to public life following her recovery, it will be interesting to see whether her wardrobe continues to mirror the changes in her life.

articles.title: IDF thwarts weapons smuggling attempt along eastern border, seizes six pistols
articles.summary: The incident follows separate police investigations earlier this month into illegal weapons possession in the West Bank, including an operation in which four protected gazelles were discovered.
paragraphs: IDF troops from the Judea and Galilee Division thwarted an attempt to smuggle six pistols along Israel's eastern border on Friday, the military announced on Saturday.
The weapons were discovered during a routine patrol in the Judea region and transferred to the police for further investigation, according to the IDF.
Israel Police investigate illegal firearms, protected wildlife possession in West Bank

Earlier this month, Israel Police investigated illegal weapons possession and the keeping of protected wildlife in the West Bank, conducting operations in the village of Shufa, near Tulkarm, and the Nablus area.
Police opened an investigation into three suspects following the discovery of illegal firearms, other weapons, and gazelles, a protected species in Israel, in Shufa.
During the operation, Israeli forces discovered three hunting rifles concealed inside a home and an adjacent greenhouse, along with a large quantity of ammunition, IDF uniform pants, and two knives.
Israeli forces also found four gazelles being held at the property. The protected animals were later transferred to the Israel Nature and Parks Authority.

In a separate operation in the Askar refugee camp on the outskirts of Nablus, Israeli forces seized an M16 rifle and a handgun concealed inside a home. A Nablus resident in his 20s was arrested in connection with the weapons.
Maya Zanger-Shamir contributed to this report.

articles.title: What to watch this week: ‘The Altruists’ turns Sam Bankman-Fried’s tech scandal into great TV
articles.summary: TV Time: Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle deliver outstanding performances in Netflix’s gripping dramatization of the FTX scandal, while Amy Poehler’s archaeological sitcom ‘Dig’ disappoints.
paragraphs: The Altruists is the best miniseries on television/streaming in a long, long time. It plays like Silicon Valley meets Billions meets The West Wing as it tells the true story of Sam Bankman-Fried, the young entrepreneur who created the cryptocurrency exchange FTX and later went to prison for various crimes connected to it.

Whether you followed Bankman-Fried’s spectacular rise and equally spectacular fall closely, you will enjoy The Altruists if you liked any of the series mentioned above. And the series isn’t only for crypto aficionados.

Even after watching the miniseries, I still have a lot of questions about crypto, and I paused it a couple of times to Google some terms, although most of them turned out to mean what I suspected from the context. But none of this should deter anyone from giving the series a try.

Just as The Sopranos was not really about organized crime as much as the characters and their very relatable problems, this is a story about nerds searching for romance and trying to rule the world more than about hi-tech or finance. People have said life is like high school with money, and in The Altruists, life is like high school with billions.

The Altruists was created by Graham Moore, who won an Oscar for his screenplay for The Imitation Game, and it has the same interplay of personal and professional life among the super-brainy that made that movie memorable.

At the core of the series is the relationship between Bankman-Fried (Anthony Boyle), a socially awkward math nerd who went to MIT and got a job on Wall Street, and the woman of his dreams, the equally nerdy math whiz Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner), who followed a similar path.

What drew the two of them together, more than just their intellect, was their commitment to “effective altruism,” a philosophy which promotes using the capitalist system to amass as much wealth as possible, so that this money can then be donated to worthy causes. This is the twist that makes it different from Wall Street, The Wolf of Wall Street, or so many other “greed is good” type stories.

The irony behind brilliant, ambitious, and self-centered people wanting to feel like they’re doing it all to help others was skewered expertly in the Silicon Valley series, which featured Gavin Belson (Matt Ross), a narcissistic founder of a giant software company, who tried to soften his image by talking endlessly about how much he wanted to make the world a better place.

The Altruists shows how Bankman-Fried and Ellison created the crypto exchange as a way to make billions that could be funneled into good causes, but somewhere along the way, they began cutting corners that led them into misusing funds, misleading investors and customers, and engaging in insider trading, as thousands of businesspeople have done before them.

Anyone with a glancing knowledge of the Bankman-Fried case knows that much, but this isn’t a whodunit so much as a why-it-was-done, and it creates two complex, initially likable characters who take a wrong turn. Their betrayal of their ideals and each other gives The Altruists a tragic dimension.

The details and nuances in the story bring it to life, like how they make sure that vegan nachos are available at the bar they frequent when they move their operations to the Bahamas to avoid US regulators.
Julia Garner delivers an Emmy-worthy performance in Netflix’s crypto drama

JUST LIKE in The Imitation Game, the clever screenplay is one key component, but the other is the acting. Boyle and Garner are never less than utterly credible and winning, and as infuriating as they can be at times, while you watch The Altruists, you will root for them to take the high road even though you know what they actually did.

Boyle, who was in The Plot Against America and The House of Guinness, turns Bankman-Fried into the George Costanza of 21st-century crypto-crime. George, you probably recall, was Jerry’s deliriously self-serving sidekick on Seinfeld, who said, “It’s not a lie if you believe it.”

Like other recent failed tycoons, among them Adam Neumann, whose life was dramatized in the series We Crashed, or Elizabeth Holmes in numerous movies and series, including the just-released documentary You Can See Everything, Bankman-Fried cultivated a cult of personality, making himself, with his hoodies, cargo shorts, and unruly curls, into the company’s public image.
You can believe that he was smart enough to build a crypto exchange and foolish enough to break the rules that sent it crashing down.

In the series, Bankman-Fried is still trying to win his parents’ approval, and his father, played by Paul Reiser (Mad About You), a professor of tax law, shows up and begins working for FTX in later episodes. Bankman-Fried’s father is a stand-in for all of us out there who don’t get what’s going on, and it’s always good to see Reiser.
But the greatest performance out of an excellent ensemble is Garner as Caroline.

Garner has been wonderful in The Americans, Ozark, and Inventing Anna, but she outdoes herself here. She’s utterly unrecognizable as the awkward Ellison, who writes erotic Harry Potter fan fiction, prattles about polyamory, and sees everything in the world as a question of probability equations.

She is just as convincing here as she was in Ozark as the tough redneck Ruth, a role for which she won three Emmys. The Altruists should net her a fourth such trophy. Hearing her utter the meticulously composed dialogue Aaron Sorkin-style as part of her performance is a joy, but she is just as good in the emotional moments as she is when she’s being clever and funny.
Acting rarely gets better than this, and as I watched her, I began to think of the young Meryl Streep. Garner’s mother is Tamar Gingold, an Israeli comedian who moved to the US years ago.

LET’S FACE it: much of what Netflix has offered in recent years is derivative and forgettable, but Netflix still occasionally hits it out of the park, and the streamer has done it again with The Altruists.
Amy Poehler and Hugh Laurie’s archaeological sitcom ‘Dig’ misses the mark

After watching the first few episodes of Dig, a new series starring Amy Poehler and Hugh Laurie that is available on Hot VOD and Next TV and will also stream on Hot 3, I tried to imagine a session in the writers’ room where anyone said they thought it was funny.

It has great stars and a great premise, but the result is a reminder of Alfred Hitchcock’s maxim, “To make a great film you need three things: the script, the script, and the script.” That’s just as true in television, obviously, and nothing proves it more than this clumsy attempt at a sitcom in an interesting setting.
The setting is an archaeological dig in Greece, and the series should not be confused with an international 2014 show of the same name about supernatural goings-on in the Old City of Jerusalem.

Laurie is perfect for his role as Neville, a charismatic archaeologist who gets all the credit and does none of the work, and Poehler is fine as Elise, his longtime associate who hopes he will retire so she can have the chance to shine. But every situation is so labored and obvious, every joke so clunky, that it’s a chore to sit through.

For example, one young intern, Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), is annoyed with Neville because she once choked on a meatball and since then, he has always called her “Meatball.” Yes, he’s a jerk, but where’s the funny part?
Another staff member, Patty (Fina Strazza), drones on about growing up in a tiny town in Maine with no one but cows around and not knowing she needs sunscreen in Greece in the summer.

Around the middle of the season, according to the press release, the series turns into a caper about a valuable statue they discover, but I doubt many people will want to stick around for that. Dig wants to be 30 Rock with archaeologists, and that’s a great aspiration, but the series misses the mark.

articles.title: Nigeria's acting legend who was loved across Africa and beyond
articles.summary: Before becoming a household name in the Nigerian film industry, Edochie built a career in broadcasting.
paragraphs: For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor.
He was Okonkwo – the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal in Things Fall Apart made him a household name and earned him a place in the hearts of millions.
Even in death, many Nigerians still refer to him by the character's name, a testament to the enduring impact of a role that defined his career.
Edochie died on 25 November, aged 79, in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

In 1987, Edochie starred in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel. His portrayal of Okonkwo would change his life, establishing him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors and bringing him international recognition.
The series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.
Joy Nnamdi, a fan of both the novel and its television adaptation, believes Edochie was the perfect choice for the lead role.
She said nobody else could have brought the character to life as convincingly.
"His character Okonkwo gave a face to the highly celebrated novel," she told the BBC in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos.
The role also cemented his reputation as a hard man, a screen persona he would maintain through much of his career.
"It was very rare to see him laugh in movies. He was the ultimate tough man," Nnamdi added.
With his deep, authoritative voice, imposing presence and effortless command of African proverbs, Edochie had a way of dominating a scene without raising his voice.
Whether playing a village elder, a wealthy businessman or a feared traditional ruler, he became an enduring embodiment of patriarchal authority on screen.
Edochie went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has grown into one of the world's largest.
From Kenya to South Africa, MultiChoice's Africa Magic channels helped take his films into millions of African homes as Nollywood became a cultural phenomenon across the continent.
Although many of his films were rooted in his Igbo culture, their themes of family loyalty, inheritance disputes, spiritual beliefs and the abuse of power resonated with audiences far beyond Nigeria.
Before becoming a household name in the film industry, however, Edochie had built a successful career in broadcasting.
Born on 7 March 1947 in Zaria, northern Nigeria, he attended primary and secondary school in Kaduna before studying journalism and television at the School of Journalism and Television in the UK.
He joined the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967, the year Nigeria's civil war broke out.
He joined the pro-separatist Voice of Biafra, and recently described the war years as the greatest personal challenge he ever faced.
"During the war, the experience that we had as Biafrans, you know, survival was difficult. Hunger was driving us into eating all sorts of nonsense," he recalled.

He rose through the ranks to hold senior management positions but then switched to acting. Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals and Billionaire's Club.
His career also bridged the transition from home-video productions to global streaming platforms.
The 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart, which became Netflix's first original Nigerian film, introduced his work to a wider international audience.
He also worked in Ghana, where he starred alongside some of the country's biggest film stars in the 2017 comedy John and John.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
He also received several other accolades, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.
In recent years, Edochie found an unexpected new audience online.
His distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films became popular social media memes, introducing his work to a younger generation of Africans.
For many who had never watched Things Fall Apart or his early Nollywood films, his stern expressions became a humorous way of conveying disbelief, disapproval or exasperation at everyday situations.
But his reputation as a formidable screen presence was no joke to those who grew up watching him.
Sani Muazu recalls that parents in the northern Nigerian city of Kano would sometimes invoke Edochie's name to keep misbehaving children in check.
"They would tell you: 'Okonkwo will come and visit you if you don't stop' and we would begin acting right," he said.

"To be honest, we grew up scared of him. Even though he was on the screen and not physically present, some of his roles added to our fears because he played some popular occultic roles, and villain roles suited him."
Tributes poured in from fans and fellow actors following news of his death, with many describing him as a giant who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.
Popular actress Genevieve Nnaji paid her tribute in a post on X.

"I will let the assurance of the fact that you are a chosen one; and therefore, have returned to the most high God override my grief and heartbreak. May the heart of a true lion forever rest in peace. We love you," she wrote.
Patience Ozokwor, popularly known as Mama G, who appeared alongside Edochie in several productions, remembered him as a brilliant actor and a source of wisdom.
"He has been a father to stories that are told, like an elder sitting down telling you how things were done in those days," she told BBC News Pidgin.
"I called him any time, any day. He'll tell you what to do and what not to do."
Film director Babangida Bangis told the BBC that Edochie's death was a loss not just for Nigeria or Africa, but for the global film industry.
"Just days ago, during a seminar for filmmakers across the country, his name popped up as an example of brilliance on the screen, longevity and professionalism," he said.
"I think his loss is one for the world, not just Nigeria or Africa. We all grew up watching and loving him."
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu also mourned the veteran actor, describing his death as a major loss to the country's film industry and cultural heritage.
The president, like many admirers, singled out Edochie's portrayal of Okonkwo, saying the performance and his subsequent roles had established him as one of Nigeria's most accomplished actors.
But beyond the fame and formidable character he portrayed on screen, his family remembers a man whose greatest legacy was the importance he placed on honesty and speaking the truth.
Leo Edochie, his son, told the BBC that his father was a strong-willed man.
"Of all his legacies, I think the whole world would agree that these two were the most important: telling the truth and remaining honest," he said.
He described his father as a man who lived an exemplary life, offering a model that young people could learn from and aspire to follow.
"I don't really have a choice, but the truth is that I have to carry on that legacy for our family," he added.
Edochie's influence also extended to his family, with two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, following him into the Nigerian film industry.
Yet, for an actor so closely associated with stern expressions and intimidating characters, some of his most endearing moments came when he let his guard down.
In 2021, he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for the song Highway, surprising fans with a display of dance moves that showed a lighter, more playful side of the septuagenarian.
It was a refreshing reminder that the man behind the formidable screen persona could also laugh, dance and enjoy himself.

articles.title: צה"ל: חיסלנו בעזה שני מחבלים שעבדו במקביל בארגון "רופאים ללא גבולות"
articles.summary: לפי צה"ל, המחבלים פעלו לשקם את כוחו של חמאס, ואחד מהם אף שימש כמפקד חוליית ארטילריה בזרוע הצבאית. בארגון הסיוע האשימו: "התקיפה כוונה לעבר אחת המרפאות שלנו"
paragraphs: לפי צה"ל, המחבלים פעלו לשקם את כוחו של חמאס, ואחד מהם אף שימש כמפקד חוליית ארטילריה בזרוע הצבאית. בארגון הסיוע האשימו: "התקיפה כוונה לעבר אחת המרפאות שלנו"

צה"ל חיסל אמש (שישי) בעיר עזה שני מחבלים שעבדו במקביל כמאבטחים בארגון ההומניטרי הבינלאומי "רופאים ללא גבולות" (MSF). לפי דובר צה"ל, המחבלים, אחמד סופיאן מוחמד עלי אבו חסירה ומועאד יוסף עלי סבאח, ששימש כמפקד חוליית ארטילריה בזרוע הצבאית של חמאס, חוסלו מהאוויר.
לדברי צה"ל, התקיפה לא כוונה לעבר בית חולים ולא נגרם נזק לתשתיות רפואיות, זאת בניגוד לדיווחים פלסטיניים קודמים על תקיפה סמוך למבנה של הארגון באזור בית החולים שיפא.
(צילום: AP Photo/Abdel Kareem Hana)

דובר צה"ל מסר כי "זו דוגמה נוספת להיטמעות של ארגון הטרור חמאס בארגונים בינלאומיים. לאורך המלחמה ובעת האחרונה בפרט, המחבלים קידמו מתווי טרור נגד הכוחות ופעלו לשקם את יכולות ארגוני הטרור ברצועה, תוך הפרה שיטתית של הפסקת האש. לפני התקיפה ננקטו אמצעי זהירות על מנת לצמצם ככל הניתן את הנזק הצפוי לאזרחים כתוצאה מכך, לרבות שימוש בחימוש מדויק ותצפיות מהאוויר".

ארגון "רופאים ללא גבולות" (MSF) פרסם הודעה חריפה בעקבות התקיפה: "התקיפה הישראלית כוונה לעבר אחת המרפאות שלנו. אנחנו המומים וזועמים בעקבות מותם של שניים מעמיתנו ששימשו כמאבטחים. מספר עובדי הארגון שנהרגו ברצועת עזה עלה ל-17". הארגון טען כי מבניו סומנו בבירור ומיקומם אף הועבר לידי צה"ל, אך לא התייחס בהודעתו לדברי צה"ל, לפיהם שני המאבטחים היו חלק מחמאס.
בתי החולים בעזה הפכו לחלק ממנגנון השליטה של חמאס

בתחילת השנה, ישראל החלה לשלול את רישיונות הפעילות של הארגון ביהודה ושומרון וברצועת עזה, בצל בדיקות שבוצעו על-ידי גורמי ביטחון שבהן עלה כי עובדיו היו מעורבים בפעילות טרור. מאז ההחלטה התנהלה מערכה מתוקשרת של האשמות הדדיות, שבמהלכה המתפ"ש חשף כי אחד מעובדי הארגון שימש כמחבל חמאס ופרסם תמונה שלו במדי ארגון הטרור.

צה"ל ושב"כ חשפו שלשום כי חמאס הפעיל מתקן חקירות ועינויים בתוך בית החולים מעמדאני (אל-אהלי הערבי), בשכונת זייתון שבצפון רצועת עזה. בצה"ל טענו כי פעילות חמאס בבית החולים המחישה את ניסיונו של הארגון לשמר את שליטתו ברצועה, תוך ניצול תשתיות אזרחיות ורפואיות.

עוד נמסר כי על פי המידע המודיעיני, לא רק בבית החולים מעמדאני, אלא גם בתי חולים נוספים ברצועת עזה, שאמורים היו לשמש מקלט עבור חולים ופצועים, הפכו לחלק ממנגנון השליטה והפעילות הצבאית של חמאס. לדברי צה"ל, לא רק שבמקומות אלו מוקמו מפקדות, חדרי פיקוד ושליטה עבור מחבלים, אלא גם מתקני חקירות ועינויים שבהם פעלו מנגנוני הביטחון של ארגון הטרור נגד תושבי הרצועה.

articles.title: IDF eliminates two Hamas terrorists working for Doctors Without Borders in Gaza, military says
articles.summary: The IDF says two Hamas terrorists eliminated in Gaza worked as security guards at a Doctors Without Borders clinic and were planning attacks in violation of the ceasefire; the aid group condemns the strike, saying its clinic was directly hit
paragraphs: The IDF says two Hamas terrorists eliminated in Gaza worked as security guards at a Doctors Without Borders clinic and were planning attacks in violation of the ceasefire; the aid group condemns the strike, saying its clinic was directly hit

The IDF said overnight Friday that it had eliminated two Hamas terrorists in an airstrike in Gaza City earlier that evening, adding that both worked as security guards at a clinic operated by Doctors Without Borders (MSF).
The military identified the two as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, an artillery cell commander in Hamas' military wing.
Destruction in Gaza City, Gaza Strip
(Photo: AP Photo/Jehad Alshrafi)

According to the IDF, the two had been planning attacks against Israeli troops and civilians throughout the war, particularly in recent weeks, while working to restore the military capabilities of terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip in violation of the ceasefire agreement.
"This is another example of the Hamas terrorist organization embedding itself within international organizations," the military said.

The IDF denied reports that the strike had targeted a hospital, saying no medical infrastructure in the area had been damaged. It added that precautionary measures had been taken to minimize potential civilian casualties, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance.
Doctors Without Borders condemned the strike, saying the two men were employed as watchmen and had been killed in a direct strike on one of its clinics in Gaza, contradicting the military's account.

"We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight," MSF said, adding that the deaths brought the total number of its employees killed in Gaza to 17.
The organization said the premises were clearly marked with MSF logos and that their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military.

MSF expressed solidarity with the families of those killed and called for accountability. The organization did not address the military's allegations regarding the men's involvement in terrorist activities.

The allegations come against the backdrop of a long-running dispute between Israel and Doctors Without Borders over the organization's operations in Gaza and the alleged involvement of its employees in terrorist activities.

In January, Israel revoked the operating licenses of more than a dozen international organizations, including MSF, after they failed to complete a mandatory registration process. Israeli security officials said checks had revealed that some employees of international aid organizations had been involved in terrorist activities.
MSF said at the time that it was awaiting the renewal of its registration and warned that Israel's requirements threatened its ability to provide essential medical services in Gaza and the West Bank.

The Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) accused the organization of refusing to provide Israeli authorities with a list of its employees, as required under a government decision. It also alleged that MSF employees had previously been identified as members of Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad.

MSF said it had facilitated 22,700 surgeries and assisted with 10,000 births in Gaza in 2025. COGAT disputed the organization's figures and its characterization of the extent of its contribution to Gaza's health care system.
