Friday's strike was the latest in a series of Israeli operations targeting Hamas figures accused of rebuilding the terrorist organization's military capabilities and planning attacks during the ceasefire.
Destruction in Gaza City's Shati refugee camp following Israeli strikes that killed Muhammad Majed Abu al-Ouf
(Photo: Omar AL-QATTAA / AFP)

On Thursday, Israel killed Khaled Abu Anza, head of Hamas' economic department and director-general of its Education Ministry, who security officials said played a central role in managing the organization's finances.
The military said its forces remained deployed in Gaza in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and would continue to operate against immediate threats.

articles.title: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
articles.summary: The Canadian man, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding and abetting suicide earlier this year, said he was remorseful for his actions.
paragraphs: Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.
Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
The 61-year-old will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.
If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.
As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".
"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.
She also said Law's motives were financial.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.
Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for many of their battles with mental illness.
He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims.

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."
Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.
The sentencing hearing on Friday followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.
Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.
Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

articles.title: Mark Ruffalo clipped Chuck Schumer's quote, and kept the old antisemitic trope - opinion
articles.summary: Either Ruffalo never read past the sentence he posted, or he read the whole thing and kept only the line he could pass off as theocracy.
paragraphs: On November 21, Mark Ruffalo told Senate Democrats who should lead them. Senator Chris Van Hollen was the right man, he wrote on X/Twitter, and Israel was “just one issue in a whole host of reasons.”
Then he added: “We need leadership that follows the will of the people, not entrenched religious beliefs and loyalties.”
The man Ruffalo wants gone is Chuck Schumer, often described as the highest-ranking Jewish elected official in American history.

The justifiably horrified reactions came fast. Anti-Defamation League chief Jonathan Greenblatt asked the two questions any honest reader would ask: “Which religion? Loyal to whom?” Rep. Ritchie Torres called it “insidious antisemitism.”
Rabbi Yaakov Menken of the Coalition for Jewish Values observed that Van Hollen is far more tied to the Episcopal Bishop of Washington than Schumer has ever been to any leading rabbi.

Ruffalo dug in. The next day he served up an alleged receipt: Schumer at AIPAC in 2018, saying, “Of course, we say it’s our land, the Torah says it, but they don’t believe in the Torah. So that’s the reason there is not peace.” Ruffalo added: “These are Senator Schumer’s words, not mine.”

Schumer, he allowed, “is entitled to his religious beliefs,” but those beliefs “cannot determine the rights of another people.” They are Schumer’s words. They are also a fragment, and Ruffalo cut away everything that gave them meaning.

Schumer opened that passage by naming the actual obstacle: “Too many Palestinians and too many Arabs do not want any Jewish state in the Middle East.” He then laid out the Palestinian Arab narrative: Europe persecuted the Jews, culminating in the Holocaust, and supposedly handed them Arab land as compensation.

Then he gave part of the Jewish claim, rooted in the Torah. “That’s the reason” points back to Arab rejection, not to scripture. He went on to dismantle the excuses. Settlements? Israel pulled every settler out of Gaza and got rockets on Sderot. Borders? Ehud Barak offered sweeping concessions in 2000, and Yasser Arafat walked away.
In that same speech, Schumer endorsed a two-state solution.

A senator who believes scripture should draw borders does not stand before AIPAC and call for partition. So Ruffalo’s proof that Schumer’s faith dictates his policy is a speech in which Schumer set his faith’s claims aside and backed dividing the land.

Either Ruffalo never read past the sentence he posted, or he read the whole thing and kept only the line he could pass off as theocracy. A man who has made Israel his signature cause can find a transcript. A newspaper editor who trimmed a quote that way would be fired. Ruffalo got retweeted.
Now read his defense again. Ruffalo used two words and defended one. He misleadingly explained “beliefs.” He never touched “loyalties.”
He couldn’t, because every honest answer to Greenblatt’s question is worse than the original post. Loyal to Israel? Loyal to the Jews?

The IHRA working definition of antisemitism, embraced by Washington under both US President Donald Trump and former president Joe Biden, lists as a textbook example “accusing Jewish citizens of being more loyal to Israel, or to the alleged priorities of Jews worldwide, than to the interests of their own nations.”
Ruffalo set “the will of the people” on one side and a Jewish senator’s “loyalties” on the other, then refused to say which loyalties he meant.

In March 2024, in the middle of a war, Schumer stood on the Senate floor and called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu an obstacle to peace and urged new Israeli elections. None of that independence bought him immunity from the “anti-Zionist” antisemites. Every Jewish politician who trades distance from Israel for acceptance eventually learns the same lesson: the bill arrives anyway.
Van Hollen, the man Ruffalo wants in Schumer’s chair, calls his bid “a generational opportunity” and promises a “fresh start.” He is 67. Schumer is 76. Both are Baby Boomers.

Van Hollen has sat in Congress since 2003. He ran the House Democrats’ campaign arm for two cycles, then chaired the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, a post Schumer reportedly handed him in 2016. This is the “insurgent.”

Strip out his hostility to Israel and little substance separates Van Hollen from a dozen other long-serving Democrats. Israel is what makes him the candidate for Israel-hating obsessives like Ruffalo.

After an August 2025 trip, Van Hollen announced the “inescapable conclusion” that Israel was “engaged in a campaign of ethnic cleansing in Gaza.” His mendacious report accused Israel of using food “as a method of population control.”

In July 2026, a UNICEF-coordinated survey put acute malnutrition in Gaza at or below prewar levels, and among young children at 1.3%. The 2025 Global Hunger Index puts child wasting at 21% in South Sudan, 18.7% in India, 17.7% in Sudan, and 16.8% in Yemen. No celebrity open letter has ever demanded a Senate leader’s head over any of them.

Ruffalo’s endorsement of Van Hollen even opened with Sudan. Give Van Hollen his due: he has spent two years trying to halt US arms sales to the United Arab Emirates until it stops arming the Rapid Support Forces, whose members and allied militias the State Department has accused of genocide.

Yet no one in this campaign accuses senators who do not back Van Hollen on Sudan of “entrenched loyalties” to Abu Dhabi. That charge is reserved for one senator, and every Jew with any sense of history knows why.
Van Hollen’s coalition tells the same story. Bernie Sanders and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed back him. So do some 35 celebrities and donors, Jane Fonda and Robert De Niro among them.

One of their organizers said Schumer is “too old, in power too long.” Their answer? A 67-year-old who has sat in Congress for nearly a quarter century. When Ruffalo wrote “loyalties,” he wasn’t freelancing. He was saying aloud what the campaign to replace Schumer has spent weeks implying.

Van Hollen knows exactly what a religious test is. In 2017, he tweeted, “We won’t tolerate religious tests in this country.” He has led 119 Democrats in condemning anti-Muslim legislation, urging congressional leaders to “speak clearly against initiatives that stigmatize a religious community.” That is his own standard.

His most prominent celebrity backer then applied a religious test to a Jewish senator, in Van Hollen’s cause, and doubled down when challenged. As of this writing, I have seen no public repudiation from Van Hollen of Ruffalo’s use of the antisemitic loyalty trope.
Van Hollen promised Democrats a fresh start. His loudest champion handed them the oldest accusation in the antisemite’s bag of tricks, and Van Hollen has let it stand.
The writer is an attorney, former IDF soldier, and former NYPD officer. He writes widely on Israel, Zionism, antisemitism, and Jewish history. He serves on the board of Herut North America.

articles.title: The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened
articles.summary: A new Bollywood flim spotlights the remarkable life of dancer and singer Vithabhai Narayangaonkar.
paragraphs: Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage.
Not even, it would seem, the birth of her child.
In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour.
"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi.
Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?"
When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children.
"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled.

Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre.
Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December.
Directed by Laxman Utekar, Eetha is based on Yogiraj Bagul's Marathi book chronicling Vithabai's life.

Rooted in devotional poetry, Tamasha evolved into a lively mix of music, dance, comedy and drama. At its heart is Lavani, a song and dance tradition in which verses ranging from the bawdy to the politically incisive are performed to the beat of the dholki, a percussion instrument.
Eetha evokes the world of Tamasha in its heyday. Kapoor, who had never performed Lavani before, learnt to dance while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each.
"The lives of Tamasha artists have been very tough, so in their dance you see pain as well as joy," Kapoor recalled at a promotional event.
Many Tamasha performers, including Vithabai, came from oppressed castes, facing discrimination even as their artistry drew large crowds.

How much of that history Eetha will capture remains debated. Utekar says it is not a biopic, but his decision to rename the protagonist Vithabai Bhau Gavkar instead of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar has drawn criticism.

For critics, much of Vithabai's history was contained in her name – Mang identified her with a historically oppressed Dalit community, while Narayangaonkar spoke of her family's roots in Narayangaon village. Both featured in the name of the troupe she inherited from her father – Bhau-Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar Tamasha Mandal.

Vithabai spoke openly about caste and the indignities Tamasha artists faced, themes that also surfaced in her songs. In a 1960s Lavani documented by historian Shailaja Paik, she rebuked men for lewd gestures, reminding them she danced to earn a living, not to please them.
It was a livelihood she had inherited from generations of performers in her family.
Like her son, Vithabai was born during a Tamasha performance, in 1935. Her mother, Shanta, had continued touring with her husband Bhau's troupe throughout her pregnancy.

Vithabai joined a theatre group at eight and her father's troupe at 13, soon becoming its star. After her father and co-leader Bapu died in quick succession, she took over the troupe with her husband and cousin.
Her career flourished during Tamasha's golden age, when productions grew more elaborate, drawing on mythology, history and contemporary life, says folk arts scholar Sukhada Khandge.
Khandge, who watched Vithabai perform as a child, recalls her sparkling eyes and commanding presence. She was as expressive with her face as she was with her feet.
Her fame carried her beyond Maharashtra.

During India's war with China in 1962, Vithabai performed for soldiers in the North-East Frontier Agency, now largely Arunachal Pradesh, braving freezing conditions just three months after giving birth, Bansode says.
At a conference in 1996, she recalled meeting soldiers from the historically oppressed Mahar and Mang communities at the frontier.

"Our Mahar-Mang soldiers were expected to fight and lay down their lives defending the nation, but the very same people would not even allow our bridegroom to pass through the village entrance," she said.

Despite offers from leading filmmakers, including Raj Kapoor, and roles in Marathi cinema, Vithabai refused to leave theatre. Film fame, she felt, would benefit her alone, while her troupe supported some 50 families, Bansode says.
There was a tenderness, too, in her relationship with audiences.
In his book on Vithabai's life, which inspired Eetha, Yogiraj Bagul recounts a performance in Mumbai during Diwali in 1971.

Despite the threat of rain, spectators insisted on buying tickets, saying the money would be their Bhau Beej gift to Vithabai if the show was cancelled – a festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters.
When the rain came, people left chanting: "Bhau Beej, Bhau Beej."
No one asked for their money back.

But Vithabai's fortunes failed to match her fame. Her husband, Maruti Sawant, mismanaged the troupe's finances and took loans in her name, family members say. By the time she left him in 1982, she was heavily indebted.
Bagul also writes about a 1986 column in a Marathi daily that revealed how the empress of Tamasha was now travelling on public buses and staying in cheap accommodation.
Despite public support, Vithabai was forced to disband her troupe in 1990 – the same year she received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, one of India's highest performing arts honours.
Vithabai successfully campaigned for government pensions for Tamasha artists. But many of the hardships she knew persist today, says Marathi writer Pradnya Daya Pawar.

Troupes spend nearly eight months a year on the road, with performers struggling to feed their children and educate them, she says. Despite government aid, many remain indebted to private moneylenders.
Vithabai's financial struggles persisted until her death in January 2002. Her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she died, the Times of India reported.
Fellow artists and admirers chipped in to bring her body home to Narayangaon.
Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in her name.
Eetha could now introduce Vithabai to a generation that never saw her perform, though the changes to her name have left some uneasy.
Marathi writer Pragya Daya Pawar argues that omitting the reference to Vithabai's caste risks obscuring the difficulties she confronted.
"It erases the social location, struggle and resistance that shaped her remarkable journey, reducing an extraordinary artist's story to a purely individual achievement," she says.
But Bansode, who spent years performing alongside her mother, says there is much to celebrate.
"The name doesn't matter to me. I am simply proud that a film is being made about my mother," she says.

articles.title: France seeks to preserve UNIFIL’s role in Lebanon as withdrawal looms
articles.summary: With UNIFIL’s 7,500 troops due to begin withdrawing in about a month, France is drafting a proposal to retain some of its missions and prevent a security vacuum in southern Lebanon amid fierce Israeli opposition and uncertainty over a replacement force
paragraphs: With UNIFIL’s 7,500 troops due to begin withdrawing in about a month, France is drafting a proposal to retain some of its missions and prevent a security vacuum in southern Lebanon amid fierce Israeli opposition and uncertainty over a replacement force

In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press, Salam said the proposed resolution would allow UNIFIL, established nearly 50 years ago, to continue carrying out some of its duties while the U.N. Security Council considers what should replace it. He also addressed the suspension of negotiations with Israel, saying the talks had been put on hold following Israel’s elections and amid uncertainty over the composition of its next government.
US officials have indicated that Washington could be 'open to considering' such an arrangement UNIFIL forces in southern Lebanon
(Photo: REUTERS/Karamallah Daher)

Salam said UNIFIL would continue to clear mines, escort humanitarian convoys and monitor violations in southern Lebanon. U.S. officials have indicated that Washington could be “open to considering” such an arrangement, he added.
"This would not resolve the problem of so-called post-UNIFIL, but it will give us some extra time to agree on a new architecture in southern Lebanon," Salam added.

The AP noted that the Lebanese prime minister’s remarks underscore the fact that there is still no plan for a force to replace UNIFIL, about a month before its mandate is due to expire following opposition from the United States and Israel.

Israel has expressed firm opposition to the force’s continued operations, arguing that it has failed in its mission. The administration of President Donald Trump, which has already cut U.S. funding for the force, viewed it as a waste of money and argued that its continued operations were hindering efforts to weaken Hezbollah and transfer full security responsibility in the area to the Lebanese army.
Maps and markings of Israeli military positions were posted at the force's outpost. Southern Lebanon
(Photo: Ammar Ammar / AFP)

Israeli criticism of UNIFIL’s performance also emerged during a visit by a ynet reporter to the ruins of the “Hezbollah tents” compound on Mount Dov. Reserve Lt. Col. Y., commander of the 221st Battalion, told the reporter that maps marking IDF positions had been discovered in outposts vacated by UNIFIL.

"This tank position, another tank position and the deployment of our outposts," he said. "We enter one of these UNIFIL outposts, near the IDF's Balut outpost, and find maps and markings of Israeli military positions posted on its windows."

"The astonishing thing about UNIFIL is that they stood here along the border, watching and monitoring us — as if we were the enemy," Lt. Col. Y. added. "You suddenly realize that their watchtowers are facing us. Their mandate is to ensure that Hezbollah does not deploy ammunition south of the Litani River and that we do not cross the border. In practice, we did not cross, while Hezbollah moved vast quantities of weapons into the area for 18 years following the Second Lebanon War. All the roads you see crisscrossing this area were paved by the U.N. and used by Hezbollah."

Under a U.N. Security Council resolution adopted last year, the roughly 7,500 UNIFIL troops deployed in southern Lebanon are to withdraw gradually over a six-month period after the force’s mandate expires on Dec. 31, 2026. The resolution also gives UNIFIL a year to wind down its operations entirely.
The goal: 'To slow the withdrawal process to prevent a vacuum.' The border fence with Lebanon

France has not commented on the proposal to extend the force’s operations. However, a Western diplomat with knowledge of the matter said one option under discussion is to slow down the withdrawal process and “maintain certain UNIFIL missions” to avoid a power vacuum. The diplomat spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the matter.

During diplomatic talks over what would follow UNIFIL’s withdrawal, France pushed for the deployment of an international force comprising several thousand French, Italian and Spanish troops. The force would operate not only in southern Lebanon but throughout the country, helping the Lebanese army establish control over its territory. Israel opposed the proposal.
"After all, they haven't fired a single shot at Hezbollah," an Israeli official previously remarked.

France put forward another proposal under which the Security Council would issue a new mandate to establish a force of several hundred observers from European countries to monitor developments in Lebanon, with an emphasis on the south of the country and designated pilot areas.

Israel also opposed this proposal, viewing it as a form of “UNIFIL 2.0” that would be unable to fulfill its mission. Israel also feared that protecting the force would require several thousand additional troops.

Meanwhile, the United States explored the possibility of establishing a smaller, 100-member observer force made up of troops from the United States and several other countries to monitor the implementation of security arrangements in designated pilot areas.

articles.title: A clinic is offering to reassess ADHD and autism diagnoses - and hundreds of people are interested
articles.summary: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
paragraphs: Image source, BBC / WOODY MORRIS
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.
Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.
But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.
This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.
At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.
But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.
Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.
"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.
If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.

The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.

The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.

And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.
Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.
Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.

This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.

Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.
When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.
Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.

But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.
Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.

Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.
What is an ADHD or autism reassessment?

Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.

The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.
"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.
The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.

Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.
But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.
"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.
"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.

Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."
Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.
During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnosis but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".
Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.
"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."
It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains.
"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.

Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.
"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.

During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.
The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.
"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."
In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.

During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.
Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.

But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.
The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.

"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.

Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.
"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.
Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.
Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.

He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.
Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.
People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.
Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed".
"It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.
Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her.

Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.
The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to.

"The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.
Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.
She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis.
"Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."

articles.title: למרות ההתנגדות בישראל: ההצעה שתאפשר ליוניפי"ל להמשיך לפעול בלבנון
articles.summary: כחודש לפני ש-7,500 חיילי הכוח אמורים לסגת בהדרגה עם סיום המנדט, צרפת מגבשת הצעה שתאפשר ליוניפי"ל להמשיך למלא גם משימות חדשות. ברקע: מאבק דיפלומטי על "היום שאחרי" והתנגדות ישראלית חריפה. סא"ל במיל' ל-ynet: "הם עקבו אחרינו כאילו אנחנו האויב". ראש ממשלת לבנון: "זה ייתן עוד זמן"
paragraphs: כחודש לפני ש-7,500 חיילי הכוח אמורים לסגת בהדרגה עם סיום המנדט, צרפת מגבשת הצעה שתאפשר ליוניפי"ל להמשיך למלא "משימות מסוימות". ברקע: מאבק דיפלומטי על "היום שאחרי" והתנגדות ישראלית חריפה. סא"ל במיל' ל-ynet: "הם עקבו אחרינו כאילו אנחנו האויב". ראש ממשלת לבנון: "זה ייתן עוד זמן"

ראש ממשלת לבנון נואף סלאם אמר אתמול (שישי) כי צרפת מגבשת הצעת החלטה במועצת הביטחון של האו"ם, שתאפשר לכוח שמירת השלום בגבול לבנון (יוניפי"ל) להמשיך לפעול גם אחרי סיום המנדט שלו בסוף 2026. כדי למלא את הוואקום התנהלו לאחרונה כמה תהליכים דיפלומטיים במקביל, ובראשם מהלך שהובילה צרפת לשלוח כוח בינלאומי מאירופה וארה"ב - תחליף שישראל פעלה לטרפד בכל הכוח בטענה שיאפשר לחיזבאללה לפעול בחופשיות.
"ארה"ב פתוחה לשקול". יוניפי"ל בדרום לבנון
(צילום: REUTERS/Karamallah Daher)

בריאיון בלעדי לסוכנות הידיעות AP אמר ראש ממשלת לבנון כי ההצעה שמתגבשת תאפשר ליוניפי"ל, שהוקם לפני כמעט 50 שנה, להמשיך למלא משימות ב"תחומים מסוימים" בזמן שמועצת הביטחון של האו"ם תדון בשאלה מה יבוא במקומו. הוא התייחס גם להפסקת המשא ומתן עם ישראל, ומסר כי מדובר במגעים שהוקפאו בעקבות הבחירות וחוסר הוודאות לגבי הרכב הממשלה הבאה.

לדברי סלאם, בין המשימות שיוניפי"ל ימשיך למלא: פינוי מוקשים, ליווי שיירות הומניטריות ופיקוח על הפרות בדרום לבנון. לטענתו, "גורמים אמריקנים רמזו שוושינגטון פתוחה לשקול הסדר כזה". סלאם הוסיף: "זה לא יפתור את הבעיה של מה שמכונה 'היום שאחרי יוניפי"ל', אבל זה ייתן לנו קצת זמן נוסף להגיע להסכמה על מתווה ביטחוני חדש בדרום לבנון".
בסוכנות הידיעות ציינו כי דבריו של ראש ממשלת לבנון ממחישים כי למעשה אין עדיין תוכנית לכוח שיבוא אחרי יוניפי"ל - כחודש לפני שהמנדט שלו אמור לפקוע בעקבות התנגדותן של ארצות הברית וישראל.
"במוצב הכוח הודבקו מפות ונקודות צבאיות ישראליות". דרום לבנון
(צילום: Ammar Ammar / AFP)

בישראל כזכור הביעו התנגדות נחרצת להמשך הפעלת הכוח בטענה שהוא נכשל במשימתו, ובממשלו של הנשיא דונלד טראמפ, שכבר קיצץ במימון האמריקני לכוח, ראו בכך בזבוז של כסף וטענו שהמשך פעילותו מעכב את הגשמת היעד של צמצום כוחו של חיזבאללה והעברת האחריות הביטחונית המלאה באזור לצבא לבנון.

הביקורת הישראלית על תפקוד הכוח עלתה גם בביקור שערך כתב ynet במתחם ההריסות של "אוהלי חיזבאללה" בהר דב. סא"ל (במיל') י', מפקד גדוד 221, סיפר לו כי במוצבים שפינה יוניפי"ל נמצאו מפות ועליהן סימונים של עמדות צה"ל. "עמדת טנק כזאת, עמדת טנק אחרת, ופריסת המוצבים שלנו", אמר. "אנחנו נכנסים למוצב יוניפי"ל שכזה, בסמוך ל'מוצב בלוט' הצה"לי, ועל החלונות שלו מודבקות מפות וציוני נקודות צבאיות ישראליות".

"כל העניין המדהים עם יוניפי"ל הוא שהם עמדו כאן בגבול והסתכלו ועקבו אחרינו - כאילו אנחנו האויב", הוסיף סא"ל י'. "אתה פתאום תופס איך מגדלי השמירה שלהם מופנים כלפינו. המנדט שלהם הוא לפקח שחיזבאללה לא פורס תחמושת מדרום לליטני, ושאנחנו לא חוצים את הגבול. בפועל אנחנו לא חצינו, וחיזבאללה במשך 18 שנה, מאז מלחמת לבנון השנייה, העביר ערמות של אמל"ח. את כל הדרכים שאתה רואה שפרוסות כאן האו"ם היה סולל, וחיזבאללה היה משתמש בהן".
המטרה: "להאט את תהליך הנסיגה כדי למנוע ואקום"

לפי החלטת מועצת האו"ם שהתקבלה בשנה שעברה, כ-7,500 חיילי יוניפי"ל שהוצבו בדרום לבנון יסוגו בהדרגה במשך כשישה חודשים לאחר פקיעת המנדט ב-31 בדצמבר 2026. עוד נקבע כי לכוח תינתן שנה כדי לסיים לחלוטין את פעילותו.

צרפת לא התייחסה להצעה להאריך את פעילותו של הכוח. עם זאת, דיפלומט מערבי שתואר כ"בקיא בפרטים" אמר כי אחת האפשרויות הנידונות היא להאט את תהליך הנסיגה ולהשאיר על כנן "משימות מסוימות" של יוניפי"ל, כדי למנוע היווצרות ואקום שלטוני וביטחוני.

במהלך הדיונים הדיפלומטיים על "היום שאחרי", צרפת קידמה מהלך שבו יישלח כוח בינלאומי של כמה אלפי חיילים צרפתים, איטלקים וספרדים שיוצבו לא רק בדרום לבנון אלא בכל שטח המדינה ויסייעו לצבא לבנון לקבל שליטה על השטח. ישראל, כאמור, התנגדה. "הרי הם לא ירו ירייה אחת על חיזבאללה", העריך בעבר גורם ישראלי.

צרפת העלתה הצעה נוספת שבמסגרתה יוענק מנדט חדש של מועצת הביטחון להקמת כוח של כמה מאות משקיפים ממדינות אירופיות שיפקחו על הנעשה בלבנון, בדגש על דרום המדינה ואזורי הפיילוט. ישראל התנגדה גם לאפשרות זו שכן ראתה בה מעין הקמת "יוניפי"ל 2" שלא יוכל לבצע את מה שנדרש וחששה שכדי להגן על כוח כזה יהיה צורך באבטחה של כמה אלפי חיילים. ארצות הברית מצידה בחנה רעיון של הקמת כוח משקיפים מצומצם שימנה 100 איש, חיילים אמריקנים וממספר מדינות שתפקידו יהיה לפקח על יישום אזורי הפיילוט.

articles.title: Purse found of woman, 24, swept from California beach three weeks ago
articles.summary: Se Nah Park was overwhelmed by a wave at the notorious Panther Beach The purse of a 24-year-old who was swept into the ocean at a notorious California beach three weeks ago was found on Wednesday, as the west coast saw record high king tides. The Santa Cruz county sheriff’s office confirmed that Se Nah Park’s purse was found by a beachgoer at 4 Mile Beach, south of Panther Beach, where she was swept away into the ocean on 8 November. Continue reading...
paragraphs: The purse of a 24-year-old who was swept into the ocean at a notorious California beach three weeks ago was found on Wednesday, as the west coast saw record high king tides.
The Santa Cruz county sheriff’s office confirmed that Se Nah Park’s purse was found by a beachgoer at 4 Mile Beach, south of Panther Beach, where she was swept away into the ocean on 8 November.
According to a GoFundMe started by Park’s friends, Park and five others had gathered around a bonfire beyond the “keyhole” archway at Panther Beach that night.
Four members of the group, including Park, attempted to make their way back through the keyhole when a powerful wave struck, sweeping Park into the ocean.
The three individuals managed to get back up the cliffslide, but tragically, Park did not.
Three weeks later, Park’s body has not been located yet, but the discovery of her purse may lead her community closer towards locating her body. .
The coast guard suspended the active search efforts to find Park on 9 November.

“Given the extensive search effort of the surrounding area and environmental conditions, we have suspended active search efforts pending further developments,” Lt Max Holloway, Sector San Francisco search and rescue mission coordinator, said at the time.

“We worked closely with our partner agencies and exhausted all available resources in our attempt to locate Ms Park. Our deepest condolences are with her family and loved ones,” the statement concluded.
In the weeks since, Park’s family and friends have not given up on their search efforts.
Her family and friends continue to “hold on to the hope that Senah can be found and brought home to rest”, her friends shared in a message on GoFundMe.

articles.title: While the imam promises Islam will rule the world, the priest calls for expelling Jews - opinion
articles.summary: The obvious question for those carrying the signs is this: What would you say to a Muslim woman who came to Germany so her daughter could choose how to dress and whom to marry?
paragraphs: “Islam will rule the world again,” Imam Karim Abu Zaid declared at a conference in Texas in May 2026. Abu Zaid, the founder and director of the Muslim Community Center in Aurora, Colorado, also founded the organization that held the conference.

Of all the words available to him, the preacher chose “rule.” Rule whom, Mr. Imam? The Muslim woman who refuses to submit to your authority? The Christian who intends to remain a Christian? The Jew whose parents left him a home in Texas without asking your permission?

How many Muslims share Abu Zaid’s vision? It is impossible to know from a speech at a conference. In England and Wales, however, it is possible to examine what happens when women turn to Sharia councils to obtain a religious divorce.
British law takes precedence over the councils’ decisions, and their rulings are not legally binding under civil law.
Nevertheless, an independent review commissioned by the British government documented discrimination against women and rulings based on Sharia law within those councils.
Anyone seeking to understand the power of a religious institution within a community should also listen to the woman seeking a divorce.

Appearing alongside Abu Zaid in Texas was Uthman ibn Farooq, an American preacher of Pakistani descent. He is known for conversations he conducts with Christians and atheists in Balboa Park in San Diego and publishes online.

In May 2025, during a lecture in Birmingham, England, he predicted that both Europe and the United States would become Muslim. A year later in Texas, he explained that turning America into a Muslim country was a goal he wanted to achieve.

Anyone waiting to see what happens to Europe before beginning this discussion in the US is already late. The discussion is taking place in English, led by an American preacher, with no interpreter required.
Ibn Farooq has said that he seeks to spread Islam peacefully through dawah, meaning an invitation to embrace the faith without coercion. But I would ask the interviewer to pose one more question.
Suppose you succeed, Mr. Preacher, and most Americans embrace your faith. The next morning, your daughter announces that she is leaving Islam.

Would you defend her right to do so with the same enthusiasm with which you now defend your right to persuade a Christian woman to convert to Islam? Your answer would tell us something about the America you envision for your fellow citizens.
On April 27, 2024, about 1,250 demonstrators gathered in Hamburg following a call from the organization Muslim Interaktiv. Some carried signs declaring that the caliphate was the solution.
Germany’s protection of their freedom to demonstrate allowed them to stand in the street and demand an Islamist regime.
The obvious question for those carrying the signs is this: What would you say to a Muslim woman who came to Germany so her daughter could choose how to dress and whom to marry?
How would you answer when she asks why you are so eager to bring to her doorstep the very regime from which she escaped?

Has Europe already been conquered? Muslims accounted for 6% of the continent’s population in 2020. According to a projection published by the Pew Research Center on November 18, that figure is expected to reach 12.7% by 2070.

When a commentator declares that Europe has fallen, he provides Islamists with a service that no propaganda budget could buy. With a single headline, he appoints a handful of preachers as the representatives of millions of people, including the woman who fled from them.
The difficult questions should be directed at the preacher seeking power and at the politician who heard him but prefers to pretend that he merely stumbled into an evening of folklore.
On November 13, America also heard a proposal from Calvin Robinson, a British Christian cleric and former GB News presenter who moved to Michigan to lead a religious community.

During a program he hosts with Joe Anders, Anders spoke of a “Jewish oligarchy” in the US. Robinson responded, “I think expelling the Jews is the solution,” and reminded American Jews that they have a homeland where they can live.
Here, old antisemitism reveals itself in all its ugliness.
No sanction to bigotry, no assistance to persecution

Jews were once told in the streets of Europe to “go to Palestine.” Now a Christian preacher tells them that Israel is available to them, as though the establishment of the Jewish state granted every antisemite in the world a license to evict Jews.
Suppose a Jewish man in Philadelphia simply tells Robinson that he is staying in his home.
What will you do now, Reverend? Who will knock on his door? Who will pack his clothes? Who will explain to his granddaughter why her grandfather must leave the country where he was born?
That is the true meaning of the word “expulsion.” It is easy to roll it off the tongue when you are convinced that the hand knocking on someone else’s door will never knock on your own.
In 1790, George Washington wrote to the Jewish community of Newport that the US government gave no sanction to bigotry and no assistance to persecution.
Now, 236 years later, a preacher from Britain arrives and issues imaginary eviction notices to the descendants of those whom America’s first president regarded as his fellow citizens.
What exactly does Robinson seek to preserve of the American legacy if saving it requires him first to tear up Washington’s letter to the Jews?
The hosts also have questions to answer. The real test comes when the speaker is your guest of honor, when your name appears on the invitation, and when your donors are sitting in the front row.
Will you stand and declare that proposals to expel Jews are not welcome in your house?

When Abu Zaid is your guest of honor, will you ask him what will happen to those who choose to remain Jewish, Christian, or without religion on the day when, in his words, Islam once again rules the world?
If you remain silent on that occasion, spare us the following day’s courageous speech about the danger posed by the opposing camp.
A free society will allow Ibn Farooq to try to persuade every American to embrace Islam, but it will defend with equal determination the Muslim who chooses to leave the faith.
It will allow Robinson to express his views while making clear to the Jewish man in Philadelphia that no one will remove him from his home.
Anyone seeking to speak in God's name should begin with a question far smaller than the fate of the world. By what right does he presume to decide the fate of the neighbor living across the street?
For centuries, antisemitism has changed its appearance and assumed different forms. Regrettably, it has always remained present among Islamist and Christian extremists.

The author is the CEO of Radios 100FM, honorary consul and vice dean of the Consular Diplomatic Corps, president of the Israeli Radio Association, and previously served as a monitor for Israel Army Radio and as a television correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title: Schools in England must set aside time for pupils to read for pleasure
articles.summary: Education secretary expected to announce measures as part of proposed reforms to national curriculum Schools in England will have to allocate time for children to read for pleasure as part of Labour’s proposed reforms of the national curriculum. The education secretary, Lucy Powell, is expected to announce to parliament on Monday that primary schools must earmark time each day for children to read. Continue reading...
paragraphs: Schools in England will have to allocate time for children to read for pleasure as part of Labour’s proposed reforms of the national curriculum.
The education secretary, Lucy Powell, is expected to announce to parliament on Monday that primary schools must earmark time each day for children to read.
Secondary schools will be required to set aside time several days a week as part of the measures to tackle declining literacy rates and increasing screen time.
There will be a statutory reading test for children in year 8, and secondary schools will be expected to ensure pupils focus on entire books, poems and other literature.

The education secretary told the Times: “Across the world, we are seeing a ticking timebomb for our future generations as reading and literacy levels are falling, with too many children seeing reading as a chore or missing out altogether.
“We cannot afford to stand idly by and let this continue. Reading fluently is the gateway to lifelong learning, opening up every subject in school.”
Powell added that in addition to setting up children for success, reading should be “enjoyed and every child should have the opportunity to discover that”.
Powell is also expected to announce the programmes of study for the curriculum in England, which could include shorter exams in some GCSE subjects.
History, geography and modern foreign languages are considered the most likely courses to be slimmed down.

Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, said she welcomed reforms that encouraged children to read more but said they “must go hand in hand with a serious effort to reduce screen time in our classrooms”.
In July, an education committee inquiry into reading for pleasure concluded that the National Year of Reading should be extended to a National Decade of Reading.
It called on the government to commit to a national reading guarantee that would ensure all children have regular opportunities to enjoy reading.
Research last year found that reading enjoyment among children and young people in the UK had fallen to its lowest level in two decades, with a sharper decline among teenage boys.
While boys’ reading enjoyment fell across most age groups – particularly among those aged 11 to 16 – for girls it remained relatively stable or slightly improved.
The National Literacy Trust’s survey found that among girls aged eight to 18, 39.1% said they enjoyed reading in their free time, compared with 25.7% of boys.

articles.title: OpenAI countersues Apple for allegedly stealing trade secrets
articles.summary: Lawsuit also alleging pressure on hardware suppliers comes after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching employees OpenAI sued Apple on Friday, accusing the company of ⁠stealing its trade secrets ​and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices. The suit, filed in northern California federal court, comes after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology. Continue reading...
paragraphs: OpenAI sued Apple on Friday, accusing the company of ⁠stealing its trade secrets ​and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.
The suit, filed in northern California federal court, comes after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology.

OpenAI filed the counterclaims ⁠in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple’s employment practices were designed to “trap” employees and prevent them from working on competitors’ technology.
OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal electronic devices that threaten to “outcompete Apple on what ⁠Apple views as its own turf”, the company said in its Friday court filing.

OpenAI said in the filing that Apple ​gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who worked ‌at OpenAI for six months. In ‌that time, the employee gained access to specific information on a new device as well as OpenAI’s roadmap for future hardware ‌products.
“Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place,” OpenAI said.
Apple denied using the rehired employee to access OpenAI’s confidential information and denied trying to suppress competition in AI device manufacturing.
“OpenAI’s counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple’s lawsuit,” Apple said in a Friday statement.
Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as the intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition for ‌talent and proprietary technology.
Apple sued OpenAI and the former Apple employees Tang Tan and Chang Liu in July, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner’s foray into consumer hardware.

Tan, ​a 24-year Apple employee who was a vice-president of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch, was part of the group that launched the AI device startup io Products before it was acquired by OpenAI in 2025.

OpenAI and the employees have denied those allegations and said that Apple’s lawsuit depended on its unauthorized monitoring of Liu’s personal messages after he stopped working for Apple. OpenAI and ⁠attorneys for Tan and Liu did not immediately respond to a request for comment on ​Friday’s court filing.

In Friday’s filing, OpenAI criticized ​Apple for encouraging employees to do work on ​their personal Apple devices and accounts, then preventing those employees from an orderly separation of work and ​personal accounts when they leave ‌for new jobs.

OpenAI said ​that Apple continues to access ​former employees’ personal devices and accounts after they leave the company, enabling Apple to “monitor and ensnare departing employees” when they leave for competitors.
OpenAI said that 400 employees have left Apple for OpenAI so far, and Apple wants to intimidate other employees from leaving to find other tech companies.

articles.title: IDF kills two Hamas terrorists who also worked for Doctors Without Borders, military says
articles.summary: Doctors Without Borders condemns the IDF strike that killed Hamas terrorists working at an MSF clinic, calling for accountability, claiming it was a "direct attack on MSF."
paragraphs: The IDF killed two Hamas terrorists in the Gaza City area on Friday night who also worked as security personnel at a clinic operated by Doctors Without Borders (MSF), the military announced on Saturday.
The two were identified as Ahmed Safian Muhammad Ali Abu Hazeera and Muayad Youssef Alizbach, the latter of whom served as an artillery unit commander in Hamas's military wing, according to the IDF.
According to the IDF, the two terrorists continued carrying out attacks against Israeli troops and civilians and were involved in efforts to rebuild Hamas's capabilities in the Gaza Strip.

The military said they were killed in an airstrike "in order to remove the threat they posed," adding that precautions were taken to minimize civilian casualties, including the use of precision weapons and aerial surveillance.
Doctors Without Borders condemns IDF strike

Doctors Without Borders (MSF) condemned the strike, describing it as “a direct attack on MSF.” The organization said the facility was “clearly marked with the organization's logos” and that its location had been communicated to the IDF, which was aware of its presence.
"We are shocked and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, who were working as guards, in an Israeli attack on one of our clinics in Gaza,” the organization said in a statement.
“This is a direct attack on MSF, and brings the number of our colleagues killed in the Gaza Strip to 17," the statement added.

IDF conducts series of operations in Gaza, killing 10 Hamas, PIJ terroristsThe strike follows a series of operations over the past week in which the IDF killed 10 terrorists belonging to Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ).

In a statement on Friday, the military confirmed that the IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) had carried out a strike in the Khan Yunis area on Tuesday, killing two terrorists: Akram Sabhi Hamdan Abu Taimah, a member of Hamas's military wing, and Wajdi Sami Suleiman Abu Salah, a PIJ operative who entered Israel during the October 7 attacks.

In a separate operation, the IDF and Shin Bet killed four Hamas terrorists, including members of the terrorist organization's elite Nukhba force, operatives who infiltrated Israel on October 7, and a battalion engineering officer.
According to the military, the terrorists were targeted after attempting to carry out attacks against Israeli troops and civilians.
IDF strikes Hamas cell commander, October 7 terrorist involved in hostage handover

In two separate incidents last Friday, the IDF struck Diab al-Rahman Radi, a Hamas military wing cell commander involved in transferring funds to the terrorist organization, and a group of Hamas terrorists who had gathered to plan attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops.

The military identified three of those killed as Mustafa Hassan Oweni, a Hamas sniper; Mohammed Abu Huishil, an anti-tank operative; and Yousef Ayidi, who entered Israel on October 7 and participated in the handover ceremony for former Gaza hostages Eli Sharabi, Ohad Ben Ami, and Or Levy.

"Throughout the war, and particularly in recent weeks, the terrorists advanced attacks against IDF troops and Israeli civilians and operated to restore the capabilities of terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip, systematically violating the ceasefire agreement," the army wrote.
The military said the strikes were carried out to eliminate the threats the operatives posed to Israeli civilians and troops.
Esther Davis contributed to this report.

articles.title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
paragraphs: Image source, Getty Images
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.
Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.

Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.
The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.
China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.
"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."

China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.
This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.

In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.

His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.
That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.
"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.
Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".
The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."
Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.
"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.
These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.
In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.
Image source, Chinese Consulate General in Istanbul's WeChat account

"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.

Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.
The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.
"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.
Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.

Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.
"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.
"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."
When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.

The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".
"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.
"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."
These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.
Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.

"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."
The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.
"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true."
Image source, Karma Rinchen

Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.

Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns: dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiananmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after. More recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.
Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.

"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target."
But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard".
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

"For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds.
For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level.
Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture.
The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi.
In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city.
"What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such plans?" the caller asked.
"What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a new page. The pen is in your own hand."
The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel says.
He declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution."
* Name changed on request to protect interviewee's identity

articles.title: Charity set up by Captain Tom Moore’s family applies to be struck off
articles.summary: Watchdog had found ‘repeated’ misconduct by veteran’s daughter and her husband in running the foundation A charity set up by the family of the pandemic fundraiser Captain Sir Tom Moore has applied to be struck off. The charity is now known as the 1189808 Foundation, having dropped Moore’s name at the request of his family last year. Continue reading...
paragraphs: A charity set up by the family of the pandemic fundraiser Captain Sir Tom Moore has applied to be struck off.
The charity is now known as the 1189808 Foundation, having dropped Moore’s name at the request of his family last year.
An application to have the organisation struck off appeared on the Companies House register on Friday.

The dropping of the captain’s name came after the charities watchdog found there had been “repeated” misconduct and mismanagement on the part of the second world war veteran’s daughter and her husband in their running of the foundation.

The Charity Commission’s report published in 2024 found a “repeated pattern of behaviour” through which Hannah Ingram-Moore and her husband, Colin, made private gains and which the regulator said would have left people feeling “misled”.

The report found that a £1.4m book deal and an £18,000 awards ceremony appearance fee were among the financial benefits the Ingram-Moores enjoyed through their family links to the Captain Tom Foundation, which was launched in May 2020.

The Ingram-Moores have already been banned from being charity trustees, and Hannah Ingram-Moore was prohibited from being a trustee or holding a senior management role in any charity in England and Wales for 10 years, and Colin Ingram-Moore for eight years.
They both resigned from the foundation.

Moore became a household name during the first Covid-19 lockdown, raising £39.4m for NHS charities by walking laps of the garden at his home in Marston Moretaine, Bedfordshire. He was honoured with a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.
The millions raised and donated to NHS Charities Together for its Covid-19 Urgent Appeal before the foundation was formed were not part of the commission’s inquiry.
Moore, a father of two who was born in Keighley, West Yorkshire, died aged 100 in February 2021 after testing positive for coronavirus.

articles.title: UK policewomen advised to consider 'cultural factors' when speaking to Muslim men - report
articles.summary: The officers were further warned to refrain from dressing immodestly when performing their duties amongst Muslims, as well as to consider having a male officer speak to Muslim men when possible.
paragraphs: Female police officers in the United Kingdom were advised to consider "cultural factors" when interacting with Muslim men, according to a National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) report cited by The Telegraph on Friday.
"Cultural factors should be considered when interacting with the opposite sex," the report read. "This applies to physical interaction and verbal communication."

The NPCC's report, titled the "National Faith Toolkit," also issued advisories for interacting with 22 other religious groups, including Jews, Buddhists and Catholics, though The Telegraph emphasized that it primarily focused on Muslims.
The Telegraph cited the NPCC as describing the purpose of the report as a means to guide policing amongst "diverse" communities in the UK.
Report requires action on 'anti-Muslim hate,' no such requirement for other groups

In addition, the section on Muslims specifically included a requirement to report "anti-Muslim hate," with other sections lacking any such requirement for their respective religious groups, including Jews, which The Telegraph noted have been increasingly targeted in recent hate crimes.

The report further warned female officers against entering mosques or Muslim households through entrances intended solely for men, noting that male officers were best-suited for interactions "in some situations."

According to The Telegraph, the report specifically advised female officers against speaking to Muslim men at all while inside a mosque or Muslim home, while UK officers in general were warned against using police dogs in Muslim areas.
UK's Farage: Report another example of 'proof of institutional two-tier policing'
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage described the NPCC report as "proof of institutional two-tier policing."

"The police should not be bending over backward to placate sexist and outdated cultures," Farage told The Telegraph. "If the police actually believed in equality before the law, the NPCC would remove this immediately, and those responsible would be fired."
An NPCC spokesperson commented on the report, saying that it is meant to serve as "a practical toolkit to help officers and staff to understand and engage effectively with different communities."

"Religious and cultural considerations do not override the law or the operational duties of police officers," the spokesperson said. "In collating the guidance, the same process has been followed for every faith group covered, and the content covers broadly the same areas for 23 different faiths and beliefs."

According to the report, the NPCC developed the toolkit through collaboration with the UK College of Policing, as well as other groups including Police Chaplaincy UK, the Christian Police Association, the National Black Police Association, the National LGBT+ Police Network, the National Sikh Police Association, the National Association of Muslim Police, the British Association for Women in Policing, and the Police Pagan Association.

Its introduction, written by NPCC Race, Inclusion, Religion and Belief Chair Rachel Kearton, emphasized the importance of police officers understanding the "cultural and religious contexts" in which they operate.

"Faith communities play a vital role in supporting policing efforts," Kearton, the former Suffolk Constabulary chief constable, wrote. "By working collaboratively, we can better protect and support some of the most vulnerable individuals in our society."

articles.title: Yarden Bibas urges Nir Oz to preserve family home as testament to October 7 massacre
articles.summary: Yarden Bibas urged Kibbutz Nir Oz to reconsider demolishing his family home, describing it as the last physical testament to the life he once shared.
paragraphs: Yarden Bibas, who lost his wife, Shiri, and his two sons, Ariel and Kfir, as a result of the October 7 massacre, called on Friday evening to halt the planned demolition of his family home in Kibbutz Nir Oz in a post shared on social media.

According to Bibas, the decision to demolish the building as part of the kibbutz's rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts would erase the last physical testament to the life he had before the tragedy.

"On October 7, Hamas tried to erase us. I cannot accept that, in the name of rehabilitation and growth, we would erase with our own hands what still remains: the lives we had and the evidence of what happened," Bibas wrote, adding that the decision made by the kibbutz members was "tormenting and crushing" him.
Bibas described the profound personal significance of the house, which represents far more to him than a place of residence.

"In this house that they want to demolish, I had a life. I had a family. In this house, Ariel learned to walk and talk. In this house, Kfir spent the first months of his life and learned to crawl. In this house, there was also Tony, an amazing and sensitive dog who immediately welcomed my boys with great love and watched over them all the time. In this house, Shiri and I built our family."
'This is the only place I have left of them'
Bibas said the house serves as a source of remembrance and comfort as he copes with his unimaginable loss.

"Within these walls, there was great love. There was children's laughter, there were small moments of happiness, and there was a loving relationship that I know I will never experience again in this lifetime. This is the only place I have left of them. Even now, I find myself returning there, trying to process what happened and feel a little closer to them. This is the last place where I saw them smiling and happy."
Bibas stressed that, in his view, preserving the house goes beyond his personal story and concerns the national memory of the October 7 massacre.

"This house is not just my personal memory. It is also a testament to what happened in Kibbutz Nir Oz on October 7, a testament to the lives that were lived here and the lives that were brutally cut short. This is the history and heritage of our people."
Bibas urges Nir Oz to balance reconstruction with commemoration
Concluding his post, Bibas called on the kibbutz's leadership and members to halt the demolition and find a way to balance rebuilding with commemoration.

"I, too, want to see Nir Oz flourish again, but I believe we can build a future without destroying everything that remains of the past. I demand that this decision be halted and reconsidered before it is too late.

"For others, it may be a painful reminder that is difficult to live alongside. For me, it is still Shiri, Ariel, and Kfir's home. I lost my family. I don't want to lose the place where we were a family, too."
Nir Oz residents oppose decision to demolish houses

Members of the kibbutz also opposed the decision to demolish the houses in a letter shared on Friday, and asked more people from the community to sign a petition asking for an alternative solution to the issue.

"As members of a kibbutz, we oppose the decision to demolish the houses in Nir Oz," they wrote. "These houses are not just buildings. They are a testament to a life that was cut short and to a horror that cannot be replaced by any photography or documentation. Their demolition would erase historical evidence that cannot be restored."
"We understand the pain and the desire to restore life, but it is possible to do so and at the same time preserve the witness houses as a site of commemoration and documentation," they added.
