"We call for a halt to the demolition and for another alternative to be formulated. Out of respect for the murdered, their families, and the residents of Nir Oz, we ask you to stop and think again," they concluded.

The decision to remove the houses was made on Thursday, when 51% of the residents from the kibbutz voted in favor of moving the burned houses and their remainin remains outside of the farmyard, while the memorial should be placed near the local cemetery.
The proposal was accepted by a majority of 38 members, with 32 voting against.

articles.title: Thousands still without power after storms that snarled Thanksgiving travel
articles.summary: Heavy rains and high winds downed trees and power lines and led to water rescues from New York to Virginia Skies cleared along the US eastern seaboard on Friday, and power was being restored to hundreds of thousands of customers whose Thanksgiving plans were disrupted by heavy rains and high winds that swept over the region a day earlier. The storms snarled travel, downed trees and power lines and led to water rescues from New York to Virginia. At its peak, nearly a million customers were without power. Continue reading...
paragraphs: Skies cleared along the US eastern seaboard on Friday, and power was being restored to hundreds of thousands of customers whose Thanksgiving plans were disrupted by heavy rains and high winds that swept over the region a day earlier.
The storms snarled travel, downed trees and power lines and led to water rescues from New York to Virginia. At its peak, nearly a million customers were without power.

The storms prompted the first-ever postponement of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City, as well as the delay or cancellation of thousands of flights. In New Jersey widespread flooding reached levels not seen since 2012, after Hurricane Sandy.
By Friday morning, conditions had significantly improved, though hundreds of thousands remained without power and air travel was still affected by significant delays.
On Friday afternoonPoweroutage.us reported 400,577 customers were still without power, including 98,597 in Pennsylvania, 63,658 in Missouri and 60,297 in New Jersey.

Flightaware said delays within, into, or out of the US on Friday stood at 2,489, and cancellations at 144. On Thursday, more than 2,200 flights to or from US destinations had been delayed and more than 400 had been cancelled.
“The bulk of the storm impacts are behind us, but tidal flooding will continue today,” the National Weather Service said early Friday.

Parts of the midwest and the south were dealing with unusual snowfalls for the time of year, with St Louis, Missouri, getting 7.3in, and snow reported in Alabama and Tennessee. An ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, was empty when the roof caved in at about 3am, according to the city.

“The south and south-east US will start with very cold morning temperatures today and Saturday as lows drop into the upper 20s and the middle 30s,” the National Weather Service said. “Freeze headlines are in effect for portions of the deep south. High temperatures Saturday will begin to moderate into the 60s.”

In New York City, authorities were rushing to clean up the damage the storm left in its wake. Several people had to be rescued from their cars amid flooding, said Zohran Mamdani, and similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities.

Strong winds and flooding disrupted train lines, toppled trees and caused power outages on Thanksgiving night, New York City emergency management officials said. Several scaffolding structures collapsed in the wind, but no injuries were reported.
New York City police said they had recovered a body of man along the Staten Island shoreline. It was not yet clear if the death was storm-related.
The storms also flooded areas from North Carolina through to New Jersey as high tide rolled in. Roads were closed, and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water.
Downtown merchants in Avalon, New Jersey, scrambled to pump out saltwater on Friday after Thanksgiving brought some of the most significant tides in the seaside community’s history.

Cheryl McKenna of Ocean City, New Jersey, said water flooded her garage and surrounded her property, keeping her family inside for six hours on the holiday. She said flooding had become more frequent since Superstorm Sandy in 2012.

“Our family’s been here for 36 years,” McKenna said. “But honestly, we’re thinking is this the right place for us to be? We’re now retired, and we want to stay down here, but how often can we continue to do this?”
Donald Trump signed a disaster declaration on Thursday for Florida in response to earlier flooding that damaged hundreds of homes and required water rescues.

The US president had approved funding earlier this week, but gathered local officials on Thanksgiving to talk about it in a small signing ceremony at his home in West Palm Beach. “Since October it has been raining continuously,” the president said. “It’s the craziest thing. It stopped now.”
Meanwhile, authorities on the west coast were assessing the damage from high-tide-driven waves and strong winds.
Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations in areas from Humboldt county in the far north to Ventura county near Los Angeles.
Workers in Pacifica, California, rushed to evaluate the damage after part of the Pacifica pier collapsed into the ocean on Wednesday amid powerful waves.

The high tides continued to affect train service on Friday. Buses were pressed into service as Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner canceled or shortened more than a dozen trains between San Diego and Los Angeles.

articles.title: IDF kills 10 Hamas, PIJ terrorists in Gaza, including four who participated in October 7 massacre
articles.summary: The IDF and Shin Bet struck and dismantled four Hamas weapons storage facilities in the Gaza Strip on Thursday, according to a Friday statement from the IDF spokesperson.
paragraphs: The IDF killed 10 terrorists in the Gaza Strip during the last week, including four who entered Israeli territory during the October 7 Massacre, the military revealed on Friday.

On Tuesday, the IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) struck the Khan Younis area, killing two terrorists, Akram Sabhi Hamdan Abu Taimah, who was part of Hamas's military wing, and Wajdi Sami Suleiman Abu Salah, a Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) terrorist who entered Israel during the October 7 attacks, the army confirmed in a statement on Friday.

In additional strikes in the northern Gaza Strip this week, the IDF and Shin Bet struck and killed four Hamas terrorists, including Nukhba terrorists, terrorists who infiltrated Israel on October 7, and a battalion engineering officer.
The army said that the terrorists were struck after attempting to launch attacks against IDF troops and Israeli civilians.
The IDF eliminated the terrorist with precision aerial munitions and surveillance to reduce the risk of harm to civilians in the Gaza Strip.
IDF confirms Nukhba, October 7 terrorist struck at Hamas meeting in Gaza

In two separate incidents last Friday, the IDF struck Diab al-Rahman Radi, a cell commander in Hamas’ military wing who was involved in transferring funds to the terrorist organization, and a group of Hamas terrorists when they gathered to plan and advance terror attacks targeting Israeli civilians and IDF troops, the IDF spokesperson said.

The military confirmed that the terrorists killed were Mustafa Hassan Oweni, a Hamas sniper, Mohammed Abu Huishil, a Hamas anti-tank operative, and Yousef Ayidi, who entered Israel on October 7 and was involved in the handover ceremony for former Gaza hostages Eli Sharabi, Ohad Ben Ami, and Or Levy.

"Throughout the war, and particularly in recent weeks, the terrorists advanced attacks against IDF troops and Israeli civilians and operated to restore the capabilities of terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip, systematically violating the ceasefire agreement," the army wrote. The terrorists were targeted to remove the threat they posed to Israeli civilians and soldiers.
IDF, Shin Bet dismantle Hamas weapons storage facilities
The army and Shin Bet struck and dismantled four Hamas weapons storage facilities in the Gaza Strip on Thursday, according to a Friday statement from the IDF spokesperson.
The facilities were being used to store weapons that Hamas terrorists would use to attack IDF troops, the statement explained.
The IDF issued warnings to the civilian population of Gaza prior to the strikes on the weapons facilities.

"Security forces will continue to operate resolutely to degrade the capabilities of terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip and thwart any attempt to restore them or possess weapons intended to harm our troops," the IDF added.

articles.title: Over 200 US lawmakers to back sanctions bill over West Bank settler violence, sources say
articles.summary: Over 200 US lawmakers reportedly support legislation that could impose personal sanctions on Israeli ministers and officials over West Bank settler violence.
paragraphs: More than 200 members of the US House of Representatives, including Republicans, support a bill that would allow personal sanctions to be imposed on individuals involved in settler violence in the West Bank, including Israeli government ministers and officials, congressional sources told Maariv.
According to the sources, the legislation is expected to pass the House as early as the first quarter of 2027.
The sources are not convinced that the bill will be blocked in the Senate or that US President Donald Trump will veto it.

The legal team drafting the legislation is making considerable efforts to prevent harm to the Israeli economy and Israeli companies. The intention is to target sanctions at individuals responsible for violence, encouraging it, or failing to prevent it.

Einat Halevy Levin, vice president of government relations at the American organization Hostage Aid, which maintains close working relations with Congress and the Trump administration, spoke to Maariv about the proposed legislation.

"The bill that is set to pass the House of Representatives as early as late January or early February is still relatively mild compared to what is planned further down the line if the violence in the West Bank is not addressed.

"Under this bill, which enjoys broad Democratic support as well as considerable Republican support, personal sanctions will be imposed on individuals who encourage Jewish violence in the West Bank or fail to prevent it. All of this will be based on established American criteria set by the US Treasury Department."

"This means that even ministers in the current government could find themselves subject to personal US sanctions, meaning that they would be unable to conduct any financial transactions through the banking system. Ultimately, their credit cards could be canceled.

"This is expected to pass by a significant majority in the House of Representatives and in the Senate, and there is no guarantee that Trump will veto the bill. There are many other bills he might prefer to veto. So we are completely exposed.
"And that is before we even discuss far more problematic legislation, such as a US arms embargo (including defensive weapons) or US sanctions against Israeli companies rather than just individuals.
"The only way to stop this is to immediately put an end to the violence in the West Bank."
US sanctions could target Israeli government officials
The West Bank Violence Prevention Act is intended to reinstate the sanctions regime introduced by the administration of former US president Joe Biden, which Trump revoked on his first day in office.

It includes asset freezes and restrictions on entry into the US and could also apply to government officials responsible for policies that encourage violence or who refrain from enforcing the law in a manner that enables it.
According to the bill's sponsors, its provisions would apply to Israelis and Palestinians alike.
Once the sanctions are enshrined in legislation, Trump will not be able to repeal the law by executive order.

The current text also allows sanctions to be imposed on individuals involved in population displacement, dispossession, and property destruction, as well as those providing financial, material, or technological support to sanctioned individuals.
The bill includes a provision for a national security waiver and requires the US Treasury Department to report to Congress every 90 days on the imposition and enforcement of sanctions.
No Israeli ministers are named in the bill. Imposing sanctions on any of them would require the US administration to determine that they meet the criteria outlined in the legislation.
Banks in Israel and other countries could also restrict the financial activities of individuals placed on the US sanctions list for fear of running afoul of enforcement and regulatory authorities.
Democratic bill has unprecedented support within the party
Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become speaker of the House in January, pledged over the weekend to advance the legislation during the first 100 days of the new Congress.
Some 174 Democrats have signed onto the bill in the outgoing Congress, including senior members of the Democratic leadership, Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar.
The companion bill in the Senate, led by Chris Coons and Cory Booker, has the backing of 45 members of the Democratic caucus.
The legislation will have to be reintroduced in January, and a new sponsor will have to be found to replace retiring congressman Jerry Nadler.
No other Democratic bill concerning Israel enjoys such broad support within the party.
According to research by the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), its supporters include 60 House members who belong to the party's pro-Israel establishment.
The list of lawmakers backing the version to be introduced in January has yet to be published.

Assuming all members of the Democratic caucus in the new Senate support the bill, they will need to secure the backing of at least six Republican senators to reach the 60 votes generally required to overcome a filibuster.
If Trump vetoes the bill, a two-thirds majority in both chambers of Congress will be required to override it.
Congressional sources are not ruling out the possibility that Republican senators will also vote in favor of the legislation.
Democrats could try to incorporate sanctions against individuals involved in West Bank violence into an appropriations or defense bill.
The president does not have the authority to veto individual provisions of a bill, meaning that Trump would have to decide whether to veto the legislation in its entirety.
Additional bills seek restrictions on Israeli settlements, military aid
Two additional bills are being advanced in the House of Representatives: the Block the Bombs Act, which seeks to restrict the transfer of offensive weapons to Israel, and the Stop Settlements Act.

The latter enjoys the support of some 60 Democrats and includes sanctions against individuals and entities involved in settlement construction and expansion, as well as a ban on the import of settlement products into the US.
Jeffries has so far refrained from committing to advancing either bill.

Under the anti-settlement legislation, construction companies, financial institutions, developers, and service providers involved in settlement development could also face sanctions, even if they were not involved in violence or dispossession.
A separate bill is being advanced in the Senate to impose sanctions on those involved in construction, financing, and infrastructure development in the E1 area.
By the end of October, it had secured the support of 21 senators, including Chris Coons, Elissa Slotkin, and Mark Kelly.

According to published voting records, 103 of the 212 members of the Democratic caucus in the outgoing House voted earlier this year in favor of a measure to eliminate annual US military aid to Israel, while another 10 abstained.
In April, 40 members of the Senate Democratic caucus voted against the transfer of certain weapons to Israel.
The House Democratic leadership has yet to commit to advancing legislation that would end US military aid in its entirety.
Democratic senators oppose expanded US-Israel defense cooperation
Twelve senators, led by Chris Van Hollen, appealed to the leadership of both chambers of Congress, demanding the removal of three provisions from the 2027 defense legislation.
The provisions would enshrine expanded cooperation with Israel in defense research, development, and production, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and intelligence.
Among other things, the senators are seeking to prevent expanded cooperation in quantum technology, autonomous systems, and biotechnology.
They are also seeking to remove a provision intended to limit the administration's ability to reduce or suspend intelligence sharing with Israel.
In their letter, the senators explicitly refer to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's plan to transition from a model of US military aid to one of a security partnership.
They oppose enshrining American commitments under the new partnership in law.

They argue that if joint research, development, procurement, and production are conducted under Pentagon oversight, transparency will diminish, and the administration will find it more difficult to change its policy toward Israel in the future.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) supports expanding technological cooperation with Israel, arguing that it serves US national security interests and American industry.

The version of the defense legislation approved by the House in July included authorization for $750 million in funding for joint defense programs, of which $500 million was earmarked for missile defense programs.

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee cast doubt this week on the possibility of ending the $3.8 billion in annual military aid as early as the end of the year, as Trump had announced on the day of the congressional elections.
Huckabee noted that the funds had been appropriated by Congress and confirmed that talks on a new agreement between the two countries had been underway for months.
The existing memorandum of understanding on defense cooperation will remain in effect until September 2028.

articles.title: ברחה מחברון, התגוררה ברמלה, נרצחה בבאר שבע
articles.summary: פאטמה אבו חולתם בת ה-19 נורתה למוות בבאר שבע, ואותרה על הכביש. קרוביה סיפרו כי "חששה לחזור לשטחים כי הרגישה מאוימת". הרקע פלילי, איש לא נעצר
paragraphs: פאטמה אבו חולתם בת ה-19 נורתה למוות בבאר שבע, ואותרה על הכביש. קרוביה סיפרו כי "חששה לחזור לשטחים כי הרגישה מאוימת". הרקע פלילי, איש לא נעצר

אותרה על הכביש בבאר שבע, מותה נקבע בבית החולים - ועדיין איש לא נעצר בחשד לרצח: פאטמה אבו חולתם, בת 19 מרמלה, היא הצעירה שנורתה למוות בבאר שבע אתמול בלילה (שישי). היא נמלטה מחברון, שם התגוררה בצעירותה, וקרובים לה אמרו כי "חששה לחזור לשטחים כי הרגישה מאוימת וחששה לחייה".
פאטמה אבו חולתם שנרצחה בבאר שבע

אזרח ששמע את הירי ברחוב התקשר למשטרה, הדיווח למד"א התקבל בשעה 03:15. "כשהגענו הובילו אותנו אל צעירה ששכבה על הכביש לאחר שנפצעה", אמרו אנשי הצוות הרפואי. "היא הייתה מעורפלת הכרה וסבלה מפציעות חודרות. הענקנו לה טיפול רפואי ראשוני במקום ופינינו אותה בניידת טיפול נמרץ של מד"א לבית החולים כשמצבה קשה ולא יציב".
בבית החולים סורוקה, לשם פונתה אבו חולתם, נקבע מותה. המשטרה פתחה בחקירה, ולפי החשד הרקע פלילי. עם זאת, כאמור, חשודים לא נעצרו.
פורסם לראשונה: 23:15, 27.11.26

articles.title: Thirteen soldiers killed in Islamic State attack in southwestern Niger as jihadist attacks increase
articles.summary: The casualty figures were provisional and the most seriously wounded soldiers were evacuated for medical treatment, the ministry said.
paragraphs: Thirteen soldiers were killed and 20 wounded in an attack on a National Guard position in southwestern Niger on Thursday, the defense ministry said, while Islamic State claimed responsibility on its Telegram channel.
The ministry said the attack was carried out by a large group of heavily armed assailants, describing them as terrorists without naming any group.
Islamic State said on Friday in a statement posted on its Telegram channel that its fighters had carried out the attack.

The West African country is battling jihadist groups linked to Islamic State and al-Qaeda. Repeated battlefield losses have fueled tensions within the armed forces, that culminated in a failed mutiny in late August.
Islamic State militants were 'neutralized,' Niger's defense ministry said
The assailants struck a National Guard post in Sanam, in the Abala department, the ministry said.
Several militants were "neutralized" and their logistical equipment destroyed, according to the statement.
The casualty figures were provisional and the most seriously wounded soldiers were evacuated for medical treatment, the ministry said.
Another 11 soldiers were killed in Baraoua, in the eastern Diffa region, earlier this week.

articles.title: Princess of Wales documentary Heal charts ‘pilgrimage’ after cancer treatment
articles.summary: BBC film follows Catherine as she undertakes Three Peaks challenge to search for what life can be post-chemotherapy On the day the Princess of Wales undertook the Three Peaks challenge, there was rain, hill fog and, finally, watery June sunshine. It is hard to not see it as a meteorological metaphor for Catherine’s journey – from cancer diagnosis through treatment and to remission – as she treks first Ben Nevis, then Scafell Pike and Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) within 24 hours, the camera capturing her physical challenge for a new documentary. Continue reading...
paragraphs: On the day the Princess of Wales undertook the Three Peaks challenge, there was rain, hill fog and, finally, watery June sunshine.

It is hard to not see it as a meteorological metaphor for Catherine’s journey – from cancer diagnosis through treatment and to remission – as she treks first Ben Nevis, then Scafell Pike and Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) within 24 hours, the camera capturing her physical challenge for a new documentary.

Titled simply Heal and premiering on the BBC from Sunday, this is far from usual royal fare. – It is powerful emotional excavation as Catherine undertakes her “pilgrimage” to search for what life is, or can be, after cancer treatment, physically and spiritually.
“I think when you’re on your hospital bed and it is so clinical around you, you haven’t got fresh air, no greenery around you, it’s very stark and alien and stripped back,” she says.

“The darkness was a really scary, disorientating experience. I think I was sort of in and out of consciousness. It was a really dark time. But also, somewhere through that, too, I became aware of someone holding my hand.
“They weren’t talking to me. They weren’t trying to fix anything. They were just there. And the presence of someone that stood by me in that time, I’ll for ever be grateful for.”
Who that hand belonged to – doctor, nurse, husband – is left unsaid. But it is implied that she is speaking not just of the physical but also of a spiritual presence.
Catherine was diagnosed with an undisclosed type of cancer in March 2024, underwent chemotherapy, and announced she was in remission in January 2025.
But what then? “It’s very hard to go back to the person you were before,” she says in the 30-minute programme.
This challenge, through which she is raising money for the Royal Marsden hospital in London where she was treated, is her “then”.
The journey “is a chance to explore what life looks like, what healing looks like beyond diagnosis, beyond treatment,” she says. There is no end goal, it is simply “what comes along the way”.
It is her ringing of the bell, which patients customarily do when hospital treatment ends but which she “weirdly didn’t realise was a thing” and so never got to do.

The main voice throughout is hers. We see her walking alone and with her brother, James Middleton, occasionally chatting with other fundraising trekkers en route, or meeting people undergoing treatment in hospitals, at pub support groups and art therapy.

We see her talking directly to the camera, shot in closeup profile, gazing occasionally into the distance as she articulates the inner turmoil, describing how with cancer you “in a way lose yourself”. She is “having to learn again to live life fully”.

We see her smiling brightly, mostly, but also in tears. At the top of Scafell Pike, James whips out his phone and plays voice notes sent by Prince William and recorded by their children Prince George, 13, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, eight.
Louis’s little-boy enthusiasm serves as poignant reminder that throughout all this she is a mother of still young children, and of the ripple effect of the disease on loved ones.

“Hello, Mummy. I really love you and I hope you do well going up the mountain,” Louis says. “Remember, I’m always in your heart with you, and I love you very much. And I’ll be following behind your back with you, and I’ll always be with you. And remember, I love you really lots and lots, and I give you lots and lots of love.”

George says he is tracking her on Flightradar up the mountains “and you look really, really strong. Keep going and we’re right behind you.” Charlotte is “so proud of you doing your walk and your challenges”.

Catherine wipes away tears. “They gave me the reason to get out of hospital. They’re going to give me the reason to finish this challenge,” she says, placing a stone on a rock. “This is for the kiddies.”

Speaking at a private screening this week, Catherine said cancer “profoundly affects every aspect of life”. She added: “I know this personally and that the journey through and beyond treatment requires more than medicine alone.”

She set out on the challenge to explore life after diagnosis “as a solitary experience – in a way, as a pilgrimage. But what I quickly realised is that our vulnerability is not something that we simply have to overcome or that separates us from others. It is an essential part of being human. It could be the very thing that connects us.”
Her hope is that the film will encourage compassion and show “the real value in standing alongside one another in the hardest of times”.
She sees every day as a day “given back to me”. Catherine says she hopes to remind people that whatever road they face, whatever challenge ahead, they are not alone.

Nature has helped her healing. “Even when I physically couldn’t get into nature, I imagined nature from my hospital bed. And now that I’m well enough, I feel a deep longing for all those spaces, for the ocean, for the trees, for the mountains,” she says in the film.
As for her pilgrimage, it has become “so much more than a personal or solitary experience but really a collective one”.

There is light. Just being alongside someone is enough, she says. “So often you think you need to fix something or say something or do something, and you don’t. You just need to be there. And that’s what love looks like.
“That’s what I think the light is that we can often find out of the darkest of times. In the midst of the fog and everything, it’s just so special. That’s a moment of consolation.”

articles.title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
articles.summary: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wants to defy the polls, and his main rivals accuse him of not telling the truth and of "betrayal".
paragraphs: If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.
The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".
Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.
A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.
A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.
Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.
She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".

Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.

While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.

The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.
Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.

Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.
Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.
Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.
"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.

One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by Sánchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".
Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".
He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign.
"These elections are about moving Spain forward, not taking it backwards," he said.

Socialist supporter Leon Felipe, 25, told Reuters news agency: "Well, I think what's at stake in these elections is a big deal, is not a change of government... but rather a return to the past - a return to Franco's dictatorship.
"So, I believe that young must mobilise."
As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

articles.title: Punk rock rebel Henry Rollins takes aim at BDS - and challenges artists weighing in on Israel
articles.summary: The hardcore rocker, author, and so much more opens up about his exceptional life, fierce beliefs, and visits to Israel.
paragraphs: Henry Rollins appeared in Israel as a spoken-word artist in 1989. He returned in 2007 to film his television special, Henry Rollins: Uncut from Israel. “This time,” he told an interviewer, “I really felt a sense of the intensity of what it means to be Israeli because in their reality, anytime, anywhere, it could be the worst day of your life. Americans can’t really identify with that feeling easily.”

A former Black Flag front man and actor, the author, radio show host, and spoken-word artist has carved out a self-made and exceptional life. He has written dozens of books. He has traveled the world as a musician, public speaker, and USO entertainer. At 65, he can still fill a room with people of all ages. He spends most of his time alone, working almost constantly.
He quotes Henry Miller. His favorite president is Abraham Lincoln. He channels Lenny Bruce in his talks. And he admires Muhammad Ali’s work ethic.

This profile draws on past interviews by others, his prolific writing, and his written answers to my questions. I read The Portable Henry Rollins, which includes excerpts from his books, poetry, and journal entries from his life on the road. Even his prose is replete with rhythm, imagery, passion, and powerful themes.
From ice cream to punk rock
In the chapter from High Adventure in the Great Outdoors, he writes of his aimless existence managing an ice cream store in Washington, DC, when he was 19:

“I watch the pretty girls pass the window that looks out onto the sidewalk. I’m the guy in the ice cream store. I have been here eleven hours. My legs ache. I just got off work; it’s 2:30 a.m. I am hungry, so I go to the only place that’s open. 7-Eleven. I get the same thing every night. I sit alone on the curb and eat. I have to walk to my apartment… I don’t want to go to the apartment. The apartment knows I’m coming. The apartment knows I have nowhere else to go. The apartment is smiling. It shuts off the heat and waits for me to fall in.”

At 20, Rollins joined Black Flag as its lead singer. The move catapulted him from a dead-end life to a formidable force in the 1980s punk rock scene. It was an intense, challenging, and even dangerous time.

The band worked around the clock booking, promoting, and performing, as well as recording and selling its music. They were often short of money and went hungry. Crowds frequently hurled objects toward the stage and spat on the musicians in a fit of chaotic energy. At times, he hated them.

Rollins, known for his fierce physical and vocal performances, gave as good as he got. “I lived for the shows,” he told the Los Angeles Times in 1987. “Violence was my girl. Getting into fist fights, smelling blood, breaking noses, that was my high, my woman. I got beat up, and I beat other people up.”

But the anger and aggression of those years were rooted in something much earlier: a childhood in which Rollins says he was often frightened, bullied, and unsure of where he belonged. That experience would eventually shape not only how he saw himself, but also the moral standards he developed for how people should treat one another.

“When I was young, I was afraid of many things,” he tells me. “I was small and got picked on. I didn’t have the courage or confidence to fight back, so I would run, or submit, or avoid groups. I think at a certain point all of that fear turned into anger and started coming out.

“I am neither tough nor brave. The experiences I had stripped me of my sense of fear. In my opinion, there is a difference between having a lack of fear and being brave. I think bravery is a conscious act. Not having fear is not necessarily being fearless. It is to lack an awareness that could very well keep you alive. I think in my case, my lack of fear isn’t proof of courage; it is a symptom, a result of trauma.”
Beyond being bullied by his peers, Rollins says he never developed a conventional sense of family. His parents were divorced when he was three years old.

“I don’t think I will ever understand the idea of family, but that’s just because of how I was raised. I might have an understanding of the concept, but it’s probably somewhat skewed. When I was young, I spent a great deal of time at my best friend’s house and in a way his family became far more familiar to me than my mother and father.”
He has described his father as racist and homophobic. I ask him how he learned to question the prejudices his father modeled instead of absorbing them.

“Because of my mother. My mother was almost the exact opposite of my father. She was very left of center, liked music, the arts, and never expressed to me any ideas of racism or homophobia. The things my father would tell me on the weekends when I would visit him simply didn’t make sense. It was amazing to me that an adult could be wrong.

“I’ve been stupid all of my life, but one thing I got right, which was pretty amazing, considering my age, was that my father was never going to teach me anything I could use in a practical way. I guess you could say what I learned from him was what not to do or how to be.”

It’s hard to reconcile that angry young man in the ’80s with who Rollins has become in recent years. In 2012, he recorded a talk called “Letter to a Young American.” It addressed the challenging economic times and the envy people sometimes feel toward those who seem to have it easy. He seems warm, open, and caring, and said in part:

“As a young person going into a very turbulent and fragile economy… it is easy to lose your moral compass, your decency, your sense of civility, and your sense of community. Very easy. People are getting a little desperate; they might not show their best elements to you. You must never lower yourself to being a person you don’t like. There’s no better time than now to have a moral and civic backbone. To have a moral and civic true north.”

“I like people,” he tells me. “It’s why I write books and do my radio show. I like the opportunity to serve them, to make things they might like, again, a book, a radio show, or a stage performance. To me, these are exercises of service, a way to be an asset. I work on these things pretty much every day. I often get very little feedback about what I do. I’m not necessarily looking for any. Of course, I hope people like the radio show and whatever else I’m doing.”

Yet he spends most of his time alone and likes it that way.. “When I was much younger, I was unable to understand people enough to be part of a group, like in school. I always felt different and deficient in many areas. As I grew older, finding myself alone a lot of the time, I concluded that I’m just one of those people who is solitary and that I shouldn’t try to be something that I’m not, because it’s obviously just not who I am.”
Does he get lonely?

“I think I got lonely when I was much younger, but I don’t remember the last time I felt lonely. I think some people need to interact with others; that’s why, like in a prison environment, solitary confinement is used as punishment. I often go days at a time without saying anything to anyone other than polite greetings at the gym or the supermarket. I answer and write emails pretty much every day and often text a couple of people I’m working with, but I live alone and don’t seek company for the sake of not being alone…
“I’ve traveled all over the world, often by myself, in countries where I don’t speak the language. I never miss being in a situation where I can understand what’s being said.”

In 2016, Rollins scheduled a speaking tour in Israel and faced pressure from the BDS campaign to cancel. His agent told him he had problems with the Israeli promoter over another client and recommended Rollins cancel his date, which he did. Rumors subsequently circulated, and the UK paper New Musical Express (NME) reported that the cancellation was in response to BDS.

Rollins immediately objected to the characterization, and NME published his clarification: “I did not, as the NME has reported, pull out of my show in Tel Aviv, Israel due to any pressure from anywhere. I canceled the Tel Aviv show on advice from my agent… I was looking forward to the show in Tel Aviv.

“I don’t think a cultural boycott is a good way to go. As much as I disagree with Israel’s dealings with Palestine, and I disagree very much, I think ideas, discussion, and other perspectives lead to change more than the silence of a boycott.”

Putting a fine point on it, he tells me, “My decision had nothing to do with the boycott, which I wasn’t aware of. I would’ve done the exact same thing had the show been in Paris or Pittsburgh. I’ve been to Israel twice, and both times the audiences were great.”
I ask what he thinks about artists weighing in on complicated political issues.

“I think a lot of political issues are extraordinarily complicated. I don’t think any artist has any specific responsibility to weigh in on any topic, but if they do, they will hopefully be informed, and that will be reflected in their answer. I think one of the problems is that questions are asked about incredibly dynamic and complex situations with the question being posed right after a question about their new album or something. I think it is in these situations where the answer can cause problems.

“I know enough to know when questions require knowledge and understanding that exceeds my intellectual pay grade. I do my best to simply say I don’t know enough to provide an answer of any merit. Artist types often get a great deal of attention paid to them, and it is my opinion that they should speak very carefully in an effort to be clear. I find it disingenuous when someone speaks about a country they’ve never been to. I don’t think visiting any country for several days makes you an expert on the place, but if you haven’t been there, I think it’s safe to say that your opinion is at best, partially informed. As well, I think it’s possible to be in a place for a long time and still not quite understand why people are the way they are there.
“I remember Tel Aviv being an amazing place. The people I met at my shows there and the interviews I did I remember as being good experiences.”

I ask for his thoughts on the rise of antisemitism. “I have no idea as to the cause of antisemitism or even why it’s still present. I think antisemitism should be rejected completely. I find any kind of discrimination to be repellent and scary. I don’t know what method of logic could bring someone out of these ideas because I don’t understand how someone gets to these ideas in the first place.”
HENRY’S NEW BOOK, a memoir titled Bait Dog Boy, will be released on March 2, through Random House. The memoir returns to the Washington, DC, childhood and adolescence that shaped him.

For someone who spent his childhood feeling frightened, alienated, and different, Rollins has built a life that seems almost entirely on his own terms. He turned his anger into art, his isolation into independence, and his experiences into a way of looking closely at the world around him.■

The writer is an attorney and 20-year entertainment veteran, the CEO of Liberate Art, and the author of the award-winning book Artists Under Fire: The BDS War Against Celebrities, Jews, and Israel. Her column, “Hollywood Stories,” spotlights Jewish and non-Jewish entertainers who voice support for Israel and the Jewish community. www.liberateart.net, / www.instagram.com/hollywoodstoriesbylanamelman

articles.title: Elderly ‘Scrooge’ severs neighbour’s Christmas lights in mobility-scooter raid
articles.summary: CCTV shows unidentified woman taking scissors to Middlesbrough home’s festive display An elderly woman has been accused of defying the season of goodwill after appearing to cut down her neighbour’s Christmas lights. CCTV footage showed her approaching a property on a mobility scooter brandishing scissors. Continue reading...
paragraphs: An elderly woman has been accused of defying the season of goodwill after appearing to cut down her neighbour’s Christmas lights.
CCTV footage showed her approaching a property on a mobility scooter brandishing scissors.

After several seconds, the Christmas lights at Beth Wilson-Croft’s house in Middlesbrough, North Yorkshire, which is surrounded by lights with an inflatable Father Christmas and Rudolph on the roof and two snowmen in the garden, went out.
The woman then fled the scene on her scooter at about 11pm on Wednesday.
Wilson-Croft said most of her neighbours enjoyed her festive display and she had never seen the alleged perpetrator before, the Daily Mail reported.
The 31-year-old said she had reported the vandalism to the police.

In an effort to find the woman, Wilson-Croft posted the footage online and wrote: “If you don’t like my Christmas decorations that’s an absolute shame for you because they’ll be back up today alongside a singing Santa and a snow machine and anything else I can get my hands on.”
After seeing the video of the incident, a man offered to help and fixed the lights by soldering them back together.
Wilson-Croft, who has a six-year-old child, has subsequently shared photographs showing her lights restored.
The footage triggered outrage from neighbours who accused the perpetrator of flouting the festive spirit and described her as a “Grinch” and a “Scrooge”.
The family’s seasonal decorations draw visitors from around the area.

articles.title: Fled Hebron fearing for her life: 19-year-old woman shot dead in Be'er Sheva
articles.summary: Fatma Abu Khultam, a resident of Ramle, was found seriously wounded on a Be'er Sheva street and later pronounced dead at Soroka Medical Center; relatives say she feared returning to the West Bank, while police suspect a criminal motive and have made no arrests
paragraphs: Fatma Abu Khultam, a resident of Ramle, was found seriously wounded on a Be'er Sheva street and later pronounced dead at Soroka Medical Center; relatives say she feared returning to the West Bank, while police suspect a criminal motive and have made no arrests

Fatma Abu Khultam, 19, from Ramle, was identified as the young woman shot dead in Be'er Sheva early Friday. She was found wounded on a street and later pronounced dead at the hospital. No suspects have been arrested in connection with her killing.
Abu Khultam had fled Hebron, where she lived when she was younger. Relatives said she "was afraid to return to the West Bank because she felt threatened and feared for her life."
Fatma Abu Khultam, who was shot dead in Be'er Sheva

A resident who heard gunfire on the street called police, and Magen David Adom received the emergency call at 3:15 a.m. "When we arrived, we were directed to a young woman lying wounded on the road," paramedics said. "She was semiconscious and suffering from penetrating injuries. We provided initial medical treatment at the scene and evacuated her to the hospital in a mobile intensive care unit in serious and unstable condition."
Abu Khultam was pronounced dead at Soroka Medical Center. Police opened an investigation and suspect the shooting was criminally motivated. No arrests have been made.

articles.title: ‘Abusive and insulting to Canadians’: campaign to oust US ambassador presented to parliament
articles.summary: Hundreds of thousands of Canadians call for Pete Hoekstra to be declared ‘persona non grata’ A petition signed by nearly 290,000 Canadians calling on Mark Carney’s government to oust Pete Hoekstra as US ambassador to Canada was formally presented to the House of Commons on Thursday, a sign of the strained relations between the neighboring countries.
