articles.title: Graham Thorpe’s widow takes legal action against NHS trust after inquest
articles.summary: Former England Test cricketer was diagnosed with anxiety and depression before he took his own life in 2024 The wife of Graham Thorpe, the former England cricketer who took his own life, has started legal proceedings against an NHS trust after an inquest identified “failings” in his mental health care. Thorpe died aged 55 in August 2024 in Surrey. His wife, Amanda, has lodged a personal injury claim at the high court against Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS foundation trust which was involved in his care, the Telegraph reported. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on…
paragraphs: The wife of Graham Thorpe, the former England cricketer who took his own life, has started legal proceedings against an NHS trust after an inquest identified “failings” in his mental health care.

Thorpe died aged 55 in August 2024 in Surrey. His wife, Amanda, has lodged a personal injury claim at the high court against Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS foundation trust which was involved in his care, the Telegraph reported.

The former batsman and coach was diagnosed with anxiety and depression and had tried to kill himself in 2022, the inquest at Surrey coroner’s court in Woking heard last year. The inquest found the trust was culpable of “failings” and “shortcomings”.
Thorpe, who played 100 Tests for England, had “spiralled into depression” after losing his job as a batting coach in 2022 at the conclusion of the Ashes series in Australia, the hearing heard.

Surrey coroner’s court was told there had been a gap of more than four months in his being seen by the local NHS trust before his death despite a “crisis” call in June 2024 when he told his care coordinator that he had “given up”. Thorpe was offered a follow-up appointment by the community mental health team but no home visit was made.

Jonathan Stevens, the assistant coroner, said at the inquest: “In my judgment, someone should have been going to see him to properly monitor and assess him, to understand his care needs. Saying ‘come and see me in two weeks’ was not an appropriate response to the crisis.

“I don’t accept that when Graham was constantly asking his wife to help end his life, which was a new presentation that hadn’t been seen before, he was not at that moment in crisis. There were shortcomings in the care that should have been provided to Graham in the last four months of his life. There were failings in the provision of his care.”
Stevens did not conclude those shortcomings were negligent, adding: “I cannot say whether it would have made any difference or not.”

Amanda told the inquest her husband was constantly asking for help to end his life and that he was sure nothing would work. She also told the inquest of Thorpe’s desire to go to Switzerland to end his life, although he did also tell his care coordinator that he had “no immediate plans” to act on his suicidal thoughts. A coroner recorded a verdict of suicide.
A statement from Surrey and Borders NHS trust read: “We understand there is an intention to commence proceedings and cannot comment further at this stage.”

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

articles.title: DWP ‘cyber incident’ knocks almost all pensions and benefits systems offline
articles.summary: Department for Work and Pensions urges people to be alert to scams related to outage and contact helpline with urgent difficulties Tell us: have you been affected by the DWP ‘cyber incident’ Benefits and pensions claimants have faced chaos after the system was hit by a “serious cyber incident”, fuelling concerns about the UK government’s ability to defend itself against malicious attacks. The government took its portal down late on Thursday after detecting “unusual activity”, meaning anyone trying to check their state pension, make an application for disability benefits or claim universal…
paragraphs: Almost all pensions and benefits systems in the UK are unavailable after a “cyber incident”.
Anyone trying to check their state pension, make an application for disability benefits or claim universal credit was not able to do so on Friday morning.
Regular benefits and pensions payments are not affected and would continue to be made as normal, the Department for Work and Pension said.
But there were reports from members of the public who said payments they had expected to be in their account had not arrived on Friday morning.
The cause of the incident, and whether it is the result of a cyber-attack, is not publicly known but the department is working with the National Cyber Security Centre.
A range of services were taken down on Thursday as a precautionary measure after “unusual activity” was detected, a government spokesperson said on Friday.

“There is no evidence to suggest that a malicious actor has targeted other government departments and we are working as quickly as possible to establish the facts,” they added. “Currently, there is no evidence of customer data loss but the investigation is ongoing and we are not going to get ahead of that process.”
It comes days after the government issued an alert warning of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks in the UK, particularly against businesses supporting Ukraine.

The incident caused concern among the public, with some reporting problems. One woman, who has two young children, told BBC Radio 4 that she normally receives a universal credit payment on the 27th day of each month and, like others, was concerned about not having enough money to cover bills due to be paid on the first.
“It’s a bit scary because when I called them [the DWP] to ask, they said they couldn’t give me any other information other than the payment would definitely be made by Monday,” she said.

“M​y weekly shop is on a Sunday so I am ​h​avin​g to go into Christmas savings, which I have​ been saving for the last six or seven months. I am having to pull mon​ey out of them ​to make up for what I don’t have and ​there are bills coming out ​also next week.”

The department said in a statement: “We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems. We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption.

“Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal. If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links.”
The DWP’s most senior official told a committee of MPs this month that cybersecurity and resilience was one of the issues “that keeps a new permanent secretary awake”.

Sarah Healey, the DWP permanent secretary, was appearing before the work and pensions select committee, where she was asked who would ensure that DWP systems would “not be the frontline in some sort of hybrid warfare from the Kremlin”.

Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries malfunctioned earlier this month, with their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F), in what was blamed on a cyber-attack. The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.
The disruption at the DWP should be a “wake-up call” for the government and public bodies, said Dame Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons science and technology committee.
“People rely on these systems for some of the most essential services the state provides, and they should be able to trust that the tech and data underpinning them are secure and resilient.

“My committee has repeatedly warned that the government cannot achieve its digital transformation of public services without addressing weaknesses in its digital infrastructure and improving standards of data hygiene. Public bodies hold citizens’ data on trust, and that demands the highest standards.”

articles.title: המהלך שמסעיר את חברי קיבוץ ניר עוז: ירדן ביבס - "זה מרסק אותי"
articles.summary: חברי קיבוץ הגישו ערעור על ההחלטה להעתיק את בתי העדות ומבקשים לצרף אליו עצומה נגד המהלך. מוקדם יותר קרא ירדן ביבס לשמר את הבתים: "בבית הזה שרוצים להרוס היו לי חיים"
paragraphs: חברי קיבוץ הגישו ערעור על ההחלטה להעתיק את בתי העדות ומבקשים לצרף אליו עצומה נגד המהלך. מוקדם יותר קרא ירדן ביבס לשמר את הבתים: "בבית הזה שרוצים להרוס היו לי חיים"

"כחברי קיבוץ, אנו מתנגדים להחלטה להרוס את הבתים בניר עוז", כתבו. "הבתים האלה אינם רק מבנים. הם עדות לחיים שנגדעו ולזוועה שאין לה תחליף בשום צילום או תיעוד. הריסתם תמחק עדות היסטורית שאי אפשר להחזיר. אנו מבינים את הכאב ואת הרצון לשקם את החיים, אך אפשר לעשות זאת ולשמר לצד זה את בתי העדות כאתר הנצחה ותיעוד".
עוד כתבו: "אנו קוראים לעצור את ההריסה ולהחזיר לדיון את חלופה 2 או לגבש חלופת פשרה אחרת. מתוך כבוד לנרצחים, למשפחותיהם ולתושבי ניר עוז, אנו מבקשים מכם לעצור ולחשוב שוב".
מגישי הערעור אינם מתגוררים כיום בקיבוץ וטרם החליטו אם לשוב אליו. למכתב צורף קישור לחתימה על העצומה, שאותה הם מבקשים לצרף לערעור שהגישו.
"בבית הזה שרוצים להרוס היו לי חיים", כתב ביבס. "זה מרסק אותי, הבן שלי למד לדבר והבן הקטן למד לזחול בבית הזה". הוא הדגיש כי אסור להרוס ולמחוק את הבתים בשם הצמיחה והשיקום.

articles.title: US military strikes cargo ship from Bandar Abbas in Gulf of Oman, says it tried to breach blockade
articles.summary: CENTCOM said the Palau-flagged Pacific Archer had left Iran’s Bandar Abbas port and ignored repeated warnings. The strike disabled the ship’s propulsion, but no crew members were injured.
paragraphs: CENTCOM said the Palau-flagged Pacific Archer had left Iran’s Bandar Abbas port and ignored repeated warnings. The strike disabled the ship’s propulsion, but no crew members were injured.

A US military aircraft struck and disabled a commercial cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday after its crew attempted to breach the US naval blockade of Iran, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Friday.

CENTCOM identified the ship as the Pacific Archer, a Palau-flagged vessel that had departed from the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas. The command said the crew received multiple warnings before the aircraft struck the ship’s stern, disabling its propulsion. The civilian crew was unharmed, according to CENTCOM, which released a brief video of the operation.

CENTCOM did not identify the ship’s cargo or intended destination, or say whether the vessel was towed after the strike. The ClassNK ship register lists the Pacific Archer as a bulk carrier, not an oil tanker.
US expands enforcement of blockade on Iran

The strike came just over a week after the US military widened the scope of its blockade enforcement. A November 18 maritime advisory said vessels could be treated as attempting to evade the blockade if they accepted cargo at sea that had originally been loaded in Iran, even if they had not called at an Iranian port. CENTCOM did not allege that the Pacific Archer had taken part in such a transfer.

On November 7, US forces disabled another merchant vessel, the Huda, in the Gulf of Oman after its crew ignored repeated warnings, according to CENTCOM. The US resumed enforcement of the blockade on July 14, according to the Joint Maritime Information Center. In an assessment published Thursday, the center said commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained below 2025 levels.
Speaking to US service members on Thanksgiving, President Donald Trump defended the blockade, calling it what he believed to be the most successful naval blockade in history.

articles.title: ההתחייבות של מנסור עבאס לגוש השינוי - והמחיר שהוא מבקש בתמורה
articles.summary: לפי דיווח ב"אולפן שישי", יו"ר רע"ם צפוי לדרוש שני תפקידי שרים בממשלה המתגבשת בראשות איזנקוט. במקביל, עבאס הביע נכונות לשיתוף פעולה גם בסוגיות ביטחוניות רגישות
paragraphs: לפי דיווח ב"אולפן שישי", יו"ר רע"ם צפוי לדרוש שני תפקידי שרים בממשלה המתגבשת בראשות איזנקוט. במקביל, עבאס הביע נכונות לשיתוף פעולה גם בסוגיות ביטחוניות רגישות

במסגרת המגעים הקואליציוניים דורשת רע"ם גם גיבוש תוכנית למאבק בפשיעה בחברה הערבית, השקעת עשרות מיליארדי שקלים במסגרת תוכנית חומש ליישובים הערביים ולערים המעורבות והסדרת סוגיית הבנייה, בדגש על הנגב. במפלגה מוכנים ליישום הדרגתי של הדרישות, בכפוף להתחייבות מצד איזנקוט.
עוד דווח כי בעקבות ההתפתחויות וההצהרה הצפויה של עבאס בנוגע להגדרת חמאס כארגון טרור, הוחלט ברע"ם להצמיד לו אבטחה מחשש לפגיעה בו.
המסר של איזנקוט לנפתלי בנט ונתניהו

איזנקוט הדגיש כי בכוונתו להקים ממשלה בטרם יפקע המנדט שניתן לו: "נותרו לכך 8 ימים. בכוונתי להקים בהם ממשלה. אני מתחייב שגם לאחר הקמת הממשלה, אפעל להצטרפות והרחבה עבור כל מי שחפץ להחזיר את ישראל למסלול, לעבר יציבות וחוף מבטחים".

articles.title: ‘Someone just walked in’: Tel Aviv burglaries rise as residents fear sleeping in their own homes
articles.summary: Reported home burglaries in Tel Aviv have risen 12% this year, but many victims never contact police; residents describe strangers entering their homes as their children slept, while detectives turn to Facebook to identify victims and recover stolen property
paragraphs: Reported home burglaries in Tel Aviv have risen 12% this year, but many victims never contact police; residents describe strangers entering their homes as their children slept, while detectives turn to Facebook to identify victims and recover stolen property

The morning after their apartment on Mazeh Street in Tel Aviv was burglarized, Maor and his wife still had no idea someone had entered their home. Only several hours later, as they discovered one missing item after another, did they realize that a stranger had wandered through their apartment and stolen their belongings while they slept in the same room as their two young daughters.

Their experience is one of 180 apartment burglaries reported to police in Tel Aviv between the beginning of the year and mid-November, an increase of approximately 12% compared with the same period last year. Police acknowledge, however, that not every burglary is reported, and sometimes it is the officers themselves who must track down the victims.
(Photo: Uncredited / Miki Ben Shoshan)

The burglar moved through Maor's apartment just a few meters from where he, his wife and their two young daughters were sleeping. He took cash, jewelry and personal belongings before disappearing without leaving behind any significant mess. When the family woke up the following morning, it never occurred to them that someone had entered their home during the night. Only hours later, as Maor prepared to leave for a meeting, did the pieces come together. Since then, every time he locks the apartment's security bars, he recalls that night and the scenario he fears most: What would have happened if one of his daughters had woken up and encountered the burglar? "It was a nightmare," he told Ynet.

"If I had woken up and seen him, I definitely would have confronted him," Maor added. "What if he had stabbed me? What if I had stabbed him? I don't know." More than the stolen money or jewelry that held sentimental value, what troubles him is that a stranger managed to invade his family's most private space while they were defenseless.

The burglary occurred during the night of November 17-18. Maor and his wife had gone out separately that evening, and he remembers locking the front door when he returned home around midnight. The following morning, his wife discovered that her handbag was missing as she prepared for work. Assuming she had left it somewhere the previous evening, she also searched their car without success. When Maor prepared to take their daughters to preschool, he discovered that his waist bag was missing as well. At that point, the couple still believed it was a coincidence.
An apartment burglary in Tel Aviv

Only later that morning, when Maor returned home and prepared to leave for a meeting, did he notice that the necklaces he usually kept in a designated spot were missing. His wallet, however, remained in place. When he opened it, he discovered that approximately 1,000 shekels in cash had disappeared. At that moment, he realized their belongings had not been misplaced outside the apartment, but stolen while the family slept.

"Someone just walked in," he recalled. The burglar also took his waist bag, which contained personal belongings and approximately 200 shekels, and his wife's handbag, which contained documents and identification. The couple noticed that one of the living room windows was open and suspects the burglar entered through it, although they do not know for certain how he gained access.

By chance, all four family members had slept in the same room that night. One of the daughters had joined her parents during the night, while their one-year-old daughter regularly slept in their bedroom. "Forget the money," Maor said. "The main thing is that neither of the girls woke up. Thank God that's how it ended."

Police arrived shortly after Maor reported the burglary, but the family's daily routine has changed since that night. The couple now makes sure to lock the apartment's security bars, something they had not always bothered doing because of the inconvenience. Even stepping onto the balcony now involves dealing with the lock and, more importantly, being reminded of what happened. Their fear is no longer simply about losing possessions, but about the possibility of someone entering their home again.
The suspect following the young woman before allegedly breaking into her apartment and raping her, about a month ago

Maor's experience follows several other incidents in the city, including the serious case of Adam Yassin, 42, a convicted sex offender with an extensive criminal record who was under Israel Prison Service supervision. According to an indictment filed against him, Yassin followed a woman in her 20s about a month ago, entered her apartment and raped her. Approximately two weeks later, he allegedly broke into her home again and committed an indecent act before she managed to drive him away. In another incident, a Palestinian from Qalqilya who was in Israel illegally violently robbed an 85-year-old woman on Hama'apilim Street.

The figures point to an increase in reported burglaries in Tel Aviv-Jaffa. According to Israel Police data, 180 apartment burglaries were reported in the city between the beginning of 2026 and mid-November, compared with 161 during the corresponding period in 2025, an increase of approximately 12%.

Even those figures, however, do not necessarily reflect the full extent of the problem. Some victims of property crimes never file complaints with police, either because the stolen belongings have little monetary value or because they do not believe filing a complaint will lead to the arrest of the burglar or the recovery of their property. As a result, their cases do not appear in police statistics.

Among them is Yaron, who lives in central Tel Aviv and returned home one evening approximately two weeks ago to discover that a stranger had ransacked his apartment in search of valuables. As far as he knows, however, the burglar left empty-handed. "I got home and couldn't believe it," he recalled. "The entire apartment had been turned upside down. All the clothes from the closet had been thrown around, and the drawers were overturned on the floor."

"I live on the second floor, and I think he came in through the balcony overlooking the building's courtyard," Yaron said. "I don't know what he was looking for in the closet, but there really wasn't anything to find. I don't keep any valuables at home, and maybe that's what saved me. Everything is at my parents' place. I think he turned everything upside down out of frustration because he couldn't find anything."

Despite what he discovered when he opened his apartment door, Yaron decided against filing a police complaint. "I didn't go to the police because he didn't actually steal anything. He just made a mess of my apartment," he explained. Nevertheless, the burglary prompted him to change his habits and become more vigilant about securing his home. "From now on, I'll close the shutters and lock the windows. It's definitely unsettling, but I've heard from other friends whose homes were burglarized during the day. They always said burglars come at night, but apparently they come during the day too."
Burglary-related arrests have increased by more than 30%

Meanwhile, figures from the Yarkon police district show that arrests in connection with apartment burglaries increased by approximately 37% during the same period, from 46 last year to 63 this year. The number of indictments rose from 38 to 39, an increase of approximately 3%, while requests to keep defendants in custody until the conclusion of legal proceedings rose from 26 to 27, an increase of approximately 4%.

Chief Inspector Ben Goldberg, who oversees intelligence and detective operations at the Lev Tel Aviv police station, is well acquainted with the phenomenon. He said one of the challenges investigators face is the discrepancy between the number of burglaries that actually occur and the number reported to police. "As an organization, we rely on empirical data. We have actual figures for the complaints that are filed," he explained. Police are aware that some victims choose not to report burglaries, but have no way of accurately determining how many. Some simply do not want to report the crime, Goldberg said, while others do not believe contacting police will help them.

Sometimes, detectives themselves must search for burglary victims. During investigations, officers occasionally recover property suspected of being stolen without knowing who owns it. In other cases, police discover social media posts by residents describing burglaries at their homes, even though they never filed formal complaints.

Police also monitor local Facebook groups, including Secret Tel Aviv, where residents share experiences and report unusual incidents in their neighborhoods. Officers sometimes publish photographs of recovered property in an effort to identify its owners. Through these efforts, police have managed to locate burglary victims whose cases were previously unknown to investigators.

Goldberg distinguishes between two main categories of burglars operating in the city. The first, and more common, consists of opportunistic offenders who roam the streets looking for chances to commit crimes. They do not necessarily select their victims in advance, but look for weaknesses in residential security.
Chief Inspector Ben Goldberg

The second category consists of criminals who operate in a more organized and calculated manner. According to Goldberg, they may gather information about their intended victims in advance, sometimes using information shared on social media. Unlike opportunistic burglars, they may already know what valuables they are looking for. "They monitor their victims' daily routines," Goldberg explained. These organized criminal groups are less common than opportunistic burglars, but they also occupy police investigators.

One case investigated by detectives at the station illustrates how quietly a burglary can be carried out. Goldberg recalled a serial burglar who would walk between seven and 10 kilometers (4.3-6.2 miles) through central Tel Aviv every day looking for opportunities. Detectives followed him for four days before observing him enter an apartment and leave with stolen property. When officers entered the apartment, they found few visible signs that anyone had rummaged through the residents' belongings. The suspect was subsequently arrested with jewelry, cash and other property in his possession, and an indictment was filed against him following the investigation.

According to Goldberg, it is no coincidence that Tel Aviv is an attractive destination for property offenders. The combination of older buildings, apartments with inadequate security measures, affluent residents, young people living in shared apartments and elderly residents creates a variety of opportunities for burglars.

Police say that while some younger residents take unnecessary risks with their home security, criminals sometimes exploit the predictable daily routines of older residents. The physical layout of some of the city's older buildings and the absence of effective security measures also contribute to their vulnerability, Goldberg said.

Goldberg pointed to another trend: the involvement of people residing illegally in Israel in property crimes. Over the past year, he said, police have encountered more cases involving people employed in Israel without authorization, including at construction sites, who allegedly exploited their familiarity with the surrounding area to commit burglaries. No figures were provided regarding their proportion of all burglaries in the city.

Not all burglars stop after a single visit. Police are also familiar with buildings that have experienced multiple break-ins. Goldberg said a successful burglary sometimes prompts offenders to return to the same building and target additional apartments. Police identify these locations as areas requiring particular attention.

S., who lives in a small ground-floor apartment, described how a man she believes attempted to enter her home returned just hours after she discovered her apartment key was missing. "Someone broke into my home early in the morning and took my key while I was sleeping. At noon, I saw the man trying to open my door," she recalled. Her front door is only approximately 1.5 meters (five feet) from her bed. She initially dismissed noises near the entrance as a cat, but when she got up to investigate, she discovered that her key was missing and the door was unlocked.
A Nova massacre survivor chases a burglar inside her home
(Photo: Miki Ben Shoshan)

When S. went outside, she noticed that the building's lighting was also switched off. That morning, she called a locksmith and replaced the lock, a decision that proved particularly significant several hours later. When she returned home around noon, she noticed a man crouching and peering into her apartment. She asked him what he was doing, and an argument ensued. When she entered her home, she discovered that her new key was lying on the floor.

According to S., the man tried to push her inside the apartment. She began shouting, attempted to photograph him and threatened to alert her neighbors. Eventually, the man left. S. called the police, and two officers arrived at her home and recommended that she file a complaint. Looking back, she realizes how easily the encounter could have ended differently. Among her most treasured possessions is her grandmother's engagement ring, which her grandmother managed to preserve throughout the Holocaust.

An unusual encounter between a resident and a burglar was captured on video in neighboring Bat Yam. Miri Ben Shoshan, a survivor of the Nova music festival massacre, woke up at 2 a.m. on October 22 and discovered a stranger inside her home. Footage she subsequently published shows her rushing toward the intruder, who fled through a window. "My husband and I are Nova survivors, so we're very light sleepers," she recalled. "At 2 a.m., I heard noises. I woke up and thought, wait, am I imagining things?" When she realized a stranger was inside her home while her children slept, she reacted instinctively. "I lunged at him, ran and screamed."

The burglar was not located, and Miri received notification last week that the investigation had been closed. She consequently decided to publish the footage on social media, hoping someone would recognize the man. The couple installed security bars on all their apartment windows the day after the burglary, but their sense of security has not returned. "I couldn't really speak for the first two weeks," she said.

Police recommend that residents consistently lock doors and windows, avoid leaving keys outside their homes and assess the effectiveness of their security measures, particularly in older buildings. They also urge residents to report every burglary, even when the financial damage appears insignificant, because each complaint could help investigators connect incidents and identify serial offenders. Anyone encountering a burglar should avoid a potentially dangerous physical confrontation and contact police from a safe location.

Ultimately, the real damage left behind by burglars cannot easily be measured in indictments, arrests or the value of stolen property. For Maor, Yaron, S. and Miri, the burglary did not end when the stranger left their home. It continues every time they check a lock, hear an unfamiliar noise in the middle of the night or imagine what might have happened. "You can earn the money again, replace the documents and change the locks," Maor said. "But it's much harder to regain the feeling that you can close your eyes at home without worrying that someone might be walking around while you're asleep."

articles.title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
articles.summary: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
paragraphs: World affairs editorReporting fromKyiv

Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.
How does it all end?

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.
Lead image: Global Images Ukraine/Getty/EPA/Shutterstock
