articles.title: Not just tents: how Hezbollah built a fortified compound inside Israeli territory
articles.summary: Dismissed before the war as a minor provocation, the Mount Dov site reveals reinforced concrete and independent power systems; reservists report finding maps of IDF positions in abandoned UN posts as Israel returns to an outpost it left in 2000
paragraphs: Dismissed before the war as a minor provocation, the Mount Dov site reveals reinforced concrete and independent power systems; reservists report finding maps of IDF positions in abandoned UN posts as Israel returns to an outpost it left in 2000

For months during the summer of 2023, Israelis were presented with a relatively reassuring image of the compound Hezbollah had established on Mount Dov: temporary canvas tents that appeared to be little more than a provocation or a localized nuisance, perhaps even one that would disappear once winter snow covered the slopes of Mount Hermon. Since the compound was destroyed in an Israeli airstrike at the outbreak of the war, no journalists had documented what lay inside.

Now, for the first time, the ruins of what became a symbol of Israel's security failures along its northern border have been exposed. A ynet visit to the site reveals a dramatically different picture. Amid the dust, rocks and vegetation that has since grown over the area lie the remains of what appears to have been a fortified military outpost, a far cry from the temporary encampment Israeli officials described or believed it to be at the time.
An independent electrical system, reinforced concrete and cooking utensils. The Hezbollah tent compound destroyed in an airstrike at the outbreak of the war
Aerial footage from 2023 showing Hezbollah's tent compound and an armed terrorist moving around the area in broad daylight

Large fragments of reinforced concrete, protruding steel reinforcement bars, heavy rusted steel beams and metal panels twisted by the force and heat of the explosions are scattered throughout the compound. Some appear to be remnants of a container or reinforced roofing, while aluminum frames indicate the presence of permanent windows, doors or partitions.

The crater also contains remnants of the temporary structures familiar to Israelis from photographs taken at a distance: white tarpaulins and wooden platforms used as flooring over the rocky terrain. Their presence alongside construction debris suggests the tents may have concealed more substantial structures.

Among the shattered concrete are the remains of an independent electrical system, including batteries, power converters, electrical control equipment and communication cables. Together with generators stationed at the compound, the infrastructure appears to have been designed to keep the position operational and heated for months, even during Mount Dov's harsh winters. The compound, occupied by Hezbollah terrorists and occasionally members of its elite Radwan Force, was apparently much more than a temporary observation post overlooking Israel.

Evidence of everyday life is also scattered throughout the wreckage: a nearly intact red cooking pot, a blue plastic bowl and a decorated ceramic cup. Several large plastic barrels of the kind Hezbollah uses to store water, fuel or equipment remain nearby.
Israel in the background. Hezbollah's tent on Mount Dov in the summer of 2023
The bombed compound today
A close-up of the ruins of Hezbollah's tent compound

Standing on the ridge overlooking the valley, the discrepancy between Israel's assessment of the threat and what Hezbollah had actually established becomes apparent. Then-defense minister Yoav Gallant dismissed the compound as a "small, non-strategic incident," while the IDF described it as a "cheap provocation." Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu refrained from ordering its destruction. Yet the remains suggest Hezbollah had established a fortified, permanent position that extended from Lebanon into sovereign Israeli territory.

According to an analysis by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, Hezbollah erected its first tent on April 8, 2023, south of the UN-demarcated Blue Line, near a UN position. A second tent was erected in late May inside Israeli territory. Evidence at the site, however, suggests the compound consisted of more than those two tents.

The compound was destroyed in an Israeli airstrike on October 8, 2023, following Hezbollah fire toward an IDF position on Mount Dov. Troops from the IDF's 210th Division subsequently reached the site and discovered several weapons, although most had already been removed. No underground infrastructure was found at the compound itself. The visit by Ynet provides the first journalistic documentation from inside the site, which had previously been photographed only from a distance or during restricted media tours organized by Hezbollah.

Reservists from the Carmeli Brigade's 221st Battalion, who recently completed their seventh deployment since the outbreak of the war, have been working to dismantle Hezbollah's terrorist infrastructure throughout the area. Operating under the 810th Mountain Brigade of the 210th Bashan Division, they describe a security reality fundamentally different from the years of restraint that preceded the war and the 26 years since Israel withdrew from southern Lebanon.

Until approximately a year ago, the soldiers said, reaching IDF positions on Mount Dov was a dangerous undertaking dependent on weather conditions and visibility. Military convoys were frequently canceled, while others came under fire and suffered casualties. Today, following the fighting associated with Operation Roaring Lion, soldiers describe significantly greater freedom of movement in the same area where Hezbollah once established its positions largely unchallenged.
Soldiers from the 221st Battalion overlooking the area from the Fortress on Mount Dov: 'Hezbollah used to move around here freely'
The Fortress on Mount Dov
The Lebanese village of Shebaa

Not far from the former tent compound stands another prominent structure, known to the soldiers as "the Fortress." Construction was interrupted by the war, and the building overlooks the Lebanese village of Shebaa. The battalion's commander, Lt. Col. (res.) Y., said his troops had recently cleared an area associated with the Hezbollah rocket attack that killed 12 children in Majdal Shams in 2024.

The commander, a resident of the West Bank and veteran of the IDF's Egoz commando unit, assumed command of the battalion in November 2025 during its sixth deployment. He believes the Fortress was intended to provide cover for Hezbollah's activities near the Israeli border.

"This building was apparently supposed to be a vacation home that Hezbollah intended to construct, allowing it to establish a presence close to us under the guise of civilian construction," he said. "We call it the 'Beaufort of Mount Dov.' To me, what you see here represents the most significant change, even more than the tent incident. Hezbollah used to move around here freely and established actual military positions right up to the Blue Line."

The battalion's operations have also exposed extensive underground infrastructure. In recent weeks, troops operating alongside Yahalom, the IDF's elite combat engineering unit, discovered and destroyed an approximately 100-meter-long tunnel equipped with sleeping quarters, toilets and showers, as well as an underground weapons storage facility. According to the battalion commander, the infrastructure was intended to support attacks against Israeli civilians and troops, including a potential assault on Mount Dov.

Maj. H., commander of the battalion's combat support company, compared the military's current freedom of operation with his experience as a soldier in 2010, when even a minor crossing of the Blue Line required exceptional authorization. What was once Hezbollah's playground, he said, has become an area of active Israeli military operations.

As Israeli forces have gained greater control over the region and entered abandoned positions belonging to the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), officers have raised new allegations about the conduct of the international peacekeeping force. UNIFIL's mandate is due to expire at the end of December.

"We found maps in positions abandoned by UNIFIL that actually showed our outposts, individual tank positions and the deployment of our military posts," Lt. Col. Y. said. He described finding maps and markings identifying Israeli military positions displayed inside a former UN facility.
Ynet correspondent Yair Kraus inside a former UNIFIL position: 'They monitored us as though we were the enemy'
The Vered Hadash outpost on Mount Dov, recaptured by the IDF after 26 years

"The amazing thing about UNIFIL is that they stood here on the border watching and monitoring us as though we were the enemy," he said. "You suddenly realize that their watchtowers were facing us. Their mandate was to ensure Hezbollah did not deploy weapons south of the Litani River and that we did not cross the border. In practice, we did not cross, while Hezbollah spent 18 years, since the Second Lebanon War, moving enormous quantities of weapons. The UN paved roads throughout this area, and Hezbollah used them."

One of the clearest symbols of the dramatic change in the region, revealed here for the first time, is the renewed occupation of the IDF's Vered Hadash outpost. Established in the 1980s during Israel's former security zone in southern Lebanon, the position was abandoned during the withdrawal in 2000 and subsequently taken over by the Lebanese army.

In recent months, following renewed fighting associated with Operation Roaring Lion in Iran, the IDF recaptured the outpost. This week, soldiers from the ultra-Orthodox Netzah Yehuda Battalion began manning the fortified position, which has become part of Israel's renewed military presence inside southern Lebanon.

Lebanese flags still decorate the walls of the former Israeli outpost, where several company commanders from the 221st Battalion described the challenges of operating in the mountainous region. Unlike Shiite villages evacuated during the ground offensive, Shebaa and Kfar Shuba are predominantly Sunni, while nearby Ain Mari is a Druze village.

These are among the few villages whose residents are permitted to remain within the area demarcated by the Yellow Line, which the Lebanese army is prohibited from crossing. Israeli officers say Hezbollah exploits this arrangement.

"We found weapons and explosive devices in homes here that looked completely new. Some probably arrived after 2023," one officer said, alleging that Hezbollah recruits local residents to assist its operations in exchange for payment.

Another challenge facing the troops is the Lebanese Resistance Brigades, a Hezbollah-backed military organization that recruits from outside the country's Shiite population. According to Israeli officers, its members receive regular salaries to collect intelligence on IDF activities while remaining embedded in local villages.

On November 16, soldiers from the battalion arrested two brothers suspected of belonging to the organization during an operation in Shebaa. Their brother, Maher Hamdan, was arrested approximately a year earlier while reportedly herding goats near the village and has since been held in Israel.
Carmeli Brigade commanders at the Vered Hadash outpost
IDF land-clearing and security operations in the Mount Dov area

"We worked very hard to get this operation approved and insisted that we carry it out ourselves," said Capt. Y., commander of the company responsible for the arrests. "This is not something we normally do as a reserve battalion. We're a battalion accustomed to carrying out very loud and aggressive operations, and now we were dealing with something much quieter." According to the soldiers, the two suspects were completely surprised by their arrests and cooperated.

Smuggling is another challenge in the mountainous border region linking Lebanon and Syria. For years, criminal networks have transported goods between the two countries, including alcohol and drugs. Israeli forces monitor the activity to prevent weapons and terrorists from entering the newly established security zone and southern Lebanon.

The extensive military operations, from destroying Hezbollah tunnels to arresting suspects in Lebanese villages, are being conducted by reservists now completing their seventh deployment since October 2023. Capt. A., a company commander, describes soldiers whose average age exceeds 40, some of them already grandfathers, undertaking physically demanding operations in difficult mountainous terrain. Many are paying a substantial personal, financial and professional price for their continued service.

"Every citizen in Israel needs to know that there are people losing jobs, losing money and perhaps experiencing personal crises, paying an enormous price to come here even after three years of war, to find and destroy every piece of terrorist infrastructure and prevent the enemy from approaching this area again," he said. "They leave everything behind to eliminate every remaining Hezbollah capability that could threaten us or harm us again, and to provide security for northern Israel."
Lt. Col. (res.) Y., commander of the 221st Battalion: 'I cannot envision a situation in which we withdraw from here again'
Israeli forces in southern Lebanon: 'Everyone will come. They call us, and we come'

Battalion commanders say turnout during the latest deployment exceeded even the number of reservists who reported for duty immediately after the October 7 massacre. That increase was made possible by more than 100 new soldiers who joined the battalion over the past year. Many had only recently completed more than two years of intensive combat service, choosing to postpone overseas trips or academic studies and immediately join the reserve brigade, which consists predominantly of Golani Brigade veterans.

The combination of veteran reservists, some of whom served at Israeli positions in southern Lebanon before the 2000 withdrawal, and young soldiers with recent combat experience has strengthened the battalion's operational capabilities.

"Hezbollah used to move around here freely, establish positions and even allow itself to cross into our sovereign territory and build that tent compound," Lt. Col. Y. said. "I cannot envision a situation in which we withdraw from here again."

Maintaining that control will require continued military activity, and the reservists already expect to be called up again, potentially as early as August 2027. Among themselves, they discuss the political deadlock and promises to broaden the burden of military service across Israeli society. Despite growing concerns about exhaustion after repeated deployments, their commanders remain confident.
"Everyone will come. I have absolutely no doubt," Capt. Y. said. "They call us, and we come."

articles.title: Who's your rabbi? A new generation is redefining Jewish spiritual leadership beyond the synagogue
articles.summary: JEWISH AFFAIRS: A new generation of Israeli spiritual leaders is redefining the role of rabbis through unconventional approaches, even making schnitzel.
paragraphs: On a Wednesday morning earlier this month, Bill Lipsey visited Rabbi Naomi Efrat’s Reform community in Pardes Hanna-Karkur. That afternoon, he was in Rishon Lezion with Rabbi Arye Nizevich, a Russian-speaking Chabad rabbi who came to Israel from Ukraine.
When the rabbis described Shabbat in their communities, both brought up chicken soup.
Lipsey, who describes himself as “an observant Conservative Jew,” had come on behalf of the Honey Foundation for Israel, which he and his wife, Amy, founded a decade ago.
In Pardes Hanna, he told The Jerusalem Post, people had found “a leader who’s speaking to them, who’s seeing them, who’s caring about them.”
From his own synagogue in New Jersey, Lipsey brought an expectation about the job. You ought to be able to call the rabbi about something going on in your family and reach someone who knows you.
In Pardes Hanna and Rishon Lezion, the families had already decided whom to call. Lipsey’s foundation helps pay for that person’s time.
Rabbi Naomi Efrat’s spiritual leadership from Haifa to Pardes Hanna-Karkur
Efrat’s congregation, Kehilat HaPardes, posted an invitation to Friday-night prayers in a living room. Efrat and Shiri Elkabetz would lead Kabbalat Shabbat, the service welcoming the Sabbath.
There would be chai, then dinner and a jam session. Everyone was asked to bring a dish big enough to share. “Thanks to the anonymous donor who bought us all that cutlery!” the invitation added.

Efrat grew up in Haifa in a family affiliated with the Conservative movement, with roots in Turkey, Romania, Syria, and the United States. At synagogue with her father, she struggled to follow the prayer book and wished she could go outside and play.

After becoming a mother, she went looking for spiritual support herself. In Beersheba, she founded a Reform congregation with a center for parents and children. Hebrew Union College ordained her in Jerusalem in 2021.
She calls herself a Reform rabbi, and Lipsey hears a neo-hassidic influence in her Judaism.

Efrat studied literature and creative writing at Ben-Gurion University. Her rabbinical thesis explored how lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender poets who grew up Orthodox used classical Jewish texts.
Modern Hebrew verse finds its way into her holiday services alongside traditional liturgical poems.
In an interview Ynet published with the Israeli Reform movement, Efrat described whole families gathering beneath one tallit, or prayer shawl, for the priestly blessing.

A father can pray beside his daughter, and a mother beside her son. Children come close enough to touch the Torah. Efrat also wants to be there “when you get home from a date at 11 at night, and you’re upset and need someone to talk to.”
Rabbi Arye Nizevich extends open invitation to his Rishon Lezion community
Nizevich’s Chabad community in Rishon Lezion’s Neve Hof neighborhood has an invitation of its own. “We speak the same language as you!” its website says.
Visitors can sign up for an evening Torah class, find a group for teenagers, or ask for help putting up a mezuzah in a new home. There is a button for putting a question to the rabbi privately.

Some who come on Shabbat had little connection to Orthodox practice in Ukraine, Lipsey said. They fled one war and are watching their children live through what he called “the war they arrived to.” Many are still learning Hebrew.
Nizevich belongs to a worldwide hassidic movement. He also moved from Ukraine, and they can tell him in Russian what happened to them.
The synagogue an immigrant brings along

During the year the Lipseys and their youngest child lived in Israel in 2010-11, Israelis had trouble placing Bill. Here was an American who knew his way around a synagogue and generally went without a kippah. Was he religious or secular?

“Why can’t I be yes and yes?” he recalled thinking. He began asking Israelis how they saw themselves. His advice to Americans is to take the guided tour, then set aside two days for coffee shops. Tell the person at the next table you’d like to know what life is like here. “You won’t believe it. They’ll actually talk to you.”
Lipsey served as president of Congregation Agudath Israel in Caldwell, New Jersey, and on the executive committee of the Masorti Foundation for Conservative Judaism in Israel.
In 2019, his daughter, Sarah Lipsey Brokman, then president of the Honey Foundation, credited two rabbis at her own New Jersey congregation as models for community rabbis in Israel.

Lipsey spoke broadly of a temptation in Diaspora Judaism to “create its own image here.” A seminary seeking a foothold in Israel, a federation deciding how to spend its money, and an immigrant who misses the shul she grew up in each have reasons for favoring a particular kind of congregation.
In 1978, Rabbi Michael Graetz of Omer, outside Beersheba, and Rabbi Moshe Cohen went to look for American support for Israel’s emerging Conservative movement, known here as Masorti.

The name itself can confuse an American visitor. Masorti is also an everyday Hebrew word for “traditional.” An Israeli who uses it may be telling you how her family lives, regardless of whether she belongs to a synagogue.
At a Conservative synagogue in Washington, they raised $30,000. A fundraiser in Palm Beach was under discussion.

In his history of Masorti Judaism in Israel, Rabbi Harvey Meirovich recounts what happened when word reached Rabbi Gerson Cohen, chancellor of the Jewish Theological Seminary in New York. The chancellor supported the Israelis. His own institution also depended on those donors.

The seminary guaranteed the movement $50,000 a year for three years. Israeli Masorti congregations could approach American synagogues and invite their congregants to become overseas members. They agreed to coordinate their fundraising with the seminary.
Back in Omer, Graetz’s congregation had begun with 10 families after the 1973 Yom Kippur War, some from the US and South Africa, others Israelis who had encountered Conservative Judaism in America.
It ran a summer day camp open to the town. Neighbors who had never joined called on the rabbi for family occasions. By the late 1990s, most members were Israeli-born.

The Reform seminary where Efrat trained opened its Jerusalem campus in 1963. By the late 1980s, according to Rabbi Naamah Kelman, a former dean there, North American federations were directing funds to Israel’s liberal movements.
American Jewish leaders pressed the Jewish Agency to fund Reform and Masorti institutions. Synagogues in Haifa and Jerusalem ran preschools and youth groups.

New York’s federation also backed secular and Modern Orthodox initiatives. Kelman put her own movement’s dilemma this way in 2010. “When does insisting that we are Reform make us foreign to the Israeli public?”
Modern Orthodox community Ra’anana adopts American synagogue model

In Ra’anana, one Modern Orthodox community deliberately adopted the American synagogue model. Children go to Shabbat groups, members serve on committees, and a full-time rabbi takes a close interest in congregants’ lives.

Many members came from the Diaspora. For a parent who grew up in a shul like that, there’s comfort in walking in on the first Saturday morning and knowing exactly where the children go. The choice was the congregation’s.
A donor hoping to repeat the experiment a few towns over would have to ask the families there what they wanted.

The Honey Foundation starts by asking whom a community already relies on. Rabbanit Shira Marili-Mirvis was a fellow herself when she became spiritual leader of Shirat HaTamar in Efrat. She now heads the foundation in Israel.

Asked about their affiliation, some applicants wrote about observing Jewish law, others about their relationship with God. Some described themselves as secular and attached to their Jewish identity, she told the Post’s Sarah Ben-Nun.
In some kibbutzim, a member had begun leading Friday-night prayers on the lawn. One incoming fellow described a weekly Talmud class where neighbors argued about philosophy.
Lipsey also counts two Young Israel congregations, a name familiar to generations of Orthodox Americans, among the communities the foundation supports.
Of the 53 fellows introduced in Jerusalem on November 19, Lipsey said 12 were Orthodox women already leading communities without a formal title.

When Lipsey mentioned Ester Horowitz in Nahariya, he and his colleagues paused over whether she was ordained. They could readily describe her Friday-night dinners and the hundreds who came to her for Passover Seder.

Horowitz’s community, Clouds of Glory, identifies Rabbi Tzvi Hirsch Bichman as its rabbi and Horowitz as its organizer and leader. She teaches Torah in Russian, prepares children and adults for conversion, and is herself studying for ordination.

She and Bichman describe a community of around 300, among them new immigrants, elderly residents, and soldiers. Lipsey counted six Russian-speaking leaders among the incoming fellows. Their communities range from liberal to Chabad.

A fellowship pays for 10 hours a week for three years. A fellow might use an afternoon to prepare a class or sit down for coffee with someone in the congregation. Each fellow also chooses a mentor and takes at least one professional course a year.

Marili-Mirvis had studied Jewish law for five years before becoming a community leader. “Ultimately, you come into a community, and the knowledge required of you is human, social and emotional,” she said.
The foundation put a question to the fellows whose terms end in December. If money were no object, would they take the job that paid the highest salary or carry on as the community rabbi?
“One hundred percent chose rabbi,” Lipsey said. The foundation can renew a stipend after three years. For the 53 places in its incoming group, it interviewed 112 candidates.

At the foundation’s first conference in Tel Aviv in 2019, about 200 rabbis and other leaders came together. At the time, Sarah Lipsey Brokman told the New Jersey Jewish News: “We wanted all the rabbis and spiritual leaders we are supporting to learn together.”
One of Lipsey’s colleagues remembered participants who were glad to attend and anxious about being seen together. “Maybe you shouldn’t take our picture together,” he recalled them saying.
At a later gathering in a botanical garden, the organizers recalled, participants danced holding hands. At a meeting earlier this year, the fellows sat down to study together.
“Nobody feels like they’re being judged, like they’re lesser or greater when they go in that room,” Lipsey said.
Rabbi, chef Nissimmi Naim Naor combines leadership, spirituality through cooking

Asked for another example of an Israeli rabbi, Lipsey thought of a chef. Nissimmi Naim Naor leads Jerusalem’s Siah Yitzhak community. In the reserves after the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led massacre, he organized military funerals in the Jerusalem area.

In an essay he wrote with his wife, the poet Shlomit Naim Naor, for the National Library of Israel, he recalled the weekly prayer for the hostages. Hundreds of people fell silent as he read each hostage’s given name and the name of their mother.
For a time he lost his desire to cook. Then a friend whose husband had been killed asked him to bake a chocolate and pecan babka for the Shabbat that fell during shiva, the week of mourning.
When he taught a group of rabbis from New York, one remembered the cake she ate while mourning her father. They all cried, he wrote.

On his series for Israel’s public broadcaster, KAN, Naim Naor cooks with bereaved families. Mika and Boaz Zussman came on Pot of Yearning (Sir Ga’agua) to remember their brother Ben, who was killed in Gaza at 22.
On the rabbi’s program, they remembered him with schnitzel, mashed potatoes, and salad.

articles.title: Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez confident of election victory despite polls – as it happened
articles.summary: This blog is now closed Freelance journalist based in Madrid and host of the Sobremesa podcast Vox has often been portrayed in international coverage as a party of Franco nostalgists whose ultraconservative Catholicism and civil-war rhetoric towards the separatist Catalan “enemy within” threatened a return to the worst of Spain’s recent past. Continue reading...
paragraphs: 'I can’t conceive of us losing,' Sánchez says despite adverse polling

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said on Friday that he was convinced he would ⁠secure a left-wing majority ⁠in a snap ​general election despite adverse public polling, as the political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning ahead of Sunday’s vote, Reuters reported.

Amid a legal ban on publishing new ⁠opinion surveys, the Socialist leader insisted that internal data suggested his party would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller ⁠leftist allies.

“I can’t conceive of us losing,” Sanchez told radio station SER, adding that left-leaning voters were ​increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a ‌prerequisite for reaching a progressive ‌majority to tackle issues such as the country’s deep housing crisis.
double quotation mark“When progressive Spain gets going, it’s unstoppable.”

However, nearly all the polls released before ‌the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People’s Party and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.
Will Spain’s housing crisis bring the far right to power? – video
Why all of Europe should be watching as Spain’s far-right Vox closes in on power
Race hate exploded in this Spanish town last year. Now its residents are bracing for more
The polls in Spain fall mainly in … Adelaide?
Join us Sunday night for live blog on 2026 Spanish election
Spain’s ‘rambling’ closing debate sparks row over opposition leader’s ‘sexist’ remark
EU budget talks break down, set to resume in mid-December
Nato jets scrambled after drone 'briefly' enters Latvian airspace from Russia
Morning opening: Putin 'cannot be a friend,' Zelenskyy says on Trump's comments

As mass protests over a nationwide housing crisis have forced Sánchez into an early general election, the Guardian travelled to Spain’s Andalusian coast to find out what’s driving the housing crisis, what solutions are on offer and why rightwing populists are gaining ground.
You can watch our film here:
In Spain, the parties are set to hold their closing rallies this evening, ​with the Socialists ‌and the Broad ​Front choosing Madrid for their ​events.
Meanwhile, the PP and Vox have opted for Seville and Valencia.
Spaniards observe a “day of reflection” on the eve of the vote. Campaigning, rallies and political advertising are banned so voters can weigh their choices before heading to the polls.
Freelance journalist based in Madrid and host of the Sobremesa podcast

Vox has often been portrayed in international coverage as a party of Franco nostalgists whose ultraconservative Catholicism and civil-war rhetoric towards the separatist Catalan “enemy within” threatened a return to the worst of Spain’s recent past.
Yet since its disappointing showing at the 2023 general election, Abascal has purged much of the party’s original leadership and overseen an ideological renewal.

In looking to update its messaging, Vox has blended elements of Marine Le Pen’s welfare chauvinism, such as the concept of “national priority”, with ideas coming from the pan-European, white nationalist identitarian movement.

Virtually absent from Spanish political debate a year ago, national priority would give Spaniards preferential access to social housing, public services and welfare benefits, with Vox already securing PP backing for the principle in regional coalition deals.

In September, however, the European Commission warned that even the residence-based criteria used at a regional level could discriminate against citizens of other EU member states. Vox’s general election manifesto goes further, pledging to exclude all non-Spanish citizens from the country’s minimum-income benefit.

If the polls are right, PP’s Alberto Núñez Feijóo could become prime minister on a lower vote share than the PP secured in the last election. He would then owe his majority to Vox’s surge and support in coalition, and Abascal would have both the leverage and the incentive to show his voters what the party can deliver in office.

A coalition formed on those terms could also foreshadow a closer alliance between conservatives and the far right at a European level. A Le Pen victory in the French presidential election next spring would put the nationalist right at the head of one of the EU’s two most influential states, shifting the political centre of gravity in Brussels and opening the way for a durable governing bloc to the right of the EU’s traditional grand coalition.

It was not by chance that Vox opened its election campaign with a rally displaying video messages of support from Le Pen, Meloni and AfD’s Alice Weidel. Having drawn on its far-right European allies to reinvent itself, Vox could now in turn strengthen their hand if it is successful in becoming the PP’s kingmaker after Sunday’s vote.
Sánchez’s defeat would also deprive the centre left of its strongest counterweight in the European Council, where he is the only social democrat to represent one of the EU’s major powers.
Speaking to the Vox rally, Weidel proclaimed: “All of Europe is waiting for a political change in Madrid.” All of Europe may not be waiting for such a change, but it is certainly watching.
European community affairs correspondent
Sitting on a park bench, taking in the sunny day, Naima reflected on all that had seemingly changed since she moved to Spain three decades earlier.
Back then, the Moroccan national had felt warmly welcomed by Spaniards. “I had never, at any point in my life, felt like there was racism,” she said.
“But now things are changing. And the blame lies with rightwing politics.”

Over the years, she has steadily watched as a growing crop of politicians sought to win votes by demonising migrants, minorities and Muslims. The impact reverberated deeply in places such as Torre-Pacheco, whose fertile fields and constant demand for farmhands has long attracted workers from around the world.

“They peddle racism, and lots of people end up suffering,” said Naima, 53. “Here everyone knows me, but others speak of being treated differently, looked at in a certain way, or having gestures made at them.”
On Sunday, Spain is set to gain a glimpse of how deeply engrained these divisions have become as voters cast their ballots in a snap general election.

Most polls suggest the government of the Socialist leader, Pedro Sánchez, will be replaced by a rightwing coalition led by the conservative People’s party (PP) and supported by the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party.
If so, it will be the first time that a far-right party has governed Spain since the return to democracy after the death of General Franco.
No new polls are allowed to be published in Spain in the five days before a Spanish election, but one company has found a surprising solución alternativa.

The Adelaide Review ran from 1984 to 2020, covering the city’s cultural and artistic life until Covid and upheavals in the media world made it “untenable”, its editor, Amanda Pepe, wrote in the final edition.
But now it has found unexpected new life as an, erm, back passage for Spanish polls in the blackout period.
The Review site is now owned by a company called Prensa Ibérica, which also runs the Spanish newspaper El Periódico.
An article on the Periódico website that links to the poll criticises “outdated legislation” that lets political parties see polls, but not citizens.
“The Adelaide Review’s daily poll addresses this issue, giving citizens access to the same information used by politicians,” it said.

It’s probably a good moment to say that we will be running a special Europe live blog from Madrid on Sunday night to bring you all the latest in the Spanish parliamentary election, including first polls, projections, reactions, and analysis.
Make sure to tune in on Sunday late afternoon and evening.

Last night’s debate between the leaders of Spain’s four biggest political parties was a rambling, ratty and revealing spectacle in which Ada Colau, the leader of the leftwing Broad Front, is generally agreed to have come out on top.
Colau, a former Barcelona mayor, was committed and forensic in her attacks on Vox’s leader, Santiago Abascal, over his refusal to condemn gender-based violence.

She and the socialist leader and current prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, also joined forces to question the economic wisdom of the far-right party’s plans for €112bn of public spending costs, and to defend the benefits of immigration.

Sánchez – who was far more animated and engaged in this debate than in last week’s head-to-head with Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of Spain’s conservative People’s party (PP) – was happy to wind up his rival over his lack of English skills.
Before Feijóo could answer a question from Colau about the PP’s proposed tax cuts, Sánchez – a fluent English speaker – quipped:
“I’m sorry to say that Mr Feijóo’s maths are about as good as his English.”
Vox’s Abascal was keen to keep the focus on immigration and on corruption – a problem, he added, “that ruins and kills”.

Feijóo also sought to attack Sánchez’s government over corruption, the two deadly rail crashes suffered this year, and over the summer’s mass border crossing into the North African territory of Ceuta.

He argued that his 30-year political career was unblemished by corruption allegations while suggesting that Sánchez was a “corruption magnet”. That led the prime minister to bring up the infamous mid-1990s holiday photos that show Feijóo hanging out on a boat with his friend Marcial Dorado, who was later convicted of drug trafficking.

But the biggest moment of the night came when Colau asked Feijóo how he could claim to be a good leader when his party had doggedly stood by Carlos Mazón, the PP president of the Valencia region who was eventually forced to resign over his disastrous handling of the floods two years ago that killed more than 230 people.

“Look, good management is taking charge in a national emergency and not running away from Paiporta,” Feijóo said in reference to Sánchez’s hasty exit from one of the areas that was worst hit by the floods after angry locals pelted him with mud during a visit shortly after the disaster.

But it was what came next that caused a stir. Turning to Colau – who, by the time of the floods in the autumn of 2024, had left the Barcelona mayoralty and no longer held public office – Feijóo said, “Y usted calladita” which translates as, “And there wasn’t a peep out of you”.
He accompanied those words putting his finger to his lips – a gesture some took to be a sexist shushing of the Broad Front leader.
Although Feijóo seemed to be trying to claim that Colau had remained silent over the floods when they happened, some took his words as an attempt to tell her to be quiet.
Sánchez was quick to pounce. “Why are you saying, ‘Not a peep out of you’, Mr Feijóo?” the prime minister asked the PP leader. “What kind of sexism is that, Mr Feijóo,” Sánchez added.
Feijóo accused Sánchez of trying to twist his words, but the damage was done. Speaking after the debate, the PP leader issued a semi-apology.

“If I’ve offended anyone, I of course take it back,” he said, adding that he hadn’t been telling Colau to be quiet. But he couldn’t resist arguing that Sánchez leftwing allies had kept quiet “during all the years of corruption”.
Colau herself said the PP leader’s words undermined his supposed feminist credentials. Speaking after the debate, she said:

“I think it was very clear what [Feijóo] was trying to do when he said ‘calladita’. That clearly sexist behaviour was witnessed on TV by all of Spain … As women we will not stop and we will not shut up. No one will make us shut up and we will go and vote.”
And since Spain’s Pedro Sánchez skipped the summit altogether as he’s dramatically fighting for his future ahead of this Sunday’s parliamentary election…
… let’s cross to Madrid for an update on last night’s TV debate…
In yesterday’s blog, I promised to give you an update this morning on the EU summit, which continued into the small hours.
Well, not much happened, as the talks on the bloc’s next budget collapsed with no agreement, with a group of countries reportedly refusing to take part in further pointless meetings.

The format set the “Sensible Seven” of frugal countries against “Friends of Cohesion” calling for sustained EU spending. With a bit of theatre, everyone disagreed with everyone, and the talks broke down shortly after midnight.
Hungary’s PM Péter Magyar said the discussions would resume at the next summit in December, but warned “there seems to be little chance of reaching a compromise on the EU’s seven-year budget.”
But Germany’s Friedrich Merz tried to stay upbeat:
“Views on the EU budget still differ widely. What is needed now is realism and goodwill. I am confident that we can reach an agreement this year – for a strong economy and a secure Europe.”

There is a bit of urgency there, as France’s Emmanuel Macron wants the discussion on the bloc’s new €1.78tn budget for 2028-2034 to be agreed before the end of the year, and well clear of the French parliamentary elections next spring.
We will keep an eye on this for you.
Overnight, Nato fighter jets and an interceptor drone were scrambled overnight in Latvia after a drone briefly entered the country’s airspace near its border with Russia, the army said.
Since the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, several countries bordering the conflict have reported incursions or drone and missile crashes on their territory.
This year, two drones were shot down over Latvia by Nato fighter jets, which protect the skies of Baltic states, Reuters reported.

articles.title: "זה מרסק אותי": הפוסט הכואב של ירדן ביבס - והדרישה לעצור את החלטת ניר עוז
articles.summary: לאחר שב-ynet נחשף כי הקיבוץ החליט לפרק את "בתי העדות" ולא בחר בחלופה שלפיה בית משפחת ביבס יהפוך לאתר זיכרון, כתב שורד השבי: "בבית הזה שרוצים להרוס היו לי חיים. בבית הזה אריאל למד לדבר. בבית הזה כפיר למד לזחול. לא אקבל שבשם השיקום, נמחק את מה שעוד נותר". אחותה של שירי: "את הבית שלה ושל ירדן אסור למחוק"
paragraphs: לאחר שב-ynet נחשף כי הקיבוץ החליט לפרק את "בתי העדות" ולא בחר בחלופה שלפיה בית משפחת ביבס יהפוך לאתר זיכרון, כתב שורד השבי: "בבית הזה שרוצים להרוס היו לי חיים. בבית הזה אריאל למד לדבר. בבית הזה כפיר למד לזחול. לא אקבל שבשם השיקום, נמחק את מה שעוד נותר". אחותה של שירי: "את הבית שלה ושל ירדן אסור למחוק"

חלופת פירוק בתי הנרצחים והנפגעים, ושחזור של כמה מהם במתחם זיכרון חיצוני שיהיה פתוח למבקרים, קיבלה 38 קולות. לפי אותה החלטה, הקיבוץ יהיה רשאי להחליט על גורל הבתים, ובהם גם ביתה של משפחת ביבס. האפשרות השנייה, שבעדה הצביעו 32 חברים, הייתה לשמר במקומם את רוב "בתי העדות", ולהקים במתחם חיצוני מיצב ממ"דים בלבד. לפי חלופה זו, שלא נבחרה, בית משפחת ביבס אמור היה להישמר ולעבור פיתוח כאתר זיכרון ומורשת.
ביתם של משפחת ביבס בניר עוז
(צילום: AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg)

"ב-7 באוקטובר חמאס ניסו למחוק אותנו. אני לא יכול לקבל שבשם השיקום והצמיחה, נמחק במו ידינו את מה שעוד נותר - את החיים שהיו ואת העדות למה שקרה. ההחלטה של חברי ניר עוז עושה בדיוק את זה", כתב ירדן ביבס. "בבית הזה שרוצים להרוס היו לי חיים. הייתה לי משפחה. בבית הזה אריאל למד ללכת ולדבר. בבית הזה כפיר העביר את החודשים הראשונים לחייו ולמד לזחול. בבית הזה היה גם טוני, כלב מדהים ורגיש שמיד קיבל את הבנים שלי באהבה גדולה ושמר עליהם כל הזמן. בבית הזה שירי ואני בנינו את המשפחה שלנו".

"בין הקירות האלה הייתה אהבה גדולה. היה צחוק של ילדים, היו רגעים קטנים של אושר, הייתה זוגיות אוהבת שאני יודע שלא אזכה לחוות שוב בחיים האלה. הבית הזה הוא זיכרון לחיים שהיו לי לפני 7 באוקטובר ולמשפחה שאיבדתי. זה המקום היחיד שנשאר לי מהם!!! גם היום אני מוצא את עצמי חוזר לשם, מנסה לעבד את מה שקרה ולהרגיש קצת יותר קרוב אליהם. זה המקום האחרון שבו ראיתי אותם מחייכים ושמחים".
הלווייתם של שירי, אריאל וכפיר ביבס

הוא כתב כי "הבית הזה הוא לא רק הזיכרון הפרטי שלי. הוא גם עדות למה שקרה בקיבוץ ניר עוז ב-7 באוקטובר. עדות לחיים שהיו כאן ולחיים שנגדעו באכזריות. גם אני רוצה לראות את ניר עוז פורח שוב, אבל החלטת הקיבוץ להרוס את הבית שלי מייסרת ומרסקת אותי. אני מאמין שאפשר לבנות עתיד מבלי להרוס את כל מה שנותר מהעבר".

לסיכום דרש שורד השבי "לעצור ולבחון מחדש את ההחלטה הזאת, לפני שיהיה מאוחר מדי. בשביל אחרים אולי מדובר בתזכורת כואבת שקשה לחיות לצידה. בשבילי, זה עדיין הבית של שירי, אריאל וכפיר. זו ההיסטוריה והמורשת של העם שלנו. איבדתי את המשפחה שלי. אני לא רוצה לאבד גם את המקום שבו היינו משפחה".
לפי החלופה שלא נבחרה, הבית היה מיועד לשימור
(צילום: REUTERS/Amir Cohen)

עד כה נהרסו שניים מתוך ארבעת הבתים שבשורה בה נמצא בית משפחת ביבס. בית זה צמוד לזה של משפחת אלגרט ושניהם טרם נהרסו - אבל לפי ההחלטה שהתקבלה הם מיועדים לפירוק. בחלופה השנייה, שלא נבחרה, נכתב כי לצד שימור בית משפחת ביבס, יש לבחון שיוקם בו מרכז גיבורי על, כמרחב זיכרון לכל ילדי ניר עוז שנרצחו.

דנה סילברמן, אחותה של שירי ובתם של יוסי ומרגיט שנרצחו בטבח 7 באוקטובר, דרשה אף היא לא להרוס את הבתים: "אני כבת שכולה, אחות שכולה ודודה שכולה, לא יכולה להשלים עם ההחלטה להרוס את כל מבני קיבוץ ניר עוז. אני רוצה לראות את ניר עוז קמה מחדש. קיבוץ חי, שוקק ומשגשג. ילדים רצים בשביליו, משפחות בונות בו את ביתן, וקולות של חיים חוזרים למקום הזה. אבל למה השיקום חייב לבוא על חשבון הזיכרון?
(צילום: מתוך הרשותות החברתיות )

"לא כל בית הוא רק קירות. יש בתים שהם עדות לחיים שהיו כאן, למשפחות, לאהבות ולחלומות שנגדעו. ואת הבית של שירי וירדן אסור למחוק. זה הבית שלהם. חלק מהסיפור שלהם, שלנו ושל ניר עוז כולה. ב-7 באוקטובר איבדנו את האנשים שלנו. האם עכשיו אנחנו אמורים לאבד גם את המקומות שבהם הם חיו? שיקום הוא לא מחיקה. תקומה היא לא שכחה. אני קוראת למקבלי ההחלטות לעצור ולבחון מחדש את ההחלטה. לשמר בתים בעלי משמעות היסטורית ואישית, ובראשם הבית של שירי וירדן. יש דברים שאפשר לבנות מחדש. יש דברים שאם נהרוס, לעולם לא נוכל להחזיר".

היא כתבה כי היא "מכבדת את זכותה של הקהילה לקבל החלטות על עתידה, ובוודאי מבינה את הכאב, המורכבות והרצון להתחיל מחדש. אבל גם החלטה שהתקבלה ברוב קולות ראויה לבחינה מחודשת. במיוחד כשמדובר במבנים שהם לא רק רכוש פרטי או ציבורי, אלא חלק מהזיכרון והמורשת של כולנו. אני גם סבורה שלאור האירוע החריג והמטלטל של 7 באוקטובר, ההחלטה על גורל בתי הקיבוץ והמורשת שלו לא יכולה להיות נתונה רק לחברי הקיבוץ. זכות ההשפעה וההצבעה בנושא הזה צריכה להינתן לכל מי שחי והתגורר בניר עוז באותו יום, ושחייו וביתו היו חלק מהקהילה שנפגעה".

בשבוע שעבר דן בג"ץ בעתירת משפחות שכולות נגד הריסת שכונת "דור צעיר" בכפר עזה, שהפכה גם היא לאחד מסמלי טבח 7 באוקטובר. העתירה הוגשה לאחר שכמו בניר עוז, חברי הקיבוץ הצביעו ברוב קולות בעד פינוי בתי השכונה והעתקת חלק מהם לאתר הנצחה חיצוני.

articles.title: Canada’s top court upholds Quebec law barring public sector workers from wearing religious symbols
articles.summary: Closely watched decision exposes tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights Canada’s top court has largely upheld a controversial secularism law in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights. In a 6-1 ruling released on Friday morning, the supreme court found Quebec was permitted to shield the law, Bill 21, from most court challenges on the grounds that it…
paragraphs: Canada’s top court has largely upheld a controversial secularism law in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights.
In a 6-1 ruling released on Friday morning, the supreme court found Quebec was permitted to shield the law, Bill 21, from most court challenges on the grounds that it violated charter rights.
“Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society,” chief justice Richard Wagner wrote in the majority opinion.

Canada’s top court says the four days of hearings from earlier in the year marked one of the longest in its 151-year history. Fifty-one interveners participated, including six attorneys general – also a record number. The court’s website crashed on Friday morning when the judgment was released.
While the judgment was celebrated by some in Quebec who considered it a vindication of the province’s fight, it was swiftly criticised by religious civil liberties groups.

“We cannot exist in a country as free people, where governments can literally go to the electorate and say, ‘I’m gonna take away the rights of a certain group of minorities’, because it’s popular and to play wedge politics with the charter rights of Canadians,” Stephen Brown, chief executive of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, told reporters at a press conference. “If that is the case, we don’t have a charter of rights and freedoms. We have a charter of suggestions and permissions.”

Passed in 2019, Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, bars workers including lawyers, judges, police and teachers from wearing religious symbols such as a hijab, turban, kippah or a cross while on the job.

Central to the case – and the reason provincial governments across the country are closely watching the result – is the “notwithstanding clause”, a constitutional mechanism that allows elected governments to override certain fundamental rights and freedoms guaranteed by Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The clause is the result of political compromise from the 1980s, when the federal government set out to replace the existing British North America Act with a new constitution. Provinces feared that under a new constitution, courts would become too powerful, undermining the authority of the elected government. A compromise was hashed out: in cases when a government – provincial or federal – felt that the courts had overstepped, they could invoke the clause to override certain charter rights of citizens.

Some fundamental rights, including protections of religious freedom, equality and speech, could be suspended. But voting, as well as language rights, were untouchable, ensuring Canadians could remove a government if they wanted. A government could only invoke the clause for five years. Before they could renew it, they would first have to face voters.

In its decision, the supreme court rejected most arguments that Bill 21 violated portions of the charter that are not subject to the notwithstanding clause, including guarantees relating to the equality of men and women and the education rights of Quebec’s English-speaking minority.

Quebec’s use of the clause with Bill 21 was notable – and controversial – in that it was the first time the notwithstanding clause had been invoked pre-emptively in an attempt to shield the law from court challenges. Quebec also passed Bill 96, which sought to strengthen French language protections – again pre-emptively invoking the notwithstanding clause.

But groups affected by those laws can still challenge them and many teachers, religious and civil liberties groups argued it was a clear violation of constitutional rights and reflected government overreach. Quebec’s government has defended the law, saying it is constitutionally valid.

In April 2021, a Quebec superior court judge described the effects of the law as “cruel”, saying it “dehumanises” the people it targets, but conceded the statute could not be struck down because it was protected by the notwithstanding clause. Quebec’s court of appeal also upheld the law in February 2024 on the same grounds.

In its 520-page judgment, the court did find that element of the law infringed on democratic rights protected by the charter, including preventing elected members of Quebec’s National Assembly who wear face coverings for religious reasons from participating in the legislative process.

In a 4-3 decision, the court also endorsed the ability of lower courts to issue “judicial declarations” on laws protected by the notwithstanding clause, giving judges the power to declare a law in violation of the charter, even though the law would be permitted to stand.
The court’s decision was celebrated in Quebec, where the governing Parti Québécois has looked for wedges with the federal government and institutions like the supreme court.
The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, had previously said his province’s right to decide its own laws was at risk.

Canada only recently fended off a threat to national unity after voters in Alberta rejected the initial stages of a separatist push. But Quebec’s newly elected government has shown an eagerness to clash with the prime minister, Mark Carney.

The supreme court’s judgment comes on the same day an appeal will be heard regarding a superior court decision that forces Quebec’s members of the national assembly to swear allegiance to King Charles to sit in the Salon Bleu – the chamber of the assembly. Lawmakers from a number of parties in the province recently refused to swear the oath of allegiance.

articles.title: "הגבר הפופולרי ביותר" בטינדר נאשם באונס
articles.summary: הדוגמן סטפן-פייר טומלין, שכונה "מר טינדר" לאחר שקיבל הכי הרבה החלקות ימינה, נאשם באונס אישה במועדון המפורסם גרוצ'ו שבלב שכונת סוהו בלונדון
paragraphs: הדוגמן סטפן-פייר טומלין, שכונה "מר טינדר" לאחר שקיבל הכי הרבה החלקות ימינה, נאשם באונס אישה במועדון המפורסם גרוצ'ו שבלב שכונת סוהו בלונדון

דוגמן שתואר בעבר כ"גבר שקיבל את מספר ההחלקות ימינה הגדול ביותר בטינדר" נאשם באונס במועדון במרכז לונדון. סטפן-פייר טומלין, בן 36, כונה "מר טינדר" לאחר שהתברר כי קיבל יותר "לייקים" מכל אדם אחר באפליקציית ההיכרויות - 14,600 בשנה אחת.
ב-BBC נכתב כי החודש הוא התייצב בבית המשפט, ולאחר ששוחרר בערבות הוא צפוי להתייצב שוב ביום שני - בעקבות ההאשמות שתקף מינית אישה במועדון המפורסם גרוצ'ו שבלב שכונת סוהו בלונדון.
טומלין על השטיח האדום בפרמיירה בלונדון, החודש
(צילום: Kate Green/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures)

חקירת משטרת המטרופולין של לונדון החלה שאישה דיווחה כי נאנסה בתוך המועדון הפרטי ב-13 בנובמבר 2024. טומלין נעצר בעקבות התלונה, ובמשטרה בלונדון אמרו כי האישה מקבלת תמיכה מקציני משטרה המתמחים בטיפול במקרים מסוג זה.

לטומלין 454 אלף עוקבים באינסטגרם, ובפרופיל שלו הוא מציג את עצמו כטייס, שחקן וכ"גבר שקיבל את מספר ההחלקות ימינה הגדול ביותר בטינדר". מאז שפתח את פרופיל הטינדר שלו בשנת 2015, הוא קיבל בו יותר מ-48 אלף "סווייפים" ימינה, והפך לתופעה ויראלית לאחר שהוכתר כ"מר טינדר" - כינוי שהביא לו פרסום והופעות בתוכניות טלוויזיה.
טומלין, לפני שבוע וחצי. נאשם באונס במועדון גרוצ'ו

מועדון גרוצ'ו נפתח בשנת 1985 בשכונת סוהו כחלופה פחות רשמית למועדוני הגברים המסורתיים, וסלבס רבים פקדו אותו לאורך השנים. ב"דיילי מייל" הוזכרו בין היתר ג'ורג' מייקל, ריטה אורה, קארה דלווין, נואל וליאם גלאגר, רובי ויליאמס ופרדי מרקיורי.

המקום נסגר זמנית בסוף 2024 בעקבות תלונת האישה, ולאחר שרישיונו של המועדון הושעה בעקבות בקשה של משטרת המטרופולין. אולם כעבור חודש הוא נפתח מחדש. חברי המועדון הוגבלו להזמנת ארבעה אורחים בלבד למקום, ונדרשו להתלוות אליהם בכל עת.

articles.title: Danon demands public correction from UN aid chief over Gaza tent deliveries
articles.summary: Israel’s UN ambassador demanded a formal apology from Tom Fletcher over his BBC remarks, citing nearly 65,000 additional tents cleared for entry into Gaza.
paragraphs: Israeli ambassador to the UN Danny Danon demanded a formal apology and public correction from UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher on Wednesday over remarks he made to the BBC regarding delays in delivering winter supplies to the Gaza Strip.
In a November 25 letter to UN Under-Secretary-General for Global Communications Melissa Fleming, seen by The Jerusalem Post, Danon described Fletcher’s remarks as “a gross distortion of the facts.”
Danon also called on the UN to review how it verifies factual claims made by senior officials and corrects inaccuracies after publication.

“We’ve got 150,000 tents ready to go into Gaza, and we’ve got to get them through,” Fletcher told BBC Radio 4’s Today program on November 14, in an excerpt he posted on November 15. “Rain should not be a death sentence,” he said.
Asked whether talks with the Israeli government had improved humanitarian access, Fletcher said aid agencies continued to encounter obstacles, including difficulties getting crossings opened.
He also accused Hamas of interfering with humanitarian operations inside Gaza, saying its members had entered some aid warehouses and intimidated staff.
Fletcher called on both Israel and Hamas to allow aid agencies to deliver supplies.
In a November 11 statement, Fletcher said waiting for the formation of a new Israeli government was not an acceptable reason to delay the delivery of winter aid.
Danon cites COGAT figures on Gaza winter aid deliveries

Danon cited figures from the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) showing that 99,900 tents and 9,000 trucks carrying winter supplies had entered Gaza since the launch of an initiative in August.

In a November 19 letter to aid agencies, COGAT said it had approved nearly 65,000 additional tents at the request of UNICEF, the International Organization for Migration, and other organizations, but that the tents had yet to enter Gaza.
Danon said the UN should expedite the delivery of supplies that had already been cleared for entry.
The figures reflect different categories: cumulative deliveries, supplies approved for entry that had yet to arrive, and stocks remaining outside Gaza at a given time.
The UN’s humanitarian office reported on November 18 that more than 150,000 tents procured by aid organizations and governments remained outside Gaza, mostly in Egypt’s El-Arish.
The documents do not establish how many of those tents, if any, were among the nearly 65,000 Israel said it had cleared for entry.

In its Thursday update, the UN estimated that 1.36 million people in Gaza were still living in tents or makeshift shelters, adding that entry restrictions and funding shortfalls were hindering preparations for winter.
Danon challenges Fletcher’s previous claims on Gaza aid
Danon also cited Fletcher’s May 2025 warning on the BBC that 14,000 babies would die within 48 hours unless aid reached them. Fletcher later expressed regret over his wording.

The underlying food security assessment projected approximately 14,100 severe cases of acute malnutrition among children between the ages of six months and five years over nearly a year, rather than deaths within 48 hours.
No public response from Fletcher or the UN to Danon’s latest letter was found.

articles.title: ‘What do you owe Netanyahu?’: Spanish election debate erupts over Israel and Hamas
articles.summary: Former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau challenges Vox leader Santiago Abascal over his ties to Netanyahu, prompting a furious response; candidates clash over Gaza, immigration and sexism ahead of elections that could bring Spain’s far right into government for the first time since Franco’s dictatorship ended
paragraphs: Former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau challenges Vox leader Santiago Abascal over his ties to Netanyahu, prompting a furious response; candidates clash over Gaza, immigration and sexism ahead of elections that could bring Spain’s far right into government for the first time since Franco’s dictatorship ended

A heated televised debate ahead of Spain's snap parliamentary elections on Sunday erupted into a confrontation over Israel and Hamas on Thursday, as Ada Colau, leader of the radical-left Broad Front party, clashed with Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right Vox party. Referring to remarks by Israeli Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli, who praised Abascal's political positions and described him as a "true friend," Colau asked: "A minister in Netanyahu's government said you are Israel's best spokesperson in Spain. What do you owe Netanyahu after that?" Abascal fired back: "You want me to answer? Fine. What do you owe Hamas?"

The televised debate, organized by Spain's Television Academy and broadcast simultaneously by several media outlets, brought together the leaders of the country's four main political parties: Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, one of Europe's most outspoken critics of Israel; his conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo, a supporter of Israel; former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau, who participated in the Global Sumud Flotilla to Gaza and was detained by Israel; and Vox leader Santiago Abascal. A coalition between Feijóo and Abascal would mark the first time a far-right party has entered Spain's national government since the end of Francisco Franco's dictatorship in 1975.
Spain's leading election candidates, from right: Ada Colau, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, Pedro Sánchez and Santiago Abascal
(Photo: Oscar DEL POZO / AFP)

The exchange between Colau and Abascal occurred during a segment devoted to foreign policy and immigration. Abascal had sharply criticized Sánchez, accusing him of mocking the victims of the devastating flash floods that killed more than 230 people in Valencia in 2024 and declaring that the prime minister should not be standing on the debate stage. He also attacked Sánchez's immigration policies, claiming his government had allowed six million immigrants into Spain over five years, placing an increasing burden on the country's health care, welfare and security systems. He accused the government of allowing "criminals, murderers, rapists and thieves" into the country.

Colau responded by recalling her detention following the Gaza-bound flotilla, which also included Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg. "Let's talk about criminals, Mr. Abascal. It turns out that you and I have something in common. We have both been to occupied Palestine. But you were welcomed with great honor in the office of the genocidal Netanyahu, while I was kidnapped by the genocidal army alongside hundreds of people who were on a humanitarian mission to Gaza."
Ada Colau following her detention in Israel in 2025
(Photo: AP Photo/Joan Mateu Parra)

Colau then referred to Chikli's remarks, asking Abascal to explain what he owed Netanyahu after being recognized as Israel's best spokesperson in Spain. Abascal responded by accusing Colau of supporting Hamas and promoting immigration that he claimed was changing the identity of entire regions of Spain, particularly Almería, Valencia and Catalonia.

"This is immigration by people who despise women, hate homosexuals and have brought female genital mutilation to Spain. These are the people you defend," Abascal said. He has previously directed similarly harsh criticism at Sánchez, describing him as a "servant of Morocco" following a mass influx of migrants into the Spanish-controlled enclave of Ceuta.

Earlier in the debate, Colau had challenged Abascal over his support for Israel, saying: "Tell us here that you think it is justified that Netanyahu massacred tens of thousands of boys and girls in Gaza. Say it."

The confrontation between Colau and Abascal was not the only heated exchange during the debate. Feijóo and Sánchez also disagreed over how to characterize Israel's military actions in Gaza following the Hamas-led October 7 attack. "It is a massacre. I am using the terminology of our head of state and the European Union," Feijóo insisted, referring to remarks made by Spain's King Felipe VI at the United Nations last year. Sánchez disagreed: "It is genocide, Mr. Feijóo. Use the term genocide."
Feijóo's silencing gesture that sparked controversy

Another controversy erupted when Feijóo addressed the deadly 2024 Valencia floods, a recurring issue throughout the debate due to questions surrounding the responsibility of Carlos Mazón, the conservative politician who headed Valencia's regional government at the time of the disaster. Although Mazón resigned from the position, he remains a member of Valencia's regional parliament, granting him parliamentary immunity.

Sánchez and Colau criticized their right-wing opponents for supporting Mazón. Feijóo hit back, accusing Sánchez of fleeing an angry crowd during a visit to one of the towns devastated by the floods, while Spain's king and queen remained at the scene despite residents throwing mud at them. "Good leadership means taking responsibility for national disasters, not running away. And you, be quiet," Feijóo told Colau, placing a finger to his lips in an apparent gesture telling her to stop speaking.

"Why are you silencing her, Feijóo? Show some respect. What kind of sexism is this?" Sánchez immediately responded. Feijóo dismissed the accusation, telling the prime minister not to manipulate the situation.

Another contentious moment came during a discussion of Spain's economy, when Sánchez criticized Feijóo's proposed tax policies and mocked his command of English, which the conservative leader had previously acknowledged was limited. "Feijóo's mathematical skills are on the same level as his English," Sánchez quipped. Feijóo did not respond.

In Sunday's elections, opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo will seek to unseat Sánchez, who has served as Spain's prime minister for the past eight years. Opinion polls put Feijóo's conservative People's Party ahead of Sánchez's Socialist Party, although the incumbent has a reputation for surviving difficult political contests.
The candidates receive instructions from the debate moderator
(Photo: REUTERS/Juan Medina)

The two leaders faced off in a televised debate last week, during which Feijóo repeatedly attacked Sánchez over corruption scandals involving his wife and associates, his handling of the economy, the country's housing crisis and two deadly railway disasters that struck Spain this year. He also focused heavily on immigration, a controversy that intensified in July when tens of thousands of migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, Spain's enclave in North Africa.

Sánchez adopted a more restrained approach, acknowledging that his government had made "mistakes" while defending its record. He argued that his opposition to U.S. President Donald Trump, the war in Iran and what he again described as "genocide in Gaza" had turned Spain into a "beacon" for the international community.

The prime minister also defended his relatively open immigration policy, which contrasts with the approach taken by much of Europe. Earlier this year, his government advanced an unprecedented plan to grant legal status to one million undocumented immigrants. Sánchez maintains that immigration is essential to Spain's economic growth, while his right-wing opponents accuse him of encouraging mass immigration, straining the country's social fabric, exacerbating its housing shortage and undermining public safety.
Migrants entering Ceuta en masse in July
(Photo: AP Photo/Antonio Sempere)

Just this week, a daily record was set for migrant arrivals in Spain's Canary Islands, with approximately 2,000 people reaching the archipelago within 24 hours. One person died during the journey, while a baby was born along the way.

Sánchez announced the November 29 snap elections just a month ago, following the collapse of his minority government amid the housing crisis and public outrage over the eviction of an elderly woman, Maricarmen Abascal, from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for 70 years, just two weeks before her death. Spain's parliamentary elections had originally been scheduled for the middle of next year. His decision was widely viewed as an attempt to capitalize on the protests and win back voters disillusioned by corruption scandals surrounding his administration and the immigration crisis.
According to Politico's polling average, Feijóo's People's Party (PP) stands at 31%, followed by Sánchez's Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) at 29%, Vox at 18% and Colau's party at 6%.

As in Israel, the party that receives the most votes does not necessarily determine who becomes prime minister. Instead, candidates must secure the support of a parliamentary majority in Spain's 350-seat lower house. If Feijóo forms a coalition with Vox, it would mark the first time a far-right party has entered Spain's national government since Franco's dictatorship ended in 1975.

articles.title: סערות ענק ושיאי חום: 7 ימים רצופים שלא נראו כמותם - והאזהרה של החוקרים
articles.summary: נתוני האקלים חושפים שיא היסטורי: הטמפרטורה העולמית חצתה את רף שתי המעלות מעל הממוצע הטרום-תעשייתי במשך שבעה ימים רצופים. במקביל, סערות עוצמתיות מכות בארה"ב והמדענים מזהירים מפני הבאות
paragraphs: נתוני האקלים חושפים שיא היסטורי: הטמפרטורה העולמית חצתה את רף שתי המעלות מעל הממוצע הטרום-תעשייתי במשך שבעה ימים רצופים. במקביל, סערות עוצמתיות מכות בארה"ב והמדענים מזהירים מפני הבאות

ההתחממות הגלובלית מגיעה לשיאים חדשים: על פי דיווח ב"פייננשל טיימס", נתונים ראשוניים מצביעים על כך שהטמפרטורה העולמית הייתה גבוהה ביותר משתי מעלות צלזיוס מהממוצע בתקופה הטרום-תעשייתית במשך שבעה ימים רצופים במהלך חודש נובמבר. רצף הטמפרטורות החריג נרשם במקביל לאירועי מזג אוויר קיצוניים ולכישלון מדינות העולם להגיע להסכמות בנוגע למאבק בהתחממות הגלובלית.
ניתוח נתונים של קופרניקוס, תוכנית תצפית כדור הארץ של האיחוד האירופי, העלה כי ביום שני האחרון נרשם שיא חדש, כאשר הטמפרטורה העולמית הייתה גבוהה ב-2.25 מעלות מהממוצע הטרום-תעשייתי.
"ככל שאנחנו רואים שיאים כאלה בתדירות גבוהה יותר, כך עולה הממוצע ארוך הטווח. זהו סימן אזהרה", אמר דאוראס ל"פייננשל טיימס".
סערות עוצמתיות ומאות אלפי בתים ללא חשמל

במקביל לנתוני החום החריגים, סערות עוצמתיות פוקדות את החוף המזרחי והמערבי של ארצות הברית. סערה שהתקדמה ביום שישי לאורך החוף המזרחי הביאה לביטולי טיסות ולהפסקות חשמל ביותר מ-675 אלף בתי אב, כאשר פנסילבניה וניו ג'רזי היו בין המדינות שנפגעו בצורה הקשה ביותר.

מושלי ניו יורק וניו ג'רזי הכריזו על מצב חירום, ומצעד חג ההודיה בניו יורק נדחה ליום שבת בשל הרוחות העזות. שירות מזג האוויר הלאומי האמריקאי הזהיר מפני רוחות חזקות, גשמים כבדים והצפות משמעותיות באזורי החוף.
בחוף המערבי פורסמו אזהרות מפני הצפות לאורך חופי קליפורניה, אורגון וושינגטון. על פי התחזיות שהובאו בדיווח, הסערות צפויות להימשך גם בשבוע הבא ולהביא עמן גשמים, שלג בהרים, רוחות עזות וגלים גבוהים.
תופעת אל ניניו החריפה גם את אירועי הגאות הקיצוניים בחוף המערבי של ארצות הברית. מחקרים קודמים מצאו כי חורפים שבהם מתרחשת התופעה מלווים בגלים עוצמתיים ובשחיקה משמעותית של קו החוף במערב צפון אמריקה.
העולם מתחמם - ומדינות העולם לא מגיעות להסכמות

רצף הטמפרטורות החריגות נרשם במקביל לכישלון שיחות האקלים בוועידת האו"ם COP31 שנערכה בשבוע שעבר בטורקיה. קרוב ל-200 מדינות לא הצליחו להגיע להסכמה על הצהרה בדבר המעבר משימוש בדלקים מאובנים, הנחשבים לגורם מרכזי בשינויי האקלים.

חשוב להדגיש כי שיאי הטמפרטורה היומיים אינם מעידים בהכרח על חציית הרף שנקבע בהסכם פריז בשנת 2015, שנועד להגביל את ההתחממות הגלובלית ל-1.5 מעלות או הרבה מתחת לשתי מעלות. ההתחממות במסגרת ההסכם נמדדת לאורך תקופה של שני עשורים לפחות.
עם זאת, על פי הדיווח, דו"ח האו"ם שפורסם בחודש שעבר קבע כי כבר לא ניתן למנוע תקופה שבה ההתחממות הנגרמת מפעילות אנושית תחרוג מרף 1.5 המעלות.
השירות המטאורולוגי הבריטי צופה גם עלייה חריגה בריכוז הפחמן הדו-חמצני באטמוספרה בשנת 2027, בעקבות השפעת אל ניניו על יכולתם של צמחים, קרקעות ואוקיינוסים לספוג פחמן.
עשרה ימים בחודש אחד: השיאים נערמים

תופעת אל ניניו הנוכחית, שהחלה בחודש יוני, צפויה להימשך לפחות עד חודש מרץ. מינהל האוקיינוסים והאטמוספרה הלאומי של ארצות הברית (NOAA) מעריך כי הסיכוי להתפתחות אירוע היסטורי עד חודש ינואר עומד על 60%, לעומת הערכה קודמת של 70%.
טמפרטורות פני הים באזורים במזרח האוקיינוס השקט כבר חרגו ביותר מארבע מעלות מהממוצע. התופעה צפויה להביא עמה גם עומסי חום כבדים ומסוכנים באזורים הטרופיים.
הפעם הראשונה שבה הטמפרטורה העולמית חצתה את רף שתי המעלות ביום בודד הייתה ב-17 בנובמבר 2023. מאז נחצה הרף ב-15 ימים נוספים, עשרה מהם בחודש הנוכחי בלבד.
"אל ניניו יבוא ויחלוף, אבל ההתחממות הנובעת מפליטת גזי חממה לא תיעלם, אלא אם נפחית את הפליטות הללו", הזהירה ברג'ס.

articles.title: Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
articles.summary: France's president made the comment while speaking to French farming representatives, months after the EU banned Brazil beef and poultry products.
paragraphs: Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron calling Brazilian meat "doped".

France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry, which took effect in September.
The Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".

Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat, poultry and other animal products owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.

In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.
Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at the Élysée Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.

"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.
Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".

Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".
Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

articles.title: Norse Atlantic Airways files for bankruptcy and cancels all future flights
articles.summary: Norwegian airline tells customers not to come to airports after surging fuel costs caused by Iran war ruin finances Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances. The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical. Continue reading...
paragraphs: Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances.

The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical.

The carrier operated low-cost, long-haul flights around the world, including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia. Flights from Gatwick and Manchester next month to Thailand are among those now scrapped, along with London flights to South Africa and the US.

The Norse board concluded operations were no longer viable after a year in which airlines across the world were hit by spiralling oil prices that doubled the cost of jet fuel as well as dampening consumer demand, after the Iran war began in February.
Rival airlines have predicted surging air fares and the collapse of weaker carriers.

In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Eivind Roald, the chief executive of Norse, said: “The board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution.
“We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners.”

He said the owning group and Norse’s UK subsidiary – which was set up to comply with aviation rules after Brexit – were “working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations”.
However, all UK flights were similarly cancelled and ticket sales halted.

In a message on its website, Norse advised passengers to contact their travel agents, flight bookers, insurers or credit card companies, but made clear those travelling were on their own and should ask airport information desks.
It said: “We know this will disrupt travel plans and may leave some passengers away from home. Customer service for both airlines is no longer available by phone, email, chat or social media.”

The abrupt end came after Norse announced it was on the brink of collapse on Thursday morning. On Friday morning, it reported that aircraft lessors had served termination notices for the 12 planes in its fleet.
Norse was founded in 2021, attempting to emulate the model of Norwegian Air, whose attempts to forge a new low-cost long-haul market ended with the pandemic.
Norse briefly revived the transatlantic routes using the same plane types, Boeing 787 Dreamliners.

However, it eventually hit similar financial turbulence and this summer told investors it was exploring a sale or merger, embarking on a $50m (£38m) cost-cutting programme, including shedding jobs and its Norwegian HQ.

articles.title: Newly released documents suggest CIA did more post-9/11 waterboarding than previously acknowledged
articles.summary: Declassified documents appear to support belief that waterboarding was more common and may have occurred beyond two acknowledged sites Newly released documents suggest that the CIA waterboarded more detainees during the post-9/11 “war on terror” than previously acknowledged, utilizing a site north of Kabul, Afghanistan, for the practice of simulated drowning. The agency has acknowledged waterboarding three men: Abu Zubaydah, believed to be a high-ranking member of al-Qaida; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, suspected architect of the 11 September 2001 attacks; and Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, accused of…
paragraphs: Newly released documents suggest that the CIA waterboarded more detainees during the post-9/11 “war on terror” than previously acknowledged, utilizing a site north of Kabul, Afghanistan, for the practice of simulated drowning.

The agency has acknowledged waterboarding three men: Abu Zubaydah, believed to be a high-ranking member of al-Qaida; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, suspected architect of the 11 September 2001 attacks; and Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, accused of planning the 2000 bombing of a navy destroyer.

But declassified documents obtained under a freedom of information lawsuit by the New York Times, includes an account from a former CIA contract translator that appears to support the belief that waterboarding was more common and may have occurred beyond two acknowledged “special rendition” sites in Thailand and Poland.
The outlet reported on Friday that the linguist worked at a secret prison, or black site, one north of Kabul, Afghanistan, known as Salt Pit or Detention Site Cobalt.
The translator told an FBI agent in 2012 he had seen a man he called “Bahir” strapped to a board tilted downward into water.

“There were approximately three to four people ‘doing this,’” the FBI agent summarized in the account, saying that the witness “saw the incident in passing but did not participate himself. The waterboard session was in the hallway and there was not a lot of room.”

The account comes from an investigation into the CIA’s use of torture and its destruction of waterboarding videotapes from 2008 to 2012 conducted by then-special prosecutor John Durham. No charges were ever brought.
In the new documents produced by the Times, the linguist told the FBI in that “Bahir” was “a relative of Hekmatyar”, seemingly a reference to Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, the former Afghan prime minister.
That may correspond to a man named “Ghairat Bahir”, who was apprehended in a raid in Islamabad in 2002, appears in CIA records, and was subjected to “enhanced” interrogation techniques.

articles.title: רשת KFC בישראל תימכר ב-2.7 מיליון שקל
articles.summary: לאחר שנקלעה לחובות, רשת המזון המהיר קנטאקי פרייד צ'יקן בישראל צפויה להימכר בסכום של 2.7 מיליון שקל ל"א.א.א. שיווק מזון בע"מ" • בתחילת החודש אישר בית המשפט לנאמני החברה לפרסם הזמנה להגשת הצעות לרכישת החברה המפעילה או את הפעילות שלה
