Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.
Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”

William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”
Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.
“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”

articles.title: From £250 job to £9,000 bill: Inside the rogue trader networks scamming customers at scale
articles.summary: Networks of plumbers and electricians are scamming people on a large scale, the BBC reveals.
paragraphs: Organised networks of rogue plumbers and electricians have been scamming people on a large scale, a BBC investigation has found.

Nessar Khawaja, who used the online name ThatGuyNess, regularly posted TikTok videos showing his work as a plumber, explaining how he made thousands of pounds from "desperate" customers, and recruiting online to expand his network.
"Me and my team, we're top of the food chain," he said in one video.
The investigation found the 23-year-old is a key figure within an organised group that is systematically ripping off customers and teaching others to do the same.
The BBC put these allegations to Khawaja in writing. He denied any wrongdoing and said his social media posts were intended as light-hearted comedy that did not reflect how he operated in practice.
In a recorded phone call, Khawaja insisted he was an entertainer, was joking and that the BBC had "taken things out of context".
In another video, Khawaja made claims he had electricians working for him who made more than £40,000 a month.
"I've got 100-120 engineers. Imagine how much money I am making them and making from them," he said.
One of Khawaja's associates told an undercover BBC journalist during a secretly-recorded recruitment call that engineers working for them had to hand over 60% from every job to the network.
After being approached for comment, TikTok said it banned the account for "breaching its rules on fraud and scams".
Trading Standards said the average rogue trader call-out scam now costs the victim about £10,000.
The impact can be devastating.
Clive, who lives in London, is undergoing treatment for cancer.
He said he had felt forced to pay the rogue trader who came to his home and charged £9,153 for installing an outdoor socket to fit garden lights he already owned.
An independent electrical expert told the BBC the job had not been done properly, was left in an unsafe state and should have cost no more than £250.
Clive said he no longer feels safe in his home.
He explained how he had searched for a local electrician on Google when his usual tradesperson was unavailable and came across Chriss Electrician Ltd.
Clive said the engineer spent about two hours at the property before presenting him with the bill.
"I was shocked," said Clive.
He added he had felt pressured into paying as the work had already been completed.
He went to his local bank branch to move money between accounts before returning home and making the payment through the engineer's portable card reader.
Despite his doubts about the costs, Clive said he had feared what might happen if he refused to pay.
"If I hadn't paid him, I thought something might happen," he said.
"When people come to the door now, I think, 'Oh God, who's that?' I don't feel safe any more."
Like Clive, another man, who the BBC has named as Tom, felt he had no choice but to settle the bill when he mistakenly called a rogue trader to his property in Essex after finding a leak.
He says he was initially quoted £49 over the phone after calling a listing at the top of Google purporting to be an established business.
But on arrival, the plumber increased the call-out fee to £250 and the costs kept on climbing.

"He charged us for the first load of repairs, and then the second load with the water cylinder. Basically, he was running my taps constantly saying, 'Look, it's coming out this hot', which caused me to panic."
By the end, the plumber presented a bill for £6,237.60.
"I noticed afterwards that the invoice said Ibby & Co. Ltd. That was when alarm bells started ringing because I had never heard of that company. It wasn't the company I called out, essentially."
Lee, not his real name, spent a year working for Khawaja as a plumber until, he says, his conscience got the better of him.
"It got a bit too much for me," he said. "I didn't like scamming people. So, I left.
"I've worked for London's biggest plumbing company and, no word of a lie, this lot have more jobs. They're giants."
Rather than relying on solid reputations and recommendation, rogue traders rely on search engine traffic.
They either pay to get their details at the top of Google, which means they are seen first, or they mimic the names of reputable companies by making tiny changes to the business name.
Reached by the BBC's undercover journalist posing as a plumber seeking to work with them, one of Khawaja's associates said: "We're a lead company. We'll send you jobs, and then you go to the jobs.
"We sort the jobs through online advertisement. Usually we'll try and get emergencies so we can charge more. You make up the pricing."
The associate told the undercover reporter they had to charge in the region of £400 for every job, regardless of what work was actually needed.
Both Clive and Tom reported what happened to the Metropolitan Police and Essex Police.
Khawaja said he was not a party to the phone call with the undercover journalist and could not comment on its contents.
He said the alleged statements did not reflect how he operates.
He separately told the BBC in the recorded phone call: "You guys should know I am an entertainer and you guys are taking it out of context."
"I am clearly joking and I'm entertaining and I am engaging with the comments, it is not literal," he added.
He said the right of reply sent to him by the BBC contained "false information which has nothing to do with me".

articles.title: Major Thanksgiving storm brings flooding, flight delays across US
articles.summary: Almost one million customers in the US had no power on Thursday evening as storms descended on both US coasts, bringing wind gusts, heavy rain and flooding.
paragraphs: On Thursday, a powerful storm hit the eastern US, bringing damaging winds of up to 70mph, torrential rain, and major coastal flooding.
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency as several communities along the Jersey Shore saw widespread flooding.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.
In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds and waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
In Maryland, almost two million customers have been asked by the water utility to use water for essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport, according to the National Water Prediction Service.
More than 980,000 households were reporting power outages by Thursday evening, with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey hit particularly hard.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said that utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. Meanwhile, energy companies in Virginia and New Jersey warned it may take some time, even days, for power to return, as crews had to wait until it was safe to access damaged areas.
On Thursday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds for the east coast as it faces down the holiday storm.
Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.
In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.
A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".

It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."
An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.

"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," they said.
Wednesday's incident in Miami came 11 weeks after a cargo plane crashed on landing at the same airport, killing five people and injuring five others in vehicles on the ground with which it collided.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.
Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

articles.title: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly convicted over attack on UK couple
articles.summary: Evidence from a British police officer helped convict Ali Kololo over a 2011 attack in the Kenyan resort of Lamu.
paragraphs: A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.
Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.
Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.
Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.
In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.
We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.
It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.
Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.
"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.

Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.
"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."
Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.
"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."
Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.
"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".
The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.

Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.
But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.
In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.

The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.

At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.
"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.

Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".
"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."

Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.

In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.
They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.
"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."

More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."
He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.
Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.
"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."

He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.
"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."
For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.
"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."
The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.
"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.

The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."
Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".

"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."
"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
articles.summary: The ousted prime minister's December homecoming plan deepens Dhaka-Delhi tensions and risks fresh unrest.
paragraphs: Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images
Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.
Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.
The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.

Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.

She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.
The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.
Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.
"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."
Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.

"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."
India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.
Sheikh Hasina: The pro-democracy icon who became an autocrat
Hasina's conviction for crimes against humanity is testing India-Bangladesh ties
Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.

They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.
The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile.
Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images

Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile.

Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".

The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".
"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.

That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.
Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.
Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.
Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.

Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, external, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked, external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn, external amid fears of further attacks.

Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.
The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.
Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.

Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.

Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".

He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, external, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).

"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising."

Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.
The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.
For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.

Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.
The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.
A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.
Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi".

Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner, external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".

"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."
Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.
Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.

"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."
That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.

"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty, external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.
"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."
A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".
Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."
Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.
"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.
For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore.

"December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again.
"Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst.

But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table".

articles.title: After Huang affair, NVIDIA's ex-sales head Puri found to have wed Super Micro executive - report
articles.summary: The revelation follows Jensen Huang's affair with a Megaspeed executive suspected by some US officials of working with Chinese intelligence.
paragraphs: Jensen Huang was not the only NVIDIA executive romantically involved with a senior officer at one of the chipmaker's customers, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday. Jay Puri, Huang's longtime lieutenant and NVIDIA's former head of global sales, dated Super Micro Computer executive Cenly Chen for several years, while the server maker was competing for access to NVIDIA's chips.

According to the WSJ, which cited current and former co-workers, the two married in March in Big Sur, California. Staff at Super Micro have since been charged with smuggling NVIDIA-powered servers into China.

As Super Micro's chief growth officer, Chen frequently dealt with Puri, and she accompanied Super Micro's CEO on visits to NVIDIA's offices to press for chip supplies for the company's customers, employees at both companies told the WSJ. In sales meetings, she presented herself as the go-to contact for NVIDIA-related questions, the report said. At the time, Puri led NVIDIA's global sales team, which decided how its newest chips were allocated among customers.

Chen declined to comment on her personal life, saying it had no bearing on her work. "I never had to rely on personal relationships for professional gain," she told the WSJ in an email. "I dealt with Super Micro's customers and the customer decided the chips they bought. I was not involved in the selection or procurement of the chips." NVIDIA and Puri did not respond to the WSJ's requests for comment.
Super Micro co-founder charged with smuggling NVIDIA chips

On March 19, 12 days after the wedding, the Justice Department unsealed charges against Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw, a Taiwan-based Super Micro sales manager, and a third-party broker. Prosecutors allege the three directed a Southeast Asian company to order about $2.5 billion worth of Super Micro servers in 2024 and 2025. They then allegedly diverted at least $510 million worth of servers containing high-end NVIDIA chips to China.

Liaw has pleaded not guilty and resigned from Super Micro's board. The broker has pleaded guilty under an agreement with prosecutors. Super Micro was not named as a defendant and has said it was a victim of the scheme.

Chen was not named in the indictment. She told the WSJ that federal law enforcement had not contacted her. However, FBI agents recently interviewed a person familiar with Super Micro and sought information about top executives, including Chen, according to that person.

The report comes as NVIDIA reels from revelations about Huang's extramarital affair with an executive at Megaspeed International, another NVIDIA customer. That executive is suspected by some US officials of having worked with Chinese intelligence. Huang resigned from NVIDIA but returned this week, after US President Donald Trump intervened with the company's board. Both Megaspeed and Super Micro face Justice Department investigations into alleged chip smuggling to China, the WSJ has reported.
Super Micro says Chen didn't manage NVIDIA relationship

Super Micro said in a statement that Chen "did not manage Supermicro's overall relationship with Nvidia or our procurement of Nvidia GPUs." It said chip allocation to its customers was determined by a multi-department process. In August, the company said a review led by independent board members found no evidence that any current senior manager knew of the alleged diversion scheme.

Chen, 50, spent nearly two decades at Super Micro before leaving weeks after NVIDIA's annual conference in March. She became CEO of ChronoScale, a cloud services firm spun out of Applied Digital, another NVIDIA partner. Puri, 72, joined NVIDIA in 2005. He announced in July that he was stepping back from his role but would stay on as a senior adviser.

Applied Digital CEO Wes Cummins, who chairs ChronoScale, told the WSJ that Chen "went to bat" with NVIDIA for Super Micro's customers. He acknowledged that her relationship with Puri created the appearance of a conflict of interest, but he said he was not aware of Super Micro receiving any special treatment. Cummins added that the disclosed conflict has actually kept ChronoScale and Applied Digital from using some of the assistance NVIDIA offers customers.

articles.title: Son of ‘Israeli godfather’ extradited from US over two alleged murder plots
articles.summary: Crime boss Eran Haya allegedly orchestrated two failed attempts to kill rival Eli Musli from Turkey; wiretaps, surveillance footage and testimony from two state witnesses underpin the case, while his attorney challenges the scope of the investigation
paragraphs: Crime boss Eran Haya allegedly orchestrated two failed attempts to kill rival Eli Musli from Turkey; wiretaps, surveillance footage and testimony from two state witnesses underpin the case, while his attorney challenges the scope of the investigation

Israeli crime boss Eran Haya, who was extradited from the United States to Israel on Thursday, is suspected of orchestrating two attempts to murder one of his biggest underworld rivals, crime boss Eli Musli, in the heart of Tel Aviv while living in Turkey.

Two foiled murder attempts, extensive surveillance, video calls with Haya abroad and testimony from two members of his criminal organization who became state witnesses are at the center of the case that led to the extradition of Haya, the son of Eitan Haya, dubbed the "Israeli godfather."
Eran Haya arrives in Israel and is taken into custody

Haya and Shlomo Niamchik headed the criminal organization, with Avi Nisani serving as Niamchik's right-hand man. The group was embroiled in a feud with a rival criminal organization led by members of the Musli family, whose associates included Eli Musli, Ben Cohen and Shimon Ravivo, who was murdered in October 2023 in the central Israeli city of Or Yehuda.

Prosecutors allege that between January 2022 and January 2024, Haya's associates committed serious criminal offenses, including murder, attempted murder and intimidation of rivals, and carried out crimes on behalf of others who hired their services.

According to the indictment, Haya and Niamchik supplied their associates with weapons, vehicles and other resources to commit the crimes and cover their tracks. Members of the organization allegedly received tens of thousands of shekels for each criminal operation.

The indictment detailing the two attempts to murder Musli describes how one of the state witnesses, identified only by the initials A.A., met Haya several times in Turkey during 2023. Prosecutors allege that the two established business ties as part of the organization's criminal activities and that Haya told the witness about his feud with the Musli family. Upon A.A.'s return to Israel, Haya allegedly provided him with a handgun through an intermediary, as well as a cellphone to maintain contact.

Prosecutors allege that Haya and Niamchik initiated the plot to murder Musli and directed those involved. In December 2023, Haya allegedly asked A.A. to gather information about Musli and his daily routine before recruiting him to participate in the murder plot.

A.A. agreed, and several other members of the organization became involved. According to prosecutors, Haya's associates conducted a series of rehearsals with his alleged knowledge and direction. Throughout January 2024, Haya received updates from his associates in Israel on their preparations. Both murder attempts, on January 8 and 16, failed. Police arrested Ofek Harush and A.A. during the second attempt.

Among the evidence allegedly linking Haya to the plot is a video call he held with A.A. on January 9, 2024, during which the witness updated him on surveillance of Musli. According to the indictment, Haya was also involved in deciding when his associates would make another attempt to carry out the murder.

In their motion to keep the defendants in custody, prosecutors outlined the evidence gathered during the investigation, including testimony from two state witnesses identified as A.A. and B.B., wiretaps, security camera footage, surveillance reports and data extracted from cellphones belonging to one of the witnesses.

Wiretaps conducted inside one of the vehicles allegedly captured Haya's associates discussing the murder plot, the division of responsibilities and the roles of Haya, Harush and Niamchik within the organization.

The detention motion said the conversations identified Haya and two others as "the planners, initiators and financiers of the murder plot." The recorded conversations also included references to approximately 10 million shekels allegedly invested in efforts to kill Musli.
Footage of Shimon Ravivo's murder, about which Haya was also questioned

Haya is also named in a separate count concerning the attempted murder of Ben Cohen in November 2023. He allegedly conspired with his associates to kill Cohen and requested that a vehicle be rented for them as part of the plot. Police defused an explosive device attached to Cohen's vehicle.

However, Haya's extradition request focused specifically on the attempts to murder Musli. During Thursday's detention hearing, it emerged that police had also questioned him about Ravivo's murder and another attempted murder.
Attorney Nir Rotenberg Photo: Alon Grego

His defense attorney, Nir Rotenberg, strongly objected, arguing that questioning his client about additional cases violated the terms of his extradition, which he said permitted prosecutors to indict Haya only in connection with the attempts to murder Musli.

"The extradition request concerned a specific charge, and police intend to question him about incidents unrelated to that request," Rotenberg said, adding that the defense had formally objected and would maintain its opposition.

"I have not yet read the court's decision, and I hope the court will address the issue," he added. "Police and prosecutors have announced that they will file an indictment regardless of the suspect's account. Police are prepared to rely on state witnesses who have given false testimony."

articles.title: Qantas and Air New Zealand planes too close at Sydney airport as ‘mental models’ of crews to be investigated
articles.summary: Aborted descent on Wednesday morning is latest in a series of landing incidents at Sydney airport Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast The Australian Transport Safety Bureau is investigating flight crews’ “mental models” after a Qantas plane aborted its landing at Sydney airport on Wednesday after noticing another aircraft crossing the runway while on its descent. The ATSB said Qantas flight 426 from Melbourne was due to land just before 10.15am on Wednesday, with the Boeing 737 jet told to expect a late landing clearance due to aircraft crossing the runway. Continue…
paragraphs: The Australian Transport Safety Bureau is investigating flight crews’ “mental models” after a Qantas plane aborted its landing at Sydney airport on Wednesday after noticing another aircraft crossing the runway while on its descent.
The ATSB said Qantas flight 426 from Melbourne was due to land just before 10.15am on Wednesday, with the Boeing 737 jet told to expect a late landing clearance due to aircraft crossing the runway.
As the Qantas plane continued to approach the airport, and before it received a clearance to land, the crew reported seeing an Air New Zealand plane crossing the runway.
The Qantas crew decided to conduct a go-around, aborting the landing before trying again.

The ATSB said it would investigate what it called an “aircraft separation issue”. The agency will gather evidence, including interviewing flight crew, looking at flight data and monitoring air traffic control audio and any available CCTV into the incident.
“In particular, the investigation will seek to ascertain what information was provided to the crews of both aircraft, and what mental models those crews held,” the agency said in a statement.
“The ATSB notes that, during the occurrence, important safety defences were in place and operated, such as the flight crew’s go-around decision.”
A preliminary report should be complete in about eight weeks, the ATSB said.
Qantas did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
“Our pilots were following air traffic control instructions and elected to conduct a go-around as the other aircraft was crossing the runway,” the airline told the Sydney Morning Herald.
Sydney airport has seen a series of near-miss incidents this year, including when a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided a collision with a Qatar Airways plane on the tarmac in August.
In another incident, a Virgin plane was forced to abort takeoff when a Qantas plane began to cross the runway in front of it.

Angus Mitchell, the ATSB chief commissioner, released preliminary investigation reports in September that found staffing levels at Sydney airport had “emerged as a recurring area of inquiry”, with a review finding runway incursions and near misses at 20% above national averages there.
“This should be viewed in the context of Sydney airport being the most complex in the country,” Mitchell said at the time.

The ATSB stressed it “has yet to determine whether staff resourcing factors directly contributed to any occurrence, or whether they were simply underlying conditions that were recognised and being effectively managed by Airservices, Australia’s air traffic services provider”.

The ATSB added Friday its examination of the recent incident would seek to look at safety defences in place “and to establish or rule out any underlying safety issues and contributing factors common across the other occurrences at Sydney airport currently under investigation”.

articles.title: German LGBT group adopts resolution combating antisemitism, anti-LGBT hate, all forms of extremism
articles.summary: The move comes amid a dramatic deterioration in the security situation facing minorities in Germany, particularly following the Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin’s Christopher Street Day (CSD).
paragraphs: The federal general assembly of Germany’s Christian Democratic LGBT organization (LSU Deutschlands, affiliated with the CDU/CSU political alliance,) adopted a comprehensive resolution by a nearly unanimous vote titled “Living in Security and Freedom: A Rule of Law That Protects Queer Life.”

The resolution, adopted at the organization’s conference in Koblenz on November 21, 2026, at the initiative of its Hesse branch (LSU Hessen), establishes a stringent policy framework for combating antisemitism, anti-LGBT hatred, and all forms of political and religious extremism.

The move comes amid a dramatic deterioration in the security situation facing minorities in Germany, particularly following the Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin’s Christopher Street Day (CSD) Pride celebrations on July 25, 2026.
During the attack, the terrorist rammed his vehicle into a crowd celebrating at the Tiergarten park, and then attacked individuals using a machete.

The attack killed one woman and wounded 31 others, some seriously. The attacker was known to police for his involvement in Islamist circles. The organization's resolution noted that a memorial established at the site had since been vandalized several times.
The document draws on 2025 figures from Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), which indicate record levels of hate crime:

Some 2,070 offenses motivated by sexual orientation, a 17% increase compared with 2024, and 1,294 offenses motivated by gender identity, a 12% increase. The figures reflect a nearly tenfold increase since 2010.
Some 6,548 antisemitic offenses were recorded in 2025, an increase of 5%, alongside 1,983 offenses motivated by religious ideology.
A 35% increase in offenses motivated by far-left extremism, with 13,490 recorded cases, and a 42% increase in violent offenses committed by such groups.
Of the 245 Pride events held across Germany in 2025, at least 110 were disrupted or attacked, 53 of them by organized far-right activists.
One of the resolution’s central provisions focuses on the growing ties between far-left groups and Islamist circles.

Citing findings by Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the country’s domestic intelligence agency, the organization warned that hatred of Israel and antisemitism had become the “glue that binds” the two camps together.

The resolution strongly criticizes activists who participate in joint demonstrations, justify Hamas terrorism, and spread overt antisemitism while advancing an Islamist agenda that seeks to deprive Jews, women, and LGBT people of their rights.

“Jewish life must be possible in Germany without any restrictions, and equally, every person, regardless of their sexual orientation or gender identity, must be able to live freely, safely, and without fear,” the resolution stated, emphasizing that “the constitution stands above any religious or political ideology.”
The LSU called on the German government, the Bundestag, and state interior and justice ministers to adopt a series of practical measures.
Combating political Islam and incitement

The organization called for a comprehensive investigation into the circumstances surrounding the Berlin attack, particularly why an individual classified as a security threat (Gefährder) remained at large.

It also demanded nationwide standards for electronic monitoring and preventive detention, restrictions on foreign funding for religious institutions that spread hatred, the complete withdrawal of public funding from organizations that support antisemitism or anti-LGBT hatred, and the prosecution of hate preachers.
Reforming criminal and immigration laws

The organization called for adult criminal law to apply as a general rule from the age of 18 in terrorism and extremism cases, noting that the Berlin terrorist had been tried under juvenile law just months before the attack.
It also called for the full use of existing legal mechanisms to deport dangerous foreign offenders and revoke citizenship in serious cases involving violations of the democratic order.
Equal protection for Jewish institutions and Pride events

The resolution calls for Jewish institutions and LGBT centers to be included equally in security agencies’ threat assessments, the installation of effective vehicle barriers at Pride events, and government funding for security at smaller events in rural areas.

The organization also demanded mandatory instruction on respect for Jewish and LGBT life in integration courses for immigrants, rejecting any form of “cultural relativism” that excuses hatred on religious grounds.
Stronger enforcement against far-right and far-left extremism

The organization called for the revocation of firearms licenses held by individuals with ties to extremism, an end to government funding for projects that justify political violence, and the dispersal of demonstrations where terrorism is glorified or incitement against Jews takes place.
Technological tools and tougher penalties

The resolution supports mandatory retention of IP addresses for three months to combat cyberbullying and threats, the regulated use of AI-based video analysis in high-risk areas subject to judicial approval, and the establishment of dedicated LGBT liaison officers at all police stations and public prosecutors’ offices across Germany.
The resolution was inspired in part by a visit by members of LSU Hessen’s executive board to the European Jewish Association (EJA) conference in Krakow and the Auschwitz-Birkenau extermination camp.

Rainer Zuber, chairman of LSU Hessen, who initiated the proposal, said his time in Poland had left a profound impression on him, emphasizing that the resolution made clear that the protection of Jewish and LGBT communities was inextricably linked.
Laurence de Donges-Amis, the EJA’s ambassador to Germany, who invited members of the organization to join the Auschwitz delegation, welcomed the adoption of the resolution.

“The impressions from Krakow and Auschwitz-Birkenau strengthen my conviction that our historical responsibility does not end with remembrance, but obliges us to act today for the freedom and security of every individual. Jewish life and queer life must be safe. Freedom must never surrender to its enemies,” de Donges-Amis said.

articles.title: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics?
articles.summary: The pay is good and there's lots of work, so what's behind the shortage of elevator mechanics?
paragraphs: Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users.

Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped, external in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays.
In the US, the average salary for a lift mechanic, external is $110,000 (£83,000). And yet people in the industry say it is difficult to attract new workers.

Sure, says Lembesis, you do encounter some dangers in a job like this. There are risks of falling from a great height – or being electrocuted. Once, he was even hit on the head with an umbrella by an elderly lady after he rescued her from a stuck lift.

But there are so many skills to learn, and great camaraderie and knowledge-sharing among mechanics, he says. As one recruiter puts it, these technicians amaze people with their ability to fix things. They are like "wizards". The overall-clad shamans who know how to get modern life running again.

Nine times out of 10, the problem is with the doors, says Lembesis. These components repeatedly move back and forth. "People hit them with carts, and dirt and debris [falls into them]," says Lembesis. "[The doors] take the most beating."
Mechanics often keep various spare door parts in their vehicles, ready to use.

But technicians like Lembesis don't just have to get lifts working, they also have to verify the lifts are safe. He remembers one case, decades ago, getting called out to a burning building. His role was to ensure the lifts, which were being drenched with huge volumes of water, were still safe to use while firefighters tackled the blaze.
"I was there for 15 hours that night," he says. "Everyone, on the way out of the door, shook my hand."

Finding good lift technicians is "becoming more difficult" says Matt Hollinshead, president of the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. "We have a four-year apprenticeship," he says. That's the first hurdle. And many states require certification or licensing before you can work on lifts.
"We have a vast array of equipment that has to be maintained in the United States." Some lifts are 100-years-old. As time goes on, the technological knowledge required to repair them only grows.

Hollinshead says that weeks or months-long delays to lift repairs are not typically due to staff shortages but that, in such cases, it's likely that a particular part isn't readily available. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes.
But the lack of technicians does mean that that building managers might have to wait days before someone can even diagnose what's wrong with a lift after it stops working.
Hollinshead says teaching the basics of the trade in high schools or technical schools could entice more people into the role.

Matt Allred, a recruiter and host of The Elevator Careers Podcast, emphasises the many skills that lift mechanics require. "You're a little bit of a wizard, right? You show up and if you can fix it – 'Wow!'."
He blames major lift companies, in part, for locking down maintenance contracts, making it difficult or impossible for third-party repairers to intervene when a lift fails.

Two large lift manufacturers approached by BBC News declined interviews. The chief executive of Otis, one of the firms, said in May that her company was struggling to hire enough staff, external to meet demand. The firm also states on its website, external that the shortage of lift mechanics affects "almost every part of the world".
However, a spokesman for Otis claimed its "US talent pipeline" was healthy, and declined an interview.

Everyone else who spoke to BBC News said hiring was challenging in the US. Allred was recently contacted by a major lift company and asked to help them find a technician. "I was surprised that a major company would reach out to a little recruiting shop," he says, suggesting that this reflects the extent of the labour shortage.

That shortage is also a problem in the UK. "It is bad and getting worse," says Dave Cooper, president of the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers, who is also chief executive of a lift and escalator engineering consultancy.
"We've known food delivery companies to refuse to deliver to flats above the ground floor because the lift is out of service."
Offering better tax breaks to companies that train lift mechanics could help ensure that plenty of workers continue to enter the industry, he adds.

Training to be a lift mechanic is "not a quick route to competency – and it requires people to stick at it for the long term" says Karen Slade, head of assessment at the Lift and Escalator Industry Association (Leia).
Continued investment in training and attracting new workers is "essential", according to Leia. There are currently 259 active lift and escalator apprentices in the UK, the body adds.
Back in Chicago, Lembesis is working with two younger mechanics who have been "really good", he says, so there's at least some hope for the future.
He stresses again how rewarding he finds his work. The people for whom he fixes lifts tend to be very appreciative.
"I love that. You get that reaction from the customers," he says. "Without them, you got nothing."

articles.title: Coalition teams up with Labor to pass 20% gas reservation scheme for Australia’s largest exporters
articles.summary: Labor passes final major piece of legislation for 2026, denying Greens’ bid for 25% tax on exports Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast A federal gas reservation scheme requiring Australia’s largest exporters to keep up to 20% of their product for domestic use will go ahead with the Coalition’s support. The opposition waved through the government’s plans in the in a late night Senate sitting on Thursday night, giving Labor the numbers it needed. A short sitting of the lower house rubber stamped changes, seeing the legislation pass parliament. Sign up for Guardian…
paragraphs: A federal gas reservation scheme requiring Australia’s largest exporters to keep up to 20% of their product for domestic use will go ahead with the Coalition’s support.
The opposition voted with the government in the Senate on Thursday night in a late sitting, giving Labor the numbers it needed.
The scheme will begin in January 2028.
On Friday, the resources minister, Madeleine King, said the scheme would mean cheaper gas prices for Australians but could not say by how much.
“We don’t want to set a figure at this time because the experience with price caps when you name a figure is that also becomes the floor, the lower price,” she said.
“And we want to make sure the market’s able to operate to drive prices down as far as they can.”
Speaking in the upper house on Thursday, the shadow resources minister, Susan McDonald, said the Coalition would not oppose the scheme after weeks of hard negotiations between the two major parties.
“The Coalition will act in the national interest,” she said.
“We will allow the government’s proposal to move forward because we do believe in a domestic gas reservation and more gas being made available to Australia.”
Labor granted Western Australia a permanent carve-out after lobbying from the federal Coalition and the state’s premier, Roger Cook.
On Friday, King said: “WA is really the inspiration for this national scheme because they’ve had a scheme since 2008, which has been really important for gas prices and supply in WA.”
WA has an existing scheme that requires exporters to reserve 15% of liquified natural gas (LNG) for the domestic market over the life of a development.
That target has not yet been met. Cook said in August the proportion of LNG delivered to the domestic market was 8.7% in 2021 and rose to 12.5% by 2025.
Business groups and gas companies pressured the federal Coalition to do a deal with Labor to keep the Greens out of negotiations.
The industry minister, Tim Ayres, said the changes would deliver “fundamental economic reform that will make Australia stronger”.
“Australia’s gas is a national asset, and that national asset should be managed in the national interest,” he said.
“This is not an export ban, nor is it an export cap. It is a predictable and proportional contribution to domestic supply.”
Ayres said Australia would remain a reliable supplier of gas for its key partners.

The key sticking point between the parties was the government’s requirement for gas companies to oversupply the market by 10%, which is designed to drive down prices for households and industry. This will remain in place.
The Coalition originally argued this would lower prices to a level that would dry up future gas investment.
They have secured a statutory review to assess the impact of a reservation policy on investment after five years.
The Greens demanded a 25% tax on gas exports in return for their support and voted against the scheme in its current form.
The minor party’s leader, David Shoebridge, condemned the scheme as a “stitch-up” against the Australian public.
“This week, parliament ends with Labor and the Coalition cutting their deal for the gas industry, delivering for the 1% of their corporate donors,” he said before the vote in the Senate.
The lower house is set to sit for a short period on Friday morning, a day later than expected, in order to pass legislation amended in the Senate.

articles.title: Water firms to identify 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts
articles.summary: Department for Work and Pensions to provide data about households missing out on WaterSure support scheme Water companies will use government data to identify as many as 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts, after criticism that not enough people are aware of the £428 support for their annual bills. The Department for Work and Pensions will provide information to identify and contact a quarter of a million households who are missing out on support to which they are entitled under the WaterSure scheme. Continue reading...
paragraphs: Water companies will use government data to identify as many as 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts, after criticism that not enough people are aware of the £428 support for their annual bills.

The Department for Work and Pensions will provide information to identify and contact a quarter of a million households who are missing out on support to which they are entitled under the WaterSure scheme.
The scheme is open to people on benefits who need to use a lot of water either for medical reasons or because their household has three or more children under 19.

The government said that 300,000 customers are signed up to WaterSure, but fewer than half of eligible households claim it because either they are unaware or they may have difficulty proving they qualify.

The Labour government has sought to portray itself as tough on the water industry. However, Andy Burnham has yet to outline his plan for the sector, despite saying he would bring in “more public control” of companies.
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said it was “common sense” to share information about eligible households with companies.

“Hundreds of thousands of the most vulnerable people aren’t getting help with their water bills because they don’t know how to access it,” she said. “That’s not right. By sharing data across government and water companies, we’re fixing that problem – meaning getting that help will be far easier for those who need it.”
The changes received the backing of Martin Lewis, founder of the MoneySavingExpert advice website.

He said: “Too many people miss out on help they desperately need and are entitled to. Water companies shoulder some blame for confusing applications and underpublicising support. Yet it is important the government joins the dots too. If one part of the state knows someone needs help, another shouldn’t leave them in the dark. Help is only effective if it actually reaches those who need it.”

Eagle also announced that the Consumer Council for Water, which helps households with complaints, will be given new powers to investigate water companies’ customer service and work with regulators to rectify problems. It will be named the Water Watchdog.

A spokesperson for Water UK, a lobby group for the industry, said: “Water companies have long called for government to automatically provide us with the information needed to give people heavily discounted water bills. As a result, hundreds of thousands more people will now benefit from WaterSure.”

articles.title: Nearly half of ethnic minority people in UK have faced racism at work in last year, survey finds
articles.summary: Figures show impact on mental health, with majority having no confidence HR will take their concerns seriously Nearly half of people from minority ethnic backgrounds have experienced racism at work and the majority have no confidence that HR would take their concerns seriously, a survey has found. It also found that 75% of people from the UK’s five largest minority ethnic communities had experienced racism or unfair treatment linked to their race, ethnicity or religion in the previous year, and three-quarters of those who had experienced racism said it had affected their mental health to…
paragraphs: Nearly half of people from minority ethnic backgrounds have experienced racism at work and the majority have no confidence that HR would take their concerns seriously, a survey has found.

It also found that 75% of people from the UK’s five largest minority ethnic communities had experienced racism or unfair treatment linked to their race, ethnicity or religion in the previous year, and three-quarters of those who had experienced racism said it had affected their mental health to some degree.

Susan Solomon, a senior research manager and lead author of the Centre for Mental Health’s report, said: “When three-quarters of people who have experienced racism report an impact on their mental health, it is clear that racism is not just an equality issue. It is a public mental health issue.”
The findings of the survey of 2,506 adults come amid reports that racial equality is worsening and discrimination is becoming more common in the UK.

Jabeer Butt, the chief executive of the Race Equality Foundation, said the research demonstrated “how widespread racism remains in everyday life and the cumulative toll it takes on the mental health of Black, Asian and minoritised ethnic people”.

In the workplace, 45% of ethnic minority workers said they had experienced racism at work in the past year, most often passed off as “banter”, while 56% had no confidence that HR would take them seriously.

The research also revealed that 42% of ethnic minority people who had faced racism linked it to anti-immigrant protests and demonstrations, 57% saw negative posts about immigrants or minorities on social media every week, and 46% heard politicians blaming immigrants for the UK’s problems just as often.

Butt said the results showed that “racism does not occur in a vacuum”. He said: “Hostile anti-immigration rhetoric, amplified in politics and across social media, can legitimise racist attitudes and behaviour, echoing our findings following the racist riots of 2024.

“The response cannot be to ask people to become more resilient or simply to report individual incidents. Political leaders, employers, public institutions and social media platforms must challenge the narratives that fuel racism and take effective action to prevent it.”

The research highlighted a gap between experiencing racism and seeking support and help. Of the respondents who had experienced racism or unfair treatment, half said they felt they had to be constantly “on guard” and ready for racist encounters, while only 5% of people who experienced racism sought professional mental health support.

Solomon said: “Our findings show that the harm does not come only from overt acts of discrimination but from the constant effort of anticipating, managing and responding to racism in everyday life. People described living in a state of vigilance, weighing decisions about where they go, how they behave and whether it is safe to speak up.”

She added: “The research also shows that the mental health impact of racism is not limited to personal experiences of discrimination. It is compounded by exposure to anti-immigration and discriminatory rhetoric in political speeches, newspaper coverage and social media. If we are serious about protecting mental health, action must be taken to prevent the harm caused by racism before it reaches crisis point.”

articles.title: Sam Wood to spend Christmas in jail after again being denied bail over alleged assault of wife Snezana
articles.summary: Former Bachelor star and fitness influencer stands accused of assaulting wife at Noosa in Queensland during family holiday in October Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Reality star Sam Wood will spend Christmas in jail after again being denied bail on domestic violence charges over allegations he strangled and assaulted his wife while the family was holidaying at Noosa on the Sunshine Coast in October. The court of appeal today heard a third application by Wood, 46, for bail. He has spent eight weeks in custody since being arrested. Continue reading...
paragraphs: Reality star Sam Wood will spend Christmas in jail after again being denied bail on domestic violence charges over allegations he strangled and assaulted his wife while the family was holidaying at Noosa on the Sunshine Coast in October.
The court of appeal today heard a third application by Wood, 46, for bail. He has spent eight weeks in custody since being arrested.
Wood is accused of assaulting his wife, Snezana, whom he met on Network Ten’s hit reality show The Bachelor in 2015.

Wood is charged with two domestic violence offences: assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation in a domestic setting. The strangulation charge had placed Wood in a “show cause” position where there was a presumption against bail unless he could demonstrate he did not pose a risk of reoffending.
His legal team has indicated he will fight the charges and he has not yet entered a plea.
Queensland appeal justice David Boddice on Friday delivered the court’s judgment on the bail appeal.
“The appeal is dismissed,” Boddice said.

Boddice found that a phone call from prison between Wood and his father provided “a sound evidentiary basis” to conclude that, if Wood were granted bail, there was “a real risk that he would seek to interfere with witnesses, namely [his wife, Snezana]”.

Boddice was referring to a recording of that conversation, played in court, in which an “obviously distressed” Wood was sobbing as he told his father that he needed to talk to Snezana, and that his domestic violence charges would be dropped if she recanted her statements to police.
“I need to be able to talk to my wife,” Wood said in the recording. “There is no way she would want this.”

After Wood’s father responds by saying he did not believe it would be so simple, as police were pressing charges, Wood replied that police would not “have a leg to stand on” if his wife changed her statement and made “a stat dec to say this actually did not happen”.

“[H]is express words are consistent with an attempt to indirectly contact his wife for the express purpose of having her change her statement to falsely claim that nothing had taken place between her and [Wood] on the night in question,” Boddice found.
Wood’s lawyer had argued that the risk of Wood interfering with witnesses could be overcome by “the inclusion of conditions that he not contact the complainant, either directly or indirectly”.

“The difficulty with accepting that contention,” Boddice found, was that Wood had provided sworn evidence to the primary judge to whom he first applied for bail that he understood and would meet those conditions.

Wood’s fresh appeal, Bodice found, “amounts to no more than a repeating of that intention”, even though there was evidence that “immediately upon a refusal of bail, he sought to have an intermediary contact [Snezana] for the express purpose of having her alter her evidence”.
“Against that background, there can be no confidence that conditions could be imposed, which would render the risk of interference with witnesses no longer unacceptable,” Boddice found.
“This court can have no confidence that the appellant would comply with those conditions.”
Wood is now seeking mediation with his wife.
Lawyers for the Melbourne-based fitness influencer made the mediation request days after his distressed prison call, asking to speak to his wife.
Justice mediation in Queensland provides a chance for the alleged offender and victim to discuss the matter, but can only occur if the latter consents.
The mediation matter was adjourned until 7 December.

articles.title: גורם מדיני: "נתקדם מהותית ביישום תוכנית טראמפ לעזה - כבר בימים הקרובים"
articles.summary: על רקע ביקורת עזה על גרירת רגליים מצד ישראל, הגורם המדיני הדגיש כי "ישראל מחויבת לתוכנית 20 הנקודות - הכוללת את פירוק חמאס מנשקו". גורם במועצת השלום אמר ל-ynet כי בארגון "מעודדים מהשיחות האחרונות עם לשכת רה"מ"
paragraphs: על רקע ביקורת עזה על גרירת רגליים מצד ישראל, הגורם המדיני הדגיש כי "ישראל מחויבת לתוכנית 20 הנקודות - הכוללת את פירוק חמאס מנשקו". גורם במועצת השלום אמר ל-ynet כי בארגון "מעודדים מהשיחות האחרונות עם לשכת רה"מ"

בצל הביקורת על התנהלות הממשלה סביב הפסקת האש ברצועת עזה, גורם במועצת השלום אמר ל-ynet כי "אנו מעודדים מהשיחות האחרונות עם לשכת ראש הממשלה ומהמשך מחויבותה של ישראל לתוכנית 20 הנקודות של הנשיא טראמפ". במקביל, הגורם הדגיש כי "המועצה מצפה שישראל תתרגם את הדברים הללו למעשים - בימים הקרובים".
גורם מדיני בירושלים אמר מצדו כי "ישראל מחויבת לתכנית 20 הנקודות, ובימים הקרובים נתקדם מהותית לפי מתאר תכנית הנשיא טראמפ לעזה, הכולל את פירוק חמאס מנשקו".
(צילום: Omar AL-QATTAA / AFP, AP Carlos Osorio, אלכס קולומויסקי)

בשבוע שעבר פורסם ב-ynet כי בצל העיכובים הרבים ביישום התכנית, זמן רב כל כך לאחר שהפסקת האש נכנסה לתוקף, במועצת השלום, בארה"ב ובאיחוד האירופי - וכן במערכת הביטחון בישראל - התגבשה ההבנה כי ממשלת נתניהו תוקעת את הוצאתה לפועל.

אנשי מועצת השלום הזמינו גורמים ישראלים כדי להסביר להם עד כמה המצב חמור ודוחק, והכינו תדרוך ומצגת שמהם עלה מסר חד: הממשלה בישראל עומדת לאבד את ההזדמנות הנוכחית. השקופית האחרונה במצגת נקראה "אלטרנטיבות אחרות לעזה", בהן תוכנית שונה לשיקום עזה שעליה יחליט ממשל אמריקני עתידי או מועצת הביטחון של האו"ם, "אולי באמצעות אונר"א", כלשון הכותבים.

גם "הרשות הפלסטינית" צוינה כעוד אפשרות, ואחריה מיד: "חמאס". במצגת הקצרה הודגש כי "ישראל הופכת לאחראית באורח מלא לכל העלויות האדמיניסטרטיביות וההומניטריות למען אנשי עזה", באופן שהבהיר כי אם לא תפעל ליישום תכנית טראמפ, הרצועה עלולה לשוב לידי חמאס.
(AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

גם ג'ארד קושנר, חתנו ויועצו של הנשיא טראמפ, הזהיר בריאיון ל"ניו יורק מגזין" כי ישראל עלולה להפוך למדינה מוקצית בעולם אם תמשיך במדיניותה הנוכחית. "ישראל ניצבת בפני צומת דרכים", אמר. "היא יכולה לצמוח מתוך הטרגדיה של 7 באוקטובר, להפוך לבטוחה הרבה יותר ומשולבת בעולם, או להמשיך במסלול הנוכחי, שמוביל אותה למעמד של מדינה מוקצית בזירה הבינלאומית".

לדבריו, הוא ניסה בחודשים האחרונים לשכנע את נתניהו לאפשר את קידום תוכנית השיקום של רצועת עזה, אך נתקל בסירוב, שהותיר את התהליך בקיפאון. קושנר שוחח ביום שלישי עם נתניהו, והפציר בו ליישם את חלקה של ישראל בתוכנית 20 הנקודות. במהלך השיחה, קושנר דחק בנתניהו לקדם כניסה של אוהלים וסיוע הומניטרי לרצועת עזה לקראת החורף, וגם לקדם את האישורים שיאפשרו לכוח הייצוב הבינלאומי להיכנס לרצועת עזה.

במועצת השלום אמרו שהשיחה בין הצדדים הייתה טובה, ושתיתכן התקדמות להבנות. לצד זאת הם הדגישו כי "כרגע אין מה להודיע על הבנות", וכי "אנו פועלים לקדם את העניינים". גורם שמעורה בפרטים אמר כי "הייתה אווירה חיובית, ונתניהו הביע רצון לקדם את תוכנית 20 הנקודות. הדבר ייבחן בביצוע בפועל בימים הקרובים".

articles.title: Why Eisenkot's bloc is rushing to scrap four laws passed by Netanyahu's coalition - explainer
articles.summary: All four laws were passed with delayed start dates or frozen by the High Court, so repealing them now would stop them before they change anything.
paragraphs: With the 26th Knesset sworn in and the race to form a new government underway, the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot has launched an accelerated legislative blitz to repeal a series of laws passed by the outgoing coalition in the 25th Knesset.

The four main laws on the agenda have one thing in common. Each was passed with a delayed start date or has been frozen by the High Court of Justice. Repealing them quickly now is meant to stop them before they can actually change how the systems they target work.
Sa'ar-Levin law reshapes the Judicial Selection Committee

In March 2025, the 25th Knesset approved Amendment No. 4 to Basic Law: The Judiciary and Amendment No. 105 to the Courts Law. Together, they fundamentally changed the makeup of the Judicial Selection Committee and its voting rules. The law gave politicians from both the coalition and the opposition the decisive say at the expense of the legal establishment's representatives. It reduced the judges' influence, removed the Israel Bar Association's representatives, and eliminated the need for Supreme Court justices to agree to appointments to the top court.

Under the new law, the committee would be made up of the justice minister, a second minister chosen by the government, two MKs (one from the coalition and one from the opposition), two public representatives chosen by the Knesset (one by the coalition and one by the opposition), and three Supreme Court justices.

The law's sponsors, Justice Minister Yariv Levin and Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, said its purpose was to diversify the bench, correct what they called a lack of representation for certain communities, and shift power to elected officials. Opponents argued that it politicized the judicial appointments process and would undermine the independence of the judiciary.

In practice, the law has changed nothing. It was written to take effect only once the 26th Knesset convened and new representatives were appointed to the committee. Technically, the law is already in force, but the committee has not convened or chosen new members.

The bills to repeal both amendments have already passed a preliminary reading. They are now being advanced in a special committee chaired by MK Gilad Kariv. If the repeal is completed before the new committee is formed in the 26th Knesset, the original nine-member model would remain in place. That model has three Supreme Court justices, two ministers, two MKs, and two Bar Association representatives. It also requires a special majority of seven of the nine members to appoint Supreme Court justices, a mechanism that forces agreement between the political and professional ranks.
Attorney-general law strips binding status of legal opinions

The original bill sought to split the attorney-general's role entirely into two separate positions, a legal adviser and a prosecutor-general. It also sought to overhaul the process for appointing and dismissing the attorney-general. Toward the end of the 25th Knesset, however, the bill was split, and only part of it passed its second and third readings.

The law that passed did not split the role, but it made three major changes. First, it allows the government, and ministries with the government's approval, to disregard the attorney-general's legal opinions on noncriminal matters. Second, it ends the attorney-general's exclusive right to represent the government: the government may hire separate legal representation in court, and the attorney-general may not appear in court without the government's approval. Third, it places the attorney-general under the justice minister's oversight, and it requires the government to set new rules for appointing the attorney-general within 30 days of the law taking effect.

The coalition argued that the law was needed to ensure governability and to let an elected government carry out its policies without a "legal veto." Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara and petitioners to the High Court argued that it would hollow out the role of the government's legal gatekeeper and turn the attorney-general into the ministers' private lawyer.

The law has not changed anything in practice. Its start date was set from the outset for Jan. 1, 2027, so that it would not apply during the election campaign. On top of that, the High Court has suspended it following petitions against it.

Repealing the law before January 2027, through a special committee chaired by MK Efrat Rayten, would keep it from ever taking effect. That would preserve the legal status quo that has existed since the Agranat and Shamgar commissions, even though it was never enshrined in legislation. The attorney-general's opinion would continue to reflect binding law for the government unless a court rules otherwise. Separate representation for the government in court would be allowed only with the attorney-general's approval, in exceptional cases.
Karhi's broadcasting law creates minister-picked regulator

Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi's sweeping broadcasting reform ran into legal difficulties and sharp criticism from the Knesset's and the government's legal advisers. It was therefore split ahead of its approval in July 2026. The parts that were removed and postponed included involvement in appointing officials at news organizations, direct oversight powers over the "reliability" of news content, and rules on prohibited broadcasts and investments by international channels.

Even so, the core version that passed, the Communications (Broadcasting) Law, 5786-2026, brought a structural revolution. It abolished the Second Authority for Television and Radio and the Cable and Satellite Broadcasting Council. In their place, it created a new nine-member council, six of whose members would be appointed by the communications minister through a search committee headed by his ministry's director-general. The council would be empowered to impose fines of up to 1% of a company's revenue, and to cancel or suspend content providers' registrations without a court order. It would also be able to demand internal data from broadcasters, and it would take over ratings measurement from the independent ratings committee.
