paragraphs: אחד הדברים הטובים ביותר שאתם יכולים לעשות לאבטחת המידע שלכם זה להשתמש במנהל סיסמאות. במקום למחזר סיסמאות, לשכוח אותן ולהזין אותן בכל פעם מחדש, מנהלי הסיסמאות יכולים לג'נרט לכם סיסמאות חזקות הרבה יותר, לשמור על ה-Passkeys שלכם, להתחבר באמצעותם ולהזין עבורכם את הסיסמאות בלי שתצטרכו לזכור אותן. לשימוש יומיומי בדרך כלל מספיק לזכור את סיסמת המאסטר שלכם. בחשבון 1Password שמוגן במפתח סודי, תצטרכו גם אותו בכניסה הראשונה ממכשיר חדש. אבל מה קורה כשהאקרים מצליחים לפרוץ דווקא למנהל הסיסמאות עצמו? ובכן, זה כבר סיפור אחר לגמרי. הנה מה שאתם חייבים לדעת על האירוע החמור.
מחשבון ה-GitHub של העובד היישר למערכות הפנימיות

1Password, ממנהלי הסיסמאות הפופולריים וגם המוערכים ביותר בעולם, דיווח על "אירוע אבטחה" שכלל בין היתר פריצה למערכות הפנימיות וגניבת מידע רגיש ביותר. בחברה טוענים כי ב-19 בנובמבר זוהו סימנים לחדירה לחשבון ה-GitHub הארגוני של אחד מעובדי החברה. כמו בלא מעט מתקפות על שרשרת האספקה, התוקף נעזר בחשבון של העובד כדי לגשת לקוד המקור ולהחדיר קוד זדוני לשרת של החברה, וכך הצליח גם להניח את ידיו על מידע של משתמשים ולקוחות של החברה.

בין היתר, התוקף הצליח להשיג מידע כמו שמות, כתובות מייל, מזהי משתמש, מועדי פתיחת החשבון והכניסה האחרונה, מפתחות פומביים, פרמטרים של פרוטוקול ההתחברות, טוקנים מחלק מקישורי ההזמנה ושחזור החשבון שנשלחו במייל ועוד. בנוסף, התוקף השיג גישה למערכת ה-CI/CD של החברה והעתיק קוד מקור ממאגרים פרטיים שלה.

ב-1Password אומרים ש"קבוצה קטנה" של משתמשים קיבלה הודעה פרטנית על חשיפת טוקנים מתוך קישורי ההזמנה או השחזור שנשלחו אליהם. לפי החברה, התוקף לא הצליח להניח את ידיו על סיסמאות בכספות או מפתחות הצפנה, כך שהנתונים הקריטיים ביותר של המשתמשים, והסיבה שהם משתמשים במנהל הסיסמאות בכלל, לא דלפו לכאורה. עם זאת, יש כאן כמה סימני שאלה גדולים מאוד: בחברה לא נקבו במספר החשבונות והמשתמשים שהושפעו מהדליפה ולא הסבירו כיצד הצליח התוקף לחדור לחשבון ה-GitHub של העובד ולהכניס קוד זדוני לשירותי השרת של החברה.

למרות הפריצה, 1Password הוכיחה שגם חדירה ללב המערכות של החברה לא חושפת לכאורה את הכספות או התכנים שבהן, כיוון שרק המשתמשים מחזיקים במפתח ההצפנה. אבל למרות שהכספות עצמן לא דלפו, ישנה סכנה למשתמשים בדמות קמפיין פישינג ממוקד היטב. כשהתוקף יודע את הפרטים האישיים שלכם, ואפילו מידע שאמור להיות חשוף רק למערכות הפנימיות של 1Password, הוא יכול לשכנע אתכם הרבה יותר בקלות "לבצע החלפת סיסמה לחשבון שלכם", במהלכה תזינו כמובן את הסיסמה הנוכחית, שתעבור לידיו, או שהוא ינסה לגנוב את טוקן ההזדהות שלכם. בנוסף, התוקף עשוי לנסות לשכנע אתכם לתת לו את המפתח הסודי. בחברה מבהירים שבשום שלב הם לא יבקשו את הפרטים הללו, ובכל מקרה, הזינו אותם רק באפליקציית 1Password הרשמית, או באתר של החברה, ובתנאי שאתם אלה שהזנתם את הכתובת או פתחתם את האפליקציה. אז אולי המידע הסודי ביותר לא דלף, אבל זה לא אומר שהתוקפים מרימים ידיים ולא ינסו עכשיו להניח את היד שלהם עליו. ראו הוזהרתם.

articles.title: Thirteen dead as mine disaster highlights illegal hunt for gold
articles.summary: Indonesian authorities say another 13 are missing in the illegal gold mine, which flooded on Monday.
paragraphs: It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground.

Rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. On Monday night, he and at least 25 other miners were digging in an open-pit mine about 100m (328ft) deep, when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood the two shafts.
Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site. At least 13 more are thought to still be missing.
Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with personnel using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow and slippery mine shafts, which are continually being flooded from below.
Above ground, ambulances and medical personnel are ready and waiting to transport victims.

"We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement on Wednesday.
"The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely."
Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but remains widespread in rural parts of the mineral-rich archipelago.

Multiple studies show that over the past ten years the illegal industry has rapidly flourished, often in correlation with rising gold prices. In early 2026, those prices reached an all-time high – spurring a gold rush that prompted mine operators across the country to expand their operations.

This included state-owned mining company Aneka Tambang (Antam), which owns the business permit for the area in which this week's flooded mine is located. Antam have said the mine was not theirs and was operating without their authorisation.

On Wednesday, while rescue operations there were underway, West Java Regional Police separately announced that they had uncovered 24 cases of illegal mining across the province between October and November alone.

But Bisman Bakhtiar, Executive Director of the Center for Energy and Mining Law Studies, told the BBC earlier this year that the actual number of illegal mines in Indonesia is higher than the government's figures.
"[The government figures are] what's been recorded. That means there must be more than that," he said, noting that law enforcement operations have had little impact on the sector.
"It's still very massive and very big because this has been going on for a very long time."
Others allege that the illegal industry is underpinned by corruption.

Laode M Syarif, former deputy chairman of the Corruption Eradication Committee, said that unofficial mining is difficult to eradicate because every illegal mine has "backing", usually from "police and military or high-ranking officials in local and provincial governments".
"As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue," he said.
In many cases, though, the allure of these mines is simple: they offer an economic lifeline to people with few other viable prospects.
Despite the value of gold having dipped in recent months, countless illegal miners throughout Indonesia are still eagerly digging for paydirt.

But the lack of regulation and poor construction in the pits also means accidents are relatively common – whether from landslides, floods, or exposure to hazardous gases, all of which have claimed lives in recent years.
Earlier this year, in the same area as this week's flooded mine, 11 illegal gold miners reportedly died after a carbon monoxide leak inside a shaft.
Elsewhere, in West Sumatra, nine people were killed at an illegal gold mine in May after heavy rain triggered the collapse of a 30-metre cliff, burying 12 miners in total.
There are numerous reports of other such incidents across the Indonesian archipelago. But the illegal nature of the small-scale gold mining sector obfuscates the true number of casualties.

Even this week, when asked how many miners were in the pits in Bogor when they flooded, M Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency, said the total casualty figure "is still unclear".
"Some say 20 people, others say 29 people," Hamdani told Indonesian news outlet Detik. "The problem is that no one reported it and no one wants to report it."
The Indonesian Ombudsman on Thursday urged law enforcement officials to conduct a thorough investigation of the incident and to address the larger systemic issue behind it.

"This should be a momentum for all parties to resolve the [illegal gold mining] problem comprehensively, not just taking action after the incident or closing the holes discovered," said Abdul Ghoffar, a member of the Indonesian Ombudsman.

"We need to uncover the entire [illegal gold mining] chain," he continued. "We must not allow only the miners in the field to be seen and prosecuted, while those who control the activities, provide capital and facilities, store, and market the mined products remain untouched.
"Law enforcement must target the actors and networks that keep this illegal activity going."
As rescue operations continue and more bodies are recovered, the picture is becoming less murky. But even if there are survivors among those who remain missing, time may be running out.
More than three days since the shafts flooded, the relatives of the anonymous men in the mines are desperately waiting to hear whether their loved ones survived.
As she waits for news of her father, Rani says: "I hope he's found soon."

articles.title: DR Congo demands answers over Ugandan general's threats
articles.summary: Gen Kainerugaba threatened a rebel takeover of a mineral-rich area in DR Congo in controversial X posts.
paragraphs: The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.

In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns.
The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.
The Ugandan government has yet to respond.
The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours.
Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.
Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.
In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahima ethnic community.
The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province.
They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.
He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.
Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.
Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.
It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.
During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed."
The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels, with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.
Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo.

"These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
"The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future".
The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".
It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.
In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.
In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.
The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.
In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

articles.title: Battlefield experience is not enough: IDF returns to training after three years of war
articles.summary: With troops still deployed across multiple fronts and renewed fighting with Iran a possibility, IDF seeks to restore combat readiness, address command failures exposed on Oct. 7 and adapt to emerging threats through shorter, more flexible training
paragraphs: With troops still deployed across multiple fronts and renewed fighting with Iran a possibility, IDF seeks to restore combat readiness, address command failures exposed on Oct. 7 and adapt to emerging threats through shorter, more flexible training
After three years of nearly uninterrupted warfare, the IDF is returning to training, or at least hoping to.

With military operations continuing in the Gaza Strip, Lebanon and the West Bank, troops deployed along Israel's borders and the possibility of renewed fighting with Iran looming, senior military officials recognize the need to reinvest in combat readiness, soldiers' professional skills and command and control capabilities alongside ongoing operational commitments.
IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir visits an exercise conducted by the Nahal Brigade's 50th Battalion at the National Ground Training Center
That message was at the center of IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir's visit to an exercise conducted by the Nahal Brigade's 50th Battalion at the National Ground Training Center.

Zamir was accompanied by Southern Command chief Maj. Gen. Yaniv Asor, Ground Forces commander Maj. Gen. Nadav Lotan, 162nd Division commander Brig. Gen. Sagiv Dahan, National Ground Training Center commander Brig. Gen. Yaniv Barot, Nahal Brigade commander Col. Arik Moyal and other senior officers.
The exercise, designed to improve combat readiness, included offensive operations and urban warfare scenarios incorporating advanced military capabilities.

“After three years of fighting, the IDF is returning to training,” Zamir said. “We continue to strengthen defenses along all borders and protect communities from forward defensive zones. At the same time, we are improving the IDF's readiness to return to combat.”
Zamir stressed that the exercises were intended not only to rehearse operational scenarios but also to reinforce the military's professional fundamentals.
“I expect you, the commanders, to make the most of this valuable training time and strengthen military fundamentals, norms, standards, individual proficiency, discipline and unit cohesion,” he said.
His remarks reflect one of the military's central conclusions after three years of war: Extensive battlefield experience cannot substitute for structured training.

Soldiers and commanders who have accumulated considerable combat experience must also have opportunities to review their performance, practice their skills and improve their capabilities. At the same time, the military must incorporate new operational methods, experiment with technologies developed during the war and reestablish the professional standards expected of a well-trained standing army.
One of the central issues addressed during the exercise was commanders' ability to direct multiple forces simultaneously, establish a common operational picture and coordinate combat operations.

The importance of those capabilities became particularly apparent during the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, which exposed serious failures in situational awareness, coordination between units and the military's ability to exercise effective command and control during a large-scale attack unfolding at multiple locations simultaneously.

The current exercises therefore extend beyond training individual soldiers or platoons. They are designed to test the military system as a whole, examining how senior commanders make decisions, how operational information is communicated between command levels, how units coordinate their activities and how commanders manage large numbers of troops deployed across different sectors.

The approach represents a significant shift in the military's training doctrine. The IDF must not only restore soldiers' tactical proficiency but also improve its ability to operate as a cohesive force under conditions of uncertainty and intense operational pressure.
Establishing an accurate operational picture, communicating orders rapidly and synchronizing operations between units will be critical to any future military campaign.

The need for such training has become more pressing because some career officers advanced rapidly through the ranks and assumed new command positions during the war amid operational demands and shortages of command personnel.

Many commanders completed their professional training, assumed new roles and were quickly dispatched to combat zones. While some gained substantial battlefield experience, they had insufficient opportunities to practice their new roles, develop a thorough understanding of the capabilities of the forces under their command and work through complex scenarios in a controlled environment.
With a limited window now available to resume training, the military hopes to address some of the gaps in professional proficiency and leadership that emerged during the war.

The return to training, however, is not taking place under normal peacetime conditions. The IDF continues to maintain forces across multiple sectors, conduct military operations and defensive missions and prepare for the possibility of renewed escalation.
As a result, it cannot allocate lengthy, uninterrupted training periods to every unit as it would during quieter years.

The National Ground Training Center is seeking to address those constraints by developing shorter, more flexible training programs that allow units to conduct meaningful exercises even when operational schedules remain unpredictable.
The goal is to provide effective training for every unit, even when troops cannot be withdrawn from their ongoing assignments for extended periods.

The challenge is to balance immediate operational requirements with the military's long-term readiness. The IDF cannot abandon its border deployments or defensive commitments, but without allowing units to train, refresh their skills and improve their capabilities, it risks entering its next military campaign without adequate preparation.
Zamir also emphasized that new threats had emerged over the past year, requiring troops to adapt their operational methods.
“A trained military is a professional military, and it is measured by its ability to arrive prepared for the challenges of the changing battlefield,” he said.

Training is also central to the military's adaptation to a new operational reality. Three years of war have changed the nature of the threats Israel faces, the tactics employed by its adversaries and the technology at their disposal.

The military must draw lessons from its battlefield experience, integrate new technologies, reassess existing doctrines and develop new operational methods. Those capabilities require dedicated training and cannot be developed through combat operations alone.

articles.title: Parents cutting basics at Christmas, charity warns
articles.summary: The chief executive of Worthing Soup Kitchen says some families choose between food and presents.
paragraphs: Christmas is likely to see families cut back on essentials to try and meet the expenses of the festive period, a West Sussex soup kitchen has warned.

Katrina McCormack, chief executive of the Shout Worthing Soup Kitchen, told BBC Radio Sussex that they are forced to limit the amount of support they can give due to high demand at Christmas, and make sure their shelves are stocked.
It comes at the start of a campaign to raise thousands for turkey and other Christmas trimmings for struggling families, which the charity says is a "driving force" for their work in December.
McCormack said: "We ran an afternoon tea with Father Christmas, and last year we had children asking him for food."
She added: "A lot of families are struggling to pay that extra, they are struggling to put food on the table.
"Most of our families won't have a Christmas dinner without this."
New research from charity Save the Children found that, of those surveyed, 65% of parents of children under 16 in the UK were concerned about being able to afford Christmas.
It added that nearly a third of parents will buy fewer presents than normal, and 16% will reduce heating use in December to save money.

McCormack said that, due to increasing cost of living, the charity had seen an increase in the number of people needing support, including families who are asking for help when they would not be needed in other parts of the year.
"Poeple have come up and asked us if we can help them get an air fryer because they can't afford to put a cooker on," she added.

articles.title: Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests
articles.summary: Female protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, a rights group says.
paragraphs: Image source, Supplied by family
Taraneh Rahimi is on death row in Iran.
In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.
She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.
He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.

When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.
He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.
Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.

The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.
Image source, Anonymous/Getty Images
The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".

It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".

It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".
The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.

It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.

The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.

The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.

Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.
Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.

Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".
Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".

According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.
Image source, Supplied to human rights groups
Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.
Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.

She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.

Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.
"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.

In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.
The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.
The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."
Image source, Supplied to Hrana
Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".

In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".
At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.

She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".
Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".
Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.

However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".
In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.

The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned – though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".
Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.
Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."

The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."
Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.
Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.
Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.
Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.
Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

articles.title: Foreign volunteers return to kibbutzim along Lebanon border for first time since October 7
articles.summary: More than three years after war emptied northern kibbutzim, young volunteers from the US and Poland arrive at Kibbutz Baram, just a few hundred feet from the border, offering hope for a historic program struggling to revive international interest
paragraphs: More than three years after war emptied northern kibbutzim, young volunteers from the US and Poland arrive at Kibbutz Baram, just a few hundred feet from the border, offering hope for a historic program struggling to revive international interest

For the first time since October 2023, foreign volunteers are returning to kibbutzim along Israel's northern border with Lebanon, marking another step toward restoring normal life in communities that were evacuated during the war.

The first two volunteers, from the United States and Poland, arrived last week at Kibbutz Baram, located just 300 meters (about 1,000 feet) from the Lebanese border. Marek Ruchla, 24, from Warsaw, and Fred Schwenke, 19, from Raleigh, North Carolina, are now settling into their new jobs in the kitchen of the kibbutz dining hall. Yesterday, for example, they were preparing schnitzels for their fellow kibbutz members, just as volunteers did before the war.
Marek Ruchla, 24, from Warsaw, and Fred Schwenke, 19, from Raleigh, North Carolina, are settling into their jobs in the kibbutz kitchen

Both are excited to become part of the kibbutz movement's six-decade tradition of welcoming volunteers from around the world. "I came for nine months," Fred says. "I'm here mainly to help, and I also need the experience of living independently."
Asked about the proximity to the Lebanese border, he seems unconcerned. "Honestly, it doesn't even cross my mind. I love being here."

Standing beside him, Marek explains that his decision was motivated by curiosity about Israel and kibbutz life. "I came to the kibbutz to explore Israel and learn about the kibbutz," he says. "I heard this was the best kibbutz. I know we're about 300 meters from the border, but it's safe here. There's no problem. Everything is fine."
The return of foreign volunteers to the northern kibbutz is a milestone in Baram's history.

On October 6, 2023, the kibbutz was home to 33 volunteers from more than 10 countries. They lived in the kibbutz's large volunteer campus and worked in its orchards, packing facilities, laundry and dining hall. When Baram was evacuated following the outbreak of the war, the volunteers left. Now, after more than three years, the kibbutz has decided to restart the program as part of its return to normal life.
Volunteers on the kibbutz
(Photo: The Kibbutz Movement)

But nationwide figures illustrate just how difficult restoring the program to its former scale may be. The Kibbutz Movement's international volunteer program has operated for more than 60 years, welcoming over 400,000 young people from around the world.

On the eve of October 7, 155 foreign volunteers, most of them not Jewish, were working in 20 kibbutzim across Israel. Today, just 30 remain in the country, although seven more are expected to arrive over the next month.

"Our goal is to return within a year to the level of activity that characterized the program before the Iron Swords war," the Kibbutz Movement says. "However, we are now dealing with a reality very different from the one we knew before the war. Israel's standing in the world has deteriorated, public discourse about it is difficult and polarized, and we are seeing a significant decline in interest among young people abroad in coming here."
Despite those challenges, the movement sees the program as an opportunity to rebuild connections between Israel and the wider world.

"The volunteer program allows young people from abroad to experience Israeli society up close, not through news headlines, but through the people and everyday communal life," says Keren Pardo, director of the Kibbutz Movement's international department.
Volunteers who came despite everything

Lior Simcha, secretary-general of the Kibbutz Movement, believes such personal encounters are particularly important today. "Precisely at a time when Israel is facing a growing wave of antisemitism, personal encounters with Israel are enormously important," he says.

Hagar Reuveni, CEO of the Kibbutz Movement, also emphasizes the practical benefits for communities still recovering from the war. "The volunteer project provides assistance to kibbutzim that have been on the front line for three years, while also offering volunteers a positive Israeli experience."

Over the decades, the program has attracted a number of well-known figures, including former British prime minister Boris Johnson, Duran Duran lead singer Simon Le Bon and actors Anthony Hopkins and Helen Mirren.

In the coming months, the Kibbutz Movement also plans to resume its volunteer program at Kibbutz Sasa, another community near the Lebanese border. Officials acknowledge, however, that attracting young people from abroad remains a considerable challenge, particularly given the security situation and Israel's changing international image.
Even former British prime minister Boris Johnson volunteered on a kibbutz in Israel
(Photo: Ammar Awad/Reuters)

"We understand that under the current circumstances, this is a significant challenge, one that also depends on diplomatic and security developments and Israel's standing in the world," the movement said in a statement.

For now, the arrival of just two volunteers at Baram is a modest beginning compared with the dozens who lived there before the war. But their presence in the kibbutz kitchen, preparing meals for residents just a few hundred meters from Lebanon, represents a return to a tradition interrupted more than three years ago.

articles.title: ‘Trapped in grief’: wife of Japanese journalist detained by Russia pleads for his release
articles.summary: Yuki Imai being held in Moscow on allegations he conducted ‘espionage’ while working for a newspaper in Sakhalin island in Russia’s far east The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying has issued an emotive appeal for his release. Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid-October as he was preparing to return to Japan from a two-year assignment at the Japanese newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the island of Sakhalin in Russia’s far east. Continue reading...
paragraphs: The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying has issued an emotive appeal for his release.

Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid-October as he was preparing to return to Japan from a two-year assignment at the Japanese newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the island of Sakhalin in Russia’s far east.

Russian authorities alleged that Imai had been “conducting espionage activities” on the island, collecting information about Russian defence capabilities he intended to pass on to Japanese intelligence. Both the newspaper and Japan’s prime minster, Sanae Takaichi, have denied the claims.

His detention has inflamed tensions between Tokyo and Moscow and prompted Takaichi to request Imai’s release during a meeting with the Russian leader Vladimir Putin at last week’s Apec summit in China.

The arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over islands in the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido – which Russia has administered since the dying days of the second world war.
In a statement released to media organisations through the Hokkaido Shimbun, Imai’s wife, Nozomi Imai, said her husband’s plight meant his family were “trapped in grief”.

“Since his detention, his parents and I have spent every day worrying about him” she said in the statement, published in Japanese, English and Russian. Recalling the moment she saw TV footage of her husband being taken away by Russian authorities, she said: “I could hardly breathe. It felt as if my heart were being ripped apart.”

She added: “No one could remain calm after seeing a beloved family member with his arms bound behind his back. In the video, I could even see the souvenirs in his suitcase – the gifts he was bringing home for us. I could not sleep even for a moment that night. When morning came, it still did not feel real. I could not even cry.”

Imai, 34, has barely seen his infant daughter, who was born during his posting to Russia. “He had been so looking forward to coming home,” Nozomi Imai wrote. “During his posting, our daughter was born. She is now 21 months old, and he loves her more than words can say. He had even said excitedly that he wanted to be the one to pick her up from daycare on the very day he got home.”
Japanese diplomats have been permitted to visit Imai only twice since he was detained, although he has had several meetings with lawyers appointed by his employer.

Japan’s ambassador to Moscow, Akira Muto, said he had met the journalist at Lefortovo detention centre in Moscow this week and that he appeared to be in good health. Japanese embassy officials were also granted access to Imai at the end of October.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai had been engaged in “ordinary news gathering” on Sakhalin, adding the newspaper did “not conduct reporting or gather information based on government directions”.

Shortly after his arrest, Takaichi denied Imai had been spying. “There is no such fact,” she told reporters, adding that “the protection of Japanese nationals is extremely important right now, and we intend to focus our efforts on that.”
Concerns are growing that Moscow will seek to make an example of Imai in protest at Japan’s support for sanctions imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Russia’s Federal Security Service, which is investigating Imai, has not commented publicly since it announced the reporter’s arrest. His detention is scheduled to expire on 12 December but could be extended, the Kyodo news agency said.

The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai, whose grandfather was born on Sakhalin, was an admirer of Russian culture who had used his position to promote grassroots exchanges.He even hosted Russian visitors at his home in the Hokkaido city of Nemuro.
Nozomi Imai, who said she and her husband had met as students through their shared love of Russian films and novels, said his detention was taking a toll on his ageing parents.

“They worry whether they will ever see their beloved only son again in their lifetime,” she wrote. “Yuki Imai is not only a journalist. He is a beloved son, husband, and father. Please – please return this precious papa to his little daughter.”

articles.title: Shekel slides to 14-month weakest against dollar
articles.summary: Wall Street losses, the global strength of the dollar, political and geopolitical uncertainties and interest rate differentials are all weighing on the Israeli currency.
paragraphs: Wall Street losses, the global strength of the dollar, political and geopolitical uncertainties and interest rate differentials are all weighing on the Israeli currency.

The shekel slid to its 14-month weakest against the US dollar yesterday as the Bank of Israel set the representative rate up 1.046% at NIS 3.38/$. The shekel-euro rate was set 0.967% higher at NIS 3.698/€. The shekel has recovered somewhat this morning in inter-bank trading to NIS 3.358/$ and NIS 3.682/€.
The shekel has depreciated by 12% against the US dollar in less than a month and by 22% since the end of May.

The shekel weakened by nearly 3% in less than two days this week, after wiping out all the gains it had recorded following the Nvidia-driven rally on Wall Street. However, it is not just the declines on Wall Street weighing on the Israeli currency as Israeli institutional investors buy dollar and sell shekels to hedge their portfolios. The strengthening of the dollar globally and the interest rate differentials between Israel and the US are also playing a role.

On top of all this the shekel, which has not been trading at these levels since September 2025, is adversely affected by the political uncertainty in Israel and lack of a stable government as well as geopolitical tensions as the possibility of renewed fighting with Iran looms on the horizon.
Published by Globes, Israel business news - en.globes.co.il - on November 26, 2026.
