articles.title: Watch: BBC confronts German man suspected of supplying migrant gangs with small boats
articles.summary: Marvin Reuter is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.
paragraphs: A German boat dealer is suspected of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings to the UK, in the first four months of 2026, allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.
His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.
We confronted the 35-year-old at his business, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

articles.title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
articles.summary: Nearly a third of crossings in early 2026 allegedly involved boats or engines from the German man's firm.
paragraphs: ByJessica ParkerBerlin correspondent and Tom BealBBC News Investigations
A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.
Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.
His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.
We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.
Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.
Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.
Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.
Image source, Getty Images
At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.
There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.
In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."
It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.
French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.
The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.
While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".
Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.
In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.
In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.
Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.
News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.
He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.
The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.
The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.
Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.
The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.
"Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."
Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boats
Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.
Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.
Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.
On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.
The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.
Meanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.
Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.
The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.
When we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.
He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.

We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.
It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.

In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.
The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.
Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".

While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.
The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

articles.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
articles.summary: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
paragraphs: The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.

The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.
The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%.
The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce.
The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings.
Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products.
Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.
The proposed tariffs will affect goods from China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.
The USTR's Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".
He said that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression".
They also employ "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base", Greer said.
But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.
Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.
Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.
Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.
These new levies are build on a "stronger legal foundation" under US law compared with Trump's April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs, Singapore Management University economics lecturer Chang Pao-Li said.

Trump previously invoked emergency presidential powers to impose tariffs that have since been struck down, while his latest approach relies on the USTR's authority to impose tariffs to address certain foreign trade practices, she said.
The levies are still likely to face legal challenges, but there has been a "historical precedent" for such tariffs remaining in force, Chang said.

Many tariffs imposed under Section 301 - a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices - during Trump's first term remained in effect during his successor Joe Biden's administration.

However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.

"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.
The additional tariff burden is likely to be small because a limited number of goods are subject to the new duties, Brown added.
Jurisdictions affected by the new wave of tariffs have voiced their disapproval over the Trump administration's move.
Washington has also proposed a 10% tariff on goods from Brazil, as part of a separate investigation over what it says are "harmful trade practices" undercutting American workers.
Brazilian authorities expressed their "outrage" at the announcement, saying that the move is aimed at pressuring the government to change regulations around issues like digital trade.
The South American nation faces duties on finished aircraft and sugar sold to the US.
"Brazil will not yield to such threats," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's office said.
The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.
The latest tariff rate is "not consistent" with the reality of bilateral economic-trade cooperation between the US and Vietnam, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Bui Thanh Son said.

The Japanese government said the US tariffs were "regrettable", while the Singapore government said it disagrees with the White House's findings and that it is engaging the USTR to explore ways to reduce the tariff.
South Korea's trade minister said the proposed 15% tariff will be "more than a decent outcome" as it would fall in line with a previously agreed limit with Washington.
Last year, Seoul pledged $350bn (£267bn) in US investments in exchange for lower tariffs as part of a trade deal.

US trading partners have been "waiting for this shoe to drop" and have argued that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much, said the Asia Society Policy Institute's Wendy Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator.
"Many believe that China, not them, should be the target for US action," she added.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun described the new tariffs as a form of "political manipulation", describing as "false" the US claim that China produces more than it can consume.
The tariff announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.
The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.
Beijing has remained vague on how it will respond but for now seems "prepared to live with the new rates provided they don't exceed 20%", Cutler said.
Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi in Seoul

articles.title: IDF, Shin Bet target senior Hamas terrorist in overnight Gaza strike
articles.summary: The IDF has not disclosed the target’s identity or confirmed whether he was killed; Palestinians report three dead in a strike on the Shati refugee camp, following the killing of two senior Hamas internal security officials in recent days
paragraphs: The IDF has not disclosed the target’s identity or confirmed whether he was killed; Palestinians report three dead in a strike on the Shati refugee camp, following the killing of two senior Hamas internal security officials in recent days

The IDF and Shin Bet domestic security agency struck a senior Hamas terrorist in the Gaza Strip early Thursday, the military announced. Neither the identity of the target nor the outcome of the strike was immediately disclosed.

Meanwhile, Palestinian reports from Gaza said three people were killed and several others wounded in Israeli strikes that allegedly targeted a "group of civilians" in the Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City.
An Israeli strike in Gaza
(Photo: AP Photo/Leo Correa)
Earlier, the Palestinian Shehab news agency cited hospital sources in Gaza as saying that at least 11 people, including two girls, had been killed in Israeli strikes since Wednesday morning.
The latest operation follows a series of targeted killings of senior figures in Hamas' internal security apparatus.

On Wednesday, an Israeli airstrike killed Muhammad Majed Abu al-Ouf, also known as Abu Hamza, who was set to assume a senior command position in Hamas' internal security apparatus in northern Gaza. Palestinian reports said his wife and two daughters were also killed in the strike.

Abu al-Ouf was expected to replace Naim Abu Nahal, who was killed in an Israeli strike a day earlier. Abu Nahal had assumed the position in September after his predecessor, Muin al-Arabid, whom Israeli officials described as Hamas' equivalent of the Shin Bet chief, was captured in a special operation.
The IDF and Shin Bet also revealed that Abu Nahal had been part of a secret circle within Hamas that held the remains of Israeli Staff Sgt. Oron Shaul for years.
Israeli security officials accuse Hamas' internal security apparatus of stealing food intended for civilians and interrogating and torturing Palestinians suspected of collaborating with Israel.
Security officials refer to the apparatus as "Hamas' Basij," a reference to the Iranian paramilitary militia operating under the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Israeli officials consider the successive killings a significant operational achievement, particularly because both senior Hamas figures possessed extensive knowledge of the terrorist organization's internal operations.

articles.title: ‘Scenes you wouldn’t see even in Africa’: Video of Iran’s president sparks outrage
articles.summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was filmed working in a dark office to encourage electricity conservation as winter approaches; Iranian media accused him of humiliating the country, while his government defended the move as leading by example
paragraphs: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was filmed working in a dark office to encourage electricity conservation as winter approaches; Iranian media accused him of humiliating the country, while his government defended the move as leading by example

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's attempt to set a personal example of energy conservation has backfired after footage showing him working in a dark office drew fierce criticism from Iranian media, with some accusing him of projecting weakness and humiliating the country.

In recent weeks, Pezeshkian has been urging Iranians to conserve electricity and energy ahead of winter as the Islamic Republic grapples with an energy crisis exacerbated by the war and the U.S. blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
The footage that triggered backlash: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian sitting in his darkened office

While the president has repeatedly addressed the issue, a video released over the weekend by Iran's state broadcaster, intended to showcase his personal commitment to conservation, instead triggered a wave of criticism.

In the footage, a state television reporter visits Pezeshkian's office. The broadcaster shared the video with the caption: "Have you ever seen the president's office?" Yet the office itself was barely visible, as the interview was conducted with the lights off.
The criticism was swift. One Iranian newspaper wrote that the government's communications team had "failed to properly advise President Pezeshkian."
Another critic suggested that the footage was intended to prepare the public for worsening conditions.

"The footage of Pezeshkian in his office, with the lights off and wearing warm clothing, may have been intended to psychologically prepare the public for the worst-case scenarios ahead. But the message of weakness it conveys is far more damaging."

Other criticism was even harsher: "Pezeshkian put Iran's dignity up for a clearance sale. The image you see, of him working in a dimly lit office while wearing a coat, is something you would not see even in the poorest countries in Africa."

Iranian government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani sought to defend the president, saying the entire administration was fully committed to the task at hand, while some were attempting to cast doubt on Pezeshkian's transparency, integrity and approach to solving problems.
Pezeshkian in his office: 'I'm simply avoiding switching on unnecessary lights'

"How can someone who eats dates tell others not to eat them?" she asked. "When the president asks the public to conserve energy, he leads by example. We accept all criticism directed at us, but remain firm in our belief that we must get through the winter by conserving resources."

Following the backlash, Pezeshkian himself addressed the controversy, clarifying that he had not turned off any lights but was "simply avoiding switching on unnecessary lights." He said he considered it his duty to prevent excessive consumption of resources.
In recent weeks, Pezeshkian has repeatedly emphasized the need for conservation as Iran struggles with an energy crisis and drought.
About two weeks ago, footage from an Iranian Cabinet meeting showed the country's interior minister getting up to switch off the lights, earning praise from the president.

The following day, Pezeshkian said: "Given the challenges facing domestic gas production as a result of the enemy's military aggression, it is essential to adopt conservation policies and manage consumption, particularly during the colder months of the year."

Last week, the Iranian president called on all government institutions and agencies to ensure an adequate energy supply and maintain production facilities through responsible consumption and appropriate conservation measures.

He also claimed that he had stopped heating his own home because of the crisis. "I am the president, and yet I sleep wearing a coat and fully dressed," he said. "I don't use any form of heating in my home."

articles.title: Nazi salute at 10 Downing Street: Influencers turn PM's residence into a 'circus'
articles.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces criticism after an influencer filmed himself making a Nazi salute outside the PM's official residence while mouthing explicit lyrics; Downing Street condemned the video but defended inviting social media stars to reach younger audiences
paragraphs: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces criticism after an influencer filmed himself making a Nazi salute outside the PM's official residence while mouthing explicit lyrics; Downing Street condemned the video but defended inviting social media stars to reach younger audiences

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has faced fierce criticism from political opponents over the past 24 hours after videos filmed during a gathering of social media influencers at his official residence, 10 Downing Street, sparked outrage across the United Kingdom.

The most controversial video shows TikTok star Max Balegde making a gesture resembling a Nazi salute outside the historic residence while miming along to a viral song featuring explicit lyrics. Although the clip was posted three weeks ago, it attracted widespread attention only recently and was deleted Tuesday following mounting criticism.
The video from 10 Downing Street that caused a stir

Burnham's opponents accused him of turning 10 Downing Street into a "circus," pointing to the clip and several other videos recorded during the event, including one featuring the prime minister himself alongside an influencer dancing inside the building.

Burnham, who succeeded Keir Starmer as Labour leader and prime minister in July, has long made extensive use of social media. Since taking office, he has significantly expanded Labour's efforts to reach younger audiences through online influencers.

That strategy culminated in a November 9 event at Downing Street attended by approximately 50 influencers with a combined following of 470 million people. According to reports, guests were required to surrender their personal phones and cameras upon entering the residence and were instead provided with devices by Downing Street staff to film content for their followers. The footage was subsequently sent to them after the event.
TikTok star Max Balegde's Nazi salute in front of 10 Downing Street

The video that drew the strongest criticism was filmed by Balegde outside the residence using his personal phone. In it, he appears to make a gesture resembling a Nazi salute while lip-syncing to an AI-generated song that has recently become a TikTok trend.

Balegde, who has 3.6 million TikTok followers and another 600,000 on Instagram, mouths the lyrics: "Bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets." "Bomboclaat" is a Jamaican profanity referring to a sanitary napkin, but in recent years the term has also become popular online slang used to express surprise, anger or frustration.
Downing Street described the video as "unacceptable," although reports indicated that the prime minister's social media accounts had previously liked the post before it was removed.

Other videos filmed during the same event also attracted attention. In one, TikTok personality Luke Hamnett recreates a famous scene from the film "Love Actually," in which Hugh Grant plays a British prime minister who is caught dancing by a member of his staff.

Hamnett's video shows him dancing to the Pointer Sisters' "Jump," moving between a mirror, the staircase lined with portraits of former British prime ministers and several rooms inside the residence. He is eventually "caught" by Burnham, who then sits down for an interview with him.

In another video, lifestyle influencer Rebecca Murphy dances in front of Downing Street's famous fireplace, flanked by British flags. A further clip featuring Balegde at the same fireplace also emerged. He edited the footage to include the caption: "They hate when you serve cunt at Downing Street," using a provocative slang expression popular in online culture.
Although these and other videos had been available online for several weeks, the controversy erupted only after attention shifted to Balegde's original clip outside the residence.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said at a news conference that she was "appalled" by the videos, accusing Burnham of encouraging people around the world to view Britain as a joke. She called on the prime minister to apologize for what she described as turning the historic residence into a personal studio for filming "silly TikTok videos."
Balegade in front of Downing Street's famous fireplace
Lifestyle influencer Rebecca Murphy dances in front of Downing Street's famous fireplace
TikToker Luke Hammett dances down the 10 Downing Street staircase
And in other rooms of the residence

"Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and all sorts of people who are hostile to Britain will see these things, receive reports about them and conclude that our prime minister is not a serious person, and that we are not a serious country," Badenoch said.

Referring specifically to Balegde's video, she added that it was disgraceful for 10 Downing Street, whose famous front door symbolizes British democracy, authority and international standing, to be treated in such a manner. She noted that the same entrance is used to welcome foreign leaders such as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, demonstrating Britain's public support for Ukraine.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage also condemned Balegde's video as "childish" and "degrading," although he stressed that he would not ban influencers from Downing Street if he became prime minister. "I would not have allowed them to behave in the way they behaved in this case," he said. "It showed a lack of respect for the place and the office, and it was highly inappropriate."

Burnham's spokesperson acknowledged that Balegde's video was unacceptable and said removing it from social media was the right decision. However, British media reported that the prime minister's social media accounts had liked the video before the controversy erupted. The spokesperson emphasized that Burnham has great respect for Downing Street's history but said the prime minister did not regret inviting the influencers.

"He understands that today there are millions of people who do not get their news from traditional media outlets, but receive their information through a variety of other channels, and he is determined to reach people wherever they are," the spokesperson said.
The government maintained that engaging with content creators was an important way to communicate with audiences who increasingly rely on social media rather than conventional news organizations.
Balegde, who found himself at the center of the controversy, posted a response video Tuesday explaining that he had filmed the deleted clip at the end of the Downing Street event.

He said he had only "10 seconds" to record something in front of the prime minister's famous black door and had made a spontaneous decision to use the viral TikTok song. He described the result as a "silly video," insisting there had been no malicious intent.
British Prime Minister Andy Burham is not sorry he invited the influencers
(Photo: Oli Scarff / AFP)
According to Balegde, nobody had objected to the clip during the three weeks it was online until "right-wing commentators" gave it what he described as a "horrible spin."
"It is completely clear that there was no malicious intent, and of course I apologize if any offense was caused," he said. "It must be a slow news day."

The controversy has nevertheless raised questions about the boundaries between political communication and online entertainment, as Burnham's efforts to engage younger audiences collide with criticism that the dignity of the prime minister's office is being undermined.

articles.title: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
articles.summary: Blaze on ring road surrounding Egyptian capital injures at least 21 people and leaves cars and motorcycles charred A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said. The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the health ministry. Continue reading...
paragraphs: A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.

The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the health ministry.

State media reported that the fire broke out when the fuel truck overturned. The stretch of the highway where it occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, the health ministry said.

At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene.
Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic as the road was blocked after the accident, saw the fuel truck and many cars on fire. He said he saw at least eight bodies being removed from burned cars.
“It was a huge fire, the cars got stuck together because of the fire,” he said, describing the fear and panic that followed. “It was a shocking scene.”
The Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The public prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were under way to identify the victims.

The health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further. He later travelled to the scene and to the hospitals, the health ministry said.
The minister’s spokesperson told the state-linked Al-Qahera News that the ring road had been reopened and the remnants of the accident cleared.

Deadly traffic incidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.
In January 2016, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

articles.title: France's political mainstream risks presidential vote debacle with no clear candidate
articles.summary: Hard-right and hard-left candidates dominate the polls ahead of next year's presidential election.
paragraphs: France's political mainstream faces wipe-out at the presidential election in April-May 2027, unless it acts fast to choose who it wishes to stand.

With every poll confirming the dominance of hard-right and hard-left leaders Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, candidates of the middle-ground – the old "legacy" parties – are being squeezed out of the game.
In theory any contender from centre-right or centre-left who was chosen in the first multi-candidate round of voting in April should be in a strong position to win in the play-off a fortnight later.
That is because at their separate ends of the spectrum both Le Pen and Mélenchon have more people who oppose than support them.
But personal rivalries, lack of preparation and differing political visions have so far put paid to any hope of a meaningful challenge.
"The game in the centre is totally blocked," says political writer François Fressoz at the left-leaning Le Monde newspaper. "The partisans of reason have lost their reason."
On the left – the old Socialist Party and its acolytes – there is at least agreement on a candidate: European Parliament MP Raphaël Glucksmann.

His problem is that allies who he might once have counted on – Greens, Communists and other small left-wing parties, not to mention many Socialist voters – are being pulled inexorably into the Mélenchon orbit.

In the last two weeks, Green party leader Marine Tondelier, a majority of Communist parliamentary deputies and one-time Socialist presidential hopeful Benoît Hamon have all thrown in their lot with the leader of France Unbowed (LFI).
Another prominent figure of the left – François Ruffin – has also withdrawn from the race, bowing to the unbowed Mélenchon's now almost total command of the field.

So with the soft-left emasculated, the main hope for an alternative to Le Pen and Mélenchon has to be focused on the right. But here the prospects – which until recently seemed bright – are now clouded with gloom.
"A Mélenchon–Le Pen duel in round two is not yet inevitable," says Guillaume Tabard, political analyst at the conservative Le Figaro newspaper. "But it is looking increasingly probable."

In recent weeks the poll ratings of the main centre-right hopeful Edouard Philippe – a former prime minister under President Macron – have fallen sharply, and he is now consistently placed behind Mélenchon in the first round of the vote. Marine Le Pen is way ahead of both.

Other candidates for command of this centre-right "space" are circling. They include another former Macron prime minister, Gabriel Attal; the leader of the right-wing Republicans (and former Macron interior minister), Bruno Retailleau; and now – a surprise new challenger – the mayor of Cannes, David Lisnard.

Lisnard, who stands on a liberal economic platform of less state and lower taxes, has emerged from nowhere to become the man of the hour. Membership of his micro-party Nouvelle Energie (New Energy) has shot up to more than 100,000, and he is being taken seriously as a possible Philippe replacement.

But this very multiplicity of names – not to mention others like judoka Teddy Riner, journalist Natacha Polony and former prime minister Dominique de Villepin – betrays the essential weakness of the centre-right challenge.

According to veteran commentator Nicolas Baverez, "If you want to win an election, it's quite simple: you need a strategy, a programme, and activists. Right now in the space between Le Pen and Mélenchon we have none of that: there is a total vacuum.
"The most glaring absence is digital. Mélenchon especially, but Le Pen too, are running extremely effective social media campaigns. In the middle… nothing."
Guillaume Tabard agrees that the lack of a shared platform is proving a serious handicap.
"In recent weeks we have seen Marine Le Pen issue her manifesto proposals for reforming pensions. We have seen Jean-Luc Mélenchon publish his programme in a best-selling book," he says.
"What do we have in between? Arguments about names and polling figures and whether or not there should be a primary. It's not, to put it mildly, an encouraging start."

For Fressoz, "There is no-one in the centre who is taking up the fight. When Le Pen makes her proposals about pensions, there is no-one saying, 'Hang on, that doesn't add up!'. Macron – who did after all take her on and beat her – is said to be furious."

Any mention of Macron, though, is most unwelcome for the camp that nominally is his heir. Philippe, Attal and Retailleau all served under a president who Baverez now calls "as toxic as Trump", so deep is his unpopularity in the country. Lisnard, by contrast, makes much of his refusal to serve under Macron – but he faces another handicap.

According to Fressoz, "Lisnard has shot up in the polls because he is on the right of the right, and there is always an appetite for a figure who is not Le Pen, but who speaks her kind of language on immigration.
"But Lisnard is an economic liberal, and in France that is a minority taste. He'll have his moment but then he will deflate."

With five months to go to until the election, all is not lost for the mainstream. Optimists in its ranks say that come the new year, opinion polls will start settling behind one or other centre-right candidate, and the others will feel obliged to step aside.

Talk of a centre-right primary – as occurred ahead of the 2017 election – is beginning to ebb. The two strongest candidates, Philippe and Lisnard, are opposed. Lisnard says he supports one but his conditions are designed to be unacceptable to the rest. Retailleau and Attal are in favour – but that, says Tabard, is "mainly as a way to keep their hopes alive."

In theory then it is possible a name will emerge in January or February, and start pulling behind him (or less likely, her) the mass of voters who do not want a disruptive radical as France's next head of state.
Possible, but hardly a good bet.
For Fressoz of Le Monde, "After years of Macron's 'neither left nor right', the left and right are once again shaping French politics. But now it is the extremes who are in control."

Le Pen and Mélenchon have both already run three times for the presidency. Their visions were defined long ago, their strategies laid, their activists trained. Polarisation is their friend, so is the social tension of recent weeks, and both are undisputed masters in their own camps.
The 2027 dénouement has been in their sights for years. That is their massive advantage.

articles.title: Has global jihadism failed, or is it simply changing shape?
articles.summary: Jihadist groups appear to be focusing on local issues rather than global terror. Does it signify a real change?
paragraphs: Chief jihadist media specialist, BBC Monitoring

Rice, pasta, sugar, cooking oil and beans are hardly what you'd expect to see in jihadist propaganda. Yet these were among the supplies that al-Qaeda's Somali branch, al-Shabab, said its "charity" had handed out to hundreds of struggling families in August, as it publicised the aid through its social media accounts and radio station.
The group, which controls large parts of rural southern and central Somalia, has been keen to show off its so-called humanitarian work throughout 2026.
"May God reward them," said a local woman in one of al-Shabab's videos.
It's all part of an effort to win over local communities and present itself as more than just a jihadist group.

A quarter of a century after al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks in the US, and 12 years after Islamic State group (IS) declared its so-called caliphate in Iraq and Syria, the jihadist movement looks very different.

Rather than focusing on attacking the West or fighting for a global Islamic state, some - especially those linked to al-Qaeda - are putting more effort into winning power closer to home. And they seem increasingly willing to make compromises along the way.

Because of this, a debate is growing within the movement. While hardliners reject compromise, pragmatists see working with local groups and former enemies as a way to gain power. But do the pragmatists represent a genuine change or simply a shift in tactics to achieve the same ultimate goals: establishing a state that applies their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law both at home and in its dealings with the outside world?
Neither al-Qaeda nor IS has achieved its ultimate dream: taking over one or more countries and ruling them according to their strict interpretation of Islam.

Both have suffered major defeats, lost leaders and faced years of international pressure. IS, which once controlled vast areas of Iraq and Syria, lost its last territorial stronghold in 2019. But jihadism hasn't gone away.

Africa is now the main battleground for jihadism, with al-Qaeda's powerful branches, JNIM in the Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger) and al-Shabab in Somalia, fighting long-running insurgencies. IS, its bitter rival, has active branches in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Sahel, Mozambique and Somalia.

One major source of inspiration, and envy, whether jihadists admit it or not, is Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa. The former IS and then al-Qaeda commander was once wanted by the US but rose to power in Syria in December 2024 and was welcomed by Western leaders.
Once known by his militant nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, he led the jihadist group Nusra Front - initially linked to IS and then al-Qaeda - and later the group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS).
He gradually broke ties with both IS and al-Qaeda and distanced himself from their calls for global jihad.
Instead, he focused on Syria, building a local power base in the north-western Idlib province.

What surprised everyone was his growing willingness to work with non-Islamist groups and engage with foreign powers. As HTS advanced on Damascus, its leadership sought to reassure the international community, reaching out even to Russia, a key ally of then-president Bashar al-Assad, to allay fears of an Islamist takeover.
That pragmatism, combined with favourable geopolitical conditions - including a weaker Russia and Iran - helped him take power in Syria.
But the sight of him being welcomed by world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, was even more remarkable.
During Sharaa's visit to the White House in November 2025, Trump sprayed him with his own branded cologne, jokingly asked how many wives he had and praised him as a "very strong leader".
For some jihadists, Sharaa's success has been inspiring. Others, however, see his actions as a betrayal of everything they believe in.

IS has declared jihad against Syria's new Islamist government, branding Sharaa and his officials "apostates", and has carried out attacks against government forces on that basis. Other hardline clerics have taken a similar stance, but have stopped short of openly calling for jihad against Sharaa.

The divide between hardline jihadists and their more pragmatic counterparts has fuelled a bitter online debate since 2025, with rival voices trading accusations of betrayal and even publishing competing books to defend their positions.

For hardliners, going too far can mean abandoning their core beliefs. This might include holding back from imposing their strict version of Islamic law, accepting "man-made" laws or a constitution, taking part in elections, working with non-Islamist groups, or building ties with governments they consider "infidel".

Another source of inspiration for jihadists was the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in 2021, as it showed that an Islamist movement could eventually take control of a country after years of fighting Western-backed forces. It engaged local groups, slowly secured power across the country, used international diplomacy, and bided its time before taking the capital, Kabul, in a lightning offensive.
A means to an end?
Two groups are especially worth watching: al-Qaeda's branches in Mali and Somalia.

In late April, al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, known as JNIM, showed considerable pragmatism by joining forces with nationalist Tuareg separatists - whom it had occasionally fought - to launch a major offensive that threatened Mali's military rulers. It even went as far as to call the Tuaregs "brothers".
But it's not just JNIM's growing military strength that's attracting attention. It's also how the group is presenting itself.
Its propaganda once prominently featured al-Qaeda's leaders, slogans and calls for global jihad. Since late 2024, however, its videos have dropped the familiar al-Qaeda branding.
And instead of talking about global Muslim causes, JNIM has increasingly focused on local problems, portraying itself as a defender of ordinary people against corrupt and abusive rulers.
It has repeatedly accused Mali's military government and its Russian allies of killing civilians and making people's lives worse.
In April, it appealed to "all sincere patriots" to help build a "new Mali", promising security, justice and prosperity alongside Islamic law.

It has even suggested it could have "balanced relations" with Russia, despite the fact they're fighting Russian forces backing Mali's government. Its wording echoed that of HTS to Russia as it advanced on Damascus.
There are parallels with Sharaa's approach in Syria: build local alliances, reassure potential enemies and avoid giving outside powers a reason to intervene.
Africa security specialist Aman Bezreh sees similarities between the two groups, but says JNIM's shift may take time.

"JNIM has indeed shown signs of pragmatism similar to HTS", she says. "However, its rebranding has progressed more slowly because the group is simultaneously focused on expanding into new territories and recruiting from diverse pools."
The debate over which path to follow is also taking place within JNIM's leadership, according to Wassim Nasr, a France 24 journalist and jihadism expert.

He says one camp favours the Taliban's approach of taking power through force with minimal concessions. The other, which he says currently has the upper hand, favours an approach closer to that of Syria's HTS - making compromises and building wider alliances to gain power more quickly.
Nasr believes JNIM may borrow from both models, but that a break with al-Qaeda is inevitable as a result of its political evolution.
Like JNIM, al-Shabab in Somalia appears willing to make deals with former enemies.

According to Abdullahi Guji, BBC Monitoring's Somalia specialist, al-Shabab reached a truce in October with a powerful Somali tribe, the Ma'awisley, whose fighters had been at the forefront of the fight against the group.
The tribe has since withdrawn its fighters from the front line, dealing a serious blow to the government's campaign against jihadists, says Guji.
Guji believes the group may soon have a chance to test whether it can seize power and establish itself as an alternative government across wider parts of the country.

African Union forces are withdrawing from Somalia amid funding cuts and the approaching end of their mandate in December. Meanwhile, the Somali government is facing political crises and rebellions, creating vulnerabilities al-Shabab could exploit, he adds.
There's another reason some jihadists may see an opportunity to expand: they believe Western governments have bigger fish to fry.
With the war in Ukraine, US-Iran conflict in the Middle East and growing rivalries with China and Russia, fighting jihadists is no longer the priority it was after 9/11.
The US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban's return to power, followed by Sharaa's rise in Syria, have reinforced that belief.

Colin Clarke, executive director of the Soufan Center, a non-profit research group that focuses on security, says some jihadist groups have learnt that avoiding confrontation with the US can help them escape Western military action and "live to fight another day".
That doesn't mean the West has stopped fighting terrorism. But if jihadists believe it is distracted or less willing to intervene, they may feel emboldened to pursue power.
Unlike its fiercely uncompromising rival IS, al-Qaeda has long shown some flexibility in pursuing its goals. But history offers a warning.

After the 2011 Arab uprisings, which largely sidelined al-Qaeda, affiliated jihadist groups in Yemen, Libya and Tunisia began using the name Ansar al-Sharia (Supporters of Sharia) to win local support without carrying the al-Qaeda brand.

In Mali in 2012, al-Qaeda leaders advised jihadists who had seized the north alongside Tuareg separatists not to rush into imposing strict Islamic rules. Instead, they urged them to work with local allies, avoid alienating communities and play down their al-Qaeda links.
The message wasn't to give up their ambitions. It was to show strategic patience until the time was right. That same thinking could be at work today.

So are these groups really changing their ambitions, or just their tactics? Even those advocating compromise aren't necessarily abandoning their dream of establishing a state ruled by their strict interpretation of Islamic law.
Clarke wonders whether this more pragmatic approach could be a "Trojan horse strategy" – a way for jihadist groups to gain power without giving up their longer-term goals.
"The big question is whether being in power actually moderates these groups, or whether they're simply changing their tactics to survive and strengthen their position," he says.
But not everyone is changing tactics.

IS remains firmly committed to its global ambitions and rejects compromise. Al-Qaeda's Yemen branch, AQAP, continues to call for attacks against the US and Israel, and urges "lone wolf" attacks against Western and Jewish targets.
And it's too early to say whether groups like JNIM and al-Shabab will follow the Taliban or Syrian examples, and whether they're willing to make compromises.
Some jihadist groups may become more focused on local politics as they face the challenges of governing. Others may simply be hiding their wider ambitions until they're strong enough to pursue them.
The global jihadist dream may have failed, but jihadism is far from finished.
Lead image: Reuters/Getty
