articles.title: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules
articles.summary: Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza. The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of…
paragraphs: A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

The nine workers had their contracts terminated in January 2024 “in the interests of the agency” and were told in termination letters that the allegations against them were “very serious and credible”. The dismissals were confirmed after a UN investigation found they might have been involved in the 7 October attacks.

The decision, which was taken by former Unrwa commissioner general Philippe Lazzarini after consultation with the UN secretary general, António Guterres, was apparently made in the hope that appeasing Israel and its allies would allow humanitarian work to continue in Gaza.
Critics warned at the time that the decision, on the basis of allegations rather than evidence, compromised the UN’s integrity and had the opposite effect, giving credence to unproven allegations.
The dismissals failed to prevent the Biden administration ordering a pause in funding, a measure that was echoed temporarily by other backers, leading to a financial shortfall of $450m (£340m).

“I have always said on the record that the Israeli allegations against Unrwa were the mother of all lies,” said Chris Gunness, a former Unrwa spokesperson. “Sacking the workers without any evidence confirmed their guilt unfairly, in the minds of journalists, led 16 top donors to abandon Unrwa and produced the worst financial crisis in the agency’s history, from which it may never recover.”
The Unrwa dispute tribunal that ruled in favour of one of its sacked workers, Abu Awad, described the Israeli allegations as unsupported and of “limited evidentiary value and reliability”.

The tribunal also found that an internal UN investigation had not interviewed the 19 staff members initially accused by Israel of involvement in the 7 October attacks because of “safety and security” concerns.
“The allegations against the applicant and the other staff members, it seems, are therefore based almost entirely on information in Israel’s possession,” the tribunal said.

It cast doubt on intercepted mobile phone conversations and messages offered by Israel as evidence, noting that one case had involved mistaken identity based on a cloned sim card, a common phenomenon in Gaza.

It also said that voice recognition claims made by Israel were dubious and some transcripts of conversations were found by UN investigators not to support claims that they proved links to Hamas or the 7 October attacks.

The allegation against Awad was that he was a “platoon commander” in Hamas’s military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, a claim he rejected. He was not alleged to have physically taken part in the 7 October attack and witness statements to the tribunal said he was on an Unrwa staff bus as normal.

The specific allegation against Awad was that he “had been instructed in a telephone call intercepted by Israeli intelligence to monitor the events of 7 October 2023, while simultaneously receiving Hamas intelligence updates related to the attacks”.
The tribunal said the Israeli security services had failed to clarify who was alleged to have made the call to Awad and in what way the mobile phone that received the call was associated with him.

Unrwa did not respond to a request for comment. Asked by the tribunal to provide evidence underpinning the dismissal of the workers, the agency cited the Israeli government as well as a report in the Times of Israel and another on the website UN Watch, a pro-Israel pressure group that has campaigned against Unrwa.

In its ruling, the tribunal said Unrwa’s claim that the cited sources had informed the decision to dismiss the workers was “open to some doubt” because all the supporting documents it had submitted were produced after the disputed decision was made on 26 January 2024.

Lazzarini, a Swiss humanitarian expert who left the commissioner general post in March, said he understood the tribunal’s finding might be appealed so he could not discuss the case in detail. In February 2024, he admitted his decision to sack the workers represented “reverse due process” in that the investigation followed the dismissal.

“My judgment, based on this going public, true or untrue, was I need to take the swiftest and boldest decision to show that as an agency we take this allegation seriously,” he said, adding that “the ability of the entire agency to continue to operate and deliver critical humanitarian assistance was at stake”.

The tribunal said it could not decide on the allegations against Awad but ruled that Unrwa had failed to produce evidence supporting its decision to sack him. It awarded him a year’s pay and $5,000 for “moral damages”.

In the wake of its allegations against the sacked workers, Israel claimed that Unrwa was heavily infiltrated by Hamas and its parliament voted in 2024 to ban the agency from operating in Israel or in the occupied Palestinian territories.

The international court of justice stated in October 2025, however, that “Israel has not substantiated its allegations that a significant part of Unrwa’s employees are members of Hamas … or other terrorist factions”.

articles.title: Guitar wars - the transatlantic battle over the Stratocaster
articles.summary: US company Fender is in dispute with a German firm that makes generic versions of its key model.
paragraphs: Image source, Getty Images
BBC foreign correspondentReporting fromBavaria
Hans Thomann leads the way through his music store in central Germany to the large electric guitar department, where the walls are hung with hundreds of instruments.
Brands on show include famous names Fender and Gibson, plus Harley Benton.
The latter is a low-price range of guitars owned by the family-run company that Thomann leads – Thomann, one of the world's largest online retailers of musical instruments.
The shop, together with warehouses and offices, are at the company's headquarters in the tiny village of Treppendorf in rural Upper Franconia, in Bavaria.
The business was founded by Thomann's father, Hans Thomann Senior, in 1954.
In one corner of the store, a young man is trying out a Fender Stratocaster, one of the world's most iconic electric guitars.
Designed in the US in the early 1950's, the "Strat" became the instrument of choice for many famous rock and pop musicians, such as Jimi Hendrix, Eric Clapton and Buddy Holly.
Hendrix famously set one on fire at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967, and his performances helped make the guitar a symbol of modern rock music.
These days, the Stratocaster is very much on Hans Thomann's mind, because it's the subject of an intense copyright dispute.
When the guitar was first made, California-based Fender did not trademark the body shape. So, since the 1960s Strat-shaped guitars have been made and sold around the world by countless manufacturers.
The shape is so ubiquitous that many musicians consider it to be a generic design.

But since March of this year, Fender has begun a new campaign to defend its right to the guitar's sinuous shape. It follows a decision by a court in Düsseldorf last December which granted Fender copyright protection, external of the Stratocaster design in Germany.

The defendant, Chinese seller Yiwu Philharmonic Musical Instruments, did not appear. The Düsseldorf court accepted Fender's arguments and ruled in its favour. According to German law the court makes its decision based on the facts presented by the plaintiff if the defendant doesn't raise objections.
The ruling said that Fender's design for the Stratocaster was "an outstanding, free creative achievement" that "clearly reflects the personality of its author".
It described the guitar as "a body without edges" with "soft curves that evoke associations with the female torso consisting of hips, waist and arms".

On its website, Fender announced in March, external the decision created "enforceable rights" against any guitars using the Strat body shape, that are manufactured, sold or distributed into Germany or other EU countries, "regardless of where those guitars are produced".
Fender began to send out cease and desist letters to dozens of retailers and manufacturers, both large and small, asking them to stop making and selling Strat lookalikes heading for Europe.
One of these letters, seen by the BBC, said Fender "insists that you immediately stop manufacturing, marketing, selling and producing the infringing products".
The letter also demanded that companies recall and destroy the guitars.
Image source, David Redfern/Redferns
The move caused an outcry in the guitar world, among manufacturers and musicians.
"Time to boycott Fender," one person wrote on the Facebook page of the boutique US guitar maker, LSL Instruments.
Thomann received a cease-and-desist letter shortly after a visit to Treppendorf in March by Fender's chief executive Bud Cole.
"We remember the meeting as a very positive and constructive exchange," says Thomann. "At the time we had no indication that Fender was considering legal action."
The letter, he says, came as a shock.

"For more than 70 years, we have carried Fender instruments with great appreciation for the brand and many of us are Fender players ourselves. We were therefore surprised and disappointed by Fender's recent actions."
In 2025, Thomann sold over 112,000 Strat-style guitars, including more than 16,000 made by Fender and Fender subsidiary brand Squier.

"As a retailer, we want to continue offering our customers everything that is available in the world of guitars," adds Thomann. "We would have welcomed to the opportunity to discuss the matter openly before receiving a formal legal demand for such extreme action."
In June, Thomann the company started legal action against Fender, filing an "action of non-infringement" that said that Fender does not have a valid copyright claim to the Stat shape.
Thomann says that the Düsseldorf ruling was simply a default judgement based on missed deadlines and didn't represent a "comprehensive review of the legal claims".

For its part, Fender, which is majority-owned by Hawaii-based company Servco Pacific, says it has a responsibility to protect the Stratocaster's iconic design. In July, it sued Thomann in a German court, for copyright infringement.
In a statement to the BBC, Fender said it remained "confident" in the original Düsseldorf court judgement.
"Our preference has always been to keep lines of communication open and resolve these matters through constructive dialogue rather than litigation," it added.
With the legal cases continuing, Thomann says he believes it is important to get "legal clarity – not only for us but for the wider guitar industry."
"Ultimately, we want to help preserve an environment in which innovation, diversity and creative development can continue to thrive," he adds.
Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Thomann says he was taking legal action not just for his company, but for smaller music companies too.
"We used to be a small music shop ourselves," he says.
"Many of the smaller manufacturers, guitar makers and dealers affected simply don't have the financial and legal resources to conduct a legal dispute like this."

One such company is LSL Instruments, a family-owned boutique guitar maker in California. Its director of sales, Johny Miller, told me that when they first received Fender's letter they were "pretty terrified and blown away".
"They were asking us to retrieve guitars from dealers out there and destroy them and send them proof.

"So when we heard Hans Thomann got the same letter and responded by suing them… so that everybody in the guitar community could understand exactly what's going on… we were so thankful and grateful," he says.
Fender tells BBC that it agrees that "legal clarity was important", and that it was now focusing more on targeting larger manufacturers.

It also says it realises that "our outreach has caused concern and frustration, particularly among smaller, independent guitar builders. "To them we say: we continue to hear you, and we're listening."

articles.title: A renovation was meant to improve these Hong Kong homes - it ended in a blaze that killed 168
articles.summary: A year after one of Hong Kong's deadliest fires, families left behind are still waiting for justice.
paragraphs: It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.
At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.

It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.
"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.
When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.
She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.

Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.
It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.
"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.
She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.
The body of Lau Man Kwong was eventually found by rescuers - he had locked himself inside the toilet.
"He was wearing his slippers, sitting on the toilet and clutching his identity card," said his wife, who added that she escaped death "by the narrowest margin".
"I would have held onto my husband and died with him.
"He was such a good person. I just don't understand why he had to die in such a terrible way."
Mr Lau and his wife moved into Wang Fuk Court in 1983 - the year the building was completed.
She recalls an idyllic life - a family with three children who were able to grow up close to the sea and spend weekends playing at a nearby park.
"All three of my children adored my husband… He could be very stern, and I was the only woman who could make him laugh."
In 2024, mandated renovations began in Wang Fuk Court.
In Hong Kong, all buildings over 30 years old have to undergo an inspection - and any necessary renovations as a result.

Like many building complexes in Hong Kong, Wang Fuk Court had a management committee that oversaw things like building repairs. As many as 57 construction companies submitted bids. But the company that won, Prestige Construction and Engineering (PC&E), submitted the most expensive bid at HK$336m ($42.8m; £32.4m).

Residents, many of whom were over 65, had to bear the cost. The hefty bills triggered protests but eventually, the contract was signed. But once the renovations began in July 2024, residents were unhappy.
Among the complaints was that workers constantly smoked on site, dropping cigarette butts everywhere.
The 1,154 page report suggested the fire was caused by a lit cigarette.

There were also complaints about most of Wang Fuk Court's eight buildings having their windows taped over with foam boards to stop debris falling in - blocking daylight or any sort of view at all, for months.
All eight buildings were also covered in a protective mesh netting and bamboo scaffolding.

The report also found that after typhoons damaged the original scaffolding nets in 2025, cheaper non-fire-retardant replacements were chosen - something that was done as a "cost-saving measure at the expense of the safety of the residents".

Residents had filed nearly 140 complaints to six government departments, including the fire services and the buildings departments, in and after 2024, but these were largely ignored, the report went on to say.
It also revealed that a staff member of the estate's property manager, ISS, had turned off the power supply to the fire alarms in all eight buildings - which is why no alarms rang on the day itself.
ISS later told the BBC it had "reviewed and reinforced its procedures [and] staff training" in Hong Kong, adding that it takes the findings of the report "very seriously".

But for those who did manage to flee their homes - the emergency staircase turned out to be another death trap. Windows were removed from some fire escape stairwells to create temporary openings for workers - letting in smoke and cutting off vital escape routes.
Dozens, including Christy's husband, died in such stairwells.

Christy, who wanted to be identified only by her first name, says her husband was at home alone when the fire broke out. She only found out about it when her friends sent her messages about it. By the time she made it to the apartment complex, it was already cordoned off.
She found out later that he had died of smoke inhalation in the stairwell, something she says that is at least of some consolation to her.
"My husband's body would have been burnt and he would have been in more pain if he was at home. At the very least… his suffering was minimal."
Christy says her family had just celebrated their eldest child's ninth birthday the day before - they had saved some leftover cake in the fridge to eat the next day. Their father never got to eat it.
Both children have been deeply affected by the loss of their father.
Her youngest child, a seven-year-old boy, had "covered his ears and yelled" when he was first told what had happened to his father.
He now often comforts his mother, saying he will take care of her as he is the only man in the family.
"He hides his emotions. A seven-year-old child should not behave this way, and I feel heartbroken," says Christy, who has herself been diagnosed with PTSD and depression.
Her daughter has "extreme thoughts" she says, and channels her emotions through art.
She turned 10 on Wednesday, but this year, there was no birthday celebration in sight.
Her birthday, she says, will now instead be a day to commemorate her father.
Wang Fuk Court's problems date back to before the renovations began.

The management company hired to oversee and supervise the project, Will Power, conspired with PC&E to defraud residents in Wang Fuk Court, according to the city's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

Although PC&E was found to have breached safety requirements and violated building department rules for multiple previous projects, homeowners at Wang Fuk Court were told that they had a clean record.

The ICAC alleges that this was part of a lucrative scheme, with Will Power's director Wong Hap-yin, along with other individuals, laundering over $5m in suspected proceeds from the tendering process from Wang Fuk Court, among other housing projects.

Once PC&E cinched the contract, Will Power's registered inspector - an individual meant to oversee the renovations - merely rubber-stamped the documents, without having actually conducted any inspections personally, the report added.
Will Power has been since liquidated and PC&E could not be reached for a response.

Both companies - Will Power and PC&E - and seven individuals have been charged with 25 counts of offences including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.
Four of them are still in custody but none of the cases have gone to trial yet.
The report said both companies involved were the "main culprits responsible".

But it also directed heavy criticism at authorities, saying that "no government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum".

One expert, Prof John Burns of Hong Kong University, had called the tragedy the "largest governance crisis" that authorities have faced since 2020 - a reference to the controversial National Security Law that was passed in that year.

On the day the report was released, almost one year after the fire, Hong Kong's housing chief Winnie Ho resigned and the city's top leader John Lee apologised for the first time, promising that a "large number" of reforms would be rolled out.

Her children, who came with her, described the house as a "war zone". Among the rubble, they found broken pieces of a piggy bank that Mr Lau had dutifully filled with coins every day for the past 20 years.
"Everyone in our family knew it was his favourite possession. The piggy bank died with him," said Mrs Lau.
Mrs Lau and her daughter have since rented a place nearby to live - and she is worried about how she is going to afford a new house.
The government has said it will spend $867m (£663m) to acquire affected flats - but Mrs Lau says it is not nearly enough to buy a similarly sized flat in the area.
Still, her family was in a better position than many others, she said.
"Should I say that we are fortunate?
"I lost my husband but many families lost multiple family members... Babies less than a year old died. "
Stories have emerged of some of the other victims - a six-month-old who died alongside her 68-year-old grandmother when the fire broke out.
The bodies of an Indonesian domestic helper and the elderly person she worked for were found huddled together.

articles.title: Palestinian journalist killed by Israel in Gaza wins Rory Peck prize
articles.summary: Mariam Dagga shares award with two of her colleagues from AP for ‘powerful coverage’ of human cost of war Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in Gaza in an Israeli strike, has posthumously won the prestigious Rory Peck prize for freelance video journalists, the organisers announced on Wednesday. She shares the award with two of her colleagues from the Associated Press (AP), Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi, “for their powerful coverage of the human cost of the war” in the Palestinian territory, the Rory Peck Trust said. Continue reading...
paragraphs: Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in Gaza in an Israeli strike, has posthumously won the prestigious Rory Peck prize for freelance video journalists, the organisers announced on Wednesday.

She shares the award with two of her colleagues from the Associated Press (AP), Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi, “for their powerful coverage of the human cost of the war” in the Palestinian territory, the Rory Peck Trust said.
Dagga, who has a teenage son named Ghaith, was killed in August 2025 in an Israeli airstrike on a southern Gaza hospital, which claimed the lives of four other journalists.
The independent photographer and reporter had been working with the AP news agency since the beginning of the current conflict, triggered by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.

Dagga was renowned for her relentless reporting despite the personal losses she suffered throughout the war. She filmed the death of a protester who was shot during the 2018 Great March of Return in Gaza, when Israeli forces shot protesters marching towards the Gaza border fence, killing more than 220 people and wounding more than 9,200. She later discovered that the protester was her brother.
The war correspondent continued her work as a journalist during the war in Gaza over the last 22 months, working as a freelancer with the AP and Independent Arabia.
The AP’s executive editor, Julie Pace, said: “Journalists play an essential role in documenting events and informing the public, often at enormous personal risk.
“We honour Mariam and all journalists killed during this conflict and other conflicts – and remain committed to seeking answers about their deaths.”
French photographer Robin Tutenges was the recipient of the first Rory Peck award for photojournalism in recognition of his work on the conflict in Ethiopia’s northern Amhara region.

Sudanese freelance photographer and video journalist Ahmed Mohamed Abdalla, who works with Agence France-Presse, was shortlisted for the same award for his coverage of the fall of El Fasher to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Sudan’s civil war.
Abdalla was not allowed to attend the prize-giving ceremony in London as the UK government refused to grant him a visa.

In a recorded video message shared during the ceremony, he told of how the capital of the North Darfur region’s besieged inhabitants had to eat livestock feed to survive amid the daily deluge of missiles.
The prize has been awarded since 1995 in memory of Northern Irish video journalist Rory Peck, who was killed in Moscow in 1993, to celebrate the work of freelance video journalists.

articles.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
articles.summary: The credit rating agency may lower Nvidia's credit rating to AA-, the fourth-highest rating.
paragraphs: Posted:
2:44 PM PST · November 25, 2026
S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.

Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.
The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.

Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.
A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

articles.title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
articles.summary: All three main US indexes were down in early trading, with the tech-dominated Nasdaq down almost 4%.
paragraphs: Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.

The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down by closing time. The tech-dominated Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower.
The declines came amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment, which has rattled investors in recent weeks.
Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and Microsoft closed the day lower, though Meta and SpaceX were in positive territory by the end of the trading day.
Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. At close, it ended up 3.4% lower.
The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia's CEO after revelations of his extramarital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.
Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.
The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.
The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs.
But share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry.
Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off.

"It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending, but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management.

Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by just over 3%.
The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.

articles.title: Netanyahu’s corruption trial at a turning point: Two cases in doubt, one still unresolved
articles.summary: In a dramatic 10-minute hearing, judges signaled little chance of conviction in the Bezeq-Walla and Netanyahu-Mozes cases, but urged prosecutors and defense lawyers to reach an agreement in the gifts affair, leaving Netanyahu's trial unresolved
paragraphs: In a dramatic 10-minute hearing, judges signaled little chance of conviction in the Bezeq-Walla and Netanyahu-Mozes cases, but urged prosecutors and defense lawyers to reach an agreement in the gifts affair, leaving Netanyahu's trial unresolved
Regarding Case 1000, known as the gifts affair, the judge said prosecutors and defense lawyers could reach an agreement and emphasized the need to "work toward ending the trial."

The hearing lasted only about 10 minutes, with the charges against the prime minister discussed only in broad terms. The developments could have significant implications for the trial, although the court's assessment does not itself constitute a formal dismissal of any charges.
Here is a breakdown of the cases at the center of the proceedings:

In Case 1000, Netanyahu is charged with fraud and breach of trust over allegations that he received gifts and other benefits, including cigars, champagne and jewelry, while acting in a conflict of interest and allegedly providing favors in return.

According to the indictment, Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, received various benefits from businessman Arnon Milchan between October 2011 and December 2016. The indictment also states that Milchan introduced Netanyahu to Australian businessman James Packer in 2013 and that the Netanyahus received additional benefits from Packer between 2014 and 2016.

Prosecutors argue that Netanyahu's conduct constituted "acts of breach of trust that substantially harmed public confidence and integrity in public office." According to the indictment, the prime minister maintained an improper relationship with Milchan and Packer for years, during which he and his wife received benefits of considerable value connected to his public positions and status as Israel's prime minister.
Friends forever: Arnon Milchan, Benjamin Nertanyahu, James Packer
(Photos: Getty Images, Yoav Dudkevich, AP)
The indictment states that, because of Netanyahu's numerous connections to Milchan, he should have refrained entirely from handling matters affecting the businessman in his official capacity.

Nevertheless, prosecutors allege that Netanyahu intervened on Milchan's behalf on several occasions. In 2013 and 2014, he contacted U.S. government officials in efforts to secure Milchan a visa to enter the United States. In 2013, Netanyahu also approached then-Finance Minister Yair Lapid regarding an extension of the income tax reporting and payment exemption granted to returning Israeli residents, a benefit Milchan enjoyed.

In 2015, Netanyahu allegedly intervened personally and instructed Shlomo Filber, then-director general of the Communications Ministry, to assist Milchan with regulatory matters relating to a proposed merger between the Israeli television broadcasters Reshet and Keshet. According to the indictment, the intervention was intended to make a potential investment Milchan was considering financially worthwhile.
Unlike the allegations involving Milchan, the indictment does not attribute any governmental favors granted to Packer.
Netanyahu has denied wrongdoing, arguing that the gifts were exchanged within the framework of longstanding, close friendships with Milchan and Packer, were reciprocal and were permitted by law.
Wednesday's hearing indicated that Case 1000 remains a live issue for the judges, who urged the prosecution and defense to discuss the matter and seek an agreement.
Case 2000 concerns meetings and conversations between Netanyahu and Arnon Mozes, publisher of Yedioth Ahronoth and ynet, during the previous decade.

According to the indictment, the two discussed the possibility of improving coverage of Netanyahu in Mozes' media outlets in exchange for promoting legislation that would restrict the circulation of the newspaper Israel Hayom. Netanyahu is charged with fraud and breach of trust in the case.
The prime minister has argued that his conversations with Mozes were tactical, comparable to negotiations with a political rival, and that he never intended to carry out any agreement.
(Photo: Haim Goldberg/Flash90)

Wednesday's remarks by the judges, indicating doubts about whether Netanyahu committed a criminal offense, significantly weakened the prospects of a conviction in this case. However, the charges have not been formally dismissed.

Case 3000 is not part of Netanyahu's corruption trial, and the prime minister is not a suspect in the investigation. The affair is included here because, when it first came to light, it was frequently mentioned in media coverage alongside the investigations that eventually led to criminal charges against Netanyahu.

The case concerns allegations of corruption, bribery, fraud and breach of trust surrounding the procurement of submarines and naval vessels from the German company ThyssenKrupp between 2009 and 2017. Communications adviser Tzachi Lieber was recently convicted in connection with the affair.
Shaul Elovitch, the former controlling shareholder of telecommunications company Bezeq and the Walla news website

Case 4000 centers on allegations that Netanyahu intervened in regulatory decisions at the Communications Ministry to benefit the business interests of Shaul Elovitch, the former controlling shareholder of telecommunications company Bezeq and the Walla news website.

According to the indictment, Netanyahu allegedly sought, directly and indirectly, to influence Walla's editorial content and coverage in ways that would benefit himself and members of his family in exchange for regulatory decisions favorable to Elovitch's business interests. The case has been one of the most significant components of Netanyahu's trial, involving allegations of bribery, fraud and breach of trust.

Wednesday's judicial assessment cast serious doubt on the likelihood of a conviction in Case 4000, suggesting that the judges see substantial weaknesses in the prosecution's case. Although the court has not formally dismissed the charges, its remarks place renewed pressure on prosecutors and defense lawyers to consider how the proceedings should conclude.

After more than six years of litigation, the judges' intervention signals a possible turning point in Netanyahu's trial, with the future of two major cases now in doubt and the court explicitly calling for efforts to reach an agreement on the remaining gifts affair.

articles.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
articles.summary: The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.
paragraphs: SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.

The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.”
The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.
FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”
Musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”
This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent.

SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.

The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document.

SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.
The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

Kirsten Korosec is a reporter and editor who has covered the future of transportation from EVs and autonomous vehicles to urban air mobility and in-car tech for more than a decade. She is currently the transportation editor at TechCrunch and co-host of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast. She is also co-founder and co-host of the podcast, “The Autonocast.” She previously wrote for Fortune, The Verge, Bloomberg, MIT Technology Review and CBS Interactive.

articles.title: These are the promises Eisnekot's Change Bloc will be forced to break to form a government
articles.summary: Opposition leaders face difficult choices over Haredi military conscription, Arab party support, state funding and religion; the challenge will be deciding which campaign pledges survive the coalition negotiations on the way to forming a government
paragraphs: Opposition leaders face difficult choices over Haredi military conscription, Arab party support, state funding and religion; the challenge will be deciding which campaign pledges survive the coalition negotiations on the way to forming a government
Each of the leaders of the Change bloc of opposition parties will have to break a campaign promise to form a new government
(Photos: Shalev Shalom, Yair Sagi, Yuval Chen, Alex Kolomoisky)

If a government is formed, the central question will be which of these promises remain intact and which are set aside to secure coalition agreements. Ynet examines the commitments that could complicate negotiations.

Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar! party, has identified ultra-Orthodox military conscription as one of his principal red lines. Speaking at a conference of municipal corporations in Eilat in May, he said that Israel could no longer tolerate widespread draft evasion.

"We cannot allow draft evasion. The State of Israel cannot accept a situation in which only 48% of its people, men and women, serve during a national emergency," Eisenkot said. "The draft issue is the only one on which I will not compromise. I will not agree to a breach of that principle in exchange for forming a government and allowing the current situation to continue."
Gadi Eisenkot has identified ultra-Orthodox military conscription as one of his principal red lines
(Photo: Maya Levin / AFP)
In keeping with that position, the anti-Netanyahu bloc voted down legislation proposed by the ultra-Orthodox parties on Wednesday that would have frozen arrests of draft evaders.

Eisenkot has also established clear conditions for potential coalition partners. In an interview with Channel 12's "Meet the Press," he said Ra'am would not be part of his government because its chairman, Mansour Abbas, had refused to define Hamas as a terrorist organization.

"I established three rules, and then added another," Eisenkot said. "The three are a Jewish and democratic state, the Declaration of Independence and the obligation to serve. Two or three months ago, I added another rule: recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organization that must be destroyed."

"Therefore, at the moment, I do not see any Arab or ultra-Orthodox party accepting these rules, including Mansour Abbas. That is why he will not be part of the government, because they do not accept the three rules."
These conditions could complicate efforts to assemble a parliamentary majority, particularly if Eisenkot needs support from parties he has publicly ruled out.

Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman also placed ultra-Orthodox conscription at the center of his election campaign. One of his main slogans was "100% for those who serve, 0% for draft evaders," accompanied by repeated declarations opposing military service exemptions.
In August, Liberman sought to tie Eisenkot's hands with an unequivocal pledge: "I will not enter a minority government. There will be no exemptions for the ultra-Orthodox."

His election campaign also featured the slogan "On October 28, I'll draft all the draft evaders." In another campaign message, he promised to end ultra-Orthodox religious coercion and promote public transportation on Shabbat.
Avigdor Liberman strongly opposes forming a minority government dependent on Arab parties

"Only a strong Yisrael Beytenu will put an end to ultra-Orthodox coercion! Only voting 'L' at the ballot box will guarantee public transportation on Shabbat and a live-and-let-live approach. Go vote!" he wrote.

"All this talk about a minority government is dangerous. We cannot rely on Knesset members from Ra'am and the Joint List who, after the October 7 massacre, describe Hamas as a charitable organization and accuse IDF soldiers of genocide and crimes against humanity," he wrote. "A minority government, by definition, is unstable and vulnerable to blackmail. All this talk about a minority government conveys weakness and defeatism."

Liberman has been equally uncompromising on state funding. "Starting October 27, anyone who does not enlist will not receive a single shekel from the state, and anyone who does not study the core curriculum will not receive even one agora in funding!" he declared.
His statements could become a major obstacle if Eisenkot seeks to establish a minority government or reach agreements with ultra-Orthodox parties to secure parliamentary support.
Naftali Bennett, chairman of the Beyahad party, has also adopted a firm position on ultra-Orthodox conscription and government funding for those who do not serve.

Speaking at the "2026: From Frontline to Growth" conference, Bennett rejected claims that demands for military service and core curriculum studies amounted to persecution of the ultra-Orthodox religious community. "Guys, I study Torah. Nobody is persecuting anything," Bennett said.

He clarified that he did not intend to imprison ultra-Orthodox men who refused to enlist. Instead, he would deny government funding to those who neither served in the military nor worked. "Today there are 50 channels through which money flows, and I will shut that down if I become prime minister," Bennett said. "Anyone who does not enlist will not receive a single shekel from the state. I will not put him in prison, but he will not receive a shekel from the state. Anyone who does not work will not receive a shekel from the state."
"Let's call it the Brooklyn model. In Brooklyn, if someone studies Torah and does not work, America does not finance him. Get over it."
Naftali Bennett: 'Anyone who does not enlist will not receive a single shekel from the state'

Bennett reinforced that position in a post on X, insisting that military conscription would be a binding condition for any future government he joined. "There will be no compromises on conscription with us. No 30% exemptions and no 'frameworks.' There will be one simple rule: Not a Zionist? Not on my dime," he wrote.

"Everyone must enlist, and anyone who does not serve the country will not receive a single shekel from the state for the rest of their life. We will transfer the tens of billions received by draft evaders to those who serve," he added.

"That's it. This is the only way to save the country, and that is why it is an ironclad condition for the next government. A government that does not draft the ultra-Orthodox and repair Israel has no right to exist. Together, we will fix things and draft everyone."

Like Eisenkot and Liberman, Bennett has therefore left himself little public room to compromise on conscription, a potentially significant challenge if coalition negotiations require concessions to ultra-Orthodox parties.

The Democrats chairman Yair Golan has outlined a different set of coalition demands, focusing primarily on religion and state. His proposals include ending gender segregation in public spaces, introducing public transportation on Shabbat and expanding religious freedom.

"Removing religion from the public sphere means eliminating religious coercion," Golan said. "Sidewalks and buses will not be divided by gender. In places that want it, businesses will be able to open on Shabbat and public transportation will operate."
Yair Golan: Education is a central priority for his party

"The Western Wall will be a place for all streams of Judaism. Every community will be able to live according to its own way, without others forcing it to decide how to marry, travel or live," he also said.

Alongside these demands, Golan has identified education as a central priority for his party. He has said the Democrats will demand control of the Education Ministry in the next government and outlined plans to prioritize the state education system.

"Education Minister Yoav Kisch has turned teachers into enemies and Kahanists into partners," Golan said. "We will put state education at the top of the agenda. Anyone who does not study the core curriculum will not receive funding."

Golan's demands could become another source of tension in coalition talks, particularly if Eisenkot seeks the cooperation or support of parties opposed to changing the existing arrangements governing religious life.

The challenge facing the prospective coalition is therefore broader than simply reaching agreement on ministerial portfolios. Its leaders have made public commitments on issues that could determine both the composition of the government and its ability to survive.

For Eisenkot, the immediate test will be whether he can reconcile those promises with the parliamentary support needed to take office, without forcing his potential partners to abandon the positions they placed at the center of their election campaigns.

articles.title: After ‘pariah state’ warning, Kushner presses Netanyahu to implement Trump’s Gaza plan
articles.summary: Trump’s son-in-law and adviser urged Netanyahu to facilitate humanitarian aid ahead of winter and approve the entry of an international stabilization force into Gaza; Board of Peace officials described the talks as positive but said progress would be measured by Israel’s actions in the coming days
paragraphs: Trump’s son-in-law and adviser urged Netanyahu to facilitate humanitarian aid ahead of winter and approve the entry of an international stabilization force into Gaza; Board of Peace officials described the talks as positive but said progress would be measured by Israel’s actions in the coming days

Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law and adviser, urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a phone call Tuesday to implement Israel's commitments under Trump's 20-point peace plan for the Gaza Strip.
The conversation followed Kushner's recent warning that Israel was "at a crossroads" and risked becoming a "pariah state" if it continued along its current path.
(Photo: Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP, Reuters, AP Photo/Peter Morrison)

During the call, Kushner pressed Netanyahu to facilitate the delivery of tents and humanitarian aid to Gaza ahead of winter. He also urged the prime minister to advance the necessary approvals for an international stabilization force to enter the Palestinian enclave.
Officials at the Board of Peace, which is tasked with advancing Trump's Gaza plan, described the conversation as constructive and said it could pave the way for agreements between the sides.
"There are currently no agreements to announce," officials said, adding that efforts were underway to make progress.

"There was a positive atmosphere, and Netanyahu expressed a willingness to advance the 20-point plan," a source familiar with the discussion said. "This will be tested by actual implementation in the coming days."

Netanyahu's office said in a statement: "Prime Minister Netanyahu and Jared Kushner held a constructive conversation. They discussed humanitarian assistance to the Gaza Strip and preparations for winter. The two agreed that the sides would continue working together to advance these issues."

In a recent interview with New York magazine, Kushner warned that Israel faced a choice between emerging from the October 7, 2023, attacks more secure and better integrated into the international community or continuing down a path toward becoming a "pariah state."

His remarks came amid mounting tensions between Israel and the Board of Peace, whose officials accuse Netanyahu's government of stalling progress in Gaza and impeding efforts to implement Trump's postwar vision for the territory.

articles.title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, police say
articles.summary: Unclear if ‘hostage-taker’ who was killed may have been a hostage as daylong siege in Cartagena shopping centre ends Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one man police described as a hostage-taker was killed. Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.…
paragraphs: Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one man police described as a hostage-taker was killed.

Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.

When masked and armed assailants stormed the supermarket at about 8am on Tuesday local time, customers and employees were taken hostage – the president initially said there were 30 hostages, but after the final count, police put the number at about 70.
Many of them could be seen through windows with their hands and feet tied. Ten had already been released over the course of the day.
When, after 17 hours in captivity, the final people were freed at about 1.30am on Wednesday, four of the hostage-takers were arrested.
One man was killed, whom De la Espriella and police described as one of the criminals who had allegedly resisted.

“One of the criminals was killed. They were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages; they rejected that opportunity and we acted forcefully,” said De la Espriella in a video posted outside the supermarket – about 6 miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls, which are visited by thousands of tourists every year.

Local media identified the dead man as Haider Muñetón Zapata, 51, whose wife had spent the day searching for him as one of the hostages. She gave an interview to Blu Radio on Tuesday, saying they lived near the supermarket and that he had gone there to buy buñuelos, a type of fried dough ball, before picking her up to take her to work, but had stopped responding to her WhatsApp messages at 8.12am.

Zapata reportedly had no criminal record. Cartagena’s mayor, Dumek Turbay, told local media that when special forces stormed the supermarket, Zapata had allegedly resisted and attacked one of the officers, prompting police to shoot him dead.

In a video released shortly after the operation, De la Espriella described the police action as “extraordinary”, speaking with a gun tucked into his waistband, as he has done on several other public occasions as part of his populist tough-on-crime rhetoric.

The president arrived in Cartagena late on Tuesday afternoon from Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he had been dealing with the aftermath of another attack on Monday night, when a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).

De la Espriella, however, denied that the supermarket hostage-taking had been carried out by a “terrorist group”, as he describes the groups involved in Colombia’s decades-long armed conflict, saying instead that those responsible were common criminals.
The president said they had tried to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle but, after being spotted by private security – who then alerted police – they took refuge in the supermarket.
As the lengthy negotiations continued into the night, police used water cannon to disperse dozens of onlookers who had gathered outside the supermarket.

Cartagena’s mayor said that when police stormed the supermarket, some of the hostage-takers tried to blend in with the hostages by removing their hoods and changing out of their black clothes into civilian clothing.
According to Turbay, police then had to screen the hostages before eventually identifying the four who were arrested.
Supermarket employee Héctor Puello, who was taken hostage, told Caracol Radio that he had started his shift in the store’s bakery about two and a half hours before the gunmen arrived.
“First of all, I felt like I had come back to life because those armed men were mistreating us,” he said.

Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, said that when he realised what was happening, he hid inside a cold-storage room with four other employees. “After four hours, we couldn’t stand the cold any longer and came out,” he said, at which point they were captured and taken hostage.
Commenting on the rescue operation, De la Espriella said his government was acting out of “the need to defend our people and go after all the criminals with an iron fist”.
The daylong hostage siege took place on a symbolic day for security in Colombia: the 10th anniversary of the country’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas.

In office for just over three months, the president – previously a lawyer and businessman – is a fierce critic of the peace deal and has focused his government on returning to a strategy of full-on confrontation with criminal groups, breaking completely with the “total peace” plan of his predecessor, the leftist Gustavo Petro.

Although some indicators show slight improvements in areas such as homicides and kidnappings, recent days have been marked by a strong response from criminal groups: in addition to the car bombing, another guerrilla group carried out the first-ever drone attack on a departmental capital on Monday.
On Tuesday night, five departments were left without electricity, and De la Espriella said criminals used explosives to bring down power pylons.
“These criminal acts constitute the response of terrorist groups to the forceful offensive being carried out by the national government to restore order and security across the country,” he said.

articles.title: Moment Nasa spacecraft hit asteroid - and what happened next
articles.summary: The crash was "like something out of a disaster movie", the BBC's science editor Rebecca Morelle says.
paragraphs: The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.
Video released by Nasa showed the moment of impact in 2022, while new images show the extent of the damage done to the asteroid.
Dimorphos, the asteroid, posed no threat to Earth, but the crash was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.
Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.
The BBC's science editor Rebecca Morelle explains.

articles.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
articles.summary: OpenAI will introduce a single usage meter across ChatGPT as it combines the Chat and Work experiences.
paragraphs: 12:03 PM PST · November 25, 2026
OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.

The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.

That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees.

Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.
While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.
Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.

The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

articles.title: Lululemon founder stuns Canadian women’s leadership conference with sexist comments
articles.summary: Chip Wilson said men importing brides from Thailand was due to women waiting too long to have children The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in Canada are having too few children and this could lead some men to bring in brides from Thailand, in remarks that stunned audience members at a women’s leadership conference. Chip Wilson, who built the Vancouver yoga-wear startup into a global athleisure empire, was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary earlier this week, an event organized by Axis Connects to advance women in leadership. The organization says it…
paragraphs: The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in Canada are having too few children and this could lead some men to bring in brides from Thailand, in remarks that stunned audience members at a women’s leadership conference.

Chip Wilson, who built the Vancouver yoga-wear startup into a global athleisure empire, was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary earlier this week, an event organized by Axis Connects to advance women in leadership. The organization says it aims to create space for “candid conversations about the barriers women face both in business and society”.

Wilson’s talk on 23 November, titled “Little Black Stretchy Pants” after his memoir, was billed as an “intimate, fireside chat” offering insight into the “mind and instincts of the man himself”. It was moderated by Nuvyn Peters, CEO of Axis Connects.

There is no publicly available video of the event, but the Guardian spoke with people who attended it and reviewed social media posts from those present. Outrage over the event was first reported by the Globe and Mail.

According to people who were there, Wilson told the audience that companies would be reluctant to hire a 22-year-old woman because she might become pregnant at 23 and take maternity leave. He went on to suggest that women were waiting too long to have children, prompting men to import brides from Thailand.
“There were audible gasps in the room and everyone was clearly uncomfortable. It was a mix of disengaging, walking out and also just complete shock of what was being said on stage,” one person said.

“I am floored that Axis gave this man a platform. We all were saying before the event it was surprising he was there – and it’s clear that [Wilson] runs in the organizer’s circles after she opened with the fact that they go on walks [at a Vancouver mountain] together.”
The event, which was supposed to run for an hour, was cut short at 45 minutes.

The remarks are not the first time Wilson has attracted criticism for his comments about women and their bodies. He stepped down as chair of Lululemon’s board in 2013 after the company’s signature black yoga pants were criticized for being see-through and Wilson blamed the problem on the body types of some customers.
On Monday, he reportedly told the group that those prior comments about body types had been “misconstrued” and said he was referring to women who wear sizes that are too small.
Wilson, who is believed to be worth more than C$6bn, has not had a leadership role at Lululemon for several years but remains a major shareholder.
He also reportedly told the audience that poverty had largely been eradicated, and that he was looking forward to going to space with Elon Musk.

Audience members also said Wilson suggested that men were better suited to helm clothing companies that catered to women, because they knew what looked good on women’s bodies. He said the same was true of women who lead companies focused on men’s fashion.

“We recognize that several comments made by Chip Wilson at the Leadership Forum were offensive and inconsistent with the values and mission of Axis Connects,” Peters said in a statement. “We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community. His comments also underscore an uncomfortable reality: attitudes and assumptions that hold women back in the workplace and in leadership have not disappeared. Challenging those attitudes is central to the work and ethos of Axis Connects.”

Wilson’s spokesperson pointed to the work the Lululemon founder has done to mentor and “empower” women in leadership roles over the years and said his efforts “speak for themselves”. A number of women who were early employees of the company and worked closely with Wilson became millionaires when the company went public, he has previously noted in his memoir, and have gone on to found their own businesses.

More than 700 women attended the conference, many representing organizations they worked for. One person said the experience left her “irate”, adding that it was also indicative of what women continued to tolerate.
“It’s just sad that this is what women still have to deal with, in a forum literally for women.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
articles.summary: Most codes of conduct serve as a reflection of corporate culture. In Nvidia's case, that could have consequences.
paragraphs: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.

It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.

Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.

“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”

The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.

“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”

Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”

Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.

“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”

In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company.

articles.title: The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America
articles.summary: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck last month, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared to 65.5 days for trucks overall.
paragraphs: Tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it launched. But the futuristic, steel-clad EV is finding new life in the used car market, according to analysis of sales figures by iSeeCars.com.

The automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model. The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall. Used Cybertrucks sold faster than any other truck, including the Ford Maverick Hybrid, which held the No. 2 spot, and the Rivian R1T, in third place.

According to iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric. EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market. EVs average 45.6 days on market compared to 54.5 days for hybrids and 61 days for gasoline-powered vehicles. Not every EV is selling well, however. For instance, iSeeCars.com found that the Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-selling vehicle in the study, averaging 134.3 days on the market, more than twice the overall industry average.

Karl Brauer, executive analyst at iSeeCars.com, told TechCrunch that high gasoline prices have changed consumer-buying habits, prompting more people to opt for an EV or hybrid over an internal combustion engine vehicle. If high prices persist, as they have since March, that trend could continue.

Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk announced Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027. Fuel prices and the relative rarity of Cybertrucks in the used car market were driving demand even before the cancellation announcement, Brauer said.

“The Cybertruck has only been out for a few years, so you have a lot of used ones coming off lease and entering the used car market for the first time,” he said, adding that used Cybertrucks are cheap relative to their MSRP.
The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year.

“The canceling of the new Cybertruck is making people kind of aware — it’s like, oh wow, these things aren’t going to be coming anymore,” Brauer said. “Whatever demand is for them, supply will not be continuing to grow.”
Brauer said that once production of the Cybertruck ends — which is expected in summer 2027 — sales of used versions may pop once again.
“When the last one is being produced, that’ll probably reignite things again, and for a few months after that,” he said.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
articles.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly automate their own research and model development.
paragraphs: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”

“We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”

The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”
Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”

“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”

But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.

Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”

Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.
In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”

“As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.

The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control.

Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.

In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently.

“Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.”
